wellbeing-bullying.title: Bullying: stop it, survive it, stand up
wellbeing-bullying.description: For those being bullied, those who bully, and bystanders — in school, online and on campus. Practical scripts, real scenarios, Indian laws and help numbers.

courses.title: If you're being bullied
courses.summary: What bullying is, safe moves in the moment, how to tell and get support, and how to rebuild confidence afterwards.
outcomes: Learners can identify bullying vs conflict and its types
Learners can respond safely in the moment
Learners can report using the WWW method and build a support web
Learners can rebuild confidence and know when to get extra help
courses.guardianNote: For ages 8–15. Explains what bullying is (and isn’t), safe things to do in the moment, how to tell adults and build support, and how to rebuild confidence. Includes helplines (1098, 14416). No graphic content.

lessons.title: What bullying is — and what it isn't

scenes.text: Rhea, 11, from Pune sits alone at lunch. For weeks, a group calls her ‘fatso’, hides her tiffin and laughs when she walks by.
Her mum says, ‘Maybe they’re just teasing?’ Rhea isn’t sure what to call it.
Her class teacher explains the difference between conflict, teasing and bullying.
Rhea realises: this is bullying — and it’s not her fault.

steps.title: The three signs of bullying
steps.body:
Bullying is behaviour that is:
- **Deliberate** — meant to hurt, scare or humiliate
- **Repeated** — happens again and again (or is likely to)
- **Unequal power** — the person doing it is stronger, more popular, older, or there are more of them

A one-off argument between equals is a **conflict**, not bullying. Friendly teasing both sides enjoy isn’t bullying either — but teasing that hurts and continues after ‘stop’ is.

steps.title: Types of bullying
steps.body:
- **Physical:** hitting, pushing, tripping, damaging things
- **Verbal:** name-calling, insults, threats, mocking someone’s body, caste, religion, accent, disability or gender
- **Social/relational:** leaving out on purpose, spreading rumours, turning friends against someone
- **Cyber:** any of the above online
- **Sexual:** unwanted touching, sexual comments or images

steps.title: You are not alone
steps.body: UNESCO reports that **almost 1 in 3 students worldwide** say they were bullied at least once in the past month. Being bullied is common — but it is never acceptable, and it is **never the target’s fault**.

steps.title: Worked example: which is it?
steps.body:
1. Arjun and Sam argue once about a cricket score. → **Conflict**
2. Friends tease each other about their favourite teams and both laugh. → **Playful teasing**
3. Every day older boys call Kabir names about his stammer and he looks upset. → **Bullying**
4. A group creates a chat to mock Rhea’s photos. → **Cyberbullying**

steps.title: Effects bullying can have
steps.body: Stomach-aches, headaches, poor sleep, not wanting to go to school, lower marks, feeling anxious, sad or worthless. If you feel hopeless or think about hurting yourself, **tell someone today** or call **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7) or **1098** (Childline).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write what has been happening: what, when, where, who. This helps adults act.

activity.prompt: Conflict, playful teasing, or bullying?

items.text: Two friends disagree once about a game rule
Friends joke about each other’s football teams and both laugh
A group hides someone’s bag every day
Mocking a classmate’s accent daily even after they ask to stop
A one-time argument between equals over a seat
Leaving someone out of every group on purpose

quiz.q: Which three features define bullying?
quiz.why: Bullying is deliberate, repeated and involves unequal power. These three signs separate it from a one-off conflict between equals.

quiz.q: Spreading rumours to turn friends against someone is…
quiz.why: Spreading rumours to turn friends against someone is social (relational) bullying. It damages friendships and reputation without physical contact.

quiz.q: Whose fault is bullying?
quiz.why: The person doing the bullying is responsible. It is never the target's fault, whatever they look like or do.

quiz.q: How common is bullying according to UNESCO?
options: Almost 1 in 3 students in the past month
quiz.why: UNESCO reports almost 1 in 3 students are bullied in a month, so it is common. But common doesn't make it acceptable.

quiz.q: If bullying makes you feel hopeless, you should…
quiz.why: If bullying makes you feel hopeless, tell someone today or call Tele-MANAS 14416 or Childline 1098. Help is available, and keeping quiet or waiting can make it worse.

sources: UNESCO (Behind the numbers: school violence and bullying, 2019)

lessons.title: What to do in the moment

scenes.text: Kabir, 13, from Lucknow has a stammer. Older boys copy him in the corridor every day.
He used to shout back and once pushed one of them — and got into trouble himself.
The school counsellor teaches him a few safe responses and helps him plan his route.
The next time, Kabir says calmly ‘Whatever,’ walks to the staffroom, and reports it.

steps.title: Safety first
steps.body:
In the moment, your goal is to **get safe**, not to win.
- **Stay calm-looking** (even if you feel scared inside) — bullies often want a reaction
- **Use a short, firm line**: ‘Stop.’ ‘Leave me alone.’ ‘Not funny.’
- **Walk away** towards adults or other people
- If you’re in danger, **shout for help** and go to an adult

steps.title: Worked example: lines that work
steps.body:
- Fogging (agree without caring): ‘Maybe.’ ‘If you say so.’ ‘Okay.’
- Broken record: ‘Stop.’ (repeated calmly)
- Humour (if natural to you): ‘Wow, that’s original.’
- Leaving: ‘I’m going.’

**Avoid:** insults back, threats, or hitting — they can escalate and get you in trouble too.

steps.title: Reduce chances
steps.body:
- Stay near friends or in supervised areas
- Change routes or timings if bullying happens at a certain spot
- Keep valuables out of sight
- Note where cameras and teachers are

steps.title: Don’t
steps.body:
- Fight back physically (unless it’s the only way to escape danger)
- Carry anything as a weapon
- Blame yourself or change who you are to ‘fit in’
- Keep it secret

steps.title: Practise with someone
steps.body: Role-play with a parent or friend: they say a mean line, you practise a calm reply and walking away. Practice makes it easier under stress.

a.text: In the corridor, two older students block your way and mock you.

choices.label: Say ‘Let me pass’ calmly and walk towards the staffroom
choices.feedback: Calm and moving towards adults is safest.

choices.label: Shout insults back
choices.feedback: That may escalate and get you blamed.

choices.label: Push one of them
choices.feedback: Physical fights often get everyone in trouble and can cause injury.

b.text: They follow and laugh but you reach a teacher.

choices.label: Tell the teacher exactly what happened
choices.feedback: Reporting helps the school act.

choices.label: Say ‘nothing’ because you’re embarrassed
choices.feedback: Many targets feel this. Telling is still the best step.

c.text: It gets worse; a teacher arrives and sees you shouting.

choices.label: Explain calmly what led up to it
choices.feedback: Honesty helps, but next time choose to walk away.

d.text: The bullying happens again the next day.

choices.label: Go to the counsellor and tell them everything
choices.feedback: It’s never too late to tell.

end1.text: The school puts a plan in place and the behaviour is addressed.

end2.text: Lesson learned: staying calm and leaving protects you better.

quiz.q: Your main goal in the moment is to…
quiz.why: In the moment, your aim is to get safe. Revenge or winning can make things worse.

quiz.q: Which reply is ‘fogging’?
quiz.why: Fogging is a calm, non-reactive reply like 'Maybe. If you say so.' It gives the person nothing to feed on, unlike crying, insults or hitting.

quiz.q: Why avoid hitting back?
options: It can escalate and get you blamed or hurt
quiz.why: Hitting back can escalate things and get you blamed or hurt. Safer choices are to walk away and tell an adult.

quiz.q: Which reduces bullying chances?
options: Staying near friends and supervised areas
quiz.why: Staying near friends and in supervised areas reduces the chance of being targeted. Being alone in hidden places raises it.

quiz.q: Why practise responses?
options: Under stress, practised responses come more easily
quiz.why: Practised responses come to mind more easily when you are stressed. Rehearsal also builds confidence.

sources: UNESCO (Behind the numbers: school violence and bullying, 2019)

lessons.title: Telling adults and building support

scenes.text: Divya, 12, in Bhubaneswar has been excluded and mocked online by her old friend group for two months.
She hasn’t told anyone, afraid it will get worse.
Her aunt notices she’s stopped eating breakfast. Divya shows her a diary she has kept of every incident.
Together they meet the class teacher. The school acts, and Divya joins the drama club where she finds new friends.

steps.title: Why telling works
steps.body: Most bullying stops only when adults know. Telling is **not snitching** — snitching is getting someone in trouble for fun; telling is **getting help** when someone is being hurt.

steps.title: How to tell (the WWW method)
steps.body:
- **What** happened (exact words or actions)
- **When** and **where** (dates, places)
- **Who** was involved, and who saw

Keep a **diary** and screenshots. Tell a teacher, counsellor, parent, or another trusted adult. If one doesn’t help, tell another, or ask a parent to write to the principal.

steps.title: What schools should do
steps.body: Many Indian school boards, including CBSE, require schools to have anti-bullying measures and committees. Schools should listen, keep you safe, deal with the people bullying, inform parents and follow up. You can ask: ‘What will happen next, and when will you check in with me?’

steps.title: Worked example: a parent’s email
steps.body: ‘Dear Principal, my daughter Divya (7B) has been excluded and mocked online by classmates since July. Attached are dated notes and screenshots. Please let us know what steps the school will take and when we can meet. Thank you.’ — factual, calm, with evidence.

steps.title: Build your support web
steps.body:
- One or two **true friends** (even outside school)
- A **club, sport or hobby** where you feel good
- A trusted adult you check in with weekly
- Helplines: **1098** (Childline), **14416** (Tele-MANAS)

Support doesn’t just stop bullying; it protects your confidence while things get sorted.

activity.prompt: Put the steps for reporting bullying in a sensible order:
items: Write down what, when, where and who
Save screenshots or evidence
Tell a trusted adult (teacher, counsellor, parent)
Ask what will happen next and when they’ll check in
If it continues, tell another adult or escalate to the principal
Keep building your support web

quiz.q: Telling an adult about bullying is…
options: Getting help when someone is being hurt
quiz.why: Telling an adult is getting help when someone is being hurt, not snitching. It protects you and others.

quiz.q: The WWW method stands for…
quiz.why: WWW stands for What happened, When/Where, and Who. Clear facts help adults act.

quiz.q: If the first adult doesn’t help…
quiz.why: If the first adult doesn't help, tell another adult or escalate. Keep telling until someone acts.

quiz.q: Why join a club or activity?
options: Builds friendships and confidence outside the bullying group
quiz.why: A club or activity builds friendships and confidence outside the bullying group. Support protects wellbeing.

quiz.q: A good question to ask the school is…
options: ‘What will happen next, and when will you check in?’
quiz.why: Asking 'What will happen next, and when will you check in?' pushes for a clear plan and follow-up. It puts the responsibility on the school to act.

sources: UNESCO (Behind the numbers: school violence and bullying, 2019)

lessons.title: Healing and rebuilding confidence

scenes.text: Tenzin, 14, from Darjeeling was bullied for a year about his looks and accent. The bullying has stopped, but he still feels small.
A counsellor explains that hurt can stay after bullying ends, and that’s normal.
Tenzin starts guitar classes and writes down three things he did well each day.
Months later, he performs at the school fest.

steps.title: The hurt can last
steps.body: Even after bullying stops, you might still feel anxious, distrustful or low. This is a normal reaction to stress — and it **can heal** with time and support.

steps.title: Talk back to the bully in your head
steps.body:
Bullies’ words can echo: ‘You’re ugly’, ‘Nobody likes you’. Practise replacing them:
- ‘That was their cruelty, not the truth.’
- ‘I have people who like me — X and Y.’
- ‘I’m learning and growing.’

Write **three things you did well** each day for two weeks.

steps.title: Things that rebuild confidence
steps.body:
- Doing something you’re good at or enjoy
- Exercise and sleep
- Spending time with kind people
- Helping others (volunteering, helping a younger child)
- Counselling, if feelings stay heavy

steps.title: When to get extra help
steps.body: If you feel hopeless, can’t stop thinking about what happened, avoid school or friends, or have thoughts of harming yourself — **talk to someone today**: a parent, counsellor, **Tele-MANAS 14416**, or **1098**. In an emergency call **112**.

activity.prompt: Write three true, kind things about yourself — and one thing you’d like to try that makes you feel strong.
activity.hint: Think about what friends or family appreciate in you.

quiz.q: After bullying stops, lingering hurt is…
options: Normal and can heal with support
quiz.why: Lingering hurt after bullying is normal, and it can heal with time and support. It isn't your fault or permanent.

quiz.q: A helpful daily habit is…
options: Writing three things you did well
quiz.why: Writing three things you did well builds a balanced view of yourself. Re-reading mean messages or avoiding everyone keeps the hurt going.

quiz.q: Which rebuilds confidence?
options: Hobbies, kind people, exercise and sleep
quiz.why: Hobbies, kind people, exercise and sleep rebuild confidence. Isolation, revenge and late-night screens make it harder.

quiz.q: You have thoughts of harming yourself. Best step?
options: Talk to someone today; Tele-MANAS 14416 or 112 in an emergency
quiz.why: If you have thoughts of harming yourself, talk to someone today. Call Tele-MANAS 14416, or 112 in an emergency; waiting or hiding it adds risk.

quiz.q: A kind reply to the bully’s voice in your head?
options: ‘That was their cruelty, not the truth’
quiz.why: Reply to the bully's voice in your head with 'That was their cruelty, not the truth.' Their words say something about them, not about your worth.

sources: UNESCO (Behind the numbers: school violence and bullying, 2019)

questions.why: Bullying is deliberate, repeated and involves unequal power. It isn't only physical and isn't every argument.
The person who bullies is at fault. It is never the target's fault.
Telling an adult is getting help, not snitching. It protects you and others.

questions.q: A one-off argument between equals is…
questions.why: A one-off argument between equals is conflict, not bullying. Bullying is repeated and has unequal power.
In the moment, the best goal is to get safe. Trying to win can make things worse.
WWW reporting means What happened, When/Where, and Who. Clear facts help adults act.
Spreading rumours and excluding is relational (social) bullying, which harms friendships and reputation. Tripping is physical bullying.
A diary of dates, places and what happened gives adults clear evidence to act on. It isn't for revenge.
Fogging means giving calm, non-reactive replies like 'maybe'. It takes away the reaction the person wants.
Tele-MANAS, the national mental-health helpline, is 14416. 101 is fire and 1930 is cybercrime.

questions.q: If the school doesn’t act, next step?
options: Escalate in writing to the principal with evidence
questions.why: If the school doesn't act, escalate in writing to the principal with evidence. Fighting or staying silent doesn't solve it.
'Their words were cruelty, not truth' helps healing because it puts the blame on the bully. Believing you deserved it keeps the hurt alive.

questions.q: Which combination is best after weeks of bullying?
options: Diary + tell adult + support web + follow up
questions.why: The best plan combines a diary of evidence, telling an adult, a support network and follow-up. Revenge, secrecy or quitting everything doesn't fix the problem.

courses.title: If you bully others: understand, repair, change
courses.summary: A non-shaming course for anyone who has bullied: why it happens, the real impact, how to apologise and repair harm, and how to change habits for good.
outcomes: Learners can identify reasons behind bullying without excusing it
Learners can explain impact vs intent
Learners can make a genuine four-part apology and take part in repair
Learners can create a personal change plan
courses.guardianNote: For ages 10–17 who have bullied or worry they might. Non-shaming: explains why people bully, the real impact, how to repair harm and change habits. Suitable for use with a counsellor or parent.

lessons.title: Why people bully

scenes.text: Varun, 14, from Delhi is popular. He mocks a quieter boy, Sid, and everyone laughs.
At home, Varun’s father often shouts and insults him. At school, mocking others makes him feel powerful.
A teacher asks him privately, ‘What do you get from it?’ Varun doesn’t know what to say.
It’s the start of him understanding his own behaviour.

steps.title: Common reasons (not excuses)
steps.body:
People bully for many reasons:
- Wanting **status** or to look tough
- **Copying** how they’re treated at home or by others
- Feeling **insecure** or jealous
- **Peer pressure** — fear of becoming the target
- Boredom, or not realising how much it hurts
- Prejudice about caste, religion, gender, body, disability or accent

Understanding the reason helps change — but it **doesn’t make the behaviour okay**.

steps.title: It harms the person who bullies too
steps.body: Research links bullying others with later problems: trouble in relationships, school discipline, and for some, getting into trouble with the law. Many people who bully are also struggling themselves — and change is very possible.

steps.title: Worked example: honest self-check
steps.body:
Ask yourself:
- Do I make jokes others don’t laugh at?
- Do people go quiet or leave when I arrive?
- Do I feel better when someone else feels small?
- Have I been told to stop and carried on?

If you answered yes to any — this course is for you, and asking is already a strong step.

steps.title: What’s under the anger?
steps.body: Many people who bully are hurting — from stress at home, being bullied themselves, or low self-worth. Talking to a counsellor or calling **Tele-MANAS 14416** can help with those feelings.

steps.title: When it becomes a crime
steps.body: Some ‘bullying’ is also against the law: assault, threats, sexual harassment, stalking, sharing private images, or attacking someone because of caste (the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act applies). This is general education, not legal advice.

items.back: Feeling powerful by making others feel small — real respect comes from kindness and skill.
Repeating how you’re treated at home or by others — you can choose differently.
Putting others down to hide your own worries.
Joining in so you don’t become the target.
Targeting someone for caste, religion, body, gender or disability — harmful and sometimes illegal.

quiz.q: Understanding why someone bullies…
options: Helps change but doesn’t excuse it
quiz.why: Understanding why someone bullies can help them change, but it does not excuse the behaviour. Reasons are explanations, not excuses.

quiz.q: Which may be a sign you’re bullying?
options: People go quiet when you arrive and you keep jokes going after ‘stop’
quiz.why: If people go quiet when you arrive and you keep jokes going after 'stop', you may be bullying. Asking before joking, apologising and mutual laughter are healthy.

quiz.q: Bullying others is linked to…
quiz.why: Bullying others is linked to later problems with relationships and discipline, so it harms the person doing it as well.

quiz.q: Caste-based bullying of SC/ST students may fall under…
quiz.why: Caste-based bullying of SC/ST students may be an offence under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, which makes it very serious.

quiz.q: Who can help with the feelings underneath?
quiz.why: A counsellor or Tele-MANAS (14416) can help with the feelings underneath bullying, such as anger or stress.

sources: UNESCO (Behind the numbers: school violence and bullying, 2019)

lessons.title: Seeing the impact

scenes.text: As part of a restorative session, Sid writes a letter about how Varun’s mocking felt.
‘I pretended to be sick so I could stay home. I stopped answering in class. I felt like nobody wanted me.’
Varun reads it and goes quiet. He hadn’t imagined it was that bad.
It changes how he sees his ‘jokes’.

steps.title: What targets experience
steps.body: Targets of bullying often experience: fear of school, headaches and stomach-aches, poor sleep, falling marks, loneliness, anxiety and depression, and sometimes thoughts of self-harm. Effects can last into adulthood.

steps.title: Worked example: intent vs impact
steps.body:
Varun: ‘I was just joking.’

Impact: Sid missed 12 days of school.

**Impact matters more than intent.** If someone isn’t laughing, it isn’t a joke.

steps.title: Empathy builder
steps.body: Imagine someone doing the same thing to you, or to your younger sibling, every day for a month. What would you feel? What would you want someone to do?

steps.title: Audience effect
steps.body: Bullying often happens in front of an audience. Laughter and silence from onlookers make it feel acceptable. Taking away the audience — by not joining in — is part of stopping it.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a short letter (you don’t need to send it) from the point of view of someone you’ve hurt.

statements.s: If I meant it as a joke, it can’t be bullying.
Bullying can affect someone’s health and school attendance.
statements.why: Physical and emotional effects are common.

statements.s: Onlookers laughing can make bullying worse.
Effects of bullying always disappear within a day.

quiz.q: Impact vs intent: which matters more?
quiz.why: Impact matters more than intent, because what counts is how the other person is affected. 'I didn't mean it' doesn't undo the hurt.

quiz.q: Sid missed school because of mocking. This shows…
quiz.why: Sid missing school because of mocking shows the real impact of bullying. Jokes that cause this are not harmless.

quiz.q: Taking away the audience means…
quiz.why: Taking away the audience means not laughing or joining in. Without the reaction, the reward for bullying shrinks.

quiz.q: An empathy exercise is…
options: Imagining it happening to you or a sibling every day
quiz.why: An empathy exercise is imagining it happening to you or a sibling every day. It helps you feel the impact.

quiz.q: Which is a common effect on targets?
quiz.why: Targets commonly feel anxious and may avoid school. It doesn't improve sleep, friendships or marks.

sources: UNESCO (Behind the numbers: school violence and bullying, 2019)

lessons.title: Repairing harm

scenes.text: The school counsellor in Mumbai runs a restorative circle with Varun, Sid and a teacher.
Each person answers: What happened? Who was affected? What needs to happen to make it right?
Varun apologises — specifically, without excuses — and agrees to stop and to tell his friends to stop.
They meet again after two weeks to check how things are.

steps.title: A real apology has four parts
steps.body:
1. **Name it:** ‘I mocked your stammer in front of others.’
2. **Own it:** ‘That was wrong and it was my choice.’ (no ‘but’)
3. **Impact:** ‘I understand it made you feel humiliated and avoid school.’
4. **Change:** ‘I will stop, and I’ll tell my friends to stop too.’

Then **give space** — the other person doesn’t have to forgive you right away.

steps.title: Fake apologies to avoid
steps.body:
- ‘Sorry if you were offended.’ (blames them)
- ‘Sorry, but you were annoying.’ (excuse)
- ‘Sorry, okay? Happy now?’ (dismissive)

steps.title: Restorative approaches
steps.body: Many schools use **restorative practice**: bringing people together (when safe and voluntary for the target) to understand harm and agree how to repair it. It focuses on responsibility and repair, not just punishment.

steps.title: Making it right in action
steps.body:
- Stop all bullying, online and offline
- Delete hurtful posts and ask others to as well
- Don’t retaliate against anyone who reported you
- Be neutral or kind if you meet the person; don’t force friendship

steps.title: Consequences still apply
steps.body: Repair doesn’t cancel school consequences. Accepting them calmly shows real change.

activity.prompt: Put the four parts of a real apology in order:
items: Name exactly what you did
Own it without excuses
Acknowledge the impact on them
Say what you will do differently

quiz.q: Which is a real apology?
options: ‘I mocked you; it was wrong; I know it hurt; I’ll stop’
quiz.why: A real apology names what you did, says it was wrong, acknowledges the hurt and promises to stop. 'Sorry, but you started it' or 'Sorry if you were offended' are not real apologies.

quiz.q: After apologising, you should…
quiz.why: After apologising, give space. Forgiveness is the other person's choice, so demanding it or posting about it is wrong.

quiz.q: Restorative practice focuses on…
quiz.why: Restorative practice focuses on taking responsibility and repairing the harm. It isn't about revenge or ignoring it.

quiz.q: Which is part of making it right?
quiz.why: Making it right includes deleting hurtful posts, which undoes harm where you can. Keeping them or retaliating makes it worse.

quiz.q: Does repair cancel school consequences?
quiz.why: No. Repair doesn't cancel school consequences, so accept them calmly as part of taking responsibility.

sources: UNESCO (Behind the numbers: school violence and bullying, 2019)

lessons.title: Changing the habit

scenes.text: Varun notices he mocks people most when he’s angry after fights at home.
He works with the counsellor on a ‘stop-think-choose’ plan and joins the school cricket team as a junior coach.
Coaching younger kids gives him respect without putting anyone down.
A year later, Sid and Varun nod hello in the corridor. Varun is proud of who he’s becoming.

steps.title: Stop – Think – Choose
steps.body:
- **Stop:** notice the urge (to mock, push, exclude)
- **Think:** How will they feel? What am I really feeling?
- **Choose:** walk away, breathe, say something neutral or kind

steps.title: Know your triggers
steps.body: Common triggers: anger from home, boredom, a certain group of friends, feeling embarrassed, being online late at night. Write yours down and plan an alternative for each.

steps.title: Earn status differently
steps.body: People respect **skill, humour that includes everyone, fairness and leadership**. Sports, music, coaching, debating or helping younger students give real respect.

steps.title: Peer group
steps.body: If your friends bully, changing may mean saying ‘Leave it’ or spending time with different people. That takes courage — and it’s leadership.

steps.title: Ongoing support
steps.body: A counsellor, coach or trusted adult can check in weekly. If anger, home stress or sadness are behind it, ask for help: **Tele-MANAS 14416**, or **1098** if you’re unsafe at home.

activity.prompt: My change plan:
items: Write down my top 3 triggers
Plan a ‘stop-think-choose’ action for each
Delete or take down anything hurtful I posted
Find one activity where I can earn respect positively
Choose one trusted adult to check in with weekly
Say ‘leave it’ when friends start bullying

quiz.q: Stop–Think–Choose helps you…
options: Pause and pick a better action
quiz.why: Stop–Think–Choose helps you pause and pick a better action. It interrupts the habit of reacting.

quiz.q: Why know your triggers?
quiz.why: Knowing your triggers lets you plan other responses in advance. Planning works better than relying on willpower in the moment.

quiz.q: Which earns real respect?
quiz.why: Real respect comes from skill, fairness and leadership. Threats, mocking and excluding earn fear, not respect.

quiz.q: Your friends start mocking someone. Leadership looks like…
quiz.why: Leadership is saying 'Leave it' when your friends mock someone. Joining in, laughing or filming supports the bullying.

quiz.q: If home stress is behind your anger, you can…
options: Talk to a counsellor or call 14416 (1098 if unsafe)
quiz.why: If home stress is behind your anger, talk to a counsellor or call Tele-MANAS 14416 (or 1098 if you feel unsafe). Taking it out on others or hiding it doesn't solve it.

sources: UNESCO (Behind the numbers: school violence and bullying, 2019)

questions.why: Reasons for bullying are explanations, not excuses. Change is still needed.
Impact matters more than intent, because the other person's hurt is what counts.
A real apology names what you did, owns it, acknowledges the impact and commits to change. 'Sorry if…' avoids responsibility.
After apologising, give space, because forgiveness is the other person's choice. Demanding it is pressure.
Taking away the audience means not laughing or joining in. That removes the reward.
Stop–Think–Choose interrupts the urge to bully, giving you time to pick a better action.
'Sorry, but you were annoying' is a fake apology because it blames the other person. 'I was wrong; I'll stop' takes responsibility.

options: What happened, who was affected, how to make it right
questions.why: Restorative circles ask what happened, who was affected and how to make it right. They focus on repair, not only blame.

questions.q: Caste-based bullying can be an offence under…
questions.why: Caste-based bullying can be an offence under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. It is a serious matter.
Coaching younger kids earns positive status and respect. Mocking earns fear.
No. Repair does not cancel consequences, and accepting them is part of responsibility.

options: Planning in advance beats in-the-moment willpower
questions.why: A trigger plan works because deciding your response in advance is more reliable than willpower in the moment. It isn't about blaming others.

questions.q: Varun bullied because of anger from home. Best combined approach?
options: Repair harm + trigger plan + counselling for home stress
questions.why: Best is to repair the harm, make a trigger plan and get counselling for the home stress. Punishment alone or ignoring misses the cause or the behaviour.

courses.title: Bystander to upstander
courses.summary: How to help safely when you see bullying — the 5 Ds, supporting the target, beating the bystander effect, and upstanding online.
outcomes: Learners can use the 5 Ds safely
Learners can support a target with helpful words and actions
Learners can explain and overcome the bystander effect
Learners can upstand online without spreading harm
courses.guardianNote: For ages 8–15. Teaches safe ways bystanders can help (the 5 Ds), how to support a target and how group dynamics work. Encourages telling adults; never asks children to put themselves in danger.

lessons.title: From bystander to upstander: the 5 Ds

scenes.text: Meera, 12, in Chennai sees older students snatch a younger boy’s cap on the bus every day.
She wants to help but is scared of becoming a target.
In a workshop she learns the 5 Ds — ways to help that don’t require being a hero.
Next day she sits next to the boy, chats about cricket (distract), and later tells the bus attendant (delegate).

steps.title: Bystanders matter
steps.body: Most bullying happens with others watching. Studies of school playgrounds have found that when a peer steps in, bullying often stops within seconds. You don’t need to be a superhero — small actions make a big difference.

steps.title: The 5 Ds
steps.body:
- **Direct:** say something — ‘Stop, that’s not okay.’ (only if it feels safe)
- **Distract:** interrupt — start a conversation with the target, ask the time, drop something
- **Delegate:** get help — tell a teacher, bus attendant, coach or parent
- **Delay:** check in afterwards — ‘Are you okay? Want me to come with you to a teacher?’
- **Document:** note what happened or screenshot online bullying — and give it to the target or an adult (don’t post it)

steps.title: Worked example: choosing a D
steps.body:
- Big older group, you feel unsafe → **Delegate** + **Delay**
- Friend mocking someone in your group → **Direct**: ‘Bro, leave it.’
- Mean group chat → **Document** + **Delegate**, and message the target privately
- Someone being excluded at lunch → **Distract**: ‘Hey, sit with us!’

steps.title: Safety rule
steps.body: Never put yourself in physical danger. If someone could get hurt, get an adult or call **112**. Helping safely is still helping.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Think of a bullying situation you’ve seen. Which D could you have used?

activity.prompt: Match each D with an example:
pairs: Screenshotting a mean chat for an adult

quiz.q: Which D means getting someone else to help?
quiz.why: Delegate means getting someone else, like an adult, to help. Direct, Delay and Distract are different actions.

quiz.q: Which is safest when a big group is bullying?
quiz.why: With a big group bullying, it is safest to delegate (get an adult) and delay (check in afterwards). Fighting or confronting alone is risky, and filming and posting spreads harm.

quiz.q: When peers step in, bullying…
quiz.why: When peers step in, bullying often stops quickly. Peer action is powerful.

quiz.q: Documenting online bullying means…
options: Saving evidence for the target or an adult
quiz.why: Documenting online bullying means saving evidence for the target or an adult. Posting, forwarding or commenting spreads it.

quiz.q: Checking in afterwards is…
quiz.why: Checking in afterwards is Delay. It's still powerful because it shows the target someone cares.

sources: UNESCO (Behind the numbers: school violence and bullying, 2019)
Right To Be (5Ds of bystander intervention)

lessons.title: Supporting the person being bullied

scenes.text: Ali, 10, is new in a Kolkata school and kids mock his Urdu accent.
Pia notices he’s always alone and invites him to play kho-kho.
She asks, ‘Are you okay? It’s not your fault.’ and offers to go with him to the teacher.
Ali says later, ‘Pia made school bearable.’

steps.title: What to say
steps.body:
- ‘That wasn’t okay. It’s not your fault.’
- ‘Do you want me to come with you to a teacher?’
- ‘You can sit with us.’
- ‘I’m here if you want to talk.’

steps.title: What not to say
steps.body:
- ‘Just ignore it.’ (often doesn’t work)
- ‘Toughen up.’
- ‘What did you do to them?’
- Sharing their story with others without permission

steps.title: Small actions that help
steps.body: Walking together between classes, including them in games and group projects, liking/commenting kindly online, telling an adult with them. Feeling that even **one person** is on their side protects wellbeing.

steps.title: If they talk about hurting themselves
steps.body: Take it seriously. Don’t promise to keep it secret. Tell a trusted adult **today**, and share **Tele-MANAS 14416** or **112** in an emergency.

a.text: A new classmate always eats alone and gets laughed at.

choices.label: Invite them to sit with your group
choices.feedback: Inclusion is powerful.

choices.label: Do nothing — it’s not your business
choices.feedback: Silence can feel like agreement to the target.

b.text: They quietly say the jokes are making them hate school.

choices.label: ‘That’s not your fault. Want me to come with you to tell a teacher?’
choices.feedback: Belief plus practical help.

choices.label: ‘Just ignore them.’
choices.feedback: Ignoring rarely stops bullying.

c.text: A week later they stop coming to school.

choices.label: Tell a teacher what you saw and message them kindly
choices.feedback: Better late than never.

end1.text: The teacher acts and your classmate has a friend. That matters hugely.

quiz.q: Which is supportive?
options: ‘That wasn’t okay. It’s not your fault.’
quiz.why: 'That wasn't okay. It's not your fault.' is supportive because it validates the target. 'Toughen up' or 'What did you do?' blames them.

quiz.q: Why does one supportive person matter?
options: It protects wellbeing and reduces isolation
quiz.why: One supportive person protects wellbeing and reduces isolation. Connection helps targets cope.

quiz.q: A friend says they want to hurt themselves. You should…
options: Tell a trusted adult today; share 14416
quiz.why: If a friend says they want to hurt themselves, tell a trusted adult today and share 14416. Keeping it secret could put them in danger.

quiz.q: Is sharing their story without permission okay?
options: No, except telling a trusted adult for safety
quiz.why: Sharing their story without permission is not okay, because it is their private story. The exception is telling a trusted adult to keep them safe.

quiz.q: Which small action helps?
quiz.why: Walking together between classes is a simple way to support someone. Avoiding them, liking mean posts or gossiping hurts.

sources: UNESCO (Behind the numbers: school violence and bullying, 2019)

lessons.title: Group dynamics: why people don't step in

scenes.text: In a Class 8 classroom in Jaipur, a student’s drawing is torn up as a ‘joke’. 30 students watch. Nobody speaks.
Later, each says they thought ‘someone else would do something’.
Their teacher explains the ‘bystander effect’ and the class makes an upstander pledge.
The next time, three students speak up together — and it stops.

steps.title: The bystander effect
steps.body: Psychologists found that people are **less likely to help when many others are present**, because responsibility feels shared (‘someone else will’), and people look to others to decide whether something is serious. Knowing about it helps you break it.

steps.title: Why we stay silent
steps.body:
- Fear of becoming the target
- Not wanting to be ‘uncool’
- Unsure if it’s ‘really’ bullying
- Thinking adults won’t help
- Liking the person who bullies

steps.title: Strength in numbers
steps.body: Speak up **with a friend**. Agree in advance with your group: ‘If we see bullying, we’ll do something.’ One voice makes it easier for others to join.

steps.title: Worked example: breaking the effect
steps.body: Instead of waiting, Neha points at a specific person: ‘Rohit, go get Ms. Kaur now.’ Naming someone overcomes shared responsibility.

steps.title: Upstander pledge
steps.body: Write: ‘When I see bullying, I will use at least one of the 5 Ds.’ Sign it.

statements.s: People are more likely to help when lots of others are around.
statements.why: The bystander effect shows the opposite.

statements.s: Naming a specific person to get help increases action.
Speaking up with a friend is easier than alone.
If nobody else reacts, it must not be serious.
statements.why: Others may be thinking the same.

quiz.q: The bystander effect means…
options: More people = each feels less responsible
quiz.why: The bystander effect is when more people are present, each person feels less responsible to act. So help often doesn't come.

quiz.q: Best way to overcome it?
options: Act yourself or name a specific person to get help
quiz.why: To overcome it, act yourself or name a specific person to get help. That gives direct responsibility.

quiz.q: Why do people stay silent?
options: Fear of being targeted, unsure if it’s serious
quiz.why: People stay silent because of fear of being targeted or unsure if it is serious. Most are not bad people.

quiz.q: An upstander pledge helps by…
quiz.why: An upstander pledge helps by making a plan in advance, so you are more likely to act when it happens.

quiz.q: Which is strength in numbers?
quiz.why: Speaking up with friends is strength in numbers. Joining, staying quiet or filming helps the bullying.

sources: UNESCO (Behind the numbers: school violence and bullying, 2019)

lessons.title: Upstanding online

scenes.text: In a Class 7 WhatsApp group, someone posts an edited photo of Sana with mean captions.
Emojis start pouring in. Ravi feels sick seeing it.
He messages Sana privately, ‘That’s not okay, I’m sorry,’ screenshots the post and shows his mother.
She informs the class teacher; the post is removed and the class discusses online respect.

steps.title: Online, bystanders are huge
steps.body: Online, hundreds can see bullying. Reactions — even one laughing emoji — spread and reward it. Silence or private support can change everything.

steps.title: Online 5 Ds
steps.body:
- **Direct:** comment ‘Not cool’ only if safe and you won’t get pulled into a fight
- **Distract:** change the topic in the group
- **Delegate:** tell a trusted adult; report the post on the platform
- **Delay:** private message to the target
- **Document:** screenshot (with date and names) for adults — **don’t forward**

steps.title: Never
steps.body:
- Forward or repost hurtful content
- Add laughing reactions
- Join a pile-on, even against someone who did something wrong
- Forward images of anyone without clothes — for under-18s it’s a crime (POCSO, IT Act)

steps.title: Reporting routes
steps.body: Platform report button · school · **cybercrime.gov.in** or **1930** · **1098** Childline. Serious threats: **112**.

activity.prompt: Helpful or harmful online?

items.text: Private message: ‘That’s not okay, are you alright?’
Adding a 😂 reaction
Reporting the post
Forwarding it to another group
Screenshotting for a trusted adult
Changing the topic in the group

quiz.q: One laughing emoji on a mean post…
quiz.why: A laughing emoji on a mean post rewards and spreads it. Reactions fuel bullying.

quiz.q: Best way to document online bullying?
options: Screenshot with date and names for an adult
quiz.why: Screenshot with date and names for an adult, so there is proof. Forwarding, commenting or reposting spreads the harm.

quiz.q: Reporting route for online harm in India?
quiz.why: In India, online harm can be reported to 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in, the national cybercrime channels.

quiz.q: Forwarding an under-18 nude image is…
quiz.why: Forwarding a nude image of someone under 18 is a crime under POCSO and the IT Act. Never forward it, even if you delete it later.

quiz.q: A private message to the target is which D?
quiz.why: A private message to the target is Delay, a check-in after the incident. It shows you care without confronting.

sources: UNESCO (Behind the numbers: school violence and bullying, 2019)

questions.q: Which D means telling an adult?
questions.why: Delegate means getting an adult to help. Distract means drawing attention away.
No. Laughing at bullying rewards it, because it gives the person bullying the audience they want.

options: Never put yourself in physical danger
questions.why: Never put yourself in physical danger. Help safely, for example by getting an adult.
'Are you okay?' afterwards is Delay, a check-in after the event.

questions.q: Which is NOT supportive to say?
questions.why: 'Toughen up' is dismissive and blames the target. 'It's not your fault' is supportive.
Online documentation means taking a screenshot for an adult. Forwarding it to everyone spreads the harm.

options: More people present → each feels less responsible
questions.why: The bystander effect is when more people present means each feels less responsible, so fewer act.

options: Name a specific person to act
questions.why: To overcome the bystander effect, name a specific person to act. Waiting for others means nobody helps.
If a friend mentions self-harm, tell a trusted adult today. Keeping it secret risks their safety.
Joining a pile-on is harmful because it adds to the hurt. Reporting helps.

questions.q: Big group bullying, you feel unsafe. Best Ds?
questions.why: With a big group and no safety, Delegate and Delay are best: get an adult, then check in later. Directly confronting alone is risky.

questions.q: Why does one supportive peer matter so much?
questions.why: One supportive peer reduces isolation and protects wellbeing. Connection is powerful for targets.

options: Deciding in advance makes action more likely
questions.why: An upstander pledge works because deciding in advance makes action more likely when the moment comes.

courses.title: Cyberbullying: respond, report, recover
courses.summary: Recognise forms of cyberbullying, respond with the 5-step plan, understand which Indian laws may apply, and protect your digital wellbeing.
outcomes: Learners can name forms of cyberbullying
Learners can respond with Stop–Save–Block–Tell–Report
Learners can explain which Indian laws may apply and how to report
Learners can protect digital wellbeing and footprint
courses.guardianNote: For ages 12–17. Covers forms of cyberbullying, how to respond (don’t retaliate, document, block, report), Indian reporting routes (1930, cybercrime.gov.in, 1098), the laws that may apply, and digital wellbeing. Non-explicit.

lessons.title: Forms of cyberbullying

scenes.text: Someone creates a fake Instagram account using photos of Ananya, 15, from Bengaluru, posting embarrassing captions.
She also gets anonymous messages calling her names and a group chat she was removed from mocks her.
She feels there is no escape — it follows her home.
Her cousin, a software engineer, helps her identify each type of harm and report them.

steps.title: Common forms
steps.body:
- **Harassment:** repeated nasty messages
- **Flaming:** angry, insulting online fights
- **Impersonation / fake accounts:** pretending to be someone
- **Outing / doxxing:** sharing private information, secrets or addresses
- **Exclusion:** deliberately removing someone from groups
- **Trolling and pile-ons:** many people attacking one person
- **Image-based abuse:** sharing private or edited images
- **Cyberstalking:** repeated monitoring, threats or contact that causes fear

steps.title: Why it feels worse
steps.body:
- It can happen **24/7** and follow you home
- It can be **anonymous**
- A huge **audience** can see it
- It can be **permanent** (screenshots)

Your feelings are valid. Help exists.

steps.title: Worked example: name it
steps.body: Ananya’s case: fake account = **impersonation**; anonymous messages = **harassment**; removed and mocked in group = **exclusion + harassment**. Naming each makes reporting clearer.

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking ‘it’s just online, it’s not real’ — the harm is real
- Responding angrily (can escalate and be used against you)
- Deleting everything before saving evidence

activity.prompt: Match the form to its description:
pairs: Fake account pretending to be someone
Sharing someone’s private information or address
Repeated monitoring or contact causing fear
Sharing private or edited images to humiliate

quiz.q: A fake account using your photos is…
quiz.why: A fake account using your photos is impersonation. Flaming is hostile arguing, and exclusion is leaving someone out.

quiz.q: Why can cyberbullying feel worse?
options: It’s 24/7, public, possibly anonymous and lasting
quiz.why: Cyberbullying can feel worse because it is 24/7, public, possibly anonymous and lasting. It can follow you home.

quiz.q: Sharing someone’s home address online to target them is…
quiz.why: Doxxing is sharing someone's private information, like a home address, online to target them. It can put them in danger.

quiz.q: Should you delete messages before saving evidence?
quiz.why: No, save evidence first. Once messages are deleted you may lose proof needed for reporting.

quiz.q: Is online harm ‘not real’?
quiz.why: False. Online harm has real impact on feelings, sleep and safety, even though it happens on a screen.

sources: UNESCO (Behind the numbers: school violence and bullying, 2019)

lessons.title: How to respond: stop, save, block, tell, report

scenes.text: Rohan, 14, from Pune receives threatening messages from an unknown number after a gaming argument.
His first urge is to fire back insults.
Instead, he follows his school’s 5-step plan.
The account is banned, and his parents report the threats at cybercrime.gov.in.

steps.title: The 5 steps
steps.body:
1. **Stop** — don’t reply or retaliate
2. **Save** — screenshots with usernames, dates, URLs; save links
3. **Block** — the person and adjust privacy
4. **Tell** — a trusted adult
5. **Report** — on the platform, to the school, and if serious at **cybercrime.gov.in** or **1930**; under 18s: **1098**; threats to safety: **112**

steps.title: Worked example: good evidence
steps.body: A good screenshot shows: the **message**, the **sender’s profile name/handle**, the **date/time**, and the **platform**. Also copy the **profile URL**. Keep a simple log: date | platform | what | who.

steps.title: Lock down your accounts
steps.body:
- Strong unique passwords + two-factor authentication
- Private accounts; review followers
- Limit who can message, tag or comment
- Turn off location in posts
- Log out of shared devices

steps.title: If you’re being threatened
steps.body: Threats of violence, sharing images, or self-harm encouragement are **serious**. Tell an adult immediately, report to police (**112**) or cybercrime (**1930**). Don’t meet the person.

steps.title: Look after your mind
steps.body: Take breaks from the app, mute notifications, spend time offline with people you trust. If it’s affecting sleep or mood, talk to a counsellor or call **Tele-MANAS 14416**.

activity.prompt: Put the five response steps in order:
items: Stop — don’t reply or retaliate
Save — screenshot with names, dates, links
Block the person and tighten privacy
Tell a trusted adult
Report to the platform, school, and 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in if serious

quiz.q: First step when cyberbullied?
quiz.why: First, stop and don't reply. Replying angrily feeds the bullying, and you can act better once calm.

quiz.q: Good evidence includes…
options: Message, sender handle, date/time, platform and URL
quiz.why: Good evidence includes the message, sender handle, date and time, platform and URL. That gives the fullest record for reporting.

quiz.q: Which national helpline handles cybercrime?
quiz.why: 1930 is the national cybercrime helpline. 181 is the Women's Helpline, 108 the ambulance and 1097 the AIDS helpline.

quiz.q: Two-factor authentication…
options: Adds a second check to protect accounts
quiz.why: Two-factor authentication adds a second check, like a code, to protect accounts. It strengthens security and doesn't share your password.

quiz.q: Someone threatens to hurt you. You…
options: Meet them to sort it out
quiz.why: If someone threatens to hurt you, tell an adult and report to 112 or 1930. Ignoring it or meeting them is unsafe.

sources: UNESCO (Behind the numbers: school violence and bullying, 2019)

lessons.title: When cyberbullying breaks the law (India)

scenes.text: A student in Kanpur morphs a classmate’s face onto an obscene image and circulates it.
The family files a complaint on cybercrime.gov.in. Police trace the account.
The student, who thought it was a prank, faces legal proceedings under the IT Act and POCSO.
The school runs a session: ‘Online actions have offline consequences.’

steps.title: Laws that may apply
steps.body:
Depending on the facts, online harassment can fall under:
- **IT Act, 2000:** identity theft (s.66C), cheating by impersonation (s.66D), violation of privacy by capturing/sharing private images (s.66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit material (s.67, 67A), and child sexual abuse material (s.67B)
- **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), in force since 1 July 2024:** offences such as stalking (including monitoring a woman’s online activity), criminal intimidation, defamation, sexual harassment and insulting the modesty of a woman
- **POCSO Act, 2012:** sexual offences against children, including online

Juveniles are dealt with under the **Juvenile Justice Act**. This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Why this matters
steps.body: ‘Prank’, ‘joke’ or ‘I didn’t create it, I just forwarded it’ are not defences in many cases. Forwarding can itself be an offence.

steps.title: Filing a complaint
steps.body: At **cybercrime.gov.in** you can report (including anonymously for some categories like child sexual abuse material). Have evidence ready. You can also go to your local police station or cyber cell. **1930** handles financial cyber fraud and guides on other complaints.

steps.title: Be careful with ‘revenge’
steps.body: Hacking back, doxxing the bully, or posting their private info can make **you** liable. Let adults and police handle it.

statements.s: Forwarding a morphed obscene image can be an offence even if you didn’t create it.
The IPC is still India’s main criminal code in 2026.
statements.why: BNS replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024.

statements.s: Impersonating someone online can be an offence under the IT Act.
Hacking a bully’s account in revenge is legal.
Juveniles are dealt with under the Juvenile Justice Act.

quiz.q: Which law has been India’s main criminal code since 1 July 2024?
quiz.why: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) replaced the IPC as India's main criminal code from 1 July 2024.

quiz.q: IT Act section 66E concerns…
options: Violation of privacy by capturing/sharing private images
quiz.why: IT Act Section 66E punishes violation of privacy, such as capturing or sharing private images without consent.

quiz.q: Is ‘it was just a prank’ a defence?
quiz.why: 'It was just a prank' is often not a defence, because the harm and consequences are real. Intent doesn't erase impact.

quiz.q: Where can you report cybercrime online?
quiz.why: cybercrime.gov.in is the national portal for reporting cybercrime online.

quiz.q: Revenge doxxing the bully…
quiz.why: Revenge doxxing can make you legally liable and escalate the problem. Report instead.

sources: UNESCO (Behind the numbers: school violence and bullying, 2019)

lessons.title: Digital wellbeing and being a good digital citizen

scenes.text: Isha, 16, from Kochi scrolls until 2 am, reading comments about herself and others.
She’s anxious, tired and snaps at everyone.
She tries a ‘phone out of bedroom’ rule, mutes toxic accounts and follows creators who make her feel good.
Two weeks later she sleeps better and feels more in control.

steps.title: Protect your mind
steps.body:
- Phone out of the bedroom at night
- Mute, unfollow or block accounts that make you feel bad
- Turn off non-essential notifications
- Take regular breaks; set app timers
- Follow accounts that teach, inspire or make you laugh

steps.title: THINK before you post
steps.body: Is it **T**rue? **H**elpful? **I**nspiring? **N**ecessary? **K**ind? If not, don’t post.

steps.title: Digital footprint
steps.body: Posts, comments and photos can last for years. Colleges and employers may look at public profiles. A good footprint shows kindness, interests and skills.

steps.title: Worked example: rewrite
steps.body:
Angry draft: ‘You’re such a loser, nobody likes you.’

THINK version: Don’t post. If there’s a real disagreement: ‘I disagree with what you said in class — can we talk?’

activity.label: How many hours a day do you spend on social media?

bands.text: Under an hour — a light, balanced amount for most people.
1–3 hours — check how you feel afterwards and protect sleep.
3–5 hours — consider app timers and offline activities; notice mood and sleep.
Over 5 hours — many studies link heavy use with poorer sleep and mood. Try a plan to cut down and talk to someone if it feels out of control.

quiz.q: THINK stands for…
quiz.why: THINK is a posting filter: is it True, Helpful, Inspiring, Necessary, Kind? It helps you decide before posting.

quiz.q: Which protects sleep?
options: Phone out of the bedroom at night
quiz.why: Keeping the phone out of the bedroom at night protects sleep. Scrolling late and notifications disturb it.

quiz.q: A digital footprint is…
options: The lasting record of what you post online
quiz.why: A digital footprint is the lasting record of what you post and do online. It can be found later.

quiz.q: An account keeps making you feel bad. You can…
quiz.why: If an account makes you feel bad, mute, unfollow or block it. That curates your feed to protect your wellbeing.

quiz.q: Heavy social media use is linked in many studies with…
quiz.why: Heavy social media use is linked in many studies with poorer sleep and mood. Balance helps.

sources: UNESCO (Behind the numbers: school violence and bullying, 2019)

questions.why: First, stop and don't reply, because replying feeds the bullying. Then save evidence and get help.
1930 is the national cybercrime helpline. 1098 is Childline, which also helps children.

questions.q: A fake account using your photo is…
questions.why: A fake account using your photo is impersonation. Flaming is hostile arguing online.
Good evidence includes the sender handle, date and time, platform and URL. Just the text is incomplete.
In THINK, K stands for Kind. Ask if what you post is kind.

options: Sharing private info to target someone
questions.why: Doxxing is sharing private information to target someone. It can put them in danger.

questions.q: India’s main criminal code since 1 July 2024?
questions.why: The BNS (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita) replaced the IPC as India's main criminal code on 1 July 2024.

questions.q: Forwarding a morphed obscene image is…
questions.why: Forwarding a morphed obscene image may be an offence under the IT Act, because it spreads harm. It is not always legal.
Revenge hacking can make you liable, since it is an offence too. Report instead of retaliating.
Section 67B of the IT Act covers child sexual abuse material, a serious offence. It is not about tax.

questions.q: Juveniles in conflict with law are handled under…
questions.why: Juveniles in conflict with the law are handled under the Juvenile Justice Act. The Companies Act is unrelated.

questions.q: Why can cyberbullying be more harmful?
questions.why: Cyberbullying can be more harmful because it is 24/7, reaches a wide audience, can be anonymous and lasts online. It isn't shorter.

options: Stop, save, block, tell, report + self-care
questions.why: A complete plan is to stop, save evidence, block, tell an adult and report, plus self-care. Deleting everything or fighting doesn't help.

courses.title: Ragging is illegal: know your rights on campus
courses.summary: For college students and parents: what counts as ragging, the UGC 2009 regulations and punishments, how to complain safely (1800-180-5522), how seniors can welcome without ragging, and campus safety.
outcomes: Learners can define ragging under the UGC regulations
Learners can report ragging safely and write a clear complaint
Seniors can replace ragging with mentoring
Learners can use campus committees and stay safe in hostels

lessons.title: Ragging is illegal: what the rules say

scenes.text: Pranav, 18, arrives at an engineering college hostel in Nagpur. Seniors order freshers to stand in a line at midnight.
They demand ‘introductions’, make him sing and insult his home state. One senior asks for his phone.
Pranav remembers the anti-ragging affidavit he signed during admission.
He calls the national anti-ragging helpline the next morning. The college anti-ragging squad acts within days.

steps.title: The legal framework
steps.body:
- The **Supreme Court of India** has directed strict action against ragging in all educational institutions.
- The **UGC Regulations on Curbing the Menace of Ragging in Higher Educational Institutions, 2009** (and similar rules from AICTE, NMC and other regulators) make ragging a punishable act in colleges and universities.
- Several states also have **anti-ragging laws** that make it a criminal offence.
- Serious acts can also be offences under the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)** — e.g. hurt, wrongful restraint, criminal intimidation, sexual harassment.

This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: What counts as ragging
steps.body:
Under the UGC regulations, ragging includes any act by students that:
- teases, treats rudely or **causes physical or psychological harm** or fear to a fresher or any student
- makes a student **do something they wouldn’t do willingly** and that causes shame or embarrassment (e.g. forced singing, dressing, ‘introductions’ at odd hours)
- **exploits** a student’s services (assignments, errands) or extorts money
- involves **physical or sexual abuse**, or anything abusive about region, language, caste, religion, gender or appearance

‘Just tradition’ or ‘harmless fun’ is not a defence.

steps.title: What colleges must do
steps.body: Every institution must have an **Anti-Ragging Committee** and **Anti-Ragging Squad**, display helpline numbers, collect **anti-ragging undertakings** from students and parents (online at the national portal), and act on complaints promptly — including informing the police where an offence is involved.

steps.title: Punishments
steps.body: Depending on seriousness, punishments include: suspension from classes, withholding scholarships or results, debarring from exams, cancellation of admission, suspension from hostel, **rustication or expulsion**, fines, and criminal proceedings. Institutions that fail to act can themselves face action by regulators.

steps.title: Helpline
steps.body: **National Anti-Ragging Helpline: 1800-180-5522** (toll-free, 24×7). Email: **helpline@antiragging.in**. Emergency: **112**.

activity.prompt: Is it ragging?

items.text: Seniors forcing freshers to sing at midnight
A senior offering to help find the library
Making a fresher write a senior’s assignments
Mocking a student’s home state and accent
A voluntary welcome event with faculty present
Demanding money or a phone ‘for initiation’

quiz.q: Which regulation governs ragging in Indian higher education?
options: UGC Regulations on Curbing the Menace of Ragging, 2009
quiz.why: Ragging is governed by the UGC Regulations on Curbing the Menace of Ragging in Higher Educational Institutions, 2009. The POSH, RTE and Motor Vehicles Acts cover other things.

quiz.q: National anti-ragging helpline?
quiz.why: The national anti-ragging helpline is 1800-180-5522, toll-free and 24×7. 1098 is Childline, 181 the Women's Helpline and 1930 cybercrime.

quiz.q: Forcing a fresher to do a senior’s assignments is…
quiz.why: Forcing a fresher to do a senior's assignments is ragging, as it exploits their services. It is not mentoring.

quiz.q: ‘It’s tradition’ is…
quiz.why: 'It's tradition' is not a defence, since ragging is illegal whatever the custom. It is never a valid excuse.

quiz.q: Which is a possible punishment?
quiz.why: Ragging can lead to severe punishments such as rustication or expulsion, and criminal cases. It is never rewarded.

sources: UGC Regulations on Curbing the Menace of Ragging in HEIs, 2009

lessons.title: If you're being ragged: what to do

scenes.text: Fatima, 18, a first-year medical student in Bhopal, is called to a senior’s room and told to ‘perform’ and answer personal questions.
She’s scared that complaining will make her life hell for 5 years.
Her roommate helps her file a complaint on the anti-ragging portal; the identity of complainants is to be kept confidential.
The Anti-Ragging Squad visits the hostel. Fatima receives support from the student counsellor.

steps.title: In the moment
steps.body:
- Get out safely if you can; stay in groups with other freshers
- Avoid isolated places and seniors’ rooms at night
- Don’t retaliate physically
- Call **112** if in danger

steps.title: Complaint routes
steps.body:
1. **Anti-Ragging Helpline 1800-180-5522** or **helpline@antiragging.in** — complaints are passed to the college and monitored
2. College **Anti-Ragging Committee/Squad**, warden, Dean of Students, principal
3. **Police** for any criminal act
4. Parents or guardians

You can complain even if you are not the victim — bystanders and parents can report.

steps.title: Worked example: written complaint
steps.body: ‘To the Anti-Ragging Committee: On 12 August 2026 at about 11:30 pm, in Room 214, Hostel B, seniors [names if known] forced me and two other first-years to sing and answer personal questions, and threatened us if we told anyone. Witnesses: [names]. I request urgent action and confidentiality. — [Name, roll no., contact].’

steps.title: Fear of retaliation
steps.body: Regulations require institutions to protect complainants and act against retaliation, and retaliation is itself treated seriously. Keep records of any further threats and report them too.

steps.title: Look after yourself
steps.body: Ragging can cause anxiety, sleep problems and thoughts of dropping out. Talk to the college counsellor, a friend, or **Tele-MANAS 14416**. If you ever feel hopeless or think of self-harm, call **14416** or **112** today.

a.text: At 11 pm, seniors knock and tell all freshers on your floor to come to the terrace ‘for introductions’.

choices.label: Stay with other freshers, refuse politely, and call the anti-ragging helpline or warden
choices.feedback: Groups and quick reporting are safest.

choices.label: Go alone so you don’t get noticed
choices.feedback: Going alone at night increases risk.

b.text: The warden arrives; seniors leave. Next day a senior threatens you in the canteen.

choices.label: Note the threat (time, place, witnesses) and report it to the committee
choices.feedback: Retaliation is taken seriously — report it.

choices.label: Apologise to the senior and agree to ‘make up’
choices.feedback: Giving in often leads to more demands.

c.text: You’re made to perform humiliating tasks and asked for money.

choices.label: Report to 1800-180-5522 and the college committee, with details
choices.feedback: Reporting stops it for you and others.

choices.label: Pay to make it stop
choices.feedback: Paying usually leads to more extortion.

end1.text: The committee acts; seniors face disciplinary action. You get counselling and feel safe in the hostel.

end2.text: Extortion rarely stops on its own. Go back and report — it’s your right.

quiz.q: Can a bystander or parent report ragging?
quiz.why: Yes, a bystander or parent can report ragging; anyone can. The victim does not have to be the only one to complain.

quiz.q: Safest response to a late-night summons by seniors?
options: Stay in a group, refuse politely and contact warden/helpline
quiz.why: Stay in a group, refuse politely and contact the warden or helpline. Going alone, fighting or paying puts you at risk.

quiz.q: A good written complaint includes…
options: Date, time, place, names, witnesses, what happened
quiz.why: A good complaint gives the date, time, place, names, witnesses and what happened. Facts help action; insults and only feelings don't.

quiz.q: Retaliation after a complaint should be…
quiz.why: Retaliation after a complaint should be reported too, because it is also a violation. Paying off or ignoring it lets it continue.

quiz.q: If ragging makes you feel hopeless, call…
quiz.why: If ragging makes you feel hopeless, call Tele-MANAS 14416 or 112. Help is available; don't stay silent or turn to the senior.

sources: UGC Regulations on Curbing the Menace of Ragging in HEIs, 2009

lessons.title: For seniors: welcome, don't rag

scenes.text: Final-year students at a Kolkata college decide to end ‘intro night’.
Instead they run a buddy system: each fresher gets a senior mentor for notes, campus tours and exam tips.
They hold a daytime welcome party with faculty, music and games anyone can skip.
Freshers later say: ‘Our seniors were the best part of first year.’

steps.title: Breaking the cycle
steps.body: Many who rag were ragged themselves and believe it ‘builds bonding’. Research and student testimony show it causes fear, trauma, dropouts and sometimes deaths. **Real bonding comes from support, not humiliation.**

steps.title: Ways to welcome freshers
steps.body:
- Buddy/mentor programmes
- Campus and city tours
- Sharing notes, previous papers and survival tips
- Daytime, supervised, voluntary welcome events
- Helping with hostel and admin hassles

steps.title: You can be liable
steps.body: Under UGC rules, **abetting** or being part of a group that rags can also lead to punishment, and institutions may take collective action where individuals can’t be identified. Don’t stand by — report.

steps.title: Worked example: stopping a friend
steps.body:
Your batchmate: ‘Let’s make the freshers do a dance tonight.’
You: ‘Bro, that’s ragging — expulsion and FIR level. Let’s do the buddy thing instead.’

activity.prompt: Senior’s anti-ragging pledge:
items: I will not rag or abet ragging
I will report ragging I see
I will volunteer as a buddy/mentor
I will speak up when friends plan ‘intro’ sessions
I will share the helpline 1800-180-5522 with freshers

quiz.q: Which is a positive alternative to ragging?
quiz.why: Buddy or mentor programmes are positive alternatives that build bonds through support. Forced dances, midnight intros and extortion harm.

quiz.q: Can abetting ragging be punished?
quiz.why: Yes, abetting ragging, meaning helping or encouraging it, can be punished under the regulations.

quiz.q: Does ragging build bonding?
options: No — it causes fear and harm
quiz.why: No, ragging does not build bonding. Evidence shows it causes fear and harm.

quiz.q: Your friend plans an ‘intro night’. You…
options: Say it’s ragging and suggest a buddy system
quiz.why: Say it is ragging and suggest a buddy system instead. Staying quiet, joining or filming allows harm.

quiz.q: Why might institutions take collective action?
options: When individuals involved can’t be identified
quiz.why: Institutions may take collective action when the individuals involved can't be identified, as the regulations allow.

sources: UGC Regulations on Curbing the Menace of Ragging in HEIs, 2009

lessons.title: Hostel and campus safety beyond ragging

scenes.text: Jaya, 18, moves from a small town in Bihar to a big university in Delhi.
She faces loneliness, a creepy message from a stranger, and pressure to drink at a party.
She uses the university’s support services: the counsellor, the Internal Committee, and a peer group.
By second semester she’s settled and mentoring newcomers herself.

steps.title: First-month survival
steps.body:
- Save numbers: warden, security, Anti-Ragging Helpline **1800-180-5522**, **112**, **14416**
- Share your timetable with a friend; let someone know when you go out
- Learn where the health centre and counsellor are
- Join one club in the first month

steps.title: Other committees
steps.body: Colleges also have: an **Internal Committee** for sexual harassment (under POSH/UGC regulations), an **SC/ST cell**, a **grievance redressal cell**, and student welfare offices. Use them.

steps.title: Pressure to drink or use substances
steps.body: You can always say ‘No thanks, I’m good.’ Never leave a drink unattended. Look out for friends; if someone is unconscious, place them on their side and call **112**.

steps.title: Loneliness is normal at first
steps.body: Most first-years feel homesick. Call home, join activities, eat in the common mess, and talk to the counsellor. If low mood lasts more than two weeks, get help — **Tele-MANAS 14416**.

cards.back: National Anti-Ragging Helpline (24×7)
Tele-MANAS mental-health helpline
All emergencies
Handles sexual harassment complaints
Unconscious person on their side; call 112
General complaints at your institution

quiz.q: Which committee handles sexual harassment on campus?
quiz.why: The Internal Committee handles sexual harassment on campus, as required by the POSH Act. A canteen or sports committee doesn't.

quiz.q: If a friend is unconscious after drinking…
options: Let them sleep on their back
quiz.why: For an unconscious friend, put them in the recovery position to prevent choking and call 112. Coffee, cold showers or lying on their back don't help and can be dangerous.

quiz.q: Homesickness in first year is…
quiz.why: Homesickness in first year is common and usually eases with time. It doesn't mean you should quit.

quiz.q: A good first-month habit?
quiz.why: Joining a club in the first month builds connection and support. Isolating or skipping meals harms wellbeing.

quiz.q: Low mood for over two weeks?
quiz.why: Low mood for over two weeks needs help, from a counsellor or Tele-MANAS 14416. Ignoring or hiding it can make it worse.

sources: UGC Regulations on Curbing the Menace of Ragging in HEIs, 2009

questions.why: The anti-ragging helpline is 1800-180-5522, toll-free and 24×7. 1098 is Childline.
No. Ragging is illegal, even if called a tradition.
The UGC Regulations 2009 govern ragging in higher education. The POSH Act deals with sexual harassment.

questions.q: Forcing freshers to do assignments is…
questions.why: Forcing freshers to do assignments is ragging, because it exploits them. It is not mentoring.
Yes, bystanders can report ragging. Anyone can.

questions.q: Safest response to a midnight summons?
questions.why: Stay in a group and contact the warden or helpline. Going alone puts you at risk.
Abetting ragging can be punished, because the regulations cover those who help or encourage it.

questions.q: Mocking someone’s region and language counts as ragging?
questions.why: Yes, mocking someone's region or language is abusive conduct and counts as ragging.

questions.q: Serious ragging acts can also be offences under…
questions.why: Serious ragging acts can also be offences under the BNS, India's criminal law, as well as under college rules.

questions.q: What must colleges collect from students and parents?
questions.why: Colleges must collect anti-ragging undertakings from students and parents, which they sign to confirm they know the rules.
Ragging can lead to expulsion and criminal proceedings. It is never rewarded.

questions.q: Why might collective punishment be applied?
questions.why: Collective punishment may be used when the individuals involved can't be identified. It isn't for fun.

options: Buddy systems and voluntary daytime welcomes
questions.why: Buddy systems and voluntary daytime welcomes support freshers without fear. Midnight intros risk harm.

wellbeing-mental-health.title: Mental health: feel, cope, heal, help
wellbeing-mental-health.description: From big feelings for little people to anxiety, depression, grief, self-harm and suicidal thoughts, sleep, loneliness, body image and addiction — always with ‘talk to someone today’: Tele-MANAS 14416, 112.

courses.title: Big feelings for little people
courses.summary: Naming feelings, taming the worry monster, a calm-down toolbox, and knowing who to tell.
outcomes: Learners can name common feelings
Learners can use worry tools and brave steps
Learners can use breathing and other calm-down tools
Learners can name helpers and know 1098
courses.guardianNote: For ages 6–10 with a parent or teacher. Helps children name feelings, understand worry, use calm-down tools (breathing, movement, talking) and know who to tell. No distressing content.

lessons.title: Naming my feelings

scenes.text: Aryan, 7, from Indore lost his favourite pencil, then got a gold star, then his best friend sat with someone else.
By evening he feels ‘bad’ but can’t say why. He throws his shoes.
His mother sits with a feelings chart. ‘Were you sad? Jealous? Proud?’
Aryan points: ‘Sad about the pencil, proud about the star, and jealous.’ Saying it makes him feel lighter.

steps.title: All feelings are okay
steps.body: Happy, sad, angry, scared, worried, excited, jealous, proud, lonely — **all feelings are okay**. Feelings are like weather: they come and go. What we **do** with feelings matters: hitting or breaking things is not okay, but talking, crying, drawing or moving is.

steps.title: Name it to tame it
steps.body: When you say the name of a feeling — ‘I feel angry’ — your brain calms down a little. Try: ‘I feel ___ because ___.’

steps.title: Feelings live in the body too
steps.body:
- Angry: hot face, tight fists
- Scared: fast heart, wobbly tummy
- Sad: heavy chest, tears
- Happy: light, bouncy

Noticing your body helps you know what you feel.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Draw a face for how you feel right now, then tell a grown-up about it.

quiz.q: Are all feelings okay?
quiz.why: Yes, all feelings are okay, including sad, angry and scared ones. What matters is what we do with them.

quiz.q: What helps calm a big feeling?
quiz.why: Saying the name of a feeling, like 'I feel angry', helps calm it. Hiding it forever or hitting does not help.

quiz.q: Hot face and tight fists often mean…
quiz.why: A hot face and tight fists often mean you are angry. Feelings show up in our bodies.

quiz.q: Is it okay to hit someone when angry?
options: No, but you can talk, draw or move
quiz.why: No, we do not hit when angry, because it hurts others. You can talk, draw or move your body instead.

lessons.title: The worry monster

scenes.text: Lily, 8, from Shimla gets a tummy-ache every Monday before school.
The doctor finds nothing wrong with her tummy. ‘I think it’s a worry tummy,’ he smiles.
At home she draws her ‘worry monster’ and gives it a silly name: Grumbleberry.
Every night she tells Dad what Grumbleberry said, and they decide together if it’s true.

steps.title: What worry is
steps.body: Worry is your brain trying to **protect** you by thinking about things that might go wrong. A little worry is helpful (like remembering your homework). Too much worry can make tummy-aches, headaches, trouble sleeping, or not wanting to go places.

steps.title: Worry tools
steps.body:
- **Draw** your worry monster and give it a funny name
- **Worry time:** 10 minutes each evening to tell a grown-up your worries, then put them in a ‘worry box’
- **Ask:** ‘Is this worry likely? What would I tell a friend?’
- **Brave steps:** do a tiny bit of the scary thing, then a little more

steps.title: Avoiding makes worry bigger
steps.body: If we always avoid what we’re scared of, the worry monster grows. Small brave steps make it shrink.

steps.title: For grown-ups
steps.body: Listen and say ‘That sounds hard’ before solving. Praise brave steps. If worries stop a child going to school, sleeping or playing for weeks, talk to a paediatrician or counsellor.

activity.prompt: Helpful or unhelpful for worry?

items.text: Telling a grown-up during worry time
Always avoiding the scary thing
Taking a small brave step
Keeping worries secret
Drawing your worry monster
Slow belly breathing

quiz.q: Worry is your brain trying to…
quiz.why: Worry is your brain trying to protect you, like an alarm. It does not want to hurt you.

quiz.q: Avoiding scary things always makes worry…
quiz.why: Avoiding scary things makes worry bigger, because the brain never learns that you are safe. Small brave steps help it shrink.

quiz.q: A worry tummy means…
options: Worry can make your tummy feel bad
quiz.why: A worry tummy means worry can make your tummy feel bad. Our body and feelings are linked, so a worried mind can give a tummy-ache.

quiz.q: A good worry tool is…
options: Hiding under the bed all day
quiz.why: A good worry tool is worry time with a grown-up, where you share your worries. Sharing makes worries feel smaller, but hiding or shouting does not.

lessons.title: My calm-down toolbox

scenes.text: Sameer, 6, from Mysuru gets so angry when he loses at Ludo that he flips the board.
