His teacher teaches ‘balloon breaths’: breathe in, fill your belly like a balloon, then let it out slowly.
Next game he loses, does 3 balloon breaths, and says ‘Good game’.
Everyone cheers — for the calm, not the game.

steps.title: Tools in my toolbox
steps.body:
- **Balloon breaths:** slow belly breathing
- **Count to 10** slowly
- **Move:** jump 10 times, stretch, run outside
- **Squeeze and let go:** squeeze fists tight, then relax
- **Calm corner:** a cushion, a book, a soft toy
- **Talk** to a grown-up

steps.title: Why breathing works
steps.body: Slow breathing out tells your body ‘I’m safe’. Your heart slows and your thinking brain switches back on.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Do 4 balloon breaths with the activity: in for 4, hold, out for 4.

steps.title: For grown-ups
steps.body: Practise tools when calm, so children can use them when upset. Model them yourself: ‘I’m frustrated, I’m going to take three breaths.’

activity.label: Balloon breaths: fill your belly (4), hold (2), let it out slowly (4), rest (2)

quiz.q: Balloon breaths are…
quiz.why: Balloon breaths are slow belly breathing, where your tummy fills up like a balloon. Slow breaths help the body calm down.

quiz.q: Breathing out slowly tells your body…
quiz.why: Breathing out slowly tells your body 'I'm safe'. That helps the alarm in your body calm down.

quiz.q: When is the best time to practise calm tools?
quiz.why: The best time to practise calm tools is when you are calm. Then they are easy to use later, when a big feeling comes.

quiz.q: Which is a calm-down tool?
quiz.why: Counting to 10 is a calm-down tool because it gives you time to settle. Shouting or flipping the board makes things worse.

lessons.title: Who can I tell?

scenes.text: Grace, 9, from Kohima has felt sad since her grandmother moved away. She doesn’t want to bother anyone.
Her teacher notices she’s quiet and asks gently, ‘How are you, really?’
Grace tells her. The teacher says, ‘Thank you for telling me. Let’s call Granny together on a video call this week.’
Grace learns telling someone makes sad feelings lighter.

steps.title: Telling helps
steps.body: When feelings are big or stay for a long time, **telling a grown-up** helps. You don’t have to fix it alone. Sharing a feeling makes it lighter.

steps.title: My helpers
steps.body: Parents, grandparents, teachers, the school counsellor, an aunt or uncle, a doctor. If you can’t talk to anyone, children in India can call **1098** (Childline) — free, any time.

steps.title: Words to start
steps.body:
- ‘Can I tell you something?’
- ‘I’ve been feeling sad/worried.’
- ‘I need help.’
- Or write a note.

steps.title: Tell straight away if…
steps.body: Someone is hurting you, you feel unsafe, or you have thoughts about hurting yourself. Tell a grown-up **today**, or call **1098** or **112**.

activity.prompt: Make my feelings helpers list:
items: Write the names of 3 grown-ups I can tell
Practise saying ‘Can I tell you something?’
Know that 1098 is Childline
Make a calm corner at home
Tell one helper how I feel this week

quiz.q: When feelings are big or last long, you can…
quiz.why: When feelings are big or last a long time, tell a grown-up you trust. Telling helps; hiding or keeping secrets does not.

quiz.q: Childline number?
quiz.why: Childline's number is 1098. Children can call it for help.

quiz.q: A good way to start is…
quiz.why: A good way to start is to say 'Can I tell you something?' It is a simple, calm way to begin telling a grown-up.

quiz.q: If you feel unsafe, tell someone…
quiz.why: If you feel unsafe, tell someone today. Telling right away keeps you safe.

questions.why: Yes, all feelings are okay, even sad or angry ones. What we do with them is what matters.
Name it to tame it. Saying the name of a feeling helps it feel smaller and calmer.
Childline is 1098. 100 is the police number.
A worry tummy means worry can cause tummy-aches. Our body and feelings are linked.
Balloon breaths are slow belly breathing. Fast breathing doesn't calm you down.
Avoiding fears makes worry bigger, because the brain never learns it is safe. Brave little steps make it smaller.
Hitting when angry is not okay, because it hurts others. Feelings are okay, but hurting is not.
Practise calm tools when you are calm. Then they are easy to use when big feelings come.

questions.q: If you feel unsafe, you tell…
questions.why: If you feel unsafe, tell a trusted grown-up today. Telling keeps you safe.

options: Doing a tiny bit of the scary thing
questions.why: A brave step is doing a tiny bit of the scary thing. Small steps make fear smaller, but avoiding it keeps fear big.

courses.title: Anxiety and panic: understand it, ride it, treat it
courses.summary: What anxiety is, how panic attacks work and how to ride them out, CBT-based tools, and what professional help is like in India.
outcomes: Learners can explain the alarm response and when anxiety becomes a disorder
Learners can manage a panic attack and know when to seek medical help
Learners can use thought records, worry time and grounding
Learners can navigate professional help and know their rights
courses.guardianNote: For ages 13+. Explains anxiety and panic attacks, grounding and breathing skills, and when and how to get professional help. Includes Tele-MANAS 14416. General education, not medical advice.

lessons.title: What anxiety is (and why it's not weakness)

scenes.text: Nisha, 16, from Hyderabad feels her heart race, hands sweat and mind go blank before every presentation.
She also lies awake worrying about marks, friends and the future.
She thinks something is wrong with her — that she’s ‘weak’.
A counsellor explains the body’s alarm system. ‘Your alarm is just a bit too sensitive right now. We can retrain it.’

steps.title: The body’s alarm system
steps.body:
Anxiety is the body’s **fight–flight–freeze** response. When the brain senses danger, it releases adrenaline: heart beats faster, breathing speeds up, muscles tense, digestion slows. This helped our ancestors escape tigers.

Today the alarm can go off for exams, social situations or ‘what ifs’ — real danger isn’t there, but the body reacts as if it were.

steps.title: Normal vs anxiety disorder
steps.body:
Everyone feels anxious sometimes. It may be an **anxiety disorder** when worry or fear is:
- **intense** and out of proportion
- **long-lasting** (most days for weeks or months)
- **interfering** with school, work, sleep or relationships
- leading to **avoidance**

WHO estimates around **300 million people** worldwide live with an anxiety disorder — among the most common mental health conditions. They are **very treatable**.

steps.title: Common types
steps.body:
- **Generalised anxiety:** constant worry about many things
- **Social anxiety:** intense fear of being judged
- **Panic disorder:** repeated panic attacks and fear of them
- **Phobias:** intense fear of specific things (heights, needles)
- **OCD** (related): unwanted thoughts and repetitive actions to reduce anxiety

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- ‘Just stop worrying’ — anxiety isn’t a choice
- Avoiding everything scary — avoidance **grows** anxiety over time
- Using alcohol, vaping or endless scrolling to cope
- Thinking it means you are weak — it’s a common health condition

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Notice your body’s alarm signs. Write: ‘When I’m anxious, my body…’ and ‘My thoughts say…’

statements.s: Anxiety is the body’s alarm (fight–flight–freeze) response.
statements.why: Adrenaline prepares the body for danger.

statements.s: Avoiding what scares you makes anxiety smaller over time.
Anxiety disorders are rare.
statements.why: They’re among the most common mental health conditions.

statements.s: Anxiety disorders are treatable.
statements.why: Therapy such as CBT and sometimes medicines help.

statements.s: Feeling some anxiety before an exam is normal.
statements.why: A little anxiety can even sharpen focus.

quiz.q: Which hormone drives the alarm response?
quiz.why: Adrenaline is the hormone that drives the body's alarm (fight–flight–freeze) response. Insulin, oestrogen and melatonin do other jobs.

quiz.q: When might anxiety be a disorder?
options: Intense, long-lasting and interfering with life
quiz.why: Anxiety may be a disorder when it is intense, long-lasting and interferes with daily life. Feeling nervous once before an exam is normal.

quiz.q: Fear of being judged in social situations is…
quiz.why: A fear of being judged in social situations is social anxiety. A phobia of spiders, depression and grief are different.

quiz.q: Avoidance tends to…
quiz.why: Avoidance gives short-term relief but keeps anxiety going, because you never learn that you can cope. Facing fears step by step helps.

quiz.q: Is anxiety a sign of weakness?
options: No — it’s a common, treatable health condition
quiz.why: No, anxiety is not weakness. It is a common, treatable health condition that can affect anyone.

lessons.title: Panic attacks: what happens and how to ride them out

scenes.text: Kunal, 22, on the Delhi Metro suddenly feels his heart pounding, chest tight, can’t breathe, dizzy. He thinks he’s having a heart attack.
At the hospital, tests are normal. The doctor says: ‘That was a panic attack.’
Kunal starts avoiding the metro, scared it will happen again.
With a psychologist, he learns what panic is and slowly returns to the metro. The attacks fade.

steps.title: What a panic attack is
steps.body:
A **panic attack** is a sudden surge of intense fear with strong body symptoms: racing heart, chest tightness, breathlessness, dizziness, shaking, sweating, tingling, feeling unreal, or fear of dying or ‘going crazy’. It usually **peaks within about 10 minutes** and then fades.

Panic attacks are **very frightening but not dangerous** in themselves.

steps.title: First time? Get checked
steps.body: Because symptoms can look like heart or breathing problems, if it’s your **first** episode, or symptoms are different from usual, or you have heart risk factors — **get medical help (112)**. Once a doctor has confirmed panic, you can use the tools below.

steps.title: Riding the wave
steps.body:
1. **Name it:** ‘This is panic. It’s uncomfortable, not dangerous. It will pass.’
2. **Slow your breath out:** breathe in for 4, out for 6–8
3. **Ground yourself** (5-4-3-2-1): 5 things you see, 4 you feel, 3 you hear, 2 you smell, 1 you taste
4. **Don’t fight it or run** — let it rise and fall
5. Stay where you are if safe; afterwards, praise yourself

steps.title: The panic cycle
steps.body: Body sensation → scary thought (‘I’m dying’) → more adrenaline → stronger sensation. Breaking the scary thought with facts breaks the cycle. **Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)** is highly effective for panic disorder.

steps.title: Worked example: Kunal’s plan
steps.body: Week 1: stand on the platform for 5 minutes. Week 2: ride one stop with a friend. Week 3: ride two stops alone. Week 4: full commute. Each step, he lets anxiety rise and fall without leaving. This is **graded exposure**.

activity.label: Long out-breath for panic: in 4, out slowly 7, rest 1

quiz.q: A panic attack typically peaks within about…
quiz.why: A panic attack typically peaks within about 10 minutes and then fades. It does not last for hours or days.

quiz.q: Are panic attacks dangerous in themselves?
quiz.why: Panic attacks are frightening but not dangerous in themselves. They don't cause heart attacks or damage the brain.

quiz.q: First-ever episode of chest pain and breathlessness. You should…
options: Get medical help to rule out other causes
quiz.why: A first episode of chest pain and breathlessness should be checked by a doctor to rule out medical causes. Don't just assume it is panic.
5-4-3-2-1 is a grounding technique that uses your senses (see 5, touch 4, hear 3, smell 2, taste 1) to bring you back to the present.

quiz.q: Graded exposure means…
options: Facing the hardest fear first without support
quiz.why: Graded exposure means facing fears in small steps, from easier to harder. Jumping to the hardest fear without support often backfires.

lessons.title: Everyday tools: thoughts, worry time and grounding

scenes.text: Ayesha, 19, from Lucknow constantly thinks ‘What if I fail? What if my friends hate me? What if something happens to Ammi?’
Her counsellor shows her a thought record and suggests ‘worry time’.
Each evening at 7 pm she writes worries for 15 minutes, then does something else.
After three weeks, the worries feel smaller and less sticky.

steps.title: Thinking traps
steps.body:
Anxious minds fall into traps:
- **Catastrophising:** jumping to the worst case
- **Mind-reading:** ‘They think I’m stupid’
- **Fortune-telling:** ‘I’ll definitely fail’
- **All-or-nothing:** ‘If it’s not perfect it’s a disaster’
- **Should statements:** ‘I should never be nervous’

steps.title: Worked example: a thought record
steps.body:
**Situation:** friend didn’t reply for 5 hours.
**Thought:** ‘She’s angry with me.’ (mind-reading)
**Evidence for:** none really.
**Evidence against:** she said she had exams; she was friendly yesterday.
**Balanced thought:** ‘She’s probably busy. I can check in tomorrow.’
**Anxiety before 80%, after 30%.**

steps.title: Worry time
steps.body: Pick 15 minutes a day. When worries pop up at other times, jot them down: ‘Later.’ At worry time, look at them: Can I do something? → plan a step. Can’t control it? → practise letting go. Most worries shrink when postponed.

steps.title: Grounding and body tools
steps.body:
- 5-4-3-2-1 senses
- Feet on the floor, notice the ground
- Cold water on face or hands
- Progressive muscle relaxation: tense each muscle group for 5 seconds, release
- Regular exercise — one of the best long-term anxiety reducers

steps.title: When to get professional help
steps.body: If anxiety is affecting study, work, sleep or relationships for weeks, see a counsellor, psychologist or psychiatrist. **CBT** is a first-line treatment; some people also benefit from medicines prescribed by a psychiatrist. **Talk to someone today.** Tele-MANAS **14416** (or 1-800-891-4416) is free, confidential and 24×7 in many Indian languages. In immediate danger call **112**. Under 18: **1098**.

activity.prompt: Match each thinking trap to an example:
pairs: ‘If I get a B, my whole life is ruined.’

quiz.q: ‘They think I’m stupid’ (without evidence) is…
quiz.why: 'They think I'm stupid' without evidence is mind-reading, a thinking trap of assuming what others think. Balanced thinking would look at the evidence.

quiz.q: Worry time works by…
options: Postponing worries to a set time and then problem-solving or letting go
quiz.why: Worry time postpones worries to a set time, then you problem-solve or let them go. That contains worry instead of letting it run all day.

quiz.q: First-line therapy for anxiety disorders?
quiz.why: CBT (cognitive behavioural therapy) is the first-line therapy for anxiety disorders. Ignoring it or using energy drinks doesn't treat it.

quiz.q: Which is a long-term anxiety reducer?
quiz.why: Regular exercise reduces anxiety in the long term. Caffeine can raise it, and alcohol and avoidance keep it going.

quiz.q: A balanced thought is…
quiz.why: 'She's probably busy; I'll check tomorrow' is a balanced thought because it considers other likely explanations. 'She hates me' and 'I'm doomed' jump to worst-case.

lessons.title: Getting help: what therapy and treatment are like

scenes.text: Rajiv, 35, an engineer in Pune, has had constant anxiety for a year. He fears that seeing a psychiatrist means he’s ‘mad’.
He calls Tele-MANAS 14416 first. The counsellor explains options and refers him.
His psychologist explains CBT. His psychiatrist explains medicine options, side effects and that they aren’t addictive in the way he feared.
Six months later, Rajiv says: ‘I wish I had gone years ago.’

steps.title: Who does what
steps.body:
- **Counsellor:** listening, support, problem-solving
- **Clinical psychologist:** assessment and talking therapies like CBT
- **Psychiatrist:** a medical doctor who diagnoses and can prescribe medicines
- **Family doctor:** a good first step, can refer you

In India: **Tele-MANAS 14416**, district mental health programmes at government hospitals, medical college psychiatry departments, NIMHANS (Bengaluru) and private practitioners.

steps.title: About medicines
steps.body: Some anxiety and depression medicines (like SSRIs) take **2–6 weeks** to work. They’re not ‘happy pills’ and don’t change your personality. **Never stop suddenly** — talk to your doctor. Some sedative medicines (benzodiazepines) can be habit-forming and are usually for short-term use only under supervision.

steps.title: What the first session is like
steps.body: You’ll talk about what’s been happening, your history, sleep, work/study and goals. You can ask: ‘What approach do you use? How many sessions? Is this confidential?’ It’s okay to try a different therapist if it doesn’t feel right.

steps.title: Your rights
steps.body: India’s **Mental Healthcare Act, 2017** gives every person the right to access mental health care, to confidentiality, to be treated with dignity, and to make an **advance directive** about future treatment.

steps.title: Avoid
steps.body: Unqualified ‘healers’ promising instant cures, self-medicating with sleeping pills, and stopping prescribed medicines without advice.

activity.prompt: Questions people hesitate to ask about therapy

items.q: Does seeing a psychiatrist mean I’m ‘mad’?
items.a: No. Psychiatrists treat common conditions like anxiety, depression and sleep problems every day — just as other doctors treat diabetes or asthma.

items.q: Will my employer or college find out?
items.a: Mental health records are confidential under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, except in limited situations such as serious risk.

items.q: Are antidepressants addictive?
items.a: SSRIs are not addictive in the way alcohol or nicotine are, but stopping suddenly can cause discontinuation symptoms — so reduce only with your doctor.

items.q: How long does therapy take?
items.a: CBT for anxiety often involves around 8–20 sessions, but it varies.

items.q: What if I can’t afford it?
items.a: Tele-MANAS 14416 is free; government hospitals and medical colleges offer low-cost or free care.

quiz.q: Who can prescribe medicines?
quiz.why: Only a psychiatrist, a medical doctor, can prescribe medicines. Counsellors and coaches can't prescribe.

quiz.q: SSRIs usually take how long to work?
quiz.why: SSRIs usually take about 2–6 weeks to work, so patience matters. They don't work in minutes.

quiz.q: Should you stop medicine suddenly when feeling better?
quiz.why: No, don't stop medicine suddenly, even when feeling better. Talk to your doctor, who can reduce it safely.

quiz.q: Which Act protects mental health rights in India?
quiz.why: The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 protects the rights of people with mental illness in India. The IT, POSH and RTI Acts cover other matters.

quiz.q: Free 24×7 mental-health helpline?
quiz.why: Tele-MANAS, 14416, is the free 24×7 mental-health helpline. 181 is the Women's Helpline, 1930 cybercrime and 1098 Childline.

questions.why: Anxiety is the body's alarm response (fight–flight–freeze). It is meant to protect us.
Tele-MANAS is the free mental-health helpline, 14416. 1930 is for cybercrime.
Panic attacks usually peak within about 10 minutes and then fade. They don't last for hours.
5-4-3-2-1 uses the senses to ground you in the present. It is not a maths trick.
Avoidance tends to keep anxiety going, since you never learn you can cope. It doesn't cure it.
Mind-reading is assuming what others think without evidence. It is a thinking trap, not telepathy.

questions.q: First panic-like episode with chest pain?
questions.why: A first panic-like episode with chest pain needs a medical check to rule out other causes. Don't ignore it.

options: Psychiatrist is a medical doctor who can prescribe
questions.why: A psychiatrist is a medical doctor who can prescribe medicines. A psychologist is trained in therapy but doesn't prescribe, so they are different roles.
Graded exposure means taking small steps toward feared situations. It works better than avoiding forever.
SSRIs typically work after about 2–6 weeks, not in an hour.
Benzodiazepines can be habit-forming, so they should be used short-term and under supervision. They are medicines, not vitamins.

options: It postpones and contains worry, then problem-solves
questions.why: Worry time helps because it postpones and contains worry, and you then problem-solve it. It doesn't increase worry.
The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 allows advance directives about future treatment. It is rights-based and doesn't allow forced treatment always.

questions.q: The panic cycle is broken by…
options: Reinterpreting sensations as uncomfortable-not-dangerous and not fleeing
questions.why: The panic cycle is broken by seeing the sensations as uncomfortable but not dangerous and by not fleeing. Running away keeps the fear going.

courses.title: Depression and grief: understanding, healing and helping
courses.summary: What depression really is, self-help and treatments, how grief works, and how to support someone who is struggling.
outcomes: Learners can recognise signs of depression and when to seek help
Learners can use behavioural activation and know treatment options
Learners can understand grief as waves and support grieving people
Learners can support a friend, including asking about suicide and connecting to help
courses.guardianNote: For ages 15+. Explains depression and grief, self-help, treatment options and how to support a friend. Includes Tele-MANAS 14416 and 112. Written following safe-messaging guidance.

lessons.title: Depression: more than sadness

scenes.text: Arnav, 17, from Guwahati loved football. Over two months he stops going, sleeps till noon, and says ‘nothing matters’.
His marks drop. He snaps at his family and stays in his room.
His parents think he’s lazy. His older cousin recognises the signs and gently says, ‘I think you might be depressed. Can we see someone?’
With therapy and support, Arnav slowly returns to the field.

steps.title: What depression is
steps.body:
Depression is a common health condition, not laziness or weakness. WHO estimates it affects around **280 million people** worldwide. It may be depression when for **at least two weeks** you have, most of the day, nearly every day:
- low, sad, empty or irritable mood, **and/or**
- loss of interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy

plus others like: sleep changes, appetite or weight changes, tiredness, slowed or restless body, poor concentration, feeling worthless or guilty, or thoughts of death or suicide.

steps.title: It can look different in teens and men
steps.body: Teens may seem **irritable or angry** rather than sad. Men may show anger, risk-taking, overworking or drinking. Physical complaints — headaches, body aches, stomach problems — are common in India and can hide depression.

steps.title: Worked example: sadness or depression?
steps.body:
- Priya felt sad for 3 days after a bad exam, then recovered. → **Normal sadness**
- Arnav has lost interest, slept 12+ hours, felt worthless for 2 months and stopped football. → **Possible depression — see a professional**

steps.title: Myths
steps.body:
- ‘Just think positive’ — depression isn’t a choice
- ‘Only weak people get it’ — anyone can
- ‘Talking makes it worse’ — talking helps
- ‘Medicines change your personality’ — prescribed properly, they help you feel more like yourself

steps.title: If you’re having thoughts of death
steps.body: Thoughts of suicide are a symptom of depression, and they can pass with help. **Talk to someone today.** Tele-MANAS **14416** (or 1-800-891-4416) is free, confidential and 24×7 in many Indian languages. In immediate danger call **112**. Under 18: **1098**.

activity.prompt: Normal low patch or possible depression (see a professional)?

items.text: Sad for two days after losing a match
No interest in anything for 3 weeks, sleeping all day, feeling worthless
Disappointed after a breakup but still seeing friends
Constant irritability, stopped eating properly, marks falling for a month
Missing home in the first week at college

quiz.q: How long do symptoms usually last for depression to be considered?
quiz.why: Depression is considered when symptoms last at least 2 weeks. A day or hours of low mood is usually normal.

quiz.q: Depression in teens may look like…
quiz.why: Depression in teens may look like irritability or anger, not only sadness. So it can be missed.

quiz.q: Is depression laziness?
quiz.why: No, depression is a real health condition, not laziness. It affects energy, mood and thinking.

quiz.q: Roughly how many people have depression worldwide (WHO)?
quiz.why: WHO estimates around 280 million people have depression worldwide. It is very common.

quiz.q: Thoughts of suicide are…
options: A symptom that can pass with help — talk to someone today
quiz.why: Thoughts of suicide are a symptom that can pass with help, so talk to someone today (Tele-MANAS 14416, or 112 in an emergency). They are not permanent or attention-seeking.

lessons.title: Helping yourself and getting treatment

scenes.text: Shreya, 24, a nurse in Kochi, has been feeling flat and exhausted for months.
Her psychiatrist diagnoses moderate depression and suggests therapy plus a medicine.
Her psychologist also suggests ‘behavioural activation’: small daily actions even when she doesn’t feel like it.
A 10-minute morning walk, one call to a friend, cooking one meal. Week by week, energy returns.

steps.title: Behavioural activation
steps.body:
Depression says ‘wait till you feel like it’. But **action often comes before motivation**. Plan small, doable activities:
- **Pleasure:** music, a favourite snack, sunlight
- **Achievement:** a small task, like washing dishes
- **Connection:** message a friend

Rate your mood before and after. Small steps add up.

steps.title: Treatments that work
steps.body:
- **Talking therapies:** CBT, interpersonal therapy, behavioural activation
- **Medicines:** antidepressants prescribed by a doctor, usually for moderate–severe depression; they take weeks to work and should be stopped only with medical advice
- **Exercise:** regular physical activity helps mild–moderate depression
- **Sleep routine, daylight, balanced food, less alcohol**
- For severe depression, specialist care, sometimes in hospital

steps.title: Daily anchors
steps.body: Get up at a fixed time, open curtains, get morning light, eat something, move for 10 minutes, connect with one person. Reduce alcohol — it worsens mood.

steps.title: Worked example: an activity plan
steps.body:
Mon: 10-min walk (pleasure), reply to one email (achievement)
Tue: call Ma (connection), shower and dress (achievement)
Wed: music while cooking (pleasure)

Mood before 3/10 → after 5/10.

steps.title: Crisis
steps.body: **Talk to someone today.** Tele-MANAS **14416** (or 1-800-891-4416) is free, confidential and 24×7 in many Indian languages. In immediate danger call **112**. Under 18: **1098**.

activity.prompt: This week’s small-steps plan:
items: Get up at the same time each day
Get 10 minutes of morning light
Move my body for 10 minutes
Do one small achievement task daily
Contact one person each day
Cut down alcohol
Book a talk with a doctor/counsellor or call 14416

quiz.q: Behavioural activation means…
options: Doing small planned activities even before motivation returns
quiz.why: Behavioural activation means doing small planned activities even before motivation returns. Action often comes first and motivation follows.

quiz.q: Antidepressants should be stopped…
quiz.why: Antidepressants should only be stopped with medical advice, since stopping suddenly can cause problems. A doctor can taper them safely.

quiz.q: Alcohol’s effect on depression?
quiz.why: Alcohol worsens mood, because it is a depressant. It doesn't treat depression.

quiz.q: Which helps mild–moderate depression?
quiz.why: Regular exercise helps mild to moderate depression and is evidence-based. Staying in bed, isolating and skipping meals make it worse.

quiz.q: A daily anchor is…
options: Fixed wake-up time and morning light
quiz.why: A fixed wake-up time and morning light act as a daily anchor that helps the body clock and mood. Random sleep and night scrolling disturb it.

lessons.title: Grief: when someone dies or something is lost

scenes.text: Mrs. Annamma Thomas, 63, from Kottayam loses her husband of 40 years.
After the funeral, visitors leave. She can’t sleep, forgets to eat, and sometimes ‘hears’ him in the kitchen.
Her son Jacob, in Dubai, worries she is ‘going mad’.
A grief counsellor explains these are normal grief reactions. With her prayer group, daily calls with Jacob and time, the pain softens.

steps.title: Grief is love with nowhere to go
steps.body: Grief is the natural response to loss — of a person, a pet, a relationship, health, a home or a dream. It can include sadness, numbness, anger, guilt, relief, longing, poor sleep, appetite changes, trouble concentrating, and even sensing the person nearby. **All can be normal.**

steps.title: Grief isn’t neat stages
steps.body: The famous ‘five stages’ (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance) aren’t a fixed sequence. Grief comes in **waves** — people move back and forth between grieving and getting on with life. Over time the waves usually become less frequent, though anniversaries and festivals can bring them back.

steps.title: What helps
steps.body:
- Let yourself feel; cry if you need
- Keep basic routines: eat, sleep, move
- Talk about the person; share stories and photos
- Rituals and faith practices if meaningful
- Accept help with practical tasks
- Be gentle with yourself on difficult days

steps.title: Worked example: supporting someone grieving
steps.body:
Helpful: ‘I’m so sorry. I’m here.’ ‘Tell me about him.’ Dropping off food. Checking in weeks later.

Unhelpful: ‘Everything happens for a reason.’ ‘At least he lived long.’ ‘Be strong.’ Avoiding them.

steps.title: When grief needs extra help
steps.body: Seek help if, after many months, grief is still so intense it stops daily life, if you feel life has no meaning, use alcohol to cope, or have thoughts of joining the person or ending your life. ICD-11 recognises **prolonged grief disorder**, which is treatable. **Talk to someone today.** Tele-MANAS **14416** (or 1-800-891-4416) is free, confidential and 24×7 in many Indian languages. In immediate danger call **112**. Under 18: **1098**.

steps.title: Children and grief
steps.body: Use clear words (‘died’, not ‘gone to sleep’, which can frighten children). Let them ask questions, include them in rituals if they wish, and keep routines.

activity.prompt: Questions people ask about grief

items.q: I sometimes feel relief after a long illness. Am I a bad person?
items.a: No. Relief that someone’s suffering has ended, or that caregiving stress is over, is very common and doesn’t mean you loved them less.

items.q: I feel guilty — I should have done more.
items.a: Guilt is a common grief reaction. Talking it through with someone often helps you see you did what you could with what you knew.

items.q: Is it normal to sense or hear the person?
items.a: Yes — many bereaved people briefly sense, see or hear their loved one. It’s a common part of grief.

items.q: How long will this last?
items.a: There’s no timetable. For many, the intensity eases over months, while love and memories remain.

items.q: How do I explain death to a 5-year-old?
items.a: Use simple, true words: ‘Grandpa died. His body stopped working and he can’t come back. We are sad and we will remember him.’

quiz.q: Are the five stages of grief a fixed sequence?
quiz.why: No, the five stages of grief are not a fixed sequence. Grief comes in waves, and people experience it differently.

quiz.q: Sensing a dead loved one nearby is…
quiz.why: Sensing a dead loved one nearby is a common grief experience. It isn't a sign of madness.

quiz.q: A helpful thing to say to someone grieving?
quiz.why: 'I'm so sorry. I'm here.' offers simple presence. Phrases like 'Everything happens for a reason' or 'At least…' can minimise their pain.

quiz.q: With children, say…
quiz.why: With children, use simple, true words like 'Grandpa died'. 'Went to sleep' or 'on holiday' can confuse or frighten them.

quiz.q: When should grief prompt extra help?
options: Months of intense grief stopping daily life, or thoughts of ending your life
quiz.why: Months of intense grief that stops daily life, or thoughts of ending your life, call for extra help. Crying at a funeral or missing someone on their birthday is normal.

lessons.title: Supporting a friend or family member who is struggling

scenes.text: Zara, 18, notices her friend Meghna hasn’t posted in weeks, cancels plans and seems flat on calls.
She’s scared of saying the wrong thing.
She invites Meghna for chai and says, ‘I’ve noticed you seem down. I’m here — want to talk?’
Meghna opens up. Zara helps her book a counselling appointment and checks in weekly.

steps.title: Notice and ask
steps.body: Signs someone may be struggling: withdrawing, changes in sleep or eating, losing interest, irritability, talking about being a burden or hopeless, drinking more. **Ask:** ‘I’ve noticed… How are you really doing?’ Ask twice — people often say ‘fine’ the first time.

steps.title: Listen well
steps.body:
- Give full attention; put the phone away
- Don’t rush to fix or compare
- Reflect: ‘That sounds really heavy.’
- Avoid: ‘Others have it worse’, ‘Just be positive’
- Ask: ‘What would help right now?’

steps.title: Encourage help
steps.body: Offer to help find a counsellor, sit with them while they call **Tele-MANAS 14416**, or go with them to an appointment. Keep checking in.

steps.title: If they mention suicide
steps.body: Take it seriously. **Ask directly**: ‘Are you thinking about suicide?’ Asking does **not** put the idea in their head. Stay with them, remove access to anything they could use to harm themselves if safe to do so, and get help now: **14416**, **112**, or take them to an emergency department.

steps.title: Look after yourself too
steps.body: Supporting someone is draining. Share the load with other people, set limits, and get support yourself.

a.text: Your friend says ‘I’m fine’ but has seemed flat for weeks.

choices.label: ‘I’m asking again because I care — how are you really?’
choices.feedback: Asking twice opens the door.

choices.label: ‘Okay, cool’ and change the subject
choices.feedback: A missed chance — but you can try again.

b.text: They say, ‘Honestly, I feel like a burden. Everyone would be better off without me.’

choices.label: ‘Thank you for telling me. Are you thinking about suicide?’
choices.feedback: Asking directly is caring and safe.

choices.label: ‘Don’t say that, you have so much to live for!’
choices.feedback: Well-meant, but it can shut them down. Ask and listen first.

c.text: A few days later they post something worrying.

choices.label: Message: ‘I’m worried about you. Can we talk today?’
choices.feedback: Reaching out again matters.

d.text: They say they’ve had thoughts but no plan. They’re scared.

choices.label: Stay with them and call Tele-MANAS 14416 together, and tell a trusted adult
choices.feedback: Connecting to help now is the right step.

choices.label: Promise to keep it a secret
choices.feedback: Safety comes before secrecy.

choices.label: ‘I’m sorry — I want to understand. I’m here. Let’s get some help together.’
choices.feedback: Repair and refocus on help.

end1.text: The counsellor helps them make a safety plan and arrange follow-up. You stay connected and look after yourself too.

quiz.q: Your friend says ‘fine’. Good next step?
quiz.why: If a friend says 'fine' but seems low, ask again and show you care. People often need a second invitation to open up.

quiz.q: Does asking about suicide put the idea in someone’s head?
options: No — it opens a door to help
quiz.why: No, asking about suicide does not put the idea in someone's head. It opens a door to help and relief.

quiz.q: Which is good listening?
quiz.why: 'That sounds really heavy' reflects their feelings, which is good listening. Changing the subject or 'Others have it worse' dismisses them.

quiz.q: If a friend has suicidal thoughts, you should…
options: Stay with them and connect them to help (14416/112)
quiz.why: If a friend has suicidal thoughts, stay with them and connect them to help (14416 or 112). Keeping it secret or leaving them alone is unsafe.

quiz.q: Why look after yourself too?
quiz.why: Looking after yourself matters because supporting others can be draining. You help best when you stay well.

questions.why: Depression symptoms last at least 2 weeks. A few hours of low mood is not depression.
Tele-MANAS, the mental-health helpline, is 14416. 1098 is Childline.
The stages of grief are not a fixed sequence. Grief comes in waves.
Behavioural activation is doing small activities before motivation returns. Waiting for motivation often keeps you stuck.
Asking 'Are you thinking about suicide?' is safe and helpful. It doesn't plant the idea.
With young children, say 'died'. 'Went to sleep' can cause fear of sleeping.
Teen depression may show as irritability, not just tears. So watch for mood changes.
Alcohol worsens mood in depression, because it is a depressant. It does not help.
'Everything happens for a reason' minimises the pain of grief. 'I'm here' is supportive.

options: Take weeks and are stopped only with advice
questions.why: Antidepressants take weeks to work and should be stopped only with medical advice. They do not work instantly.
ICD-11 recognises prolonged grief disorder, a treatable condition. Grief is not weakness.

questions.q: A friend has thoughts of suicide. Best?
options: Stay, connect to help (14416/112), tell a trusted adult
questions.why: Stay with them, connect them to help (14416 or 112) and tell a trusted adult. Promising secrecy puts them at risk.
Physical complaints, like aches or tiredness, can hide depression and are common, especially in India. So depression may be overlooked.

courses.title: Self-harm and suicidal thoughts: you are not alone
courses.summary: A hope-focused, safe-messaging course: getting through suicidal thoughts today, understanding self-harm, helping someone at risk, and building reasons for living. Always: talk to someone today — Tele-MANAS 14416, 112.
outcomes: Learners can take immediate steps to stay safe and contact help (14416, 112, 1098)
Learners can make a personal safety plan
Learners can understand self-harm and use safer coping strategies
Learners can help someone at risk using Ask–Listen–Stay–Connect
Learners can build a hope box
courses.guardianNote: For ages 14+. A careful, hope-focused course on self-harm and suicidal thoughts, following WHO safe-messaging guidance: no methods are described. Teaches that these feelings can pass and help works, how to talk to someone today (Tele-MANAS 14416, 112, 1098), how to make a safety plan, and how to help a friend by asking directly, listening and getting help. Strongly recommended that a trusted adult knows the learner is taking it.

lessons.title: If you're having thoughts of ending your life

scenes.text: Rohit, 20, an engineering student in Kota, can’t sleep. After failing an exam, he feels everyone would be better off without him.
He remembers a poster in his hostel: ‘Tele-MANAS 14416 — talk to someone today.’
At 3 a.m., with shaking hands, he calls. A counsellor listens without judging.
They make a plan to get through the night and see the campus counsellor in the morning. Rohit is still here — and months later, he says the feeling did pass.

steps.title: You are not alone, and this can pass
steps.body: Thoughts of ending your life usually come from **unbearable pain**, not from truly wanting to die. Pain makes it hard to see other options — but those feelings **can change**, and many people who once felt this way go on to live full lives. **Talk to someone today.** Tele-MANAS **14416** (or 1-800-891-4416) is free, confidential and 24×7 in many Indian languages. In immediate danger call **112**. Under 18: **1098**.

steps.title: Getting through right now
steps.body:
- **Tell someone now** — call **14416**, a friend, family member, or **112**
- **Put distance** between yourself and anything you could use to hurt yourself; ask someone to hold onto it
- **Go somewhere safer** — a room with other people, a friend’s place, an emergency department
- **Avoid alcohol and drugs** — they make impulses stronger
- **Just get through the next hour.** Feelings at their peak do fade

steps.title: Make a safety plan
steps.body:
A safety plan is a short written list you make (ideally with a counsellor) for hard moments:
1. My warning signs
2. Things I can do on my own to cope (music, walk, shower)
3. People and places that distract me
4. People I can ask for help (names and numbers)
5. Professionals and helplines (14416, 112)
6. How I’ll make my surroundings safer
7. My reasons for living

steps.title: Why it happens
steps.body: Common contributors include depression and other mental health conditions, exam or work pressure, relationship breakups, bullying, abuse, loneliness, money problems, discrimination, and alcohol or drug use. These are things that **help can address**.

steps.title: You will be cared for, not punished
steps.body: India’s **Mental Healthcare Act, 2017** presumes that a person who attempts suicide is under severe stress and directs the government to provide care, treatment and rehabilitation. Reaching out is safe.

activity.prompt: Build your safety plan — arrange these steps in the usual order of use:
items: Notice my warning signs
Use my own coping activities
Go to people or places that distract me
Ask a trusted person for help
Contact professionals or helplines (14416 / 112)
Make my surroundings safer

quiz.q: Thoughts of ending one’s life usually come from…
options: Unbearable pain that can change with help
quiz.why: Thoughts of ending one's life usually come from unbearable pain, and they can change with help. They are not weakness or just attention-seeking.

quiz.q: Tele-MANAS number?
quiz.why: Tele-MANAS, the free 24×7 mental-health helpline, is 14416. 181 is the Women's Helpline, 1930 cybercrime and 101 fire.

quiz.q: Which makes impulses stronger?
quiz.why: Alcohol and drugs make impulses stronger and lower control. Calling 14416, talking to a friend or going to a safe place helps.

quiz.q: A safety plan includes…
options: Warning signs, coping steps, people and helplines, reasons for living
quiz.why: A safety plan lists warning signs, coping steps, people and helplines, and reasons for living. It gives you steps to follow in a crisis.

quiz.q: Under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, a person who attempts suicide…
options: Is presumed under severe stress and should receive care
quiz.why: Under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, a person who attempts suicide is presumed to be under severe stress and should receive care, not punishment.

lessons.title: Understanding self-harm

scenes.text: Tanya, 15, from Delhi wears long sleeves even in May. She hurts herself when feelings become overwhelming.
She feels ashamed and thinks no one would understand.
When her PE teacher notices, she doesn’t shout — she asks gently if Tanya is okay and takes her to the school counsellor.
With support, Tanya learns other ways to cope. It takes time, and some setbacks, but she gets better.

steps.title: What self-harm is
steps.body: Self-harm means hurting yourself on purpose as a way of coping with very painful feelings — like anger, sadness, numbness or overwhelm. It’s more common than many think, especially among teens and young adults. It’s usually **not** about attention and **not** always about wanting to die — but it is a sign of distress that deserves care, and it can be linked to higher risk later, so support matters.

steps.title: Safety first
steps.body: If you have hurt yourself, get **medical care** for any injury — a doctor or nurse will help, not judge. If an injury is serious, call **112**.

steps.title: Other ways to get through the urge
steps.body:
Urges often peak and fade within minutes. Try:
- Delay: ‘I’ll wait 15 minutes’ — then 15 more
- Intense but safe sensations: hold something cold, take a cold shower
- Release: tear paper, scribble hard, punch a pillow, run, dance
- Soothe: wrap in a blanket, calming music, a pet
- Connect: message someone, call **14416**

The goal is to get through the moment while you work on the bigger feelings with support.

steps.title: Recovery is possible
steps.body: Therapies like CBT and DBT (dialectical behaviour therapy) help people find new ways to cope. Recovery often has ups and downs — a setback doesn’t mean failure.

steps.title: If a friend self-harms
steps.body: Stay calm, don’t show disgust or anger, don’t demand they stop immediately. Say: ‘I care about you. Can I help you talk to someone?’ Encourage a trusted adult, counsellor or doctor. You don’t have to keep it secret if they’re at risk — tell a trusted adult.

statements.s: Self-harm is always just for attention.
statements.why: Usually a way of coping with overwhelming feelings.

statements.s: Urges to self-harm often peak and fade within minutes.
A setback in recovery means failure.
Doctors will help, not judge, if you need care for an injury.
If a friend self-harms, reacting with anger helps them stop.

quiz.q: Self-harm is usually…
options: A way to cope with painful feelings
quiz.why: Self-harm is usually a way to cope with painful feelings. It is not just a trend, fun or attention-seeking, and the person needs support.

quiz.q: A safe alternative to get through an urge?
options: Holding something cold or tearing paper
quiz.why: Holding something cold or tearing paper gives safe sensations and release when an urge comes. Alcohol or hiding alone increases risk.

quiz.q: Which therapy is known to help?
quiz.why: DBT (dialectical behaviour therapy) is known to help people who self-harm. Isolation and shouting therapy do not.

quiz.q: If a friend self-harms, you should…
options: Stay calm, show care and encourage help
quiz.why: If a friend self-harms, stay calm, show care and encourage them to get help. Showing disgust, ignoring or posting about it hurts.

quiz.q: If an injury is serious…
quiz.why: If an injury is serious, call 112 for emergency care. Waiting or hiding it can be dangerous.

lessons.title: How to help someone who may be suicidal

scenes.text: Coach Ibrahim in Bhopal notices his athlete, Kiran, 19, has stopped training, gave away his favourite boots, and said ‘it won’t matter soon’.
Ibrahim worries he might make it worse by asking.
He takes Kiran aside: ‘I’ve noticed some things and I’m worried. Are you thinking about suicide?’ Kiran nods and breaks down.
Ibrahim stays with him, calls Tele-MANAS, and takes him to the hospital. Kiran gets help in time.

steps.title: Warning signs
steps.body:
- Talking about wanting to die, being a burden, or having no reason to live
- Saying goodbye, giving away belongings
- Withdrawing from people and activities
- Sudden calm after a period of deep depression
- Increased alcohol or drug use
- Extreme mood swings, reckless behaviour

If you see these, act.

steps.title: ASK – LISTEN – STAY – CONNECT
steps.body:
- **Ask directly:** ‘Are you thinking about suicide?’ Research shows asking does not increase risk.
- **Listen** without judging, arguing or lecturing
- **Stay** with them if they’re in immediate danger; help make the surroundings safer
- **Connect** to help now: **14416**, **112**, emergency department, a trusted adult or doctor
- **Follow up** in the days after

steps.title: Worked example: words that help
steps.body:
‘I’m really glad you told me.’
‘You don’t have to go through this alone.’
‘Let’s call someone together right now.’

Avoid: ‘You’re being selfish’, ‘Don’t be silly’, or promising secrecy.

steps.title: Safe talking online
steps.body: Don’t share details of methods or graphic stories. Share help numbers and messages of hope. If you see a worrying post, reach out privately and report it to the platform, which can connect the person to support.

steps.title: After helping
steps.body: It’s normal to feel shaken. Talk to someone about it yourself — you can call **14416** too.

a.text: A classmate posts: ‘I’m done. Goodbye everyone.’

choices.label: Message them privately now: ‘I saw your post and I’m worried. Are you thinking about suicide? I’m here.’
choices.feedback: Reaching out directly and quickly is right.

choices.label: Assume they’re joking and scroll on
choices.feedback: Always take such messages seriously.

b.text: They reply: ‘Yes. I can’t do this any more.’

choices.label: Ask where they are, stay on chat, and call 112 / alert a trusted adult who can reach them
choices.feedback: Immediate danger needs emergency help.

choices.label: Say ‘Sleep on it, you’ll feel better’
choices.feedback: If someone may be in immediate danger, get help now.

choices.label: Reach out to them and tell a trusted adult right away
choices.feedback: It’s never too late to act.

d.text: Help is on the way. They’re still talking to you.

choices.label: Keep listening, stay connected, and share Tele-MANAS 14416 for ongoing support
choices.feedback: Staying connected matters.

end1.text: Emergency services and family reach them. In the days after, you check in — and get support for yourself too.

quiz.q: Which is a warning sign?
options: Giving away belongings and saying goodbye
quiz.why: Giving away belongings and saying goodbye are warning signs of suicide risk, so act on them. Studying, laughing with friends or joining a club are usual activities.

quiz.q: ASK–LISTEN–STAY–CONNECT begins with…
quiz.why: ASK–LISTEN–STAY–CONNECT begins with asking directly about suicide. Asking is safe and opens the way to help.

quiz.q: Should you promise to keep suicidal thoughts secret?
quiz.why: No, don't promise to keep suicidal thoughts secret, because safety comes first. Get help from a trusted adult or helpline.

quiz.q: If someone is in immediate danger, call…
quiz.why: In immediate danger call 112, the national emergency number. 1930, 181 and 1097 are other helplines.

quiz.q: Sharing method details online is…
options: Harmful — share help numbers and hope instead
quiz.why: Sharing method details online is harmful, as it can influence vulnerable people. Share help numbers and hope instead (safe messaging).

lessons.title: Reasons for living and building hope

scenes.text: Ankita, 23, from Jaipur is recovering after a hard year. Her therapist suggests a ‘hope box’.
She fills it with photos of her nieces, a letter from her best friend, her favourite song list and a postcard from Goa.
On bad nights, she opens the box and calls her sister.
‘It doesn’t fix everything,’ she says, ‘but it reminds me why I’m holding on.’

steps.title: Hope is a skill you can build
steps.body: When pain is intense, the brain narrows and forgets reasons to live. Writing and collecting them **in advance** makes them available when you need them.

steps.title: Build a hope box (physical or on your phone)
steps.body:
- Photos of people and pets you love
- Kind messages you’ve received
- Future plans and places you want to see
- Favourite music, prayers or quotes
- Your safety plan and helpline numbers (**14416**, **112**)

steps.title: Connection protects
steps.body: Feeling connected — to family, friends, community, faith or pets — is one of the strongest protective factors. Even one supportive relationship helps.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write three reasons for living — big or small (a person, a pet, a dream, a favourite food you haven’t tried yet).

activity.prompt: Write three reasons for living — and one person you could contact on a hard day.
activity.hint: Small reasons count too: a pet, a song, a place you want to visit, someone who would miss you.

quiz.q: Why prepare reasons for living in advance?
options: Pain narrows thinking; having them ready helps
quiz.why: Pain narrows thinking, so it is hard to remember reasons for living in a crisis. Preparing them in advance helps.

quiz.q: What goes in a hope box?
options: Photos, kind messages, plans and helpline numbers
quiz.why: A hope box holds photos, kind messages, plans and helpline numbers. They remind you of hope in hard moments.

quiz.q: Which is a strong protective factor?
quiz.why: Connection is a strong protective factor, because feeling supported reduces risk. Isolation, alcohol and secrecy raise it.

quiz.q: On a hard night, a good step is…
options: Open the hope box and call someone or 14416
quiz.why: On a hard night, open the hope box and call someone or 14416. Staying alone with no plan or drinking increases risk.

questions.why: Tele-MANAS, the mental-health helpline, is 14416. 1098 is Childline.
112 is the national emergency number. 1930 is the cybercrime helpline.
Asking directly about suicide is helpful and safe. It does not increase risk.
Self-harm is usually a way of coping with painful feelings. It is not simply attention-seeking.

options: Warning signs, coping, people, helplines, safer surroundings
questions.why: A safety plan includes warning signs, coping steps, people, helplines and safer surroundings. It guides you in a crisis.
Alcohol in a crisis makes impulses stronger. It doesn't help.
Giving away belongings is a warning sign of suicide risk, so act. Joining a team is not.
No, don't promise secrecy. Safety comes first, so get help.
If a friend self-harms, stay calm and encourage help. Showing disgust can make them feel ashamed.
Online, share help numbers and hope. Method details can harm vulnerable people.

options: Presumes severe stress; care and rehabilitation
questions.why: The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 presumes severe stress in a suicide attempt, so the person gets care and rehabilitation, not punishment.

questions.q: Sudden calm after deep depression can be…
options: A warning sign to check in
questions.why: Sudden calm after deep depression can be a warning sign, so check in. It isn't always recovery.

options: Follow up in the days after
questions.why: The final step, Connect, also includes following up in the days after. Ongoing check-ins keep the person supported.

courses.title: Sleep, loneliness, body image and everyday mental fitness
courses.summary: The everyday foundations of mental health: sleep, connection, a kinder body image (including eating-disorder awareness), and the five ways to wellbeing.
outcomes: Learners can plan healthy sleep for their age
Learners can make a connection plan to reduce loneliness
Learners can recognise body-image pressure and eating-disorder warning signs
Learners can use the five ways to wellbeing
courses.guardianNote: For ages 12+. Covers sleep, loneliness, body image and everyday mental fitness. Discusses eating disorders factually without numbers, weights or methods, with signs to seek help.

lessons.title: Sleep: the free superpower

scenes.text: Kabir, 16, from Mumbai scrolls till 2 a.m., then wakes at 6:30 for school. He’s grumpy, can’t focus, and drinks two energy drinks a day.
His marks and mood fall. He thinks he’s ‘just not smart’.
His biology teacher explains sleep science. Kabir tries phone-out-of-room for two weeks.
He feels sharper, calmer and stops needing energy drinks.

steps.title: How much sleep we need
steps.body:
Recommended by sleep experts (AASM/NSF):
- Children 6–12: **9–12 hours**
- Teens 13–18: **8–10 hours**
- Adults: **7–9 hours** (at least 7)
- Older adults: **7–8 hours**

Teens naturally feel sleepy later at night — a real body-clock shift — which makes early mornings tough.

steps.title: What sleep does
steps.body:
- **Memory:** sleep turns what you studied into long-term memory
- **Mood:** poor sleep increases irritability, anxiety and low mood
- **Body:** growth, immunity, appetite hormones, heart health
- **Safety:** drowsy driving and accidents

All-nighters before exams usually **hurt** performance.

steps.title: Sleep habits that work
steps.body:
- Same wake-up time every day (even weekends, roughly)
- Morning daylight
- Phone out of the bedroom, or at least 30–60 minutes off before bed
- No caffeine (tea, coffee, cola, energy drinks) after about 2 pm — caffeine lasts for hours
- Cool, dark, quiet room
- If you can’t sleep after ~20 minutes, get up, do something calm in dim light, return when sleepy
- Short naps (20 minutes) before 4 pm if needed

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: Loud snoring with pauses in breathing, falling asleep during the day despite enough sleep, insomnia for over 3 months, or sleep problems with low mood or anxiety. Sleeping pills should only be used under medical advice.

steps.title: Worked example: Kabir’s plan
steps.body: Wake 6:30 → bed by 10:30 (8 hours). Phone charging in the kitchen at 10. Last tea at 1 pm. Read a novel in bed. Weekend wake by 8:30, not noon.

activity.label: How many hours did you sleep last night?

bands.text: Under 6 hours — sleep debt. Expect lower focus and mood; aim for an earlier, phone-free bedtime.
6–7.5 hours — okay for many adults, but short for teens (8–10 hours) and children (9–12).
8–10 hours — great for teens; adults usually need 7–9.
Over 10 hours regularly — fine after sleep debt or illness, but if you’re always this sleepy, check mood and health with a doctor.

quiz.q: How much sleep do teens need?
quiz.why: Teens need about 8–10 hours of sleep for growth, mood and learning. Four to six hours is too little.

quiz.q: When should caffeine stop?
quiz.why: Stop caffeine by early afternoon, because it stays in the body for many hours and disturbs sleep.

quiz.q: All-nighters before exams usually…
quiz.why: All-nighters before exams hurt memory and performance, because sleep helps the brain store what you learned. They don't improve marks.

quiz.q: Can’t sleep after 20 minutes?
options: Get up, do something calm in dim light, return when sleepy
quiz.why: If you can't sleep after about 20 minutes, get up, do something calm in dim light and return when sleepy. Scrolling, coffee or hard exercise keeps you awake.

quiz.q: Loud snoring with breathing pauses may need…
quiz.why: Loud snoring with breathing pauses may be sleep apnoea, so see a doctor. More caffeine or a later bedtime won't solve it.

lessons.title: Loneliness and connection

scenes.text: Mr. Venkat Rao, 72, lives alone in Hyderabad. His children are in the US. Days pass without talking to anyone.
Meanwhile Priyanka, 26, new in Bengaluru for work, eats dinner alone every night scrolling.
Both join a neighbourhood library reading circle. Mr. Rao teaches Priyanka Telugu; she helps him video-call his grandchildren.
‘I didn’t know how lonely I was until I wasn’t,’ says Priyanka.

steps.title: Loneliness is a signal
steps.body: Loneliness is the painful feeling that your connections aren’t what you need. You can feel lonely in a crowd, in a marriage or online. Like hunger signals a need for food, loneliness signals a need for connection. **It is common at every age** — WHO has called social isolation and loneliness a global health priority.

steps.title: Why it matters for health
steps.body: Long-term loneliness and isolation are linked with higher risk of depression, anxiety, heart disease, stroke, dementia and earlier death. Connection is not a luxury — it’s a health need.

steps.title: Ways to reconnect
steps.body:
- Start small: a message to an old friend
- Repeat contact: same class, gym, temple, club, volunteering weekly
- Shared activities beat small talk: sports, music, cooking, reading groups
- Help others: volunteering builds belonging
- Pets, neighbours, local groups
- Turn online contact into calls or meetings

steps.title: Worked example: Priyanka’s 4-week plan
steps.body: Week 1: join a weekend running group. Week 2: invite one colleague for lunch. Week 3: call her college friend. Week 4: volunteer at an animal shelter. By week 4, she has three people she sees regularly.

steps.title: When loneliness becomes heavy
steps.body: If loneliness comes with hopelessness, low mood for weeks, or thoughts of not wanting to live, talk to someone today: **Tele-MANAS 14416**.

activity.prompt: My connection plan this month:
items: Message one person I’ve lost touch with
Join one regular group or class
Have one meal with someone each week
Volunteer or help someone once
Turn one online chat into a call
Check in on someone who may be lonely

quiz.q: Loneliness is best understood as…
options: A signal of a need for connection
quiz.why: Loneliness is a signal that you need connection, like hunger signals a need for food. It is not a character flaw.

quiz.q: Long-term loneliness is linked with…
options: Higher risk of depression and heart disease
quiz.why: Long-term loneliness is linked with a higher risk of depression and heart disease. It affects health, not improves it.

quiz.q: Which builds connection best?
quiz.why: Repeated shared activities build connection best, because time together and a shared purpose grow friendships. One-off small talk or scrolling doesn't.

quiz.q: Can you be lonely in a crowd?
quiz.why: Yes, you can be lonely in a crowd. Loneliness is about the quality of connection, not the number of people around.

quiz.q: Loneliness with hopelessness for weeks?
quiz.why: Loneliness with hopelessness lasting weeks needs support, so talk to someone, such as 14416. Waiting or hiding it can make it worse.

lessons.title: Body image, filters and eating worries

scenes.text: Riya, 15, from Chandigarh never posts a photo without a slimming, skin-smoothing filter.
She starts skipping lunch and feels guilty after eating. Her brother Aman, 17, is spending hours at the gym and taking powders after seeing fitness influencers.
Their school nurse talks to the class about body image and eating disorders.
Riya and Aman both realise they’ve been comparing themselves to edited images. They talk to their parents and a doctor.

steps.title: What body image is
steps.body: Body image is how you **see, think and feel** about your body. It is shaped by family comments, friends, culture, films, advertising and social media. Many images online are **filtered, edited, posed and lit** — they are not real bodies.

steps.title: Comparison culture
steps.body: Research links frequent appearance-focused social media use with lower body satisfaction, particularly in teens. Both girls and boys are affected: girls are often pressured to be thin and fair; boys to be tall and muscular. **Colourism** — prejudice favouring lighter skin — is a common pressure in India.

steps.title: Eating disorders are serious illnesses
steps.body:
Eating disorders — such as **anorexia**, **bulimia**, **binge-eating disorder** and **ARFID** — are serious mental and physical illnesses that affect all genders, ages and body sizes. Warning signs:
- Intense fear of weight gain, constant focus on food, weight or shape
- Skipping meals, strict rules, hiding food or eating in secret
- Eating very large amounts with loss of control
- Vomiting or misusing laxatives after eating
- Excessive exercise, or exercising when ill or injured
- Periods stopping, dizziness, feeling cold, fatigue

Early help leads to better recovery. See a doctor.

steps.title: Boys and muscle pressure
steps.body: Some boys develop **muscle dysmorphia** — feeling too small despite being muscular. Warning signs: compulsive training, anxiety about missing workouts, extreme diets, or using **anabolic steroids** or unregulated supplements, which can harm the heart, liver, hormones and mood.

steps.title: Building a kinder body image
steps.body:
- Unfollow accounts that make you feel worse; follow diverse, real bodies
- Focus on what your body **does** (dance, run, hug, laugh)
- Stop body talk: no comments on others’ weight, skin or shape — including ‘compliments’ about weight loss
- Eat regular meals; food is fuel, not a reward or punishment
- Talk to someone if food or body thoughts take over

This is general health education, not medical advice. If something worries you, see a doctor, nurse or counsellor.

statements.s: Most images on social media show unedited bodies.
statements.why: Many are filtered, posed or edited.

statements.s: Eating disorders only affect thin girls.
statements.why: They affect all genders, ages and body sizes.

statements.s: Anabolic steroids can harm the heart, liver and hormones.
Focusing on what your body can do can improve body image.
Periods stopping can be a warning sign of under-eating.

quiz.q: Body image is…
options: How you see, think and feel about your body
quiz.why: Body image is how you see, think and feel about your body. It isn't just height, weight or a filter.

quiz.q: Which is an eating-disorder warning sign?
options: Intense fear of weight gain and skipping meals
quiz.why: An intense fear of weight gain and skipping meals is a warning sign of an eating disorder. Seek help early.

quiz.q: Muscle dysmorphia is…
options: Feeling too small despite being muscular
quiz.why: Muscle dysmorphia is feeling too small despite being muscular. It is a body-image disorder that mostly affects boys and men.

quiz.q: A kinder habit is…
options: Unfollowing accounts that make you feel worse
quiz.why: Unfollowing accounts that make you feel worse is a kind habit that curates your feed. Skipping meals, using filters or commenting on weight harm.

quiz.q: Colourism means…
quiz.why: Colourism is prejudice favouring lighter skin. It is a social bias, not a liking for colours.

lessons.title: Everyday mental fitness

scenes.text: The Sharma family in Noida — two parents, a teen and a grandmother — feel stressed and disconnected.
They read about the ‘Five Ways to Wellbeing’ and pick one per week.
Dadi teaches cooking; the teen starts guitar; weekend walks become a ritual.
A month later, everyone says home feels lighter.

steps.title: Five Ways to Wellbeing
steps.body:
Based on research reviewed for the UK government’s Foresight project, five simple actions support mental wellbeing:
- **Connect** with people
- **Be active** — walk, dance, play
- **Take notice** — pay attention to the present (mindfulness)
- **Keep learning** — a new skill or hobby
- **Give** — kindness, volunteering, helping

steps.title: Mini-practices
steps.body:
- 3 good things: each night write three things that went well
- 2-minute breathing
- A 10-minute walk outdoors
- Gratitude message to someone
- One ‘learn’ task weekly

steps.title: Stress vs burnout
steps.body: Some stress helps us perform. **Burnout** is long-term exhaustion, cynicism and reduced effectiveness from chronic stress, often at work or caregiving. Signs: dreading every day, exhaustion even after rest, feeling detached. Rest, boundaries, support and sometimes professional help are needed.

steps.title: Worked example: a weekly plan
steps.body: Mon: call a friend (connect). Tue: 20-min walk (active). Wed: mindful tea, no phone (notice). Thu: 15 mins on a language app (learn). Fri: help a neighbour (give).

activity.prompt: Match each ‘way to wellbeing’ with an example:

quiz.q: Which is one of the Five Ways to Wellbeing?
quiz.why: Give is one of the Five Ways to Wellbeing (Connect, Be active, Take notice, Keep learning, Give). Giving boosts wellbeing.

quiz.q: Burnout involves…
quiz.why: Burnout involves long-term exhaustion and detachment, caused by chronic stress. It is not short-term excitement.

quiz.q: ‘3 good things’ is…
options: Writing three things that went well each night
quiz.why: '3 good things' means writing three things that went well each night. It is a gratitude practice that improves mood.

quiz.q: ‘Take notice’ means…
quiz.why: 'Take notice' means paying attention to the present moment, which is mindfulness. It isn't about reading notices or noticing faults.

quiz.q: Some stress can…
quiz.why: Some stress can help performance, because moderate arousal sharpens focus. Too much leads to burnout.

sources: Foresight Mental Capital and Wellbeing (Five Ways to Wellbeing)

questions.why: Teens need about 8–10 hours of sleep. Five hours is too little.
Loneliness signals a need for connection. It isn't weakness.
Social media images are often edited and filtered, so they don't show reality.
Stop caffeine by early afternoon, because it lasts many hours in the body.
Eating disorders affect all genders and sizes. They are not limited to thin girls.
Keep learning is one of the Five Ways to Wellbeing. Avoiding people is not.
All-nighters hurt memory, because sleep consolidates what you learned.
Muscle dysmorphia is feeling too small despite having muscle. It is a body-image disorder, not strength.
Repeated shared activity builds connection best. One-time small talk rarely builds friendship.
Steroids risk the heart, liver, hormones and mood. The harms can be serious and lasting.
Burnout signs include exhaustion, cynicism and reduced effectiveness. Excitement is not a sign.

options: Get up, calm activity, return when sleepy
questions.why: If you can't sleep for 20 minutes, get up, do a calm activity and return when sleepy. Scrolling keeps the brain alert.

questions.q: Commenting on someone’s weight loss as a compliment…
options: Can reinforce harmful focus on weight
questions.why: Commenting on weight loss as a compliment can reinforce a harmful focus on weight. It may hurt someone struggling, so avoid body talk.

courses.title: Addiction: phones, gaming, porn, vaping, alcohol and drugs
courses.summary: How addiction works in the brain; healthy vs harmful use of phones and games; compulsive porn use (non-explicit); vaping, tobacco and alcohol facts and Indian laws; other drugs, overdose and how to get help.
outcomes: Learners can explain reward, tolerance, withdrawal and the habit loop
Learners can set controls for phones and gaming
Learners can recognise compulsive porn use and find help
Learners can state facts and Indian laws on vaping, tobacco, alcohol and drugs
Learners can respond to an overdose and use helplines 14446, 1800-11-2356, 14416
courses.guardianNote: For ages 14+. Explains how addiction works and covers phones, gaming, compulsive pornography use (non-explicit), vaping and tobacco, alcohol and other drugs, with Indian laws and helplines (14446, 1800-11-2356, 14416). Non-judgemental and harm-aware.

lessons.title: How addiction works

scenes.text: Manish, 19, from Chandigarh started gaming to relax. Now he plays 8 hours a day, skips classes and feels irritable when he can’t play.
In a college talk, a psychiatrist explains the brain’s reward system and how habits become compulsions.
Manish recognises himself — and realises it’s not about being ‘weak’.
He starts a plan with the college counsellor.

steps.title: The reward system
steps.body: The brain releases **dopamine** when we do things that feel rewarding — food, friendship, achievement. Substances like nicotine and alcohol, and behaviours like gaming or scrolling, can trigger strong dopamine signals. With repeated use the brain adapts: you need **more** for the same effect (**tolerance**) and feel bad without it (**withdrawal**).

steps.title: Signs of addiction (substance or behaviour)
steps.body:
- **Loss of control:** using more or longer than intended
- **Priority:** it crowds out sleep, study, work, relationships
- **Continuing despite harm**
- **Cravings**
- **Tolerance and withdrawal** (irritability, anxiety, physical symptoms)

WHO’s ICD-11 includes **gaming disorder**, defined by impaired control, increasing priority, and continuing despite negative consequences, usually over at least 12 months.

steps.title: Why some people are more at risk
steps.body: Genetics, starting young (the teen brain is more sensitive to addiction), stress, trauma, mental health conditions like ADHD, depression or anxiety, and easy availability. Addiction is a **health condition**, not a moral failure — and it’s treatable.

steps.title: The habit loop
steps.body: **Cue → craving → action → reward.** Changing cues (phone out of sight), finding healthier rewards, and adding friction (logging out, deleting apps) all weaken the loop.

steps.title: Help in India
steps.body: **National Toll-Free Drug De-addiction Helpline: 14446** · Tobacco Quitline: **1800-11-2356** · Tele-MANAS **14416** · government de-addiction centres and psychiatry departments.

activity.prompt: Put the habit loop in order:
items: Cue (a trigger — boredom, notification, stress)
Craving (the urge)
Action (using / playing / scrolling)
Reward (relief or pleasure)
Repeat — the loop strengthens

quiz.q: Tolerance means…
options: Needing more for the same effect
quiz.why: Tolerance means needing more of something to get the same effect, as the brain adapts. It is a feature of addiction.

quiz.q: Which is a sign of addiction?
quiz.why: Continuing despite harm is a key sign of addiction. Trying once, stopping easily or occasional enjoyment is not.

quiz.q: Is gaming disorder recognised by WHO?
quiz.why: Yes, WHO recognises gaming disorder in ICD-11. It involves loss of control and continuing despite harm.

quiz.q: Why is the teen brain at higher risk?
options: It’s more sensitive to reward and still developing self-control
quiz.why: The teen brain is more sensitive to reward and still developing self-control, so it is at higher risk. It is not about weakness.

quiz.q: National drug de-addiction helpline?
quiz.why: The national drug de-addiction helpline is 14446. 1098 is Childline, 112 is emergency and 1930 is cybercrime.

lessons.title: Phones, gaming and scrolling

scenes.text: In Chennai, the Iyer family — parents included — check phones 100+ times a day. Dinner is silent.
They introduce a ‘phone basket’ at meals and after 9:30 pm.
The first week is hard; their son Karthik, 14, is furious.
By week three, they’re playing carrom after dinner. Karthik sleeps better and his grades improve.

steps.title: Designed to hook you
steps.body: Many apps and games use **variable rewards** (likes, loot boxes, streaks), infinite scroll and autoplay to keep you engaged. It’s not just willpower — design matters. Recognising the tricks helps you take control.

steps.title: Practical controls
steps.body:
- Turn off non-essential notifications
- Move tempting apps off the home screen; grayscale mode
- App timers and downtime settings
- Phone out of the bedroom at night
- Replace: have a go-to offline activity
- Be wary of loot boxes and in-game purchases — they work like gambling

steps.title: Gaming: healthy vs harmful
steps.body: Gaming can be fun, social and even build skills. It becomes harmful when it **controls you**: losing sleep, skipping school or work, lying about time, irritability when stopping, losing interest in other things, or spending money you don’t have. Online real-money gaming can lead to serious debt.

steps.title: Worked example: a reset plan
steps.body: Week 1: track screen time honestly (baseline 7 h). Week 2: notifications off, no phone at meals (6 h). Week 3: no phone after 10 pm (5 h). Week 4: two offline hobbies (4 h). Reward progress.

steps.title: When to get help
steps.body: If you can’t cut down despite trying, or it’s harming school, work, sleep, money or relationships — see a counsellor. Specialised behavioural addiction clinics exist in India (e.g. at NIMHANS). Tele-MANAS **14416**.

activity.prompt: Healthy use or warning sign?

items.text: Gaming with friends on weekends after homework
Skipping meals and sleep to keep playing
Lying to parents about screen time
Using an app timer to stop after an hour
Spending borrowed money on in-game purchases
Feeling furious and anxious whenever you can’t play

quiz.q: Variable rewards are…
options: Unpredictable rewards like likes and loot boxes that hook attention
quiz.why: Variable rewards are unpredictable rewards like likes and loot boxes. They hook attention because you never know when the next one comes.

quiz.q: Which helps control phone use?
quiz.why: Keeping the phone out of the bedroom removes cues and temptation. Autoplay, notifications and infinite scroll are designed to keep you hooked.

quiz.q: Loot boxes work like…
quiz.why: Loot boxes work like gambling, since you pay for a random reward. That can encourage compulsive spending.

quiz.q: A warning sign of problem gaming?
options: Losing sleep and lying about time
quiz.why: Losing sleep and lying about time are warning signs of problem gaming, showing loss of control. Stopping easily and playing occasionally are not.

quiz.q: Best first step to cut down?
quiz.why: The best first step is to track your honest baseline screen time, so you know what to change. Throwing the phone away or ignoring it doesn't help.

lessons.title: Compulsive pornography use (non-explicit)

scenes.text: Aditya, 22, a software trainee in Pune, started watching porn at 13. Now he watches daily, late into the night, and feels he can’t stop.
He feels ashamed, tired and anxious about relationships.
He sees a psychologist, who explains compulsive sexual behaviour without judgement.
With a plan — filters, sleep routine, exercise and therapy — he cuts down and feels more in control.

steps.title: When it becomes a problem
steps.body: Many adults view pornography; for some it becomes **compulsive**. WHO’s ICD-11 includes **compulsive sexual behaviour disorder** — a persistent pattern of failing to control intense sexual urges or behaviour, continuing despite harm or little satisfaction, for at least 6 months, causing significant distress or impairment. Not everyone who watches has a disorder; the key is **loss of control and harm**.

steps.title: Legal and safety points (India)
steps.body: Any material involving under-18s is child sexual abuse material — viewing, downloading or sharing it is a **serious crime** (POCSO, IT Act s.67B). Many porn sites are blocked in India and spread malware and scams; sextortion schemes also target viewers.

steps.title: What helps
steps.body:
- Notice triggers (boredom, loneliness, stress, late night) and plan alternatives
- Content filters, phone out of bedroom
- Exercise, sleep routine, social time
- Replace shame with curiosity: ‘What was I feeling before?’
- Therapy (CBT, acceptance-based approaches); treat underlying anxiety or depression

steps.title: Avoid
steps.body: Quack ‘cures’ and ‘sex power’ medicines; myths that it ‘drains semen strength’. Shame-based approaches often increase the cycle.

steps.title: Help
steps.body: A psychologist or psychiatrist; Tele-MANAS **14416**. Partners affected can seek couples counselling.

statements.s: Everyone who watches porn has a disorder.
statements.why: Loss of control and harm are key.

statements.s: ICD-11 includes compulsive sexual behaviour disorder.
Material involving under-18s is a serious crime to view or share in India.
Shame is the most effective way to stop.
statements.why: Understanding triggers and support work better.

statements.s: Content filters and phone out of the bedroom can help.

quiz.q: The key feature of compulsive use is…
options: Loss of control and continuing despite harm
quiz.why: The key feature of compulsive use is loss of control and continuing despite harm. Curiosity or watching once isn't compulsive.

quiz.q: Which is a common trigger?
options: Boredom or loneliness late at night
quiz.why: Boredom or loneliness late at night is a common trigger. Knowing your triggers helps you plan other responses.

quiz.q: Approach shown to help?
quiz.why: CBT and treating underlying anxiety or depression is an evidence-based approach. Shame, secrecy and quack medicines do not help.

quiz.q: Porn sites are commonly linked to…
quiz.why: Porn sites are commonly linked to malware, scams and sextortion, which are safety risks. They are not free education.

quiz.q: Who can help?
