quiz.why: A psychologist, psychiatrist or Tele-MANAS (14416) can provide qualified help. Random forums and wall-poster clinics are unreliable.

lessons.title: Vaping, tobacco and alcohol

scenes.text: Sahil, 15, from Bengaluru tries a friend’s fruity vape. ‘It’s just water vapour,’ the friend says.
Within weeks he feels restless without it and buys more secretly.
A teacher finds it. Instead of only punishing, the school counsellor explains nicotine addiction and the law.
Sahil uses the Quitline and a quit plan with his parents.

steps.title: Vaping facts
steps.body:
- E-cigarettes heat a liquid usually containing **nicotine** — highly addictive — plus flavourings and chemicals; the aerosol is **not just water vapour**
- Nicotine affects the developing teen brain (attention, learning, mood) and can lead to smoking
- India’s **Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Act, 2019** bans the production, import, sale, distribution, storage and advertisement of e-cigarettes

This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Tobacco
steps.body: Tobacco — smoked or chewed (gutkha, khaini, beedi, cigarettes) — causes cancers (mouth, lung and many others), heart disease and stroke. India has a very high burden of oral cancer linked to smokeless tobacco. Under **COTPA 2003**, sale to under-18s and near educational institutions is prohibited, and smoking in public places is banned. Quitting at any age brings health benefits. **Quitline: 1800-11-2356.**

steps.title: Alcohol
steps.body: WHO states that **no level of alcohol is safe** for health. Alcohol affects judgement, coordination and memory, and is linked to accidents, violence, liver disease, several cancers, and worse depression and anxiety. The legal drinking age in India **varies by state** (commonly 18–25) and some states prohibit alcohol. Never drink and drive. Binge drinking can cause alcohol poisoning: if someone is unconscious, breathing slowly or vomiting while drowsy — put them on their side and **call 112**.

steps.title: Quitting nicotine
steps.body:
- Pick a quit date; tell friends and family
- Remove vapes/cigarettes, lighters
- Know cravings peak and pass in minutes — delay, drink water, walk, breathe
- Avoid triggers (certain friends, places, tea breaks) at first
- Use support: Quitline, doctors; nicotine replacement for adults under medical advice
- Slips happen — restart, don’t give up

steps.title: Refusing offers
steps.body: ‘No thanks, I’m good.’ ‘I’ve got a match tomorrow.’ ‘Nah, vapes are banned and they get you hooked.’ Hold a drink of your own; suggest another activity.

cards.back: Bans production, import, sale, distribution, storage and advertisement of e-cigarettes in India
Bans sale of tobacco to under-18s and near schools; bans smoking in public places
National Tobacco Quitline
WHO: no level is safe for health
Unconscious, slow breathing → recovery position, call 112
Not just water vapour — nicotine and chemicals

quiz.q: Is vape aerosol just water vapour?
options: No — it contains nicotine and chemicals
quiz.why: No, vape aerosol is not just water vapour. It contains nicotine and chemicals that harm the lungs and brain.

quiz.q: Which law bans e-cigarettes in India?
quiz.why: E-cigarettes are banned in India by the Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Act 2019. COTPA 2003 covers tobacco products in general.

quiz.q: WHO’s position on safe alcohol levels?
options: No level is safe for health
quiz.why: WHO says no level of alcohol is safe for health. Beer and wine carry the same risk because the alcohol is what harms.

quiz.q: Someone unconscious after drinking. You…
options: Let them sleep on their back
quiz.why: Put an unconscious person in the recovery position, which prevents choking, and call 112. Coffee or cold showers don't help, and lying on their back is dangerous.

quiz.q: National Tobacco Quitline?
quiz.why: The National Tobacco Quitline number is 1800-11-2356. 1098 is Childline, 1930 cybercrime and 181 the Women's Helpline.

lessons.title: Other drugs and getting help

scenes.text: Jaspreet, 24, from Punjab started using drugs offered by friends after losing his job.
Within a year he lost money, friendships and his health.
His sister called the 14446 helpline; he was referred to a government de-addiction centre.
With treatment, family support and a recovery group, he’s now two years drug-free and works as a peer counsellor.

steps.title: Common drugs and risks
steps.body:
- **Cannabis (ganja, charas):** affects memory and motivation; can trigger psychosis in vulnerable people, especially with early, heavy use
- **Opioids (heroin/‘smack’, some painkillers):** highly addictive; overdose can stop breathing
- **Stimulants (cocaine, methamphetamine):** heart problems, paranoia
- **Inhalants (whitener, glue):** can cause sudden death, brain damage — a concern among some children
- **Prescription misuse:** sedatives or painkillers without prescription

steps.title: Law in India
steps.body: The **NDPS Act, 1985** makes producing, possessing, selling, buying or using narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances an offence, with penalties depending on the quantity. It also provides for treatment: people who use drugs and volunteer for de-addiction treatment can be given immunity from prosecution under certain conditions. This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Treatment works
steps.body: Treatment may include detox under medical care, medicines (e.g. opioid substitution therapy), counselling, family therapy, and peer support (NA/AA groups). Relapse is common and part of many recovery journeys — **not** failure.

steps.title: Overdose: act fast
steps.body: Signs: unresponsive, very slow or no breathing, blue lips. **Call 112**, place in the recovery position, stay with them. Naloxone reverses opioid overdose if available.

steps.title: Help
steps.body: **14446** National Drug De-addiction Helpline · **14416** Tele-MANAS · government hospitals and Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan centres. Families can call too.

a.text: At a party, someone offers you a pill: ‘Everyone’s trying it.’

choices.label: ‘No thanks,’ and stay with friends you trust
choices.feedback: Clear refusal is enough.

choices.label: Take half to fit in
choices.feedback: Unknown pills can contain anything; risks are unpredictable.

b.text: Later you find a friend who took it, now drowsy and hard to wake.

choices.label: Call 112, put them in the recovery position and stay
choices.feedback: Fast action saves lives.

choices.label: Let them sleep it off
choices.feedback: Unresponsiveness can be an emergency.

c.text: You feel your heart racing and you’re scared.

choices.label: Tell a trusted friend and get medical help (112)
choices.feedback: Honesty with medics helps them treat you.

end1.text: Medical help arrives in time. Next day you call 14446 to learn more about support.

end2.text: Never leave an unresponsive person alone. Call 112.

quiz.q: Which law governs drugs in India?
quiz.why: The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985 governs drugs in India. COTPA deals with tobacco.

quiz.q: Signs of overdose?
quiz.why: Overdose signs include being unresponsive, slow breathing and blue lips, which need emergency help (112). Laughing or being talkative are not overdose signs.

quiz.q: Relapse in recovery is…
options: Common and part of many recovery journeys
quiz.why: Relapse is common and part of many recovery journeys. It isn't failure, so restart the plan and get support.

quiz.q: Drug de-addiction helpline?
quiz.why: The drug de-addiction helpline is 14446. 181 is the Women's Helpline, 1097 is the AIDS helpline and 1930 is cybercrime.

quiz.q: Inhalants like whitener can cause…
quiz.why: Inhalants like whitener can cause sudden death and brain damage. They are very dangerous.

options: Needing more for the same effect
questions.why: Tolerance means needing more for the same effect, as the brain adapts. It is not patience.
The drug helpline is 14446. 100 is the police number.
Vapes contain nicotine and chemicals, not only water. The 'harmless vapour' idea is a myth.
Gaming disorder is classified in ICD-11 by WHO. It means loss of control over gaming with harm.
The habit loop starts with a cue, the trigger that sets off the behaviour. The reward comes at the end.
E-cigarettes are banned in India under the Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Act 2019. They are not legal everywhere.
WHO says there is no safe level of alcohol for health. Two drinks is not considered safe.
Loot boxes resemble gambling because you pay for a random reward. They are not savings.
Put the person in the recovery position and call 112 to prevent choking. Leaving them on their back can be deadly.

questions.q: Compulsive sexual behaviour disorder key feature?
questions.why: The key feature of compulsive sexual behaviour disorder is loss of control with harm. Any viewing alone isn't the disorder.

questions.q: NDPS Act can give immunity for…
questions.why: The NDPS Act can give immunity to users who volunteer for treatment, with conditions. It focuses on treatment for users and not on protecting dealers.
A relapse means restarting the plan, because relapse is common in recovery. Giving up is not needed.

questions.q: Teen brain addiction risk is higher because…
questions.why: The teen brain is more sensitive to reward, and self-control is still developing, so risk is higher. It is not about brain size.

wellbeing-never-fear.title: Never fear: brave, step by step
wellbeing-never-fear.description: Lessons and breathing activities to face fears of exams, failure, the stage, the dark, water, heights and strangers — for little children to adults.

courses.title: Brave little hearts: dark, water, heights and new people
courses.summary: Gentle, playful lessons to help children with fear of the dark, water, heights and talking to people — with breathing games, tiny brave steps and safety rules.
outcomes: Learners can use calm tools for fear of the dark
Learners can follow water-safety rules and take brave steps in water
Learners can tell safe brave steps from unsafe risks at heights
Learners can talk to new people safely and know what to do if lost
courses.guardianNote: For ages 4–10 with a parent. Gentle lessons on fear of the dark, water, heights and talking to people, with breathing games and tiny brave steps. Water-safety content follows standard drowning-prevention advice (WHO). The ‘strangers’ lesson teaches safe helpers and tricky situations without frightening detail.

lessons.title: Not afraid of the dark

scenes.text: Chintu, 5, from Bhopal can’t sleep. Shadows on the wall look like monsters.
His Nani gives him a small torch and they go ‘shadow hunting’ together — the monster is just his school bag!
They put glow stars on the ceiling and practise ‘starfish breathing’.
Each night, Chintu turns the light down a little more.

steps.title: Why the dark feels scary
steps.body: In the dark, our eyes can’t see well, so our imagination fills in the gaps. Many children feel scared of the dark — it’s very normal, and it usually gets easier as you grow.

steps.title: Brave tools
steps.body:
- **Shadow hunt** with a torch and a grown-up
- A soft **night-light**
- A cuddly toy as a ‘night guard’
- **Starfish breathing:** trace your fingers slowly while breathing in and out
- A calm bedtime story

steps.title: Tiny brave steps
steps.body: Night 1: light on, door open. Night 3: night-light only. Night 6: door half-open. Celebrate each step with a sticker.

steps.title: For grown-ups
steps.body: Stay calm and kind; don’t tease or threaten (‘the monster will get you’). Avoid scary shows before bed. If fears are intense and don’t improve for months, talk to a paediatrician.

activity.label: Starfish breathing: trace up a finger as you breathe in (3), hold (1), trace down as you breathe out (4)

quiz.q: Why does the dark feel scary?
quiz.why: The dark feels scary because our imagination fills the gaps with things we can't see. Monsters are not real.

quiz.q: A brave tool for the dark?
quiz.why: A night-light and starfish breathing are calm tools for the dark. Scary videos or shouting make it harder.

quiz.q: Tiny brave steps means…
quiz.why: Tiny brave steps means getting a little braver each night. You don't do it all at once.

quiz.q: Is being scared of the dark normal?
quiz.why: Yes, being scared of the dark is very normal for many children. It gets easier with calm tools.

lessons.title: Water: safe and brave

scenes.text: Tara, 7, from Kochi is scared to put her face in the water at her first swimming class.
Her coach doesn’t force her. First she blows bubbles in a bowl, then in the shallow end, holding the edge.
By the fifth class she floats like a starfish with the coach’s hand under her back.
She also learns the most important rule: never swim without a grown-up watching.

steps.title: Water safety rules first
steps.body:
Drowning can happen quickly and quietly. WHO lists drowning as a leading cause of death for children worldwide, so:
- **Never go near water** — ponds, wells, rivers, buckets, tanks, the sea — **without a grown-up watching**
- Young children should always be within an arm’s reach in or near water
- Wear a **life jacket** on boats
- Swim only in safe, supervised places
- If someone is in trouble: **shout for help, throw something that floats — don’t jump in**

steps.title: Brave steps with water
steps.body:
1. Splash hands and face at the tap
2. Blow bubbles in a bowl
3. Sit in the shallow end with a grown-up
4. Blow bubbles in the pool
5. Float with support
6. Kick holding the edge

Learning to swim with a qualified teacher is one of the best ways to be safe.

steps.title: For grown-ups
steps.body: Never force a child into water — it can deepen fear. Praise small steps. Cover water containers at home, and keep toddlers away from buckets and tanks.

steps.title: Grown-ups can learn too
steps.body: Many adults never learned to swim. It’s never too late — adult beginner classes use the same gentle steps.

activity.prompt: Put the brave steps with water in order:
items: Splash hands and face at the tap
Blow bubbles in a bowl
Sit in the shallow end with a grown-up
Blow bubbles in the pool
Float with support
Kick while holding the edge

quiz.q: Most important water rule?
options: Never go near water without a grown-up watching
quiz.why: Never go near water without a grown-up watching. Supervision saves lives, because water can be dangerous very quickly.

quiz.q: Someone is struggling in water. You should…
options: Shout for help and throw something that floats
quiz.why: Shout for help and throw something that floats. Reach or throw, don't go in, because jumping in can put you in danger too.

quiz.q: On a boat, wear…
quiz.why: On a boat, wear a life jacket. It keeps you afloat if you fall in.

quiz.q: Should grown-ups force kids into water?
quiz.why: No, grown-ups should not force children into water. Praise small steps, because forcing can make the fear bigger.

lessons.title: Heights: wobbly but brave

scenes.text: Arjun, 6, from Shimla watches other kids climb the jungle gym. He freezes on the second bar.
His father stands beside him: ‘Just one more bar, then we’ll look around together.’
Arjun climbs one bar and sees the mountains. He grins.
Every weekend he climbs one bar higher.

steps.title: Some fear of heights is smart
steps.body: A little fear of heights keeps us safe near edges, balconies and terraces. It becomes a problem only when it stops us doing safe, fun things like slides or climbing frames.

steps.title: Safety rules
steps.body:
- Don’t lean over balcony railings or terrace edges
- Don’t climb on windows, furniture or water tanks
- Use playground equipment meant for your age
- Hold handrails on stairs and escalators

steps.title: Brave steps
steps.body: Climb one step higher than last time, then look at something far away (not straight down). Breathe slowly. A grown-up can stand close by.

steps.title: For grown-ups
steps.body: Fit window guards on high floors and keep furniture away from windows. Encourage safe climbing to build confidence and balance.

activity.prompt: Safe brave step or not safe?

items.text: Climbing one more bar on the playground frame with Papa nearby
Leaning over a balcony railing
Going down the small slide
Climbing on a window grill
Holding the handrail on an escalator

quiz.q: A little fear of heights is…
quiz.why: A little fear of heights is helpful for safety, because it makes us careful. It isn't silly.

quiz.q: While climbing, look…
quiz.why: While climbing, look far away, not straight down. That helps you feel less dizzy.

quiz.q: Is leaning over a balcony safe?
quiz.why: No, leaning over a balcony is never safe, because you could fall.

quiz.q: A brave step is…
options: One bar higher than last time
quiz.why: A brave step is going one bar higher than last time. Small steps build courage safely.

lessons.title: Talking to people: shy, safe and brave

story.title: Mehak orders her own ice cream

scenes.text: Mehak, 8, from Amritsar always hides behind her mother when shopkeepers or new kids talk to her.
Her mum suggests a mission: ‘Today, you order your own ice cream.’
Mehak practises at home, then says, ‘One mango ice cream, please.’ The shopkeeper smiles.
Her mum also reminds her of the safety rules for people she doesn’t know.

steps.title: Being shy is okay
steps.body: Lots of children feel shy with new people. Shyness isn’t bad — but practising small brave talks helps you make friends, ask for help and feel confident.

steps.title: Brave talk steps
steps.body:
1. Smile and wave
2. Say ‘Hi’ or ‘Namaste’
3. Say your name
4. Ask a question: ‘What game are you playing?’
5. Order or ask for something yourself with a grown-up nearby

steps.title: Safety with people you don’t know
steps.body: Talking politely to a shopkeeper or a new classmate **with your grown-up nearby** is fine. But **never go anywhere** with someone you don’t know, take gifts or sweets from them, or get into their vehicle — even if they say ‘Your mum sent me’. Families can use a **secret password** for anyone picking you up.

steps.title: Safe helpers if you’re lost
steps.body: If you get lost: **stop, stay where you are**, and look for a safe helper — a police officer, a shop counter worker, a security guard, or a mother with children. Tell them your name and your grown-up’s phone number. **112** is the emergency number.

steps.title: For grown-ups
steps.body: Avoid labelling (‘she’s just shy’) in front of the child. Praise effort. Teach the family password and help them learn your phone number.

a.text: You’re at a big mall and can’t see your parents anywhere.

choices.label: Stop and stay where you are, then look for a shop counter or security guard
choices.feedback: Staying put helps your family find you.

choices.label: Run around looking everywhere
choices.feedback: Running makes it harder for your family to find you.

b.text: A security guard asks if you’re okay.

choices.label: Tell your name and your parent’s phone number
choices.feedback: That’s how they help you find your family.

c.text: A man you don’t know says, ‘Come with me, I’ll take you to your mum outside.’

choices.label: Say ‘No!’ loudly and go to a shop counter or guard
choices.feedback: Never go with someone you don’t know.

choices.label: Go with him
choices.feedback: Never leave with someone you don’t know — find a safe helper inside.

end1.text: Your parents are called and you’re together again in minutes.

end2.text: Let’s try again: stay inside, say no, and find a safe helper like a guard or shop counter.

quiz.q: Being shy is…
quiz.why: Being shy is okay, and brave talks can help. It isn't bad or rude.

quiz.q: Someone you don’t know offers sweets to go with them. You…
options: Say no and tell your grown-up
quiz.why: Say no and tell your grown-up. Never go with someone you don't know, even if they offer sweets.

quiz.q: If you’re lost, first…
options: Stop and stay where you are
quiz.why: If you're lost, stop and stay where you are. Then it is easier for your grown-up to find you.

quiz.q: A safe helper is…
options: A police officer or shop counter worker
quiz.why: A police officer or shop counter worker is a safe helper. Anyone in a car or someone online is not safe.

quiz.q: A family password helps…
options: Know who is really sent to pick you up
quiz.why: A family password helps you know who is really sent to pick you up. If they don't know it, don't go.

questions.q: Is fear of the dark normal?
questions.why: Yes, fear of the dark is normal. Many children feel it.
Near water you need a grown-up watching, because water can be dangerous quickly.
If lost, stay where you are. Running off makes it harder to be found.
A night-light helps with fear of the dark by giving a little comfort.

options: Shout and throw something that floats
questions.why: Shout for help and throw something that floats. Don't jump in, because you could get into danger too.

questions.q: Go with someone you don’t know?
questions.why: Never go with someone you don't know, even if they have sweets.
When climbing, look far away, not straight down. It makes you less dizzy.
A security guard is a safe helper. A stranger in a car is not.
Brave steps should be small and gradual. Doing it all at once can feel too scary.
112 is the emergency number in India. 1234 is not a real emergency number.

questions.q: Why not force a child into water?
questions.why: Forcing a child into water can deepen the fear. Gentle, small steps work better.

courses.title: Never fear exams or failure
courses.summary: Understand exam fear, use study methods that work, follow an exam-day toolkit, and turn failure into a next step.
outcomes: Learners can explain the stress curve and reframe exam nerves
Learners can use retrieval and spaced practice
Learners can follow an exam-day plan including breathing and time planning
Learners can review failure constructively and know where to get help

lessons.title: Why exams feel scary — and how fear can help

scenes.text: Aditi, 15, from Kota knows her chemistry perfectly at home. In the exam hall her hands shake and her mind goes blank.
She thinks: ‘If I fail, my parents will be ashamed, I’ll never get into a good college, my life is over.’
Her teacher explains the stress curve: a little fear sharpens you; too much blocks memory.
Aditi learns to bring her fear down to the ‘helpful’ zone. Her next test goes much better.

steps.title: The stress curve
steps.body: Psychologists describe an **inverted-U**: with too little arousal you’re bored and careless; with a moderate amount you’re alert and focused; with **too much** your thinking brain goes offline and memory retrieval suffers (the ‘blank mind’). The goal isn’t zero nerves — it’s **helpful nerves**.

steps.title: Why the mind goes blank
steps.body: Under high stress, adrenaline and cortisol shift the brain into survival mode. The **prefrontal cortex**, which you use to recall and reason, works less well. Slowing your breathing and naming the feeling helps switch it back on.

steps.title: Thinking traps around exams
steps.body:
- **Catastrophising:** ‘One bad paper = my life is ruined’
- **All-or-nothing:** ‘If I don’t get 95%, I failed’
- **Mind-reading:** ‘Everyone will think I’m stupid’

Balanced version: ‘This exam matters, but it’s one step. There are many paths to a good life.’

steps.title: Worked example: reframing
steps.body:
Thought: ‘My heart is racing — I’m going to fail.’
Reframe: ‘My heart is racing because my body is getting ready. This energy can help me focus.’

Studies on **reappraisal** — telling yourself ‘I’m excited’ or ‘this is my body preparing’ — show it can improve performance compared with trying to ‘calm down’.

steps.title: When it’s more than nerves
steps.body: If exam fear causes panic attacks, stops you sleeping or eating for days, or leads to thoughts of self-harm, talk to someone today: a counsellor or **Tele-MANAS 14416**. Your life matters far more than any exam.

activity.label: Box breathing before an exam: in 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4

quiz.q: According to the stress curve, best performance comes with…
quiz.why: Performance is best with moderate arousal, as in the stress curve. No stress makes you sleepy, and extreme panic spoils thinking.

quiz.q: Why does the mind go blank?
options: Stress hormones reduce prefrontal cortex function
quiz.why: The mind goes blank because stress hormones reduce prefrontal cortex function, the part used for recall and planning. It doesn't mean you didn't study.

quiz.q: ‘One bad paper = my life is ruined’ is…
quiz.why: 'One bad paper = my life is ruined' is catastrophising, a thinking trap of jumping to the worst case. Balanced thinking looks at the facts.

quiz.q: Reappraisal means…
options: Seeing arousal as your body preparing to perform
quiz.why: Reappraisal means seeing arousal, like a racing heart, as your body preparing to perform. This reframe helps you use the energy.

quiz.q: Exam fear with thoughts of self-harm. You should…
quiz.why: Exam fear with thoughts of self-harm needs help now. Talk to someone today, such as Tele-MANAS 14416; studying more or hiding it is not enough.

lessons.title: Prepare like a pro: study methods that actually work

scenes.text: Rahul, 17, from Patna highlights every page and re-reads chapters five times. He still forgets everything in tests.
His cousin, a medical student, shows him research on ‘retrieval practice’ and ‘spacing’.
Rahul switches to self-quizzing and a spaced schedule.
Two months later his scores rise — and his fear drops because he can see his progress.

steps.title: What research says works
steps.body:
Cognitive science (e.g. Dunlosky et al., 2013) rates these highly:
- **Retrieval practice:** test yourself — close the book and recall, use flashcards, past papers
- **Spaced practice:** study a topic over several days rather than cramming

Moderately useful: **interleaving** (mixing problem types), **elaboration** (explaining why), **worked examples**.

Low value alone: **re-reading** and **highlighting** — they feel productive but lead to the ‘illusion of knowing’.

steps.title: Worked example: a spaced schedule
steps.body: Learn ‘chemical bonding’ on Day 1. Quiz yourself on Day 2, Day 4, Day 8, and Day 15. Each recall strengthens memory. Use a simple table: topic | dates reviewed | score.

steps.title: Focus and rest
steps.body:
- Work in focused blocks (e.g. 25–50 minutes) with short breaks
- Phone in another room
- Sleep 8–10 hours (teens) — sleep consolidates memory
- Exercise and eat regularly
- Practise under exam conditions to reduce surprise

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- All-night cramming
- Studying only favourite topics
- Comparing hours with friends instead of measuring what you can recall
- Energy drinks and skipping meals

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Pick one topic. Close the book and write everything you remember in 5 minutes. Check, correct, and repeat in 2 days.

activity.prompt: High-value or low-value study method?

items.text: Self-quizzing with flashcards
Re-reading the chapter five times
Spacing reviews over days
Highlighting everything
Solving past papers under timed conditions
Cramming all night before

quiz.q: Which method has strong research support?
quiz.why: Retrieval practice, testing yourself from memory, has strong research support. Cramming, highlighting and just re-reading are weaker.

quiz.q: Spaced practice means…
quiz.why: Spaced practice means spreading reviews over several days. It helps memory last better than one long session.

quiz.q: Why does re-reading feel good but work poorly?
options: Illusion of knowing — familiarity isn’t recall
quiz.why: Re-reading feels good because the material looks familiar, an illusion of knowing. Familiarity isn't the same as being able to recall.

quiz.q: Sleep and memory?
quiz.why: Sleep consolidates memory, so protect it before exams. It doesn't erase memory.

quiz.q: Interleaving means…
quiz.why: Interleaving means mixing problem types in a session. It helps you learn to choose the right method.

lessons.title: Exam day toolkit

scenes.text: Meera, 16, from Chennai wakes up on board-exam day with a knot in her stomach.
She follows her plan: breakfast, kit checked the night before, leaves early.
At her desk, she does box breathing, reads all questions, and starts with one she knows.
When she gets stuck, she marks it and moves on. She finishes on time.

steps.title: The night before
steps.body:
- Light revision only; no new topics
- Pack: admit card, ID, pens, pencils, ruler, water, watch (if allowed)
- Sleep at your usual time
- Lay out clothes

steps.title: Morning
steps.body:
- Eat a normal breakfast
- Leave early — rushing increases panic
- Avoid last-minute group panic chats; a quick calm review is fine

steps.title: In the hall
steps.body:
1. **Breathe:** 3 rounds of box breathing
2. **Read all questions** and instructions
3. **Start with what you know** to build momentum
4. **Plan time:** divide by marks
5. **Stuck?** Mark it, move on, return later
6. **Blank mind?** Breathe, write down anything related — keywords, a diagram — memory often follows
7. **Check** answers if time remains

steps.title: Worked example: time plan
steps.body: 3-hour paper, 80 marks → about 2 minutes per mark, leaving 15 minutes to read and 15 to check. A 5-mark question ≈ 10 minutes.

steps.title: After the exam
steps.body: Avoid post-mortems with friends that spiral into worry. You can’t change it now; rest and prepare for the next one.

activity.prompt: Put the exam-hall steps in a good order:
items: Do 3 rounds of slow breathing
Read all questions and instructions
Start with a question you know
Keep to your time plan
Mark tough questions and return later
Check answers at the end

quiz.q: Night before an exam, best plan?
options: Light revision, pack kit, usual sleep
quiz.why: The night before an exam, do light revision, pack your kit and keep your usual sleep. Rest helps recall more than all-nighters or new topics.

quiz.q: First thing at your desk?
options: Slow breathing then read all questions
quiz.why: At your desk, first breathe slowly, then read all the questions. Calm first, then plan, works better than panicking or looking at others.

quiz.q: Stuck on a question?
options: Mark it, move on, return later
quiz.why: If stuck, mark the question, move on and return later. This keeps momentum and saves time for other marks.

quiz.q: 80 marks in 150 working minutes — about how many minutes per mark?
quiz.why: 150 minutes ÷ 80 marks ≈ 1.9, so about 2 minutes per mark. Use this to pace yourself.

quiz.q: After the exam, best?
options: Rest and prepare for the next
quiz.why: After the exam, rest and prepare for the next one. Long worried post-mortems and comparing answers only add stress.

lessons.title: When results disappoint: failing well

scenes.text: Sundar, 18, from Coimbatore doesn’t clear his entrance exam. He locks himself in his room for days.
His father, who once failed a bank exam, sits with him: ‘I failed too. It hurt. Then I tried a different way.’
Together they analyse what went wrong, look at options — another attempt, other courses — and make a plan.
A year later Sundar is in a course he loves. ‘Failing taught me how to learn,’ he says.

steps.title: Feel it first
steps.body: Disappointment, shame, anger and grief after a bad result are normal. Let yourself feel them for a while. Talk to someone. Don’t make big decisions in the first 48 hours.

steps.title: Growth mindset (with nuance)
steps.body: Carol Dweck’s research suggests that seeing ability as something that grows with effort, strategy and help — rather than as fixed — supports learning. Later studies find effects are modest and work best combined with good strategies and support. The useful message: **failure is information, not identity.**

steps.title: Worked example: a failure review
steps.body:
1. **What happened?** Scored 40% in physics.
2. **What went well?** Chemistry improved.
3. **What didn’t?** Too much re-reading, no timed practice.
4. **What will I change?** Daily past-paper practice, ask for help with mechanics.
5. **What’s the next step this week?** Book a doubt session.

steps.title: Many paths
steps.body: There are many routes to a good career and life: other colleges, other courses, vocational paths, gap years, re-attempts. Many successful people failed exams. Your worth is not your marks.

steps.title: If you feel hopeless
steps.body: Results season is a known time of high distress. If you feel worthless or have thoughts of ending your life, talk to someone today: **Tele-MANAS 14416**, **112**, or a trusted adult. Parents: stay close and say ‘We love you no matter what.’

a.text: Results are out. You didn’t get the score you hoped for.

choices.label: Let yourself feel upset and talk to someone you trust
choices.feedback: Feelings first; connection helps.

choices.label: Lock yourself away and decide you’re a failure
choices.feedback: Isolation and labels make it heavier.

b.text: After a day or two, you feel ready to think.

choices.label: Do a failure review: what went well, what didn’t, what to change
choices.feedback: Turning failure into information.

choices.label: Decide never to try anything hard again
choices.feedback: Avoidance limits your future.

c.text: You feel worse and stop eating properly.

choices.label: Reach out to a parent, friend or call 14416
choices.feedback: Reaching out is strength.

d.text: You list options: re-attempt, another course, or a skill programme.

choices.label: Pick a next step for this week and ask for help
choices.feedback: Small steps rebuild confidence.

end1.text: You’re moving again. Failure became a turning point, not a full stop.

quiz.q: After a bad result, first…
options: Let yourself feel and talk to someone
quiz.why: After a bad result, let yourself feel and talk to someone. Feelings first, then plans; making big decisions at once or hiding doesn't help.

quiz.q: Growth mindset means…
options: Ability can grow with effort, strategy and help
quiz.why: Growth mindset means ability can grow with effort, good strategies and help. Talent is not fixed.

quiz.q: A failure review asks…
options: What went well, what didn’t, what to change
quiz.why: A failure review asks what went well, what didn't and what to change. It is a learning tool, not a way to blame yourself.

quiz.q: Your worth is…
quiz.why: Your worth is not defined by marks. There are many paths to a good life.

quiz.q: Thoughts of ending your life after results?
quiz.why: If you have thoughts of ending your life after results, talk to someone today. Call 14416 or 112; waiting or hiding it is unsafe.

questions.why: Best performance comes with moderate arousal, in the middle of the inverted-U curve. Extreme panic harms it.
Box breathing uses equal counts, 4-4-4-4: breathe in, hold, breathe out, hold. It calms the body.
Failure is information, not identity. It tells you what to change, not who you are.
Retrieval practice, testing yourself, is a high-value study method. Highlighting is weaker.
If stuck in an exam, mark it and move on. That keeps momentum.
Keep your usual sleep the night before, because sleep helps memory and focus. An all-nighter hurts performance.
Catastrophising is jumping to the worst case. It is a thinking trap, not planning.
Spaced practice spreads reviews over days. It works better than one long session.
If your mind goes blank, breathe and jot related keywords to cue recall. Leaving is not needed.

questions.q: Why does the mind go blank?
questions.why: The mind goes blank because stress reduces prefrontal function. It is not laziness.
Reappraisal is seeing arousal as preparation. Suppressing it usually doesn't work.

questions.q: Growth mindset effects in later studies?
options: Modest; best with good strategies and support
questions.why: Growth mindset effects in later studies were modest, and best with good strategies and support. It is not a huge effect on its own.
Minutes per mark = total time ÷ marks = 150 ÷ 75 = 2 minutes per mark. Use this to pace yourself in the exam.

courses.title: Never fear the stage: public speaking for everyone
courses.summary: Why stage fright happens, how to prepare a talk, what to do on the day, and how to speak up in class, meetings and life.
outcomes: Learners can explain stage fright and the spotlight effect
Learners can structure and rehearse a short talk
Learners can use voice, body and breathing on the day
Learners can build a speaking ladder for everyday life

lessons.title: Why the stage feels scary

scenes.text: Ravi, 12, from Jaipur is chosen to speak at the school assembly. His hands tremble just thinking about it.
He imagines everyone laughing at him.
His teacher tells him that most people — even famous actors — feel stage fright.
Ravi learns that the audience usually notices far less nervousness than he feels.

steps.title: Stage fright is normal
steps.body: Fear of public speaking is one of the most common fears worldwide. Your body reacts to an audience like a threat: fast heart, dry mouth, shaky voice, sweaty palms. It’s the same alarm system as other fears — uncomfortable, but not dangerous.

steps.title: The spotlight effect
steps.body: Research shows people **overestimate how much others notice** their nervousness or mistakes (the ‘spotlight effect’ and ‘illusion of transparency’). The audience mostly sees a person talking — not your racing heart.

steps.title: Worked example: thought check
steps.body:
Fear: ‘Everyone will laugh if I forget a line.’
Check: ‘When others forget lines, do I laugh? Usually I feel sympathy.’
Balanced: ‘If I forget, I’ll pause, check my notes and continue.’

steps.title: Calm the body
steps.body: Slow breathing with a long out-breath, loosening shoulders, a sip of water, and grounding your feet all calm the alarm before you go on.

activity.label: Before going on stage: in 4, out slowly 6, rest 2

quiz.q: Stage fright is…
quiz.why: Stage fright is very common, even among experienced speakers. It is not a disease or only for kids.

quiz.q: The spotlight effect means…
options: We overestimate how much others notice our nerves
quiz.why: The spotlight effect is the tendency to overestimate how much others notice our nerves or mistakes. Most people are focused on themselves.

quiz.q: A long out-breath helps because…
quiz.why: A long out-breath helps because it calms the body's alarm by switching on the calming (parasympathetic) system. It slows the heart and eases nerves.

quiz.q: If you forget a line, best plan?
quiz.why: If you forget a line, pause, check your notes and continue. Apologising repeatedly or running off makes it feel bigger than it is.

lessons.title: Prepare: structure, practice, notes

scenes.text: Kavya, 21, a college student in Pune, has a 5-minute talk on plastic waste.
She writes a clear structure: hook, three points, story, call to action.
She practises out loud six times — to a mirror, her roommate, and a phone camera.
On the day, she still feels nervous — but she knows her material, and it shows.

steps.title: A simple structure
steps.body:
- **Hook:** a question, surprising fact or short story
- **Point 1, 2, 3:** each with an example
- **Story:** a real person or moment
- **Close:** a summary and one clear action

The ‘rule of three’ makes talks easy to follow and remember.

steps.title: Practise out loud
steps.body: Thinking through a talk isn’t the same as saying it. Practise **aloud** at least 3–5 times, standing, with a timer. Record once and watch it back — you’ll usually look calmer than you felt. Practise in front of one friend, then a small group.

steps.title: Notes that help
steps.body: Use **keyword cards**, not full scripts. Number them. Memorise your first two sentences and your closing line — the start and end matter most.

steps.title: Worked example: a 3-minute talk
steps.body: Hook (20 s): ‘Every minute, a truckload of plastic enters the ocean.’ Point 1 (40 s) · Point 2 (40 s) · Point 3 (40 s) · Close (20 s) + 20 s buffer.

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading a full script word-for-word
- Too many slides with too much text
- Practising only silently
- Speaking too fast — pause after key points

activity.prompt: Put a short talk in order:
items: Hook: a question or surprising fact
Point 1 with an example
Point 2 with an example
Point 3 with an example
A short story
Close with a summary and one action

quiz.q: Which structure is easy to follow?
quiz.why: Hook, three points, story and close is an easy structure to follow, as the rule of three helps both you and listeners remember. Random facts or only jokes lack structure.

quiz.q: Best kind of notes?
quiz.why: Numbered keyword cards give you prompts without a script, so you can speak naturally. A full script tempts you to read it, and no notes can leave you stuck.

quiz.q: Why practise out loud?
options: Silent rehearsal isn’t the same as speaking
quiz.why: Practise out loud, because silent rehearsal isn't the same as speaking. Your mouth, pace and breath need practice too.

quiz.q: Which parts should you memorise?
quiz.why: Memorise the opening and closing lines, because starting and ending strongly matter most. Memorising every word makes it fragile if you forget one.

quiz.q: A common mistake?
quiz.why: Speaking too fast is a common mistake, because nerves speed us up. Slow down and pause after key points.

lessons.title: On the day: voice, body and nerves

scenes.text: Imran, 16, from Lucknow is in the inter-school debate. Just before his turn, his knees shake.
He does three slow breaths, plants his feet, and finds a friendly face in the audience.
His first sentence is slow and clear. His voice steadies.
He doesn’t win — but he’s proud he did it, and signs up for the next one.

steps.title: Body
steps.body:
- Stand with feet hip-width apart, weight balanced
- Hands relaxed at sides or gesturing naturally
- Look at friendly faces in different parts of the room for a few seconds each
- Smile at the start

steps.title: Voice
steps.body:
- Breathe from the belly
- Speak a little slower and louder than feels natural
- Pause after key points — pauses look confident
- Warm up: hum, yawn, say tongue twisters

steps.title: Nerves on the day
steps.body:
- Arrive early; check mic and slides
- Do a quick breathing round and shoulder rolls
- Say to yourself: ‘I’m excited and ready’
- Hold notes or a clicker to steady hands
- Remember: the audience wants you to do well

steps.title: Worked example: handling a mistake
steps.body: You lose your place. Pause, take a sip of water, look at your card, and continue: ‘Where was I — yes, point two.’ Most listeners won’t notice; those who do will respect your calm.

activity.prompt: Speaker’s day-of checklist:
items: Arrive early and check mic/slides
Warm up my voice
Do 3 rounds of slow breathing
Memorise first and last lines
Plant my feet and find friendly faces
Speak slower and pause
If I slip: pause, sip water, continue

quiz.q: Pauses make you look…
quiz.why: Pauses make you look confident, because they show control and give listeners time to think. They don't look nervous or lost.

quiz.q: Where should you look?
options: At friendly faces around the room
quiz.why: Look at friendly faces around the room, which connects you with the audience. Staring at your phone, the ceiling or the floor breaks that connection.

quiz.q: Shaky hands?
quiz.why: If your hands shake, hold notes or a clicker to steady them. Hiding, clenching fists or leaving doesn't help.

quiz.q: You lose your place. Best?
options: Pause, sip water, check notes, continue
quiz.why: If you lose your place, pause, sip water, check your notes and continue. Nervous laughing, repeated apologies or stopping make it worse.

quiz.q: Audience wants you to…
quiz.why: The audience wants you to do well, because they are on your side. Most people feel sympathy for a nervous speaker.

lessons.title: Speaking up in class, meetings and life

scenes.text: Neha, 23, joins a tech firm in Hyderabad. In meetings she has ideas but stays silent, afraid of sounding silly.
Her mentor suggests a ladder: ask one question this week, share one idea next week.
Her first question is simple — and her manager thanks her.
Three months later she presents to the client.

steps.title: Build a speaking ladder
steps.body:
Fear shrinks with **gradual practice** (exposure). Steps:
1. Ask one question in class or a meeting
2. Answer a question you know
3. Share one idea
4. Present for 2 minutes to a small group
5. Present to a larger group

Move up when a step feels manageable.

steps.title: Useful phrases
steps.body:
- ‘Can I add something?’
- ‘Building on what Arjun said…’
- ‘I have a question about…’
- ‘I’m not sure, but one idea is…’

steps.title: Join a practice space
steps.body: Debate clubs, drama groups, Toastmasters-style clubs and college societies give safe, regular practice.

steps.title: When fear is bigger
steps.body: If fear of being judged stops you attending classes, meetings or social events for months, it may be **social anxiety disorder** — very treatable with CBT. Talk to a counsellor or **Tele-MANAS 14416**.

activity.label: How scary is speaking up for you right now?

bands.text: Low fear — great time to take on bigger steps like presenting.
Medium — start with questions and short contributions; move up weekly.
High — begin with tiny steps (one question in a small group) and practise breathing first.
Very high — fear is stopping you. Consider talking to a counsellor; CBT works well for social anxiety.

quiz.q: A speaking ladder works by…
quiz.why: A speaking ladder works by gradual exposure, taking small steps from easy to harder. Jumping to the hardest step or avoiding keeps the fear.

quiz.q: A good phrase to join a discussion?
quiz.why: 'Building on what Arjun said…' joins a discussion by linking to someone else's idea, which is collaborative. 'You're wrong' or 'Whatever' shuts others down.

quiz.q: Where can you practise regularly?
quiz.why: Debate or drama clubs offer regular, supportive places to practise speaking. Practising only alone or never doesn't build the skill.

quiz.q: Fear of judgement stopping daily life for months may be…
quiz.why: Fear of judgement that stops daily life for months may be social anxiety disorder, which is treatable. It isn't rudeness or laziness.

quiz.q: First step on the ladder?
quiz.why: The first step on a speaking ladder is small, like asking one question. A keynote or TV interview is far too big to start with.

questions.why: Stage fright is common and happens to many people, even experienced speakers.
Keyword cards act as prompts, so you speak naturally. A full script makes you read.
Pauses look confident, because they show control. They don't look weak.
The spotlight effect is overestimating how much others notice our nerves. It has nothing to do with bright lights.
Practise out loud, since silent rehearsal isn't the same as speaking.
Memorise the opening and closing, since strong starts and ends matter most. You needn't memorise everything.
The rule of three helps memory and clarity, since three points are easy to follow and remember. It isn't meant to lengthen a talk.
If you lose your place, pause, check your notes and continue. Leaving makes the situation worse.
A speaking ladder uses gradual exposure, moving up from easy to harder steps. Avoidance keeps fear alive.

options: It activates the body’s calming system
questions.why: A long out-breath activates the body's calming system, slowing the heart rate. It isn't about being loud.

options: Thinking your nerves are obvious to others
questions.why: The illusion of transparency is thinking your nerves are obvious to others. In fact, people notice far less than you think.
CBT (cognitive behavioural therapy) is an evidence-based treatment for social anxiety disorder. Avoidance keeps it going.

questions.q: 3-minute talk with 20 s hook, 20 s close, 20 s buffer — time per point for 3 points?
questions.why: A 3-minute talk is 180 s. Subtract 20 + 20 + 20 = 60 s, which leaves 120 s, and 120 ÷ 3 = 40 s per point.

courses.title: The fear toolkit: heights, water, strangers, failure
courses.summary: For teens and adults: why avoidance backfires, how to build a fear ladder (heights, water, lifts), talking to strangers and networking, and facing fear of failure and judgement.
outcomes: Learners can explain the avoidance trap and habituation
Learners can build and climb a fear ladder
Learners can start and end conversations with strangers safely
Learners can use fear-setting and small tests to act despite fear of failure

lessons.title: How fear works and why avoidance backfires

scenes.text: Pooja, 28, from Mumbai has avoided lifts for ten years after getting stuck once. She climbs 14 floors to her office.
Her fear has spread: now she avoids metros and crowded rooms too.
A psychologist explains how avoidance teaches the brain ‘that was dangerous’.
They build a plan to face it in small steps.

steps.title: The avoidance trap
steps.body: When we avoid something scary, we feel instant relief. The brain learns: ‘Avoiding kept me safe.’ So next time the fear is **stronger** — and often spreads to similar situations. This is why avoidance makes fears grow.

steps.title: Habituation and new learning
steps.body: If you stay in a feared (but safe) situation long enough, or repeat it often, fear **comes down by itself** and the brain learns ‘I can cope’. This is the basis of **exposure therapy**, one of the most effective treatments for phobias.

steps.title: Worked example: a fear curve
steps.body: Pooja stands in a lift with the door open. Fear: 7/10 at minute 1, 8/10 at minute 2, 6/10 at minute 5, 3/10 at minute 10. Staying until it drops teaches her brain something new.

steps.title: Safety behaviours
steps.body: Hidden ‘crutches’ — always holding a friend’s arm, constant phone checking, carrying a ‘lucky’ item — can stop learning. Gradually drop them as you progress.

statements.s: Avoiding a fear makes it smaller over time.
Fear often comes down if you stay in a safe situation long enough.
Exposure therapy is one of the most effective treatments for phobias.
Safety behaviours always help long-term.

quiz.q: Why does avoidance backfire?
options: It teaches the brain the situation was dangerous
quiz.why: Avoidance backfires because it teaches the brain that the situation was dangerous, so fear grows. Facing it shows you can cope.

quiz.q: Habituation means…
options: Fear decreasing with safe, repeated exposure
quiz.why: Habituation is when fear decreases with safe, repeated exposure, as the brain learns the situation is not harmful. It doesn't rise forever.

quiz.q: A safety behaviour is…
options: A hidden crutch that blocks learning
quiz.why: A safety behaviour is a hidden crutch, such as always carrying something for comfort, that blocks learning that you can cope without it. Drop it gradually.

quiz.q: Pooja’s fear spread to metros because…
quiz.why: Pooja's fear spread to metros because avoidance generalised the fear to similar situations. Avoiding more places made her fear grow wider.

lessons.title: Build your fear ladder

scenes.text: Sanjay, 35, from Bengaluru, got a dream job on the 30th floor but freezes near windows.
He writes a fear ladder from 1 to 10.
Every few days he climbs a rung: looking at photos, standing on a 2nd-floor balcony, then 5th, then near office windows.
Two months later he enjoys the city view at lunch.

steps.title: How to build a ladder
steps.body:
1. Write your fear goal (e.g. ‘stand by a 30th-floor window’)
2. List 8–10 steps from easy (2/10 fear) to hard (9/10)
3. Start with a step that is challenging but doable (about 3–4/10)
4. Stay until fear drops by about half, or repeat several times
5. Move up when a step feels manageable
6. Practise often — several times a week

steps.title: Worked example: Sanjay’s ladder
steps.body:
1. Look at photos from tall buildings (2)
2. Watch a drone video (3)
3. Stand on a 2nd-floor balcony (4)
4. 5th-floor balcony (5)
5. Glass lift in a mall with a friend (6)
6. Glass lift alone (7)
7. 20th-floor window, 1 metre away (8)
8. 30th-floor window, touching the glass (9)

steps.title: Tools on each rung
steps.body: Slow breathing, naming the feeling, and a coping statement: ‘This is uncomfortable, not dangerous. It will pass.’ Don’t use breathing to ‘escape’ — use it to stay.

steps.title: When to get help
steps.body: If a phobia seriously limits life, or if it involves a trauma, work with a psychologist. For medical fears (needles, blood), tell your doctor — some people faint with blood/needle fear and a specific technique called ‘applied tension’ helps.

activity.prompt: Arrange this fear-of-water ladder from easiest to hardest:
items: Watch videos of people swimming
Sit by the pool with feet in
Stand in the shallow end with an instructor
Put your face in the water and blow bubbles
Float with support
Swim a width with the instructor beside you

quiz.q: First ladder step should be…
quiz.why: The first ladder step should be challenging but doable, about 3–4 out of 10 in fear. Starting with the hardest is too much, and zero fear teaches nothing.

quiz.q: Stay on a step until…
options: Fear drops by about half, or repeat several times
quiz.why: Stay on a step until fear drops by about half, or repeat it several times. That is when the brain learns it is safe. Leaving at peak panic reinforces fear.

quiz.q: Breathing should be used to…
quiz.why: Use breathing to stay in the situation, not to escape or avoid it. It supports exposure instead of replacing it.

quiz.q: Fainting with needle fear may be helped by…
quiz.why: Applied tension, tensing muscles to raise blood pressure, helps prevent fainting with needle or blood fear. Running, holding breath or avoiding doctors doesn't.

quiz.q: How often to practise?
quiz.why: Practising several times a week works best, because frequent exposure builds learning. Once a year or only when forced is too little.

lessons.title: Talking to strangers: networking, asking for help and small talk

scenes.text: Lin, 26, a PhD student from Shillong, attends her first conference in Delhi. She stands in a corner during tea breaks.
Her supervisor suggests a mission: start three conversations using a simple script.
She says to a nearby researcher: ‘Hi, I’m Lin. What did you think of the morning talk?’
By the end of the day she has two new collaborators.

steps.title: Why strangers feel scary
steps.body: We often fear rejection or awkwardness. Studies on talking to strangers (e.g. commuters asked to chat) show people **underestimate** how much others will enjoy the conversation and how much **they themselves** will enjoy it.

steps.title: Simple scripts
steps.body:
- **Open:** ‘Hi, I’m ___. What brings you here?’
- **Shared moment:** ‘That talk was interesting — what did you think?’
- **Follow-up:** ‘How did you get into that?’
- **Exit kindly:** ‘Great to meet you — I’ll grab a coffee. Let’s connect.’

steps.title: Asking for help
steps.body: Asking a stranger for directions or help is normal: ‘Excuse me, could you tell me where Platform 4 is?’ Most people like helping.

steps.title: Safety as an adult
steps.body: Be friendly but careful: meet new contacts in public places, don’t share bank details or OTPs, and be wary of strangers online who move quickly to money, romance or ‘investment’ talk — common scam patterns. Report cyber fraud at **1930**.

cards.back: ‘Hi, I’m ___. What brings you here?’
‘What did you think of that talk?’
‘How did you get into that?’
‘Great to meet you — let’s connect.’
‘Excuse me, could you tell me…?’
A new contact quickly asks for money, OTPs or ‘investments’

quiz.q: People usually ___ how much they’ll enjoy talking to a stranger.
quiz.why: Research shows people underestimate how much they will enjoy talking to a stranger. So the real experience is usually better than expected.

quiz.q: A good opener?
options: ‘Hi, I’m Lin. What brings you here?’
quiz.why: 'Hi, I'm Lin. What brings you here?' is friendly and invites conversation. Silence, abrupt questions or a CV straight away isn't.

quiz.q: A kind exit line?
quiz.why: 'Great to meet you — let's connect.' is a graceful exit. Looking at your phone, yawning or walking off silently is rude.

quiz.q: Red flag with a new online contact?
options: Quickly asks for money or OTPs
quiz.why: A new online contact who quickly asks for money or OTPs is a scam red flag. Genuine people don't rush to ask for this.

quiz.q: Cyber fraud helpline?
quiz.why: The cyber fraud helpline is 1930. 1098 is Childline, 181 the Women's Helpline and 14446 the drug helpline.

lessons.title: Fear of failure and judgement in adult life

scenes.text: Vikram, 40, from Indore has had a business idea for years. Fear of failing — and of what relatives will say — stops him.
His coach asks: ‘What’s the worst case? How likely? How would you cope?’
He tests the idea small: a weekend stall.
It doesn’t make much money, but he learns a lot — and his second version works.

steps.title: Fear of failure
steps.body: Fear of failure often protects us from shame and judgement. But avoiding risk can cost more: missed chances, regret. **Perfectionism** — needing everything flawless — is a common driver.

steps.title: Fear-setting
steps.body:
Write:
1. **Define:** worst things that could happen
2. **Prevent:** what could reduce each risk
3. **Repair:** if it happened, how would I recover?
4. **Benefits** of trying, even if partly successful
5. **Cost of inaction** in 6 months, 1 year, 3 years

steps.title: Worked example: test small
steps.body: Instead of quitting his job, Vikram ran a weekend stall, then an online page, then a small shop. Each step was a cheap ‘experiment’ — failure became data.

steps.title: Handling judgement
steps.body: ‘Log kya kahenge’ (‘what will people say’) is powerful in India. Ask: Whose opinion truly matters? Will this matter in 5 years? Most people are busy with their own lives.

activity.prompt: What’s one thing you’d try if you weren’t afraid of failing? Write the worst case, how you’d recover, and the smallest first test.
activity.hint: Think about a small, low-cost experiment you could do this month.

quiz.q: Fear-setting includes…
options: Define, prevent, repair, benefits, cost of inaction
quiz.why: Fear-setting involves defining the fear, how to prevent it, how to repair it, the benefits of trying and the cost of inaction. It makes risk clearer.

quiz.q: Testing small means…
quiz.why: Testing small means running cheap experiments before big commitments. It reduces risk without avoiding the goal.

quiz.q: Perfectionism often…
quiz.why: Perfectionism often drives fear of failure, because any mistake feels unacceptable. It doesn't prevent mistakes.

quiz.q: A useful question about judgement?
quiz.why: 'Will this matter in 5 years?' gives perspective about judgement. 'What will everyone think?' feeds the fear.

questions.why: Avoidance makes fear stronger, since the brain never learns the situation is safe.
Exposure therapy has strong evidence for phobias. It helps people face fears gradually.
A fear ladder starts at a doable step, then moves up. Starting at the hardest is too overwhelming.

options: Fear drops with repeated safe exposure
questions.why: Habituation is when fear drops with repeated safe exposure. It doesn't rise.
Safety behaviours can block learning, since you credit the crutch instead of learning you can cope. Drop them gradually.
Talking to strangers is usually more enjoyable than expected, as research shows. It isn't always awful.
The 'repair' step in fear-setting asks how you would recover if things went wrong. It is about coping, not blame.

questions.q: Breathing during exposure should help you…
questions.why: Breathing during exposure should help you stay in the situation. Using it to escape defeats the purpose.
Quick requests for money or OTPs are a scam red flag. A polite greeting is normal.
Applied tension helps with fainting from blood or needle fear by raising blood pressure. It isn't a tool for exams.
Generalising means fear spreads to similar situations. It doesn't disappear on its own.
Cost of inaction is a step in fear-setting, where you consider what staying stuck would cost you. It isn't part of exposure.

questions.q: Stay on a ladder step until…
options: Fear drops noticeably or after repeats
questions.why: Stay on a ladder step until fear drops noticeably or after several repeats. Leaving instantly reinforces avoidance.

wellbeing-puberty.title: Puberty: growing up without fear
wellbeing-puberty.description: Calm, medically accurate guides to puberty for girls and boys — first periods, nightfall, body changes, hygiene and feelings — plus a shared course on respecting each other.

courses.title: Growing up as a girl: periods, breasts and body changes
courses.summary: Everything a girl needs for puberty and her first period — calmly explained: breast development, how the cycle works, pads/cups/tampons and hygiene, cramps, PMS, PCOS and when to see a doctor.
outcomes: Learners can describe the main body changes of puberty for girls and the normal age ranges
Learners can explain the menstrual cycle and calculate their cycle length
Learners can choose and safely use pads, cups, tampons or period underwear and dispose of them correctly
Learners can manage cramps and PMS and recognise signs that need a doctor, including PCOS
Learners can reject common period myths with facts
courses.guardianNote: Covers the body changes of puberty for girls: breast development, the menstrual cycle, the first period, choosing and using pads, cups, tampons and period underwear, hygiene and safe disposal, cramps and PMS, and when to see a doctor (including PCOS awareness). Language is medically accurate, calm and non-explicit, in line with UNESCO ITGSE 2018 and NCERT ‘Reaching the Age of Adolescence’. Ideally explored with a parent or trusted adult nearby, and suitable for boys too.

lessons.title: What puberty is — and when it starts

scenes.text: Ananya, 10, from Pune notices her school uniform feels tight across her chest and she has grown 6 cm since last Diwali.
Her cousin Riya, also 10, hasn't changed at all. Ananya worries: ‘Is something wrong with me — or with her?’
Her Mausi explains: ‘Puberty is your body slowly turning from a child’s body into an adult’s. It starts at different times for everyone.’
Ananya relaxes. Both she and Riya are completely normal.

steps.title: Puberty in one sentence
steps.body:
Puberty is the set of changes that turns a child’s body into an adult body that could one day have a baby. It is controlled by **hormones** — chemical messengers. In girls the brain signals the **ovaries** to make more **oestrogen** (also spelled estrogen), and that hormone drives most of the changes.

It is not an illness and not something you can speed up or stop. It simply happens, over several years.

steps.title: When does it start?
steps.body:
For most girls puberty begins between **8 and 13 years**. The first sign is usually small, tender ‘breast buds’. Then, over the next few years:
- a **growth spurt** (you may grow 6–8 cm in a year)
- hair under the arms and in the pubic area
- hips become wider and body shape becomes curvier
- skin becomes oilier, and pimples may appear
- sweat begins to smell stronger
- a white or clear discharge from the vagina, often 6–12 months before the first period
- the **first period**, usually about 2 years after breasts start to grow (commonly between 10 and 15)

steps.title: Worked example: two normal timelines
steps.body:
**Meher** (Delhi): breast buds at 9, first period at 11.

**Grace** (Kochi): breast buds at 12, first period at 14½.

Both are healthy. The order of changes is fairly similar for most girls, but the **start age and the speed** vary a lot. Genes (when your mother started), nutrition and body weight all play a part.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Comparing yourself with friends** and deciding you are ‘too early’ or ‘too late’. A wide range is normal.
- **Believing puberty makes you ‘impure’** or that you must hide. It is a healthy sign that your body is working.
- **Dieting to delay changes** — this is harmful. Growing bodies need good food, especially iron, calcium and protein.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body:
Talk to a doctor if:
- breasts start growing **before age 8**, or
- there are **no signs of puberty by 13**, or
- there is **no period by 15**, or none within 3 years of breasts starting to grow.

Usually all is well, but a check-up can rule out problems. This is general health education, not medical advice. If something worries you, see a doctor, nurse or counsellor.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write down three changes you have noticed (or expect) and one question you are shy to ask. Keep it — by the end of this course you will be able to answer it, or you’ll know who to ask.

activity.prompt: Put these typical puberty changes for girls in the usual order (it varies, but this is most common):
items: Breast buds appear
Growth spurt speeds up
Pubic and underarm hair grow
White vaginal discharge begins
First period
Periods slowly become more regular

quiz.q: Which hormone drives most puberty changes in girls?
quiz.why: The ovaries make more oestrogen when puberty begins; it drives breast growth, body shape changes and the menstrual cycle.

quiz.q: What is usually the FIRST sign of puberty in girls?
quiz.why: Small, sometimes tender breast buds are usually first; the first period typically comes about two years later.

quiz.q: Priya is 12 and has no signs of puberty yet, while her best friend has periods. What is true?
quiz.why: Puberty commonly starts anywhere from 8 to 13. A doctor check is suggested only if there are no signs by 13.

quiz.q: A white or clear discharge before the first period is…
quiz.why: This discharge is normal and keeps the vagina clean. See a doctor only if it smells bad, itches, or is green/grey.

quiz.q: When is a doctor check recommended?
options: Periods are irregular in the first year
quiz.why: No period by 15 (or 3 years after breasts begin) is a reason for a check-up. The others are normal.

lessons.title: Breast development and choosing a bra

scenes.text: Fatima, 11, in Hyderabad feels a small, sore lump under one nipple. The other side feels flat.
She is frightened it’s something serious and hides it for a week.
Finally she tells her Ammi, who takes her to the school nurse. The nurse smiles: ‘That’s a breast bud — the very first step of growing up.’
Ammi and Fatima pick out two soft cotton beginner bras. Fatima feels relieved and grown-up.

steps.title: How breasts grow
steps.body:
Breasts develop in **stages over 3–5 years**. First a small, firm bud forms under the nipple. The area around the nipple (the **areola**) widens and darkens. Slowly fat and milk-gland tissue grow, and the breast becomes rounder and fuller.

Growth can feel **tender, itchy or sore** — especially when bumped. This is normal and eases with time.

steps.title: Uneven is normal
steps.body: It is very common for **one breast to start growing before the other**, or for one to stay slightly larger even in adulthood. Breasts come in every size and shape, and size has nothing to do with health or the ability to breastfeed later.

steps.title: Worked example: does she need a bra?
steps.body:
A bra is a **comfort choice, not a medical need**. Fatima’s nurse suggests:
- **Starter / training bra or a cotton slip** when buds feel sore or show through clothes
- **Sports bra** for running, sports or dance — reduces bouncing and discomfort
- **Fitted bra** later, measured around the ribcage under the breasts and across the fullest part

Signs of a good fit: the band is snug but you can slide two fingers under it, straps don’t dig in, nothing presses or pinches.

steps.title: Myths to drop
steps.body:
- ‘Sleeping in a bra stops growth’ — false.
- ‘Small breasts mean you are not healthy’ — false.
- ‘Massage, creams or exercises change breast size’ — false; size is mostly genes and body fat.
- ‘A lump in a growing breast is cancer’ — almost always false in children; it is usually a bud. Still, any lump that worries you should be shown to a doctor.

steps.title: If someone teases you
steps.body: Comments about your chest or bra straps are **not okay** — at school or online. You can say ‘That’s not funny, stop.’ and tell a teacher. Bodies changing is private and normal; teasing is the problem, not you.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: See a doctor if there is **fluid coming from the nipple**, redness with fever, a lump that keeps growing or feels hard and fixed, or breasts starting before age 8. This is general health education, not medical advice. If something worries you, see a doctor, nurse or counsellor.

statements.s: It is normal for one breast to grow before the other.
statements.why: Very common, and they often even out — a small difference into adulthood is also normal.

statements.s: Wearing a bra is medically required once breasts start growing.
statements.why: A bra is for comfort and support, especially during sports. It is your choice.

statements.s: Breast buds can feel sore or tender.
statements.why: Growing tissue is sensitive; it usually eases over months.

statements.s: Creams or exercises can make breasts bigger.
statements.why: Breast size depends mostly on genes and body fat. Products claiming otherwise do not work.

statements.s: A sports bra can make running more comfortable.
statements.why: It reduces movement and discomfort during exercise.

quiz.q: Fatima feels a small sore lump under one nipple at age 11. Most likely it is…
quiz.why: At this age a small tender lump under the nipple is almost always the first stage of breast development.

quiz.q: How long does breast development usually take?
quiz.why: Breast development usually takes about 3–5 years, moving gradually through several stages. It doesn't happen in weeks or finish at age 10.

quiz.q: Which shows a good bra fit?
options: Snug band, two fingers fit under it, no pinching
Cups gape and band rides up
Band so tight you cannot breathe deeply
quiz.why: A good bra fit has a snug band, with two fingers able to fit under it, and no pinching or digging. Gaping cups or a band that rides up means a poor fit.

quiz.q: Which needs a doctor visit?
options: Fluid coming out of the nipple
quiz.why: Fluid coming out of the nipple should be checked by a doctor. A darker areola, mild soreness and one breast slightly bigger are normal during development.

quiz.q: Someone snaps your bra strap as a ‘joke’. Best response?
options: Say clearly it’s not okay and tell a teacher
quiz.why: Unwanted touching is not a joke. Saying stop and telling an adult protects you and others.

lessons.title: Your first period: what is actually happening

scenes.text: Zoya, 12, from Lucknow, feels a damp feeling during maths class. In the toilet she sees a brownish-red stain on her underwear.
Her heart races: ‘Am I hurt?’ She remembers her health class — this is her **first period**.
She tells Ms. D’Souza, who quietly gives her a pad from the emergency kit and a spare pair of shorts.
Zoya calls her mother, who says ‘Congratulations, beta — your body is healthy. Let’s talk tonight.’
By evening Zoya feels proud, not ashamed.

steps.title: The menstrual cycle, simply
steps.body:
Inside the lower belly is the **uterus** (womb), a hollow muscle about the size of a fist, with two **ovaries** and two **fallopian tubes**.

Each cycle:
- Hormones make the **lining of the uterus** thicken, like preparing a soft bed.
- Around the middle of the cycle an ovary releases a tiny **egg** (ovulation).
- If the egg is not fertilised, the body doesn’t need the lining. It breaks down and leaves through the **vagina** as the period — a mix of blood and tissue.
- Then the cycle starts again.

steps.title: Numbers that are normal
steps.body:
- **First period (menarche):** usually 10–15 years.
- **Period length:** 2–7 days.
- **Cycle length** (first day of one period to first day of the next): in adults 21–35 days; in the **first 2–3 years** it is often irregular — anything from about 21 to 45 days is common.
- **Blood amount:** usually only a few tablespoons in the whole period, even though it can look like more.
- **Colour:** bright red, dark red or brown are all normal. Small clots (smaller than a ₹1 coin) can be normal on heavy days.

steps.title: Worked example: counting your cycle
steps.body:
Zoya’s period started on **3 March**. Her next started on **5 April**.

Count every day from 3 March up to 4 April (the day before the next period starts): 3–31 March = 29 days, plus 1–4 April = 4 days → cycle = **33 days**. Normal.

Tip: mark the first day of each period on a calendar or a period-tracking app. After a few months you can predict your next one and carry a pad.

steps.title: Myths that hurt girls
steps.body:
- ‘You can’t bathe or wash your hair during periods’ — **false**. Bathing keeps you clean and eases cramps.
- ‘You can’t touch pickles, cook or enter the kitchen’ — **false**. Periods are not dirty or contagious.
- ‘You shouldn’t exercise or play’ — **false**. Movement often helps cramps.
- ‘Period blood is impure’ — **false**. It is ordinary blood and tissue.

Cultural and religious practices are a family matter, but no practice is needed for health.

steps.title: Your period emergency kit
steps.body:
Keep a small pouch in your school bag:
- 2 pads (or your chosen product)
- a spare pair of underwear
- a small paper/plastic bag for wrapped used pads
- tissues or wet wipes

If you leak: tie a jumper around your waist, ask the teacher or nurse for help. Teachers deal with this often — you are not the first.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body:
- soaking a pad every **1–2 hours** for several hours
- periods lasting **more than 7 days**
- cycles **shorter than 21 days** or longer than 45 days after the first couple of years
- feeling dizzy, very tired or breathless (possible anaemia)
- pain that stops you going to school

This is general health education, not medical advice. If something worries you, see a doctor, nurse or counsellor.

a.text: You’re in class and feel your period has started unexpectedly. You don’t have a pad.

choices.label: Ask the teacher to go to the toilet, then ask a trusted teacher or nurse for a pad
choices.feedback: Great — adults at school keep supplies and know what to do.

choices.label: Sit still and hope it stops until home time
choices.feedback: Periods don’t stop on command; waiting hours can mean leaking and discomfort.

b.text: The nurse gives you a pad. There’s a small stain on your skirt.

choices.label: Tie a jumper around your waist and carry on
choices.feedback: Simple and smart. Rinse the stain in cold water at home.

choices.label: Run home without telling anyone
choices.feedback: Leaving school without permission is unsafe. Tell an adult — they can help or call home.

c.text: An hour later you feel a leak.

choices.label: Now quietly tell a friend or teacher
choices.feedback: Better late than never — help is always available.

choices.label: Keep hiding it
choices.feedback: Hiding makes it harder. Periods are normal; asking for help is brave.

end1.text: Well handled! Next time, keep a period kit in your bag and track your dates.

end2.text: Remember: teachers, nurses and friends can help. Asking is the safest choice. Try again?

quiz.q: Where does period blood come from?
quiz.why: Each cycle the uterus lining thickens; if no pregnancy happens it is shed as the period.

quiz.q: Which period length is normal?
quiz.why: A normal period lasts about 2–7 days. A month, 14 days or half a day is outside the usual range.

quiz.q: In the first couple of years, cycles are often…
quiz.why: In the first couple of years, cycles are often irregular, roughly 21 to 45 days, while hormones settle. They are not usually exactly 28 days at first.

quiz.q: Is it safe to bathe and wash hair during a period?
options: Yes, and it helps you feel fresh
quiz.why: Yes, bathing and washing hair during periods is safe and helps you feel fresh. Warm water can even ease cramps.

quiz.q: Which needs a doctor?
options: Brown blood on the last day
Soaking a pad every hour for several hours
quiz.why: Very heavy bleeding needs checking for causes such as anaemia or a bleeding disorder.

lessons.title: Pads, cups, tampons and period underwear — hygiene and disposal

scenes.text: Kavya, 15, from Chennai, has a swimming competition on day 2 of her period.
She has only used pads and wonders if a tampon or a menstrual cup could help.
Her aunt, a nurse, explains each option, how often to change it and how to throw it away safely.
Kavya chooses what feels right for her — and swims her best time.

steps.title: Sanitary pads (disposable or cloth)
steps.body:
A pad sticks to your underwear and absorbs blood.
- **How to use:** peel off the backing, stick it in the middle of your underwear, fold the wings under.
- **Change every 4–6 hours**, or sooner if heavy. Even on light days, change at least 3 times a day to prevent rashes and odour.
- **Reusable cloth pads** are washed in soap and cold water, then dried fully **in sunlight** (sunlight helps kill germs). Damp, hidden cloth can cause infections.
- **Disposal:** roll the used pad, wrap it in its wrapper or paper, and put it in a dustbin — never flush it (it blocks toilets).

steps.title: Tampons
steps.body:
A tampon is a small cotton plug inserted into the vagina to absorb blood. It is useful for swimming and sport.
- Wash hands, relax, and insert at an angle towards the lower back; the string stays outside.
- **Change every 4–8 hours. Never leave one in for more than 8 hours** and use the lowest absorbency you need.
- Rare but serious: **Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS)** — sudden high fever, rash, vomiting, dizziness. Remove the tampon and get medical help at once.
- A tampon **cannot get lost** inside you; the vagina is closed at the top by the cervix.
- Using a tampon does **not** affect virginity — that is a myth.

steps.title: Menstrual cups
steps.body:
A soft silicone cup is folded, inserted into the vagina, and opens to collect blood.
- Can be worn **up to about 12 hours** depending on flow (empty more often on heavy days).
- Empty, rinse, re-insert. Between periods **boil it for a few minutes** to clean it.
- One cup can last several years — cheaper and creates less waste.
- Many teens find it takes a few cycles to learn. That’s normal. Smaller sizes exist for teens.

steps.title: Period underwear
steps.body: Washable underwear with absorbent layers. Good for light days, nights or backup. Rinse in cold water, wash, and dry fully.

steps.title: Worked example: choosing for a day
steps.body:
Kavya’s heavy day plan:
- **Morning to lunch (school):** tampon, changed at lunch (about 5 hours)
- **Swimming at 4 pm:** fresh tampon before the event
- **Night:** a long overnight pad (tampons are best not worn for more than 8 hours, so for long sleep many choose pads)

The best product is the one **you** are comfortable with. There is no ‘right’ one.

steps.title: Hygiene essentials (and mistakes)
steps.body:
- **Wash hands** before and after changing.
- Wash the outer genital area with **plain water** (mild soap outside only). **Do not douche** or use perfumed products inside — the vagina cleans itself.
- Wipe **front to back** after the toilet.
- **Mistake:** using one pad all day to ‘save’ it — causes rashes and infection.
- **Mistake:** drying cloth pads in dark corners out of embarrassment.
- If you can’t afford products, ask your school nurse or ASHA worker — many government schemes in India provide low-cost or free sanitary pads.

activity.prompt: Match each product with its key safety rule:
pairs: Change every 4–6 hours; wrap and bin, never flush
