Never more than 8 hours; watch for TSS signs
Empty within about 12 hours; boil between periods
Wash and dry fully in sunlight
Rinse in cold water, wash and dry fully

quiz.q: What is the longest a tampon should be left in?
quiz.why: Leaving a tampon in longer than 8 hours raises the risk of Toxic Shock Syndrome.

quiz.q: How should a used disposable pad be thrown away?
options: Leave it in the toilet corner
Wrap it and put it in a dustbin
quiz.why: Wrap used pads and put them in a dustbin. Flushing blocks pipes, and leaving them around is unhygienic.

quiz.q: Can a tampon get lost inside the body?
options: No — the cervix closes the top of the vagina
quiz.why: A tampon cannot get lost inside the body, because the cervix closes the top of the vagina and its opening is too small. It can always be found and removed.

quiz.q: How do you clean a menstrual cup between periods?
options: Boil it for a few minutes
quiz.why: Boil a menstrual cup for a few minutes between periods to sterilise it. A tissue wipe, perfume or the fridge doesn't clean it.

quiz.q: Which is a hygiene MISTAKE?
quiz.why: The vagina cleans itself; douching and perfumes upset the natural balance and can cause infections.

lessons.title: Cramps, PMS, PCOS and when to see a doctor

scenes.text: Ishita, 16, in Jaipur, misses school every month because of cramps. Her periods also come only every 2–3 months.
She has also noticed more hair on her chin and pimples that won’t go. Online forums scare her.
Her mother takes her to a gynaecologist, who listens, examines her and orders blood tests and an ultrasound.
The diagnosis is **PCOS**. With a plan — exercise she enjoys, food changes and medicine for her cramps — Ishita feels in control again.

steps.title: Why cramps happen
steps.body:
During a period the uterus **squeezes** to push out its lining. Chemicals called **prostaglandins** cause these squeezes; more prostaglandins = stronger cramps. Pain is felt in the lower belly, back or thighs, often worst on days 1–2.

Mild to moderate cramps are very common in teens and often get easier with age.

steps.title: What actually helps
steps.body:
- **Heat:** a hot-water bottle or warm towel on the belly or back
- **Movement:** walking, stretching, yoga, cycling
- **Warm bath**
- **Pain relievers:** medicines such as ibuprofen or mefenamic acid work best if taken at the start of pain — **ask a doctor or pharmacist** which is right for you and follow the dose on the label
- Regular sleep, water, and less junk food

If pain makes you miss school or doesn’t improve with these, see a doctor — **severe pain is not something you must just endure**.

steps.title: PMS: the days before
steps.body: **Premenstrual syndrome** includes bloating, tender breasts, tiredness, food cravings, irritability or sadness in the days before a period. It eases when the period starts. Exercise, sleep, less salt and caffeine help. If mood changes are severe (for example, feeling hopeless or unable to function), tell a doctor — a condition called PMDD can be treated.

steps.title: PCOS awareness
steps.body:
**Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)** is a common hormonal condition — WHO estimates it affects about **8–13% of women of reproductive age**, and many don’t know they have it.

Possible signs:
- **irregular or missed periods** (well beyond the first couple of years)
- extra **hair on face, chest or belly**
- stubborn **acne**, oily skin
- weight gain or difficulty losing weight
- thinning hair on the scalp
- dark velvety skin patches on the neck or armpits

Diagnosis is by a doctor using your history, examination, blood tests and sometimes ultrasound. There is **no cure but it is very manageable**: physical activity, balanced food, and medicines when needed. Early care lowers later risks such as diabetes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Self-diagnosing from social media.** Many teens have irregular periods early on — only a doctor can diagnose PCOS.
- **Crash diets or ‘detox’ products** — these worsen health.
- **Hiding pain** because ‘every girl suffers’. Conditions like endometriosis can cause severe pain and deserve care.
- **Stopping school or sport** out of shame.

steps.title: When to see a doctor — the checklist
steps.body:
- No period by 15
- Periods stop for 3+ months (after they were regular), or come less than every 21 days
- Bleeding so heavy you change protection every 1–2 hours
- Pain that stops daily life or doesn’t improve with usual remedies
- Signs of PCOS listed above
- Fever with pain, or bad-smelling discharge

You can ask for a **female doctor** if that makes you more comfortable. This is general health education, not medical advice. If something worries you, see a doctor, nurse or counsellor.

activity.prompt: Sort each situation: usually normal, or worth seeing a doctor?

items.text: Mild cramps on day 1 that ease with a hot-water bottle
Cycle of 40 days in the first year after menarche
Pain so bad you miss school every month
Bloating and craving sweets 3 days before a period
Changing a pad every hour for a whole day
Periods stopped for 4 months after being regular, plus new chin hair
Feeling a little moody before your period

quiz.q: What causes period cramps?
quiz.why: Period cramps happen when the uterus contracts, triggered by prostaglandins, to shed its lining. They aren't caused by the stomach, bones or cold drinks.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a common sign of PCOS?
quiz.why: PCOS can cause irregular periods, extra hair and acne, but not sudden improvement in eyesight. Vision changes aren't a sign of PCOS.

quiz.q: Roughly how common is PCOS according to WHO?
options: About 8–13% of women of reproductive age
quiz.why: WHO estimates PCOS affects about 8–13% of women of reproductive age, so it is common. It isn't limited to women over 50 or rare.

quiz.q: Best first steps for mild cramps?
options: Heat, gentle movement, and a pain reliever advised by a pharmacist or doctor
quiz.why: Heat, gentle movement and a pain reliever advised by a pharmacist or doctor help most mild cramps. Skipping meals, cola or staying still for days doesn't.

quiz.q: Ishita’s friend says ‘Severe pain is just normal, deal with it.’ What’s the truth?
options: Pain that stops daily life should be checked by a doctor
quiz.why: Severe period pain can have treatable causes; nobody should have to just endure it.

questions.why: Menarche is the medical word for the first period.

questions.q: Which product should never be worn for more than 8 hours?
questions.why: A tampon should not be worn for more than 8 hours, as longer wear raises the risk of Toxic Shock Syndrome. Pads and period underwear don't carry that risk.

questions.q: Which is usually the first sign of puberty in girls?
questions.why: Breast buds are usually the first sign of puberty in girls. Acne, wider hips and the first period come later.

questions.q: A period that lasts 5 days is…
questions.why: A period of 5 days is normal, because the usual range is 2–7 days.

questions.q: Which statement about periods is a myth?
options: Cycles may be irregular at first
Periods are impure and you must not cook
questions.why: The idea that periods make girls impure, so they must not cook, is a myth. A period is a normal body process.
Cloth pads should be dried fully in sunlight, because sun helps kill germs. Drying damp or hidden away allows germs to grow.

questions.q: Shreya’s period started on 1 June and the next on 29 June. Her cycle length is…
questions.why: Count from day 1 of one period to day 1 of the next: 1 June to 29 June = 28 days.

questions.q: Why should you wipe front to back?
options: It keeps germs from the anus away from the vagina and urinary opening
questions.why: Wipe front to back so germs from the anus don't reach the vagina or urinary opening. That lowers the risk of infections.

questions.q: Which is a sign to see a doctor?
options: Changing a pad every 1–2 hours for several hours
questions.why: Changing a pad every 1–2 hours for several hours is very heavy bleeding, which needs a doctor. Brown blood on the last day, a 35-day cycle at 13 and breast tenderness before a period are normal.

questions.q: Which is TRUE about the menstrual cycle?
options: The egg is released during the period
If the egg isn’t fertilised, the uterus lining is shed as the period
Ovulation happens only once a year
questions.why: If the egg isn't fertilised, the uterus lining is shed as the period. Ovulation happens mid-cycle, not during the period.

questions.q: A girl of 9 has breast buds. What should she know?
options: This is within the normal range
questions.why: Puberty can normally start between about 8 and 13 in girls, so breast buds at 9 are within the normal range. She doesn't need surgery or special diets.

questions.q: Which combination most strongly suggests a doctor check for PCOS?
options: Missed periods for months (after the first years), excess facial hair and stubborn acne
questions.why: Months of missed periods (after the first years), excess facial hair and stubborn acne together suggest PCOS, which a doctor can check. Regular cycles and mild cramps are normal.

questions.q: Sudden high fever, rash and dizziness while using a tampon means…
options: Possible Toxic Shock Syndrome — remove tampon and get urgent medical help
questions.why: A sudden high fever, rash and dizziness with a tampon suggests Toxic Shock Syndrome, a rare emergency. Remove the tampon and get urgent medical help.

questions.q: Why are irregular cycles common in the first 2–3 years?
options: The ovaries and brain hormones are still settling into a pattern; ovulation may not happen every cycle
They aren’t — it is always a disease
questions.why: In the first 2–3 years, the ovaries and brain hormones are still settling into a pattern, so ovulation may not happen every cycle. That makes irregular cycles common.

questions.q: Which approach to PCOS is evidence-based?
options: Doctor diagnosis, regular activity, balanced eating and medicines when needed
questions.why: For PCOS, the evidence-based approach is a doctor's diagnosis, regular activity, balanced eating and medicines when needed. Crash diets and detox teas don't work.

courses.title: Growing up as a boy: voice, nightfall, hygiene and more
courses.summary: A calm, factual guide for boys going through puberty: growth, voice change, body hair, erections and nightfall explained as normal, hygiene, acne, shaving, myths and when to see a doctor.
outcomes: Learners can describe the changes of puberty for boys and normal age ranges
Learners can explain erections and nightfall as normal body processes and reject the ‘weakness’ myth
Learners can follow a daily hygiene routine and shave safely
Learners can perform a testicle self-check and know emergency signs
Learners can find trustworthy help instead of quacks and online myths
courses.guardianNote: Covers the body changes of puberty for boys: growth spurts, voice change, body hair, erections and nightfall (wet dreams) explained as normal, hygiene, acne, shaving, and myths that cause needless fear, plus when to see a doctor. Medically accurate, calm and non-explicit, in line with UNESCO ITGSE 2018 and NCERT. Suitable for girls too.

lessons.title: What changes for boys — and when

scenes.text: Arjun, 12, from Kolkata grew 8 cm this year. His trousers are short and his feet hurt in old shoes.
His friend Kabir already has a moustache shadow; Arjun has none. Arjun wonders if he is ‘behind’.
His Baba explains: ‘Boys start puberty anywhere from about 9 to 14. Kabir started early — you’ll get there in your own time.’
Arjun stops comparing and starts asking questions.

steps.title: Puberty for boys in one sentence
steps.body: Puberty is when a boy’s body grows into an adult man’s body. The brain signals the **testes** (testicles) to make more **testosterone**, the hormone behind most changes. It usually begins between **9 and 14 years** and continues for several years.

steps.title: The usual changes
steps.body:
- **Testicles grow** first (often unnoticed), then the **penis** grows
- **Pubic hair**, later underarm, facial and body hair
- **Growth spurt** — often later than girls, sometimes 7–10 cm a year
- **Voice deepens**, sometimes cracking for a while
- **Muscles and shoulders** broaden
- **Oily skin and acne**, stronger sweat smell
- **Erections** happen more often, and **nightfall** (wet dreams) may start

Boys usually start puberty about a year or two later than girls.

steps.title: Worked example: two normal boys
steps.body:
**Kabir** (Bengaluru): changes begin at 10, moustache shadow at 12.

**Tom** (London): changes begin at 13½, voice breaks at 15.

Both are healthy. Adult height and strength are not decided by how early you start.

steps.title: Mistakes boys make
steps.body:
- Comparing body hair, height or muscles in the changing room and feeling ashamed
- Taking ‘muscle powders’ or steroids sold online — **dangerous for growing bodies**
- Hiding worries because ‘boys don’t ask’ — every question in this course is one millions of boys have had

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body:
- signs of puberty **before 9**, or **no signs by 14**
- **sudden pain or swelling in a testicle** — go to a hospital the **same day** (it can be *testicular torsion*, an emergency)
- a lump in a testicle

This is general health education, not medical advice. If something worries you, see a doctor, nurse or counsellor.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: List three changes you’ve noticed or expect, and one question you feel too shy to ask. Keep it for the end of the course.

cards.back: The main hormone made by the testes that drives puberty changes in boys
About 9 to 14 years
Testicles getting larger
Often later than girls; can be 7–10 cm in a year
Sudden testicle pain or swelling — get medical help the same day
Unsafe for teens — can harm hormones, heart, liver and growth

quiz.q: Which hormone drives most puberty changes in boys?
quiz.why: Testosterone, made by the testes, drives most puberty changes in boys. Insulin, thyroxine and oestrogen do other jobs.

quiz.q: Arjun is 12 with no facial hair. This is…
quiz.why: No facial hair at 12 is completely normal, since facial hair often appears later, around 14–17 or after. It isn't a sign of illness.

quiz.q: Sudden severe pain in a testicle means…
options: Go to a hospital the same day
quiz.why: Sudden severe testicle pain could be torsion, a twisted testicle that needs emergency treatment within hours. Go to hospital the same day.

quiz.q: Compared with girls, boys usually start puberty…
options: About a year or two later
quiz.why: Boys usually start puberty about a year or two later than girls, on average. So it is normal for friends to develop at different times.

quiz.q: An online seller offers ‘growth steroids’ for teens. Best choice?
options: Avoid them and talk to a doctor about any worries
quiz.why: Avoid online 'growth steroids' and talk to a doctor about your worries. Steroids and unregulated supplements can seriously harm teenagers.

lessons.title: Voice change, growth spurts and body hair

scenes.text: Rohan, 13, in Mumbai, sings in the school choir. One day his voice suddenly jumps high, then low, mid-song.
Some classmates giggle. Rohan wants to quit choir.
The music teacher, Mr. Fernandes, explains what is happening in his throat and suggests singing gentler songs for a while.
Months later Rohan has a strong, deep voice — and is the choir’s new baritone.

steps.title: Why voices crack
steps.body:
The **voice box (larynx)** grows bigger during puberty and the **vocal cords** get longer and thicker. Longer, thicker cords vibrate more slowly, making a **deeper** voice.

While they grow, the brain is still learning to control them — so the voice can **crack or jump** suddenly. This usually settles within months. A bump at the front of the neck, the **Adam’s apple**, may become visible.

steps.title: Tips while your voice changes
steps.body:
- Don’t strain or shout to sound deeper
- Drink water; rest your voice when hoarse
- Singers: work in a comfortable range with a teacher
- If hoarseness lasts **more than 3 weeks**, see a doctor

steps.title: Growth spurts
steps.body:
During the spurt bones grow fast — sometimes faster than muscles stretch, so you might feel **clumsy** or have aching legs at night (‘growing pains’, usually harmless). Feet and hands often grow first.

Good sleep (8–10 hours for teens), protein, calcium (milk, curd, ragi, paneer, leafy greens) and outdoor play support growth. Height is mostly decided by genes; there is no pill or stretching trick that adds height.

steps.title: Body hair
steps.body: Hair appears in the **pubic area**, then underarms, then the **upper lip**, chin and cheeks, and for some the chest, arms and legs. Amount and thickness vary hugely by family and ethnicity. **More hair does not mean more manly**, and less hair is not a problem.

steps.title: Worked example: answering teasing
steps.body:
A classmate says: ‘Ha, your voice sounds like a whistle!’

Rohan’s calm answer: ‘Yeah, it’s changing. Yours will too.’

Short, confident replies take the fun out of teasing. If it continues, tell a teacher.

steps.title: Myths
steps.body:
- ‘Shaving makes hair grow thicker or darker’ — **false**; it only cuts the hair at the surface.
- ‘Hanging from bars adds 10 cm’ — **false**.
- ‘A deep voice means more testosterone, so you’re stronger’ — **not reliable**.

statements.s: Your voice cracks because the vocal cords are growing longer and thicker.
statements.why: The brain needs time to control larger cords.

statements.s: Shaving makes hair grow back thicker.
statements.why: Shaving cuts hair at the surface; it does not change the root.

statements.s: Growing pains at night are often harmless.
statements.why: They are common in growing children; see a doctor if one leg swells, is red, or pain is severe.

statements.s: Special pills can add many centimetres to adult height.
statements.why: Height is mainly genetic; good food and sleep help you reach your potential.

statements.s: Hoarseness lasting more than 3 weeks should be checked by a doctor.
statements.why: Long-lasting hoarseness needs a medical check.

quiz.q: Why does the voice get deeper?
options: Vocal cords grow longer and thicker
quiz.why: The voice deepens because the vocal cords grow longer and thicker, which vibrate at a lower pitch. The tongue, teeth and lungs don't cause it.

quiz.q: The Adam’s apple is…
options: The front of the growing voice box
quiz.why: The Adam's apple is the front of the growing voice box (larynx), which becomes more visible in puberty. It isn't a swallowed seed or disease.

quiz.q: How much sleep do teenagers need?
quiz.why: Teenagers need about 8–10 hours of sleep for growth, mood and learning. 4–5 hours is too little.

quiz.q: Which food group especially supports bone growth?
options: Calcium-rich foods like milk, curd, ragi
quiz.why: Calcium-rich foods like milk, curd and ragi support bone growth, along with vitamin D. Chips and sugary drinks don't.

quiz.q: A classmate mocks your cracking voice. A good reply?
quiz.why: A calm, short reply like 'Yeah, it's changing. Yours will too.' reduces teasing. Tell a teacher if it continues; fighting or hiding doesn't help.

lessons.title: Erections and nightfall (wet dreams) — totally normal

scenes.text: Sameer, 14, from Indore, wakes up to find his shorts and bedsheet damp and sticky. He had a confusing dream.
He panics: an older boy once told him ‘losing semen makes you weak’. He stays quiet all day, scared and ashamed.
At school, the visiting doctor gives a talk on puberty. She says: ‘Nightfall is normal and healthy. It doesn’t cause weakness.’
Sameer feels a huge weight lift. That night, he simply rinses his shorts and goes back to sleep.

steps.title: What is nightfall?
steps.body:
**Nightfall** (also called a **wet dream** or *nocturnal emission*) is when **semen** — a whitish fluid containing sperm — comes out of the penis during sleep. It often happens during a dream, but not always, and you might not remember the dream.

It happens because, from puberty, the testes make sperm **all the time**, and the body naturally releases fluid now and then. It is a **sign that your body is maturing**, not a disease.

steps.title: Facts doctors want boys to know
steps.body:
- Most boys have nightfall at some point; some often, some rarely, some never. **All are normal.**
- It usually starts around 12–16 and may become less frequent with age.
- **Semen loss does not cause weakness**, thinness, hair loss, poor eyesight, low marks or infertility. The body keeps making more.
- You cannot fully control it, and you don’t need to. There is no medicine needed for normal nightfall.

steps.title: Erections
steps.body:
An **erection** is when the penis becomes firm because extra blood flows into it. In puberty, erections can happen **without any reason** — in class, on a bus, when waking up. This is because of changing hormones.

What helps:
- Remember **nobody can usually tell**
- Think about something else, take slow breaths, it passes in a few minutes
- Untucked shirt, a bag on your lap, or standing up and walking can help
- Morning erections are a normal sign of healthy blood flow

steps.title: The ‘dhat’ myth and quacks
steps.body:
In parts of South Asia there is an old belief that semen is precious ‘vital fluid’ and losing it drains strength. Some roadside ‘clinics’, posters and websites use this fear to sell expensive, useless or harmful ‘medicines’.

**Doctors and science agree: this belief is false.** If you’re anxious, see a qualified MBBS doctor, not a poster advertisement.

steps.title: Worked example: what to do after nightfall
steps.body:
1. Wipe yourself with tissue or a cloth.
2. Rinse your underwear or shorts in water, or put them in the laundry.
3. Change the sheet if needed, or wipe the spot.
4. Wash in the morning as usual.
5. Go back to sleep. Nothing else is needed.

If you feel shy about laundry, you can rinse it yourself — but many parents already know this is part of growing up.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body:
- **pain**, burning while urinating, or blood in the semen or urine
- a lump or swelling in a testicle
- worries that are affecting sleep, study or mood (anxiety itself is worth talking about)

This is general health education, not medical advice. If something worries you, see a doctor, nurse or counsellor.

activity.prompt: Questions boys ask about nightfall and erections

items.q: Does nightfall mean I had a ‘bad’ dream or bad thoughts?
items.a: No. Dreams are not under your control, and nightfall is a body process. Having it says nothing bad about you.

items.q: I have nightfall several times a week. Is that too much?
items.a: Frequency varies widely between boys and is normal. It is not harmful. If you are very worried or it comes with pain, see a doctor.

items.q: I’ve never had a wet dream. Is something wrong?
items.a: No. Some boys never have one, especially if they release semen in other ways. It is not a test of health.

items.q: Will it make me weak or affect my studies?
items.a: No. Semen is constantly made and its release does not reduce strength, height or brainpower.

items.q: Why do I get erections at random times?
items.a: Puberty hormones make erections more frequent and sometimes unrelated to any thought. They pass in minutes, and they usually aren’t noticed by others.

items.q: Can I talk to someone about this?
items.a: Yes — a parent, an older trusted relative, a school counsellor or a doctor. You can also call Tele-MANAS 14416 if worry is affecting you.

quiz.q: What is nightfall?
options: Release of semen during sleep, normal in puberty
quiz.why: Nightfall is the release of semen during sleep, and it is normal in puberty. It isn't an infection, disease or bedwetting.

quiz.q: Does nightfall cause weakness?
quiz.why: No, nightfall does not cause weakness. That is a myth, since science shows semen release doesn't harm health.

quiz.q: An unexpected erection in class. Best approach?
options: Breathe slowly, think of something else; it passes
quiz.why: Breathe slowly and think of something else, and the erection will pass. Spontaneous erections are normal in puberty and need no medicine.

quiz.q: A roadside poster offers a cure for ‘semen loss weakness’. What should you do?
options: Ignore it; see a qualified doctor if worried
quiz.why: Ignore such posters and see a qualified doctor if you are worried. They exploit myths to sell useless or harmful products.

quiz.q: Which needs a doctor?
quiz.why: Pain or burning when urinating can mean an infection, so see a doctor. Nightfall, morning erection and not remembering dreams are normal.

lessons.title: Hygiene, sweat, acne and shaving

scenes.text: Vikram, 14, from Guwahati plays football every evening. Lately friends wave their hands near their noses when he walks in.
He’s embarrassed. At home he showers only every other day.
His older brother shows him a simple daily routine and how to shave his patchy moustache safely.
Two weeks later Vikram feels fresher and more confident.

steps.title: Why you suddenly smell
steps.body:
In puberty, **apocrine sweat glands** in the armpits and groin become active. Their sweat isn’t smelly itself, but bacteria on skin break it down and create odour.

Daily routine:
- **Bath or shower every day**, and after sport
- Wash **armpits, groin, feet** with soap
- Clean under the foreskin gently with water if you are uncircumcised (pull back only as far as it comfortably goes)
- Fresh underwear and socks **daily**; cotton is best in hot weather
- **Deodorant or antiperspirant** on clean, dry armpits

steps.title: Acne
steps.body:
Hormones make skin glands produce more oil. Oil plus dead skin can block pores, causing pimples.
- Wash your face **twice a day** with a mild cleanser
- **Don’t squeeze or pick** — it spreads infection and leaves scars
- Use oil-free sunscreen and moisturiser
- Products with benzoyl peroxide or salicylic acid help mild acne
- For painful, deep or scarring acne, see a doctor (dermatologist) — effective treatments exist

steps.title: Worked example: first shave
steps.body:
1. Wash your face with warm water to soften hair.
2. Apply shaving gel or foam.
3. Use a **clean, sharp razor**; shave **in the direction the hair grows** to reduce cuts and bumps.
4. Rinse the razor often. Don’t press hard.
5. Rinse with cool water, pat dry, apply a gentle moisturiser.

**Never share razors** (risk of infections like hepatitis B). An electric trimmer is a good gentle alternative. Shaving is a choice — you don’t have to start until you want to.

steps.title: Feet and teeth
steps.body: Wash and fully dry between toes; alternate shoes so they dry; use cotton socks. Brush teeth twice daily — teenage hormones can make gums more sensitive.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Covering smell with strong perfume instead of washing
- Wearing the same sports kit for days
- Picking at pimples before an event
- Shaving dry with a blunt razor
- Using a friend’s razor

activity.prompt: Build your daily hygiene routine — tick what you’ll do:
items: Shower or bath every day and after sport
Wash armpits, groin and feet with soap
Wear clean underwear and socks daily
Use deodorant on clean, dry skin
Wash face twice a day; don’t pick pimples
Brush teeth twice a day
Use my own razor only, and shave with the grain

quiz.q: Why does body odour start in puberty?
options: Apocrine sweat glands activate and skin bacteria break down sweat
quiz.why: Body odour starts in puberty because apocrine sweat glands become active and skin bacteria break the sweat down. It isn't due to food or too much soap.

quiz.q: Best way to deal with a pimple?
options: Leave it, wash face gently, use a suitable acne product
quiz.why: Leave the pimple alone, wash your face gently and use a suitable acne product. Squeezing or scratching spreads bacteria and can scar.

quiz.q: When shaving, it is best to shave…
options: Against the grain with a blunt razor
In the direction hair grows with a clean, sharp razor
quiz.why: Shave in the direction the hair grows with a clean, sharp razor, which lowers cuts and razor bumps. Dry shaving, blunt or shared razors are risky.

quiz.q: Why should you never share razors?
options: Risk of blood-borne infections like hepatitis B
quiz.why: Never share razors because tiny cuts can pass blood-borne infections like hepatitis B. It isn't just about being blunt or impolite.

quiz.q: Does shaving make hair grow thicker?
quiz.why: No, shaving doesn't make hair grow thicker, because it doesn't affect the hair root. It only cuts the tip.

lessons.title: Myths, worries and when to see a doctor

scenes.text: Dev, 15, from Patna watches videos claiming boys must have big muscles, lots of hair and a certain body to be ‘real men’.
He also notices one side of his chest is puffy and tender. He searches online at 2 am and becomes terrified.
He finally tells his uncle, a pharmacist, who takes him to a doctor. The doctor explains it’s common and usually goes away.
Dev learns: search engines don’t examine you — doctors do.

steps.title: Breast swelling in boys (gynaecomastia)
steps.body:
Many boys — around half in some studies — get **temporary swelling or tenderness under one or both nipples** during puberty because of normal hormone shifts. It usually **goes away by itself within months to 2 years**.

See a doctor if it is large, growing quickly, hard, one-sided and not settling, or comes with discharge. Never take pills sold online to ‘fix’ it.

steps.title: Size and shape worries
steps.body:
Penis size, testicle size and body shape vary widely, just like height or nose shape. Size is **not linked to manliness, fertility or the ability to have a satisfying relationship**. Large medical studies show most men who worry are in the normal range. It is also normal for **one testicle to hang lower** than the other.

If you have a real medical concern (for example, a testicle that is missing from the scrotum or very small), a doctor can check calmly and privately.

steps.title: Testicle self-check
steps.body:
From mid-teens, once a month, after a warm shower:
- Gently roll each testicle between thumb and fingers
- It should feel smooth and firm, like a boiled egg without shell; the soft tube at the back (epididymis) is normal
- Tell a doctor about any **new lump, hardness, heaviness or swelling**

Testicular cancer is uncommon but most often affects young men, and it is very treatable when found early.

steps.title: Media myths that harm boys
steps.body:
- ‘Real men don’t cry or ask for help’ — **false**; asking for help is strength.
- ‘You need supplements to grow’ — **false**; food, sleep and exercise are enough.
- ‘Porn shows how bodies normally look and work’ — **false**; it is staged and edited (see the Sexuality Education course).
- ‘Masturbation causes weakness’ — **false**; it is common and harmless (see ‘Questions teens never ask’).

steps.title: The see-a-doctor list for boys
steps.body:
- Sudden testicle pain or swelling → **emergency, same day**
- A lump in a testicle
- Pain/burning when urinating, unusual discharge
- Foreskin that is painful, swollen, or stuck back behind the head of the penis
- Breast swelling that is large or not settling
- No signs of puberty by 14
- Worry, low mood or anxiety that won’t go away — call **Tele-MANAS 14416** or talk to a counsellor

This is general health education, not medical advice. If something worries you, see a doctor, nurse or counsellor.

a.text: It’s 1 am. You found a lump-like tenderness under your nipple and a website says it could be cancer.

choices.label: Close the phone and plan to tell a parent or trusted adult tomorrow
choices.feedback: Good — sleep, then get real help. Late-night searching usually fuels fear.

choices.label: Keep reading forums until 4 am
choices.feedback: Forums often show worst cases; they can’t examine you.

choices.label: Order ‘chest reduction pills’ online
choices.feedback: Unregulated pills can be harmful and don’t treat the cause.

b.text: Your uncle says ‘Let’s see a doctor this week.’

choices.label: Go to the doctor and ask your questions honestly
choices.feedback: Doctors see this often. Honesty gets you the right answer.

choices.label: Say ‘Never mind, it’s nothing’ out of embarrassment
choices.feedback: Embarrassment passes; health matters. It’s okay to change your mind and go.

c.text: Now you’re exhausted and more scared.

choices.label: Tell a trusted adult in the morning
choices.feedback: Better choice — let a professional check.

d.text: The pills arrive with no ingredients listed.

choices.label: Don’t take them; tell a trusted adult and see a doctor
choices.feedback: Wise. Never take unknown medicines.

end1.text: The doctor confirms common pubertal gynaecomastia and says it should settle. You sleep well tonight.

end2.text: Worry tends to grow when kept secret. Go back and choose to get it checked.

quiz.q: Puffy, tender chest in a teen boy during puberty is usually…
options: Temporary and caused by normal hormone changes
quiz.why: A puffy, tender chest in a teen boy is usually temporary and caused by normal hormone changes (pubertal gynaecomastia). It is rarely cancer.

quiz.q: One testicle hanging lower than the other is…
quiz.why: One testicle hanging lower than the other is normal and very common. It isn't a sign of infertility or an emergency.

quiz.q: How should a testicle self-check feel if normal?
options: Smooth and firm, with a soft tube at the back
quiz.why: A normal testicle feels smooth and firm, with a soft tube at the back, the epididymis. A hard lump, pain or heat needs checking.

quiz.q: Which statement is TRUE?
options: Real men don’t ask for help
Asking a doctor about body worries is sensible and normal
Penis size is linked to fertility
quiz.why: Asking a doctor about body worries is sensible and normal, since doctors answer such questions every day. 'Real men don't ask for help' is a myth.

quiz.q: Which is an emergency?
quiz.why: Sudden testicle pain is an emergency, possibly torsion. An uneven voice, patchy moustache and acne are normal changes.

questions.why: A wet dream, or nightfall, is the release of semen during sleep. It is normal in puberty and is not bedwetting.

questions.q: Which hormone drives puberty in boys?
questions.why: Testosterone, made by the testes, drives puberty in boys. Oestrogen, adrenaline and insulin have other roles.

questions.q: How often should a teen bathe?
questions.why: A teen should bathe every day and after sport, because sweat and bacteria cause odour and infections. Weekly washing is too little.

questions.q: The voice cracks during puberty because…
options: Vocal cords are growing and the brain is adjusting
questions.why: The voice cracks because the vocal cords are growing and the brain is adjusting. It settles within months and isn't an illness.

questions.q: Shaving direction to reduce cuts and bumps?
questions.why: Shave with the direction of hair growth to reduce cuts and bumps. Against the hair growth irritates the skin.
Nightfall does not harm health. The idea that it weakens you is a myth, often used by quacks.

questions.q: Which is NOT a normal change in boys’ puberty?
questions.why: Sudden severe testicle pain is not a normal change in puberty; it is an emergency. Growth spurts, testes growing and a deepening voice are normal.

options: Caused by changing hormones and normal
questions.why: Spontaneous erections are normal in teens, caused by changing hormones, and can occur without any sexual thought. They aren't a disease.

questions.q: Best place to get advice about a body worry?
questions.why: A qualified doctor is the best place for advice, since only they can examine and advise. Posters, forums and rumours are unreliable.

questions.q: Why should razors never be shared?
questions.why: Razors shouldn't be shared because blood-borne infections like hepatitis B can spread through tiny cuts. Rust and blunting are not the main reason.

options: Settles within months to about two years
questions.why: Teen gynaecomastia usually settles within months to about two years. It isn't cancer and rarely needs surgery.

questions.q: A boy has no signs of puberty at 14. What’s sensible?
options: See a doctor for a check-up
questions.why: No signs of puberty by 14 is a reason to see a doctor for a check-up. Dieting or taking steroids is unsafe.

options: Semen loss drains strength and health
questions.why: The 'dhat' myth is the belief that semen loss drains strength and health. It is false, as semen loss does not cause weakness.

questions.q: Why can teens feel clumsy during a growth spurt?
options: Bones grow quickly and coordination takes time to catch up
questions.why: During a growth spurt bones grow quickly, and coordination takes time to catch up. So feeling clumsy is normal.

questions.q: Which combination needs urgent hospital care?
options: Voice cracks and hoarseness for 1 week
Sudden testicle pain with swelling and nausea
questions.why: Sudden testicle pain with swelling and nausea are typical signs of torsion, which needs urgent hospital care within hours. A cracking voice, acne and morning erection are normal.

courses.title: What's happening to my friends? Puberty for everyone
courses.summary: A shared course for all genders: how every body changes, moods and crushes, respecting privacy, and how to talk to trusted adults.
outcomes: Learners can describe puberty changes in all bodies, including intersex variation
Learners can use tools to manage strong emotions and respect a crush’s answer
Learners can explain why body teasing and sharing images harm others and can be illegal
Learners can identify trusted adults and start a conversation about growing up
courses.guardianNote: A shared course for all children going through puberty: how bodies of every sex change, mood swings and crushes, why teasing about bodies and periods hurts, and how to talk with parents and trusted adults. Non-explicit and age-appropriate (UNESCO ITGSE 2018, ages 9–15).

lessons.title: Everyone's body changes — girls, boys and intersex people

scenes.text: In Class 7 at a Bengaluru school, Ms. Thomas sets up an anonymous question box about puberty.
Notes pour in from boys and girls: ‘Why do girls have periods?’ ‘Why do boys’ voices crack?’ ‘Why am I so moody?’
She answers every one in front of the whole class, calmly. Nobody laughs.
By the end, students realise their friends are going through the same journey.

steps.title: Same journey, different routes
steps.body:
Puberty changes **everyone**. Some changes happen to all: growth spurt, pubic and underarm hair, oilier skin and acne, stronger body odour, mood swings and new feelings. Some depend on your body:
- **Ovaries** → oestrogen → breasts, wider hips, periods
- **Testes** → testosterone → deeper voice, facial hair, broader shoulders, nightfall

Knowing what happens to others helps you understand and **respect** them.

steps.title: Intersex people
steps.body: Some people are born with bodies that don’t fit typical definitions of male or female — this is called being **intersex** (or having differences of sex development). It is a natural variation and they deserve the same respect and privacy as anyone.

steps.title: Worked example: compare the facts
steps.body:
- **Average start:** girls ~8–13, boys ~9–14
- **Growth spurt:** girls earlier; boys later but often longer
- **Releases:** periods (girls) start ~10–15; nightfall (boys) commonly ~12–16
- **Both:** acne, sweat smell, hair growth, emotions

So in Class 6–7, many girls may be taller than boys. By Class 10–11 that often reverses. All normal.

steps.title: Being a good friend
steps.body:
- If a friend has a period leak, quietly tell them and offer a jumper.
- If a friend’s voice cracks, don’t make it a joke.
- Keep friends’ body worries **private** — don’t share or post.
- Point friends to reliable info and trusted adults.

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking periods are a ‘girls-only’ topic that boys shouldn’t know — knowing helps boys be kind brothers, friends and future partners.
- Thinking boys don’t have body worries.
- Using puberty changes as insults.

activity.prompt: Which bodies does each change usually happen to?

items.text: Periods
Breast development
Nightfall (wet dreams)
Voice deepening a lot
Acne and oily skin
Underarm and pubic hair
Growth spurt
Mood swings

quiz.q: Which change happens to everyone in puberty?
quiz.why: A growth spurt and new body hair happen to everyone in puberty. Periods, breasts and nightfall are specific to some.

quiz.q: Why might Class 6 girls be taller than boys?
options: Girls often have their growth spurt earlier
quiz.why: Girls often have their growth spurt earlier than boys, so Class 6 girls may be taller. Boys often catch up and overtake later.

quiz.q: What does intersex mean?
quiz.why: Intersex means natural variations in sex characteristics, such as chromosomes, hormones or anatomy. It is not a disease or a fashion.

quiz.q: A friend has a period stain on her skirt. Kind response?
options: Quietly tell her and offer a jumper
quiz.why: Quietly tell her and offer a jumper, which is discreet and kind. Announcing, laughing or photographing humiliates her.

quiz.q: Why should boys learn about periods?
options: So they can be understanding friends, brothers and future partners
quiz.why: Boys should learn about periods so they can be understanding friends, brothers and future partners. Knowledge reduces stigma and builds respect.

lessons.title: Moods, new feelings and crushes

scenes.text: Neha, 13, from Ahmedabad laughed in the morning, cried at lunch over a small comment, and snapped at her brother at night.
She also can’t stop thinking about a classmate, Aarav. Her stomach flips when he says hi.
She wonders: ‘Am I going crazy?’
Her Nani laughs gently: ‘No, dear. Your brain is growing too. Let’s learn some tools.’

steps.title: Your brain is under construction
steps.body:
During adolescence the **emotional parts of the brain** develop faster than the **planning and self-control parts** (the prefrontal cortex), which keep maturing into your mid-20s. Hormones add to this. Result: feelings can be **bigger, faster and more confusing**.

This is normal, and you can learn skills to ride the waves.

steps.title: Tools for big feelings
steps.body:
- **Name it:** ‘I feel embarrassed / jealous / lonely.’ Naming calms the brain.
- **Pause before reacting:** count to 10 or breathe slowly.
- **Move:** a walk, dance or sport releases tension.
- **Write or draw** it out.
- **Talk** to someone you trust.
- **Sleep, food, water** — tired and hungry brains feel everything more.

steps.title: Crushes
steps.body:
A **crush** is a strong liking or attraction to someone. It may be a classmate, a friend, a celebrity, someone of a different gender or the same gender. Crushes are a **normal part of growing up**.

You don’t have to act on a crush. It’s okay to enjoy the feeling, keep it private, or tell a trusted person. If you tell your crush and they don’t feel the same, that’s **their right** — and it hurts, but it passes.

steps.title: When feelings need extra help
steps.body: Moodiness is normal; but tell an adult or call **Tele-MANAS 14416** if for **two weeks or more** you feel sad or empty most of the day, lose interest in everything, can’t sleep or eat, or have thoughts of hurting yourself. These are signs to get support, not to hide.

steps.title: Worked example: handling a ‘no’
steps.body:
Arjun tells Priya he likes her. Priya says, ‘Thanks for telling me, but I see you as a friend.’

**Healthy response:** ‘Okay, thanks for being honest.’ Then giving space.

**Unhealthy responses:** sulking, spreading rumours, repeatedly asking, posting about her. Respecting ‘no’ is a sign of maturity.

activity.label: Calm-wave breathing: in 4, hold 4, out slowly 6, rest 2

quiz.q: Why can teen emotions feel so intense?
options: The emotional brain matures faster than the self-control parts, plus hormones
quiz.why: Teen emotions can feel intense because the emotional brain matures faster than the self-control parts, and hormones add to it. It isn't drama on purpose or bad parenting.

quiz.q: Which is a healthy response when your crush says ‘no’?
options: Accept it and give them space
quiz.why: Accepting a 'no' and giving space is mature and kind. Spreading rumours, repeated asking or posting about them is disrespectful.

quiz.q: Having a crush on someone of the same gender is…
options: One of the normal ways people feel attraction
quiz.why: A crush on someone of the same gender is one of the normal ways people feel attraction. It is not an illness or crime.

quiz.q: When should moodiness be shared with an adult or helpline?
options: When sadness or emptiness lasts two weeks or more, or there are thoughts of self-harm
quiz.why: Share moodiness with an adult or helpline when sadness or emptiness lasts two weeks or more, or there are thoughts of self-harm. Tele-MANAS 14416 is free and 24×7.

quiz.q: Which tool helps calm a big feeling quickly?
options: Slow breathing and naming the feeling
quiz.why: Slow breathing and naming the feeling calm the nervous system. Sugar, scrolling or shouting don't settle big feelings.

lessons.title: No teasing: respecting changing bodies

scenes.text: In a Delhi school, Karan secretly takes a photo of a classmate, Imran, changing for PE and posts it in a group chat as a ‘joke’.
Imran stops coming to PE. Later he stops coming to school.
The teacher finds out. Karan is shocked to learn that sharing such photos can be a serious offence, and that he hurt Imran deeply.
Karan apologises, deletes the photo, and the class discusses respect.

steps.title: Bodies are private
steps.body:
Everyone deserves **privacy** while their body changes. That means no:
- comments about breasts, chest, body hair, size, weight or skin
- jokes about periods, voices, erections or nightfall
- photos or videos of anyone changing, in toilets or without consent
- snapping bra straps, pulling down shorts, ‘pantsing’ or touching as a ‘prank’

steps.title: This can be against the law
steps.body:
Taking or sharing intimate images of a person without consent violates their privacy. If the person is **under 18**, sexual images are treated as child sexual abuse material under India’s **POCSO Act** and **IT Act** — creating, keeping or sharing them is a serious crime, even as a ‘joke’ and even if you are a minor yourself.

This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Worked example: turn teasing into support
steps.body:
**Teasing:** ‘Ew, someone’s on her period!’
**Respectful:** say nothing to embarrass her; if she needs help, offer a jumper or tell a teacher quietly.

**Teasing:** ‘Look at his moustache — so ugly.’
**Respectful:** ‘Leave him, everyone grows differently.’

steps.title: If it happens to you or a friend
steps.body:
1. Don’t forward or react with laughter.
2. Tell the person ‘Stop — that’s not okay.’ if it’s safe.
3. Report to a teacher, counsellor or parent.
4. For images online: report the post, don’t delete evidence yourself (take a note of who, when, where), and use **cybercrime.gov.in** or helpline **1930**; under 18s can also call **1098**.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Body teasing is linked with anxiety, low self-esteem, eating problems and skipping school. Respect makes school safe for everyone — including you when it’s your turn to change.

a.text: A classmate shares a video in the class group of someone’s period stain, with laughing emojis.

choices.label: Don’t react; message the sender ‘Delete this, it’s not okay’ and tell a teacher
choices.feedback: Strong and kind. You’re protecting your classmate.

choices.label: Add a laughing emoji so you fit in
choices.feedback: Reacting spreads harm and makes you part of it.

choices.label: Forward it to another group
choices.feedback: Forwarding multiplies the harm — and can be an offence.

b.text: The teacher asks you what happened.

choices.label: Explain honestly and show the group message
choices.feedback: Evidence helps adults act quickly.

c.text: The girl in the video stops coming to school. You feel bad.

choices.label: Apologise to her, delete what you shared and tell a teacher
choices.feedback: It’s never too late to make it right.

end1.text: The video is removed and the class learns about respect. Your classmate thanks you quietly.

end2.text: You’ve taken responsibility. Next time, you’ll stand up from the start.

quiz.q: Which is an example of respecting privacy?
quiz.why: Not commenting on people's bodies respects their privacy. Photographing, snapping a bra strap or joking about voices doesn't.

quiz.q: Sharing a sexual image of someone under 18 in India is…
options: Legal if you’re also a minor
Only wrong if they find out
A serious crime under POCSO and the IT Act
quiz.why: Sharing a sexual image of someone under 18 is a serious crime under POCSO and the IT Act, even as a joke or if you are also a minor.

quiz.q: Someone posts an embarrassing image of a classmate. What should you avoid?
quiz.why: Avoid forwarding the image, because that spreads harm. Report it, tell a teacher and support the classmate instead.

quiz.q: Which helpline handles cybercrime reports in India?
quiz.why: 1930 is India's national cybercrime helpline, and reports can also be made at cybercrime.gov.in. The other numbers aren't official helplines.

quiz.q: Why does body teasing matter?
options: It is linked to anxiety, low self-esteem and school avoidance
quiz.why: Body teasing matters because it is linked to anxiety, low self-esteem and school avoidance. It isn't just fun or something that makes people tougher.

lessons.title: Talking to parents and trusted adults

scenes.text: Siddharth, 12, from Chandigarh has questions about his body but feels too shy to ask anyone.
He decides to ask his dad during a long car ride, when they don’t have to look at each other.
‘Papa, can I ask something weird?’ His dad says, ‘There are no weird questions.’
They talk for 20 minutes. Siddharth realises his dad had the same worries at his age.

steps.title: Who counts as a trusted adult?
steps.body: A **trusted adult** is someone who listens, keeps you safe and wants the best for you: a parent, grandparent, aunt or uncle, older sibling, school counsellor, nurse, teacher or doctor. You can have **more than one**. If one doesn’t listen, try another.

steps.title: How to start the conversation
steps.body:
- Pick a calm moment — a walk, a car ride, cooking together
- Use a starter: ‘Can I ask you something private?’ or ‘My friend wanted to know…’
- Write a note or text if speaking feels hard
- Ask them to keep it between you (but know that if you’re unsafe, they must help — that’s their job)

steps.title: Worked example: three starters
steps.body:
1. ‘Ma, I think my period might start soon. Can we buy pads together?’
2. ‘Chachu, is it normal that my voice keeps cracking?’
3. ‘Ms. Rao, I’m being teased about my body. Can you help?’

Short, honest, specific.

steps.title: If an adult makes you uncomfortable
steps.body: A trusted adult **never** asks you to keep secrets about touching, shows you sexual pictures, or asks for photos of your body. If anyone does — even someone you know — tell another trusted adult or call **1098** (Childline). It is never your fault.

steps.title: Reliable sources
steps.body: When you look things up, prefer health information from WHO, UNICEF, government health sites and qualified doctors over random videos and forums. And remember — this course is here any time.

activity.prompt: Who are three trusted adults you could talk to about growing up, and what’s one question you’d ask?
activity.hint: Think about who listens well. Write a starter sentence you could use.

quiz.q: Which is a good moment to ask a private question?
options: In front of the whole family at dinner
A calm moment like a walk or car ride
quiz.why: A calm moment like a walk or car ride is a good time for a private question, since side-by-side settings feel less intense. Dinner in front of the family or an argument isn't.

quiz.q: A trusted adult would never…
options: Ask you to keep secrets about touching
quiz.why: A trusted adult would never ask you to keep secrets about touching. Taking you to a doctor, listening and helping you find information are what safe adults do.

quiz.q: If the first adult you tell doesn’t listen, you should…
quiz.why: If the first adult doesn't listen, tell another trusted adult. Keep telling until someone helps.

quiz.q: Childline’s number in India is…
quiz.why: Childline's number is 1098, free and 24×7. 1930 is cybercrime, 108 ambulance and 14416 Tele-MANAS.

quiz.q: Which is the most reliable source?
quiz.why: WHO or a qualified doctor are the most reliable sources. Rumours, clinic posters and random influencers can be wrong.

questions.q: Which change happens in everyone’s puberty?
questions.why: A growth spurt happens in everyone's puberty. Breasts, periods and a big voice deepening don't apply to all.

options: A normal strong liking or attraction
questions.why: A crush is a normal strong liking or attraction. It isn't an illness and isn't always love.
Childline's number is 1098. 100 is police, 101 fire and 102 ambulance.

options: Keeping a friend’s body worry private
questions.why: Keeping a friend's body worry private is respectful. Laughing, posting photos or commenting on someone's chest is not.
Teens can feel moody because of brain development and hormones. It isn't laziness or the weather.

questions.q: A trusted adult is someone who…
options: Asks you to keep touching secrets
questions.why: A trusted adult listens and keeps you safe. They never ask for secrets about touching or photos.
Intersex describes natural variations in sex characteristics. It isn't a disease or a political group.
If your crush says no, accept it and give space. Spreading rumours, posting or asking again disrespects their choice.

questions.q: Sharing a sexual image of a 14-year-old classmate is…
options: A serious crime under POCSO and the IT Act
questions.why: Sharing a sexual image of a 14-year-old is a serious crime under POCSO and the IT Act, because it is child sexual abuse material. A private group, later deleting or calling it a prank doesn't change that.

questions.q: When should a teen seek help for low mood?
options: When it lasts 2 weeks+ or there are thoughts of self-harm
questions.why: A teen should seek help when low mood lasts 2 weeks or more, or there are thoughts of self-harm. Tele-MANAS 14416 can help.

questions.q: Why are girls often taller than boys around Class 6?
options: Girls’ growth spurts tend to start earlier
questions.why: Girls' growth spurts tend to start earlier than boys', so girls are often taller around Class 6. Boys often catch up later.

questions.q: Which response best supports a friend being teased about body hair?
options: ‘Leave him, everyone grows differently’ and tell a teacher if it continues
questions.why: Say 'Leave him, everyone grows differently' and tell a teacher if it continues. Joining in, ignoring or posting adds to the harm.

questions.q: Someone forwards a classmate’s private image. The best combination of actions is…
options: Don’t share; report the post; note details; tell a trusted adult; use 1930/cybercrime.gov.in or 1098
questions.why: Don't share the image, report the post, note details, tell a trusted adult and use 1930, cybercrime.gov.in or 1098. This stops the spread and gets proper help.

wellbeing-sexuality-education.title: Sexuality education: safe, respectful, accurate
wellbeing-sexuality-education.description: Age-banded sexuality and relationships education from body safety for little ones to adult sexual health and parenting — medically accurate, non-explicit, following UNESCO ITGSE 2018 and WHO.

courses.title: My body belongs to me (body safety)
courses.summary: Gentle, picture-free lessons for little ones with a grown-up: body part names, safe and unsafe touch, the swimsuit rule, secrets vs surprises, and a safety hand of trusted adults.
outcomes: Learners can name body parts including private parts with correct words
Learners can tell safe from unsafe touch and use No–Go–Tell
Learners can tell surprises from unsafe secrets
Learners can name five trusted adults and know 1098 and 112
courses.guardianNote: For children aged 4–6 with a parent or teacher. Teaches correct names for body parts (including private parts, without pictures), that ‘my body belongs to me’, safe and unsafe touch, the swimsuit rule, secrets versus surprises, and telling a trusted adult. No sexual content. Follows UNESCO ITGSE 2018 guidance for ages 5–8, which finds that correct names and body-safety rules help children speak up and stay safe.

lessons.title: My body, my words

scenes.text: Tara, 5, is having a bath. She asks her Amma, ‘What is this part called?’
Amma answers calmly with the real name, the same way she names elbows and knees.
Later Tara tells her teddy: ‘Every part of me has a name. Some parts are private.’

steps.title: Every part has a name
steps.body:
We have names for every part of our body: head, eyes, nose, mouth, tummy, elbows, knees, toes.

Some parts are **private parts** — the parts covered by underwear or a swimsuit. Their real names are:
- **penis** and **testicles** (most boys)
- **vulva** and **vagina** (most girls)
- **bottom** (everyone)
- **chest** or **breasts** (grown-ups)

These are normal words, just like ‘elbow’.

steps.title: For grown-ups
steps.body: Use the correct words calmly. Children who know the real names can **tell an adult clearly** if something is wrong, and it shows them their bodies are nothing to be ashamed of. Family pet-names are fine at home, as long as children also know the real ones.

steps.title: Private means private
steps.body: Private parts are kept covered in public. They are **only for you**. A doctor or a grown-up helping you wash may look **only to keep you healthy**, and a parent should be told.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Play ‘Head, shoulders, knees and toes’ — then point to your body and name each part. Say together: **‘My body belongs to me.’**

items.say: Private parts are the parts under my underwear or swimsuit
If I feel unsafe, I tell a grown-up I trust

quiz.q: Which parts are private?
options: Parts covered by underwear or a swimsuit
quiz.why: Private parts are the parts covered by underwear or a swimsuit. Hair, ears and hands are not private parts.

quiz.q: Whose body is your body?
quiz.why: Your body is yours. It belongs to you, not to a friend, teacher or anybody else.

quiz.q: Is ‘vulva’ or ‘penis’ a bad word?
options: No, they are correct body words
quiz.why: No, 'vulva' and 'penis' are the correct body words, just like elbow or knee. They aren't bad words.

quiz.q: When may a doctor look at private parts?
options: Only to keep you healthy, with a parent told
If they give you a sweet
quiz.why: A doctor may look at private parts only to keep you healthy, and a parent should be told. They should never do it for a sweet or in secret.

lessons.title: Safe touch, unsafe touch and the swimsuit rule

scenes.text: Kabir, 5, loves hugging his Dadi. Hugs from her feel warm and safe.
At a party, an uncle keeps tickling Kabir even after he says ‘stop’. Kabir feels yucky inside.
Kabir tells his Papa. Papa says, ‘You did the right thing. You can always say stop.’

steps.title: Safe touch
steps.body: **Safe touches** make you feel happy, cared for and safe: a hug from family when you want it, a high-five, holding hands to cross the road, a doctor checking you with a parent there.

steps.title: Unsafe touch
steps.body: **Unsafe touches** hurt you or make you feel scared, confused or yucky: hitting, pinching, kicking, or **anyone touching your private parts** (except for keeping you clean or healthy), or asking **you** to touch **their** private parts, or showing you pictures of private parts.

steps.title: The swimsuit rule
steps.body: Nobody should touch, look at or take pictures of the parts covered by your swimsuit — **and you shouldn’t touch theirs**. If anyone tries, even someone you know and love, you can say **NO**, **GO** away, and **TELL** a grown-up you trust.

steps.title: For grown-ups
steps.body: Let children choose how to greet relatives — a hug, a wave or a namaste. Forcing hugs teaches them their ‘no’ doesn’t count. Most abuse is by someone the child knows, so the rule applies to everyone.

steps.title: Practise
steps.body: Stand tall, hold up your hand and say in a strong voice: **‘No! Stop! I don’t like that!’** Then name who you would tell.

activity.prompt: Is it a safe touch or an unsafe touch?

items.text: A high-five from a friend
Holding Mummy’s hand to cross the road
Someone touching your private parts and saying it’s a secret
Getting hit or pinched
A hug from Nani when you want one
Someone showing you pictures of private parts

quiz.q: If someone touches your private parts, what do you do?
options: Say NO, GO away and TELL a trusted grown-up
quiz.why: Say NO, GO away and TELL a trusted grown-up. That is the No, Go, Tell rule to keep you safe.

quiz.q: Do you have to hug someone if you don’t want to?
options: No — you can wave or say namaste instead
quiz.why: No, you don't have to hug anyone. You can wave or say namaste instead, because you choose how to greet.

quiz.q: Which is a safe touch?
options: Touching private parts as a game
Holding hands to cross the road
quiz.why: Holding hands to cross the road is a safe touch because it keeps you safe. Kicking, pinching and touching private parts as a game are not safe.

quiz.q: Is it your fault if someone gives you an unsafe touch?
quiz.why: It is never your fault if someone gives you an unsafe touch. The grown-up or older person is the one who did wrong.

lessons.title: Secrets vs surprises

scenes.text: Meera, 6, helps Papa hide a present for Mummy’s birthday. ‘It’s a surprise until Sunday!’
Later, a neighbour gives Meera chocolate and says, ‘Don’t tell anyone I touched you. It’s our secret.’
Meera remembers her class: surprises are happy and end soon. Secrets that make you feel bad must be told.
She tells Mummy, who hugs her and says ‘Thank you for telling me. You are safe.’

steps.title: Surprises
steps.body: A **surprise** is something happy that everyone finds out about soon — like a birthday present or a party. Keeping a surprise is fun.

steps.title: Unsafe secrets
steps.body: An **unsafe secret** is something someone tells you never to tell, especially about touching, pictures, or something that makes you feel scared, sad or confused. **You never have to keep an unsafe secret.** Telling is not tattling — it keeps you safe.

steps.title: Tricky words
steps.body: Grown-ups who want to hurt children sometimes say: ‘Your parents will be angry,’ ‘Nobody will believe you,’ or give gifts so you keep quiet. **None of that is true.** Tell anyway.

steps.title: For grown-ups
steps.body: Use ‘surprise’ for happy things in your family and avoid asking children to keep secrets from other caregivers. Say often: ‘You can tell me anything, and I won’t be angry with you.’

activity.prompt: Surprise (okay to keep for now) or unsafe secret (tell a grown-up)?

items.text: A present for Dada’s birthday
Someone says ‘don’t tell anyone I touched you’
A party plan for your teacher
A big child says ‘don’t tell or I’ll hurt you’
Someone asks you for a photo without clothes

quiz.q: A surprise is…
options: Something happy everyone will know about soon
quiz.why: A surprise is something happy that everyone will know about soon, like a birthday gift. It is not scary or kept forever.

quiz.q: Someone gives you a gift and says ‘Don’t tell your parents about our touching game.’ What do you do?
quiz.why: Tell a trusted grown-up. A 'secret touching game' is an unsafe secret, and gifts don't make it okay.

quiz.q: Is telling an unsafe secret ‘tattling’?
quiz.why: No, telling an unsafe secret is not tattling. It keeps you safe and is brave.

quiz.q: Will you get in trouble for telling?
options: No — the grown-up who asked for the secret is wrong, not you
quiz.why: No, you won't be in trouble. The grown-up who asked you to keep the secret is wrong, not you.

lessons.title: My trusted grown-ups and my safety hand

scenes.text: Ravi, 5, traces his hand on paper at school.
On each finger he draws a trusted grown-up: Ammi, Abbu, Nani, his teacher Miss Rose, and the school nurse.
He sticks it on the fridge. ‘If I need help, I have five people!’

steps.title: Your safety hand
steps.body: Pick **five grown-ups** you trust — at home, at school, and in the family. They listen, keep you safe and believe you. If you need help and one is not there, you try the next finger.

steps.title: Know important things
steps.body: Learn your **full name**, a parent’s **name and phone number**, and your home area. In India, **1098** is **Childline** — a free number for children who need help, any time, day or night. **112** is for any emergency.

steps.title: Keep telling
steps.body: If you tell someone and they don’t help, **tell another grown-up** on your safety hand — keep telling until someone helps.

steps.title: For grown-ups
steps.body: Help your child choose their five, and let those adults know they are on the list. Practise their phone number as a song. Stay calm and grateful whenever your child tells you something worrying — your reaction teaches them whether it’s safe to tell.

activity.prompt: Make your safety hand (with a grown-up):
items: Trace my hand on paper
Draw or write 5 trusted grown-ups, one on each finger
Learn a parent’s phone number
Learn that 1098 is Childline and 112 is for emergencies
Practise saying ‘No! Go! Tell!’
Put my safety hand where I can see it

quiz.q: What is a trusted grown-up?
options: Someone who listens and keeps you safe
quiz.why: A trusted grown-up is someone who listens and keeps you safe. They never ask you to keep secrets about touching.

quiz.q: Childline’s number is…
quiz.why: Childline's number is 1098. It is free and for children who need help.

quiz.q: If the first grown-up doesn’t help, what should you do?
options: Tell another grown-up on your safety hand
quiz.why: If the first grown-up doesn't help, tell another grown-up on your safety hand. Keep telling until someone helps.

quiz.q: Which number is for any emergency in India?
quiz.why: 112 is the number for any emergency in India. 1098 is Childline.

questions.why: My body belongs to me. It isn't my friend's or my teacher's.

questions.q: Private parts are the parts covered by…
questions.why: Private parts are covered by underwear or a swimsuit. That is the swimsuit rule.

questions.q: What do you say if someone gives an unsafe touch?
questions.why: If someone gives an unsafe touch, say No! Go! Tell! Say no, go away and tell a trusted grown-up.

questions.q: A present for Mummy’s birthday is a…
questions.why: A present for Mummy's birthday is a surprise, which is happy and will be shared soon. It isn't an unsafe secret.

questions.q: Someone says ‘don’t tell anyone about our touching game’. That is…
options: An unsafe secret — tell a grown-up
questions.why: 'Don't tell anyone about our touching game' is an unsafe secret. Tell a trusted grown-up.

questions.q: Do you have to hug relatives if you don’t want to?
options: No, you can wave or say namaste
questions.why: No, you don't have to hug relatives if you don't want to. You can wave or say namaste instead.
Childline's number is 1098. It is free for children.

options: No, it is the correct name
questions.why: No, 'penis' and 'vulva' are correct names, not rude words. Correct names help children speak clearly.

questions.q: If someone you know and love touches your private parts, is the swimsuit rule still true?
options: No, it’s okay if you know them
questions.why: Yes, the swimsuit rule applies to everyone, even someone you know and love. Tell a trusted grown-up.

questions.q: If you tell and nobody helps, what next?
questions.why: If nobody helps, tell another trusted grown-up. Keep telling until someone listens.

courses.title: Privacy, consent and families
courses.summary: Primary-school lessons on many kinds of families, privacy and boundaries, consent in everyday life, online safety and how to get help.
outcomes: Learners can describe different kinds of families respectfully
Learners can set and respect body boundaries and privacy
Learners can explain consent (ask, clear yes, stop on no, change your mind)
Learners can spot online grooming red flags and know where to get help (1098, 112, 1930)
courses.guardianNote: For ages 6–10. Covers different kinds of families, privacy and body boundaries, consent in everyday life (hugs, games, tickling, photos), online safety, and what abuse is and how to get help. No sexual content. Based on UNESCO ITGSE 2018 learning objectives for ages 5–8 and 9–12.

lessons.title: Families come in many kinds

scenes.text: Class 3 in Shillong makes family trees. Lalit draws his Mum, Dad and sister.
Ayesha lives with her grandparents. Jonah has two homes because his parents are divorced. Sana’s mother is raising her alone. Ben was adopted.
One child says ‘That’s not a real family.’ The teacher answers: ‘A family is people who love and care for each other.’
The wall of family trees looks wonderful — every one different.

steps.title: What makes a family
steps.body:
A **family** is a group of people who care for each other. Families can be:
- a mother, father and children
- a single parent and children
- grandparents raising grandchildren
- joint families with aunts, uncles and cousins
- adoptive or foster families
- families where parents live in different homes
- families with two mums or two dads

What matters is **love, care and safety**, not the shape.

steps.title: Rights in every family
steps.body: Every child has the right to be safe, fed, loved, educated and listened to (UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, which India has signed).

steps.title: Worked example: kind words
steps.body: Instead of ‘Why don’t you have a dad?’ try ‘Who lives in your home?’ Instead of ‘That’s weird,’ try ‘Cool, tell me more.’

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body:
- Teasing someone about their family
- Thinking only one kind of family is ‘normal’
- Assuming everyone celebrates the same festivals or has the same rules

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Draw your family — everyone who cares for you, even pets!

statements.s: A family can be grandparents raising grandchildren.
Only families with a mother and father are real families.
statements.why: Love and care make a family, not its shape.

statements.s: Adopted children are part of their family just like anyone else.
It’s kind to ask ‘Who lives in your home?’ instead of making guesses.

quiz.q: What makes a family?
quiz.why: A family is made by love, care and safety. House size, number of children or the same surname don't decide it.

quiz.q: Jonah’s parents live in two houses. His family is…
quiz.why: Jonah's family is a real family, even with two homes. Many families have parents in separate homes.

quiz.q: A kind question to ask a new friend is…
options: Why don’t you have a dad?
quiz.why: 'Who lives in your home?' is an open, kind question. Asking if a family is weird or why someone lacks a parent can hurt.

quiz.q: Which right does every child have?
quiz.why: Every child has the right to be safe and loved. Driving or having a phone are not child rights.

sources: UN Convention on the Rights of the Child

lessons.title: Privacy: my body, my space

scenes.text: Diya, 8, has started closing the bathroom door. Her little brother keeps barging in.
She feels annoyed and embarrassed. Mum explains that wanting privacy is normal as you grow.
The family agrees on a rule: knock and wait. Diya feels respected.

steps.title: What is privacy?
steps.body: **Privacy** means having some things that are just yours — your body, your space, your thoughts. As you grow, you may want to change clothes, bathe and use the toilet alone. That’s healthy.

steps.title: Body boundaries
steps.body:
A **boundary** is a line you set about what feels okay. Examples:
- ‘Please knock before coming in.’
- ‘I don’t want to be tickled now.’
- ‘Don’t take my photo.’

Other people have boundaries too, and you respect theirs.

steps.title: When others may see or touch private parts
steps.body: Only to keep you **clean or healthy**: a parent helping a young child wash, or a doctor or nurse during a check-up — and **a parent or trusted adult should know and usually be present**. Nobody else.

steps.title: Worked example: photos
steps.body: Uncle wants to post a bath-time photo of you online. You can say ‘Please don’t post that.’ Photos of people without clothes should **never** be taken or shared — by anyone.

steps.title: Practise boundary sentences
steps.body: Say out loud: ‘Please knock.’ ‘I don’t like that. Stop.’ ‘That’s private.’

a.text: You’re changing after swimming class. An older child peeps over the stall and laughs.

choices.label: Say firmly ‘That’s private! Stop!’ and tell the coach
choices.feedback: Clear words and telling an adult protect your privacy.

choices.label: Say nothing and feel bad
choices.feedback: Your feelings matter — telling helps.

b.text: The coach says she will talk to the child and keep the changing room supervised.

choices.label: Thank the coach and tell your parent at home
choices.feedback: Telling more than one trusted adult is good.

choices.label: Tell your parent and the coach
choices.feedback: It’s never too late to tell.

end1.text: Your privacy is protected and the changing room is safer for everyone.

quiz.q: What is a boundary?
options: A line you set about what feels okay for you
quiz.why: A boundary is a line you set about what feels okay for you. It protects your comfort and is not meant to be rude.

quiz.q: Who may check your private parts?
options: A doctor for health, with a parent knowing
quiz.why: Only a doctor, for health, with a parent knowing, may check your private parts. Classmates, strangers online or any adult may not.

quiz.q: Someone wants to post your bath photo. You can…
quiz.why: You can say 'Please don't post that'. You have the right to refuse a photo being shared.

quiz.q: Wanting privacy as you grow is…
quiz.why: Wanting privacy as you grow is normal and healthy. It isn't rude or strange.

quiz.q: If someone sets a boundary with you, you should…
quiz.why: Respect the boundary when someone sets one. Everyone's boundaries count.

lessons.title: Consent basics: ask, listen, respect

scenes.text: Aman, 7, tickles his cousin Rhea. At first she laughs, then says ‘Stop!’
Aman keeps going because she’s still laughing. Rhea starts crying.
Uncle explains: ‘When someone says stop, we stop — even if they’re laughing. Laughing can be nervous.’
Aman says sorry. Next time he asks: ‘Can I tickle you?’

steps.title: What consent means
steps.body: **Consent** means **asking** and **getting a clear yes** before doing something that involves someone else’s body or things — and **stopping** when they say no or seem unsure. It applies to hugs, tickling, games, borrowing things and taking photos.

steps.title: Stop means stop
steps.body:
- ‘No’, ‘Stop’, ‘I don’t want to’, a pushed-away hand or a silent, unhappy face all mean **stop**.
- You can **change your mind** any time. A ‘yes’ earlier can become ‘no’ now.
- **Silence is not a yes.**

steps.title: Worked example: asking
steps.body:
- ‘Can I give you a hug?’
- ‘Do you want to play wrestling, or something else?’
- ‘Can I take your photo and show Mum?’

If they say no: ‘Okay!’ — and pick something else. No sulking.

steps.title: When it’s not about choice
steps.body: Some things are about safety, not consent: holding hands to cross a road, vaccines, a seat belt. Grown-ups decide these to keep you safe. But **no one** gets to touch your private parts or ask for secrets, whatever they say.

steps.title: Try this game
steps.body: Play ‘Ask first’: before any high-five, hug or tag, ask. Notice how it feels to be asked.

statements.s: If someone is laughing while saying ‘stop’, you can keep going.
statements.why: Stop means stop; laughter can be nervous.

statements.s: You can change your mind after saying yes.
statements.why: Consent can be taken back at any time.

statements.s: Silence means yes.
statements.why: Only a clear, happy yes counts.

statements.s: Asking ‘Can I hug you?’ is a good habit.
Consent applies to taking someone’s photo.

quiz.q: Consent means…
options: Asking and getting a clear yes, and stopping on a no
quiz.why: Consent means asking, getting a clear yes, and stopping on a no. It isn't just doing what you want.

quiz.q: Rhea laughs but says stop. Aman should…
quiz.why: 'Stop' always means stop, even if Rhea is laughing. Aman should stop immediately.

quiz.q: Which shows ‘no’?
quiz.why: Pushing your hand away shows 'no'. Body language can mean no even without words.

quiz.q: Holding hands to cross the road is…
quiz.why: Holding hands to cross the road is about safety, not choice. Safety rules protect you.

quiz.q: Your friend says no to a hug. Good response?
quiz.why: 'Okay! High-five instead?' respects your friend's no and offers another option. Hugging anyway or sulking doesn't.

lessons.title: Online safety and getting help

scenes.text: Riya, 9, from Bhopal plays an online game. A player called ‘StarGirl12’ chats with her every day and sends gifts in the game.
One day StarGirl asks, ‘Send me a photo of you in your night-clothes. Don’t tell your mum — our secret!’
Riya remembers: secrets plus photos = tell. She shows her father.
Her father blocks and reports the account. They learn ‘StarGirl’ was actually an adult man.

steps.title: People online may not be who they say
steps.body: Anyone can pretend to be a child online. People who want to harm children may be friendly, give gifts, flatter you and then ask for **secrets, photos or meetings**. This is called **grooming**.

steps.title: Red-flag messages
steps.body:
- ‘Don’t tell your parents.’
- ‘Send me a photo’ — especially without clothes or in night-clothes
- ‘Let’s meet’ or ‘What’s your address/school?’
- ‘You’re so mature for your age.’
- Gifts, game coins or money in return for something

**Any of these = stop, screenshot if you can, tell a trusted adult.**

steps.title: Safe habits
steps.body:
- Use a nickname, not your full name
- Never share address, school, phone number or passwords
- Keep accounts private; only add people you know in real life
- Use devices in shared family spaces
- **Block and report** anyone who makes you uncomfortable

steps.title: What abuse is — and that it’s never your fault
steps.body:
**Abuse** is when someone hurts a child — by hitting, by not caring for them, by cruel words, or by **sexual abuse** (touching private parts, showing sexual pictures, asking for photos). It is **always the adult’s or older person’s fault, never the child’s**.

In India the **POCSO Act** protects every child under 18. Help: **1098** (Childline), **112**, or **cybercrime.gov.in / 1930** for online problems.

steps.title: Worked example: telling
steps.body: ‘Papa, someone in my game asked for a photo and said it’s a secret. I feel weird.’ — That’s all you need to say. A good adult will **thank you, not shout**, and help you block and report.

a.text: A game friend you’ve never met says: ‘You’re my best friend. Send a photo of you, just for me. Don’t tell your parents.’

choices.label: Don’t reply; tell a parent or trusted adult
choices.feedback: Exactly right — secrets plus photo requests are a red flag.

choices.label: Send an ordinary photo, it’s harmless
choices.feedback: Even ordinary photos can reveal where you live or go to school, and lead to more requests.

choices.label: Ask them why first
