choices.feedback: Groomers have clever answers. It’s safer to stop and tell.

b.text: Your parent thanks you and says ‘Let’s screenshot, block and report.’

choices.label: Help them take screenshots and report
choices.feedback: Evidence helps platforms and police act.

c.text: They now ask for more photos and say ‘If you don’t, I’ll tell your parents you sent one.’

choices.label: Stop, and tell a trusted adult right away
choices.feedback: Threats are a trick. You are not in trouble — tell now.

end1.text: The account is reported. You kept yourself and maybe other children safe.

quiz.q: What is grooming?
options: When someone builds trust with a child to harm them
quiz.why: Grooming is when someone builds trust with a child in order to harm them. Groomers flatter, give gifts and ask for secrets.

quiz.q: Which is a red flag online?
options: ‘Don’t tell your parents, send me a photo’
quiz.why: 'Don't tell your parents, send me a photo' is a red flag, since secrets and photo requests are grooming signs. 'Good game!' and 'Nice move' are normal.

quiz.q: Who is at fault if a child is abused?
quiz.why: The person who harmed the child is at fault. Abuse is never the child's fault.

quiz.q: What should you share online?
quiz.why: Only share a nickname online. Passwords, school names and addresses are private details.

quiz.q: Which law protects children in India from sexual abuse?
quiz.why: The POCSO Act (2012) protects children in India from sexual abuse. The Income Tax, Companies and Motor Vehicles Acts cover other matters.

options: Only mum, dad and two kids
People who love and care for each other
questions.why: A family is people who love and care for each other. It doesn't depend on surnames or on having two parents and two kids.

options: Asking and getting a clear yes
questions.why: Consent means asking and getting a clear yes. Never asking or doing what you like ignores the other person.
Stop means stop, even if the other person is laughing. Always stop.
Your home address is private information online, because someone could find you. Game scores and favourite colours are safe.
Childline's number is 1098. 108 is the ambulance, and 1930 is cybercrime.

questions.q: Someone online says ‘Don’t tell your parents’. That is…
questions.why: 'Don't tell your parents' is a red flag, because safe people don't ask for secrecy. Tell a trusted adult.

options: Not a yes — ask and check
questions.why: Silence is not a yes, so ask and check. Only a clear yes counts.

questions.q: Who may see your private parts?
options: Doctor for health, with parent knowing
questions.why: Only a doctor for health, with a parent knowing, may see your private parts. Other adults and online friends may not.

questions.q: Can you change your mind after saying yes to a game?
questions.why: Yes, you can change your mind after saying yes. Consent can be withdrawn at any time.

options: Gifts plus asking for secret photos
questions.why: Gifts plus asking for secret photos is grooming behaviour. A friend saying hi or a teacher giving homework is normal.

questions.q: A child was tricked into sending a photo and is now threatened. Best step?
options: Tell a trusted adult immediately; report via 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in
questions.why: The child should tell a trusted adult immediately and report via 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in. The child isn't in trouble, and adults and police can help; sending more or hiding makes it worse.

questions.q: Which law protects every child under 18 in India from sexual abuse?
questions.why: The POCSO Act 2012 protects every child under 18 in India from sexual abuse. RTI and consumer laws cover other matters.

courses.title: Consent, crushes and online safety
courses.summary: For Class 6–8: consent in depth (FRIES), crushes and healthy friendships, peer pressure, online safety including sextortion, and recognising abuse with POCSO protection.
outcomes: Learners can apply the FRIES model of consent offline and online
Learners can tell healthy from unhealthy friendships and resist peer pressure
Learners can recognise grooming and sextortion and follow the six response steps
Learners can recognise forms of abuse and help a friend get support under POCSO
courses.guardianNote: For ages 11–13. Covers consent in depth, crushes and healthy friendships, online safety (grooming, image requests, sextortion basics), and recognising abuse with POCSO protections and helplines. Non-explicit. Aligned with UNESCO ITGSE 2018 objectives for ages 9–12 and 12–15.

lessons.title: Consent in depth: FRIES

scenes.text: At a birthday party in Nagpur, Nikhil, 12, snaps a silly photo of his friend Tanvi mid-sneeze and wants to post it.
Tanvi says ‘Delete it please.’ Nikhil says ‘But you said I could take photos earlier!’
His sister explains: ‘Saying yes to one thing isn’t yes to everything. And she can change her mind.’
Nikhil deletes it. Tanvi trusts him more after that.

steps.title: FRIES: five parts of consent
steps.body:
A widely used way to remember consent is **FRIES**:
- **F**reely given — no pressure, threats, guilt or tricks
- **R**eversible — you can change your mind any time
- **I**nformed — you know what you’re agreeing to
- **E**nthusiastic — a real, happy yes, not a shrug
- **S**pecific — yes to one thing is not yes to everything

steps.title: Worked example: is it consent?
steps.body:
1. ‘Fine, whatever, if you’ll stop asking.’ → **Not freely given** (pressure).
2. Tanvi agreed to photos, but not posting. → **Not specific**.
3. A friend agreed to share a secret, then says ‘Actually, don’t tell.’ → Consent **reversed** — respect it.
4. ‘Yes! Let’s play cricket!’ → Clear, enthusiastic consent.

steps.title: Consent online
steps.body: Consent applies to **photos, tagging, forwarding messages and sharing passwords**. Before posting a picture of someone, ask. Before forwarding a private chat, ask. Screenshots of private conversations shared without permission break trust and can cause real harm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking ‘they didn’t say no’ = yes
- Pressuring with ‘If you were my real friend…’
- Thinking consent once means consent forever
- Ignoring body language like stepping back or going quiet

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Practise two sentences: one to **ask** (‘Is it okay if I post this?’) and one to **refuse** (‘No, I’m not comfortable with that.’)

activity.prompt: Match each FRIES letter to its meaning:
pairs: You can change your mind any time
You know what you’re agreeing to
Yes to one thing isn’t yes to everything

quiz.q: ‘Fine, whatever, just stop asking’ is…
quiz.why: 'Fine, whatever, just stop asking' is not freely given consent. It is a yes caused by pressure, so it isn't real consent.

quiz.q: Tanvi agreed to photos but not posting. Posting would break which part?
quiz.why: Tanvi agreed to photos but not posting, so posting would break the 'specific' part of consent. Agreeing to one thing isn't agreeing to everything.

quiz.q: Can someone take back their consent?
quiz.why: Yes, consent can be taken back at any time. Someone can change their mind even after saying yes.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a sign of consent?
quiz.why: Silence and stepping away is not a sign of consent; it means check in or stop. 'Yes, I'd love to', 'Let's do it!' and a smile with 'sure!' are clear.

quiz.q: Before forwarding a friend’s private chat, you should…
quiz.why: Ask your friend first before forwarding a private chat. Online consent matters too.

lessons.title: Crushes, friendships and peer pressure

scenes.text: Pooja, 13, from Kochi has a crush on Rahul. Her friends dare her to send him a love note in class.
She doesn’t want to, but they call her ‘scared’.
She remembers: real friends respect your choices. She says, ‘No, I’ll decide when I’m ready.’
One friend, Ann, quietly says ‘Good for you.’ Pooja realises who her true friends are.

steps.title: Crushes are normal
steps.body: A crush is a strong attraction to someone — a classmate, a friend, someone older, someone famous; it may be someone of another gender or the same gender. Crushes can feel exciting, confusing or painful. **You decide** whether to keep it private, share it with a friend, or tell the person. There’s no rush.

steps.title: Healthy vs unhealthy friendships
steps.body:
**Healthy:** respect, honesty, kindness, fun, supporting each other, accepting ‘no’, having other friends too.

**Unhealthy:** constant teasing that hurts, pressure, jealousy, controlling who you talk to, sharing your secrets, leaving you out as punishment, making you feel bad about yourself.

steps.title: Peer pressure
steps.body:
Peer pressure is feeling pushed by friends to do something. It can be **positive** (joining a study group) or **negative** (dares, bunking, vaping, sending photos, teasing someone).

Ways to say no:
- Clear: ‘No thanks.’
- Reason: ‘My parents would ground me forever.’
- Change subject: ‘Let’s go play instead.’
- Leave: walk away.
- Joke: ‘Nah, I’m too lazy for that.’

steps.title: Worked example: when your crush says no
steps.body: Rahul says ‘I don’t like you that way, sorry.’ Pooja feels hurt. Healthy steps: cry if needed, talk to Ann, do something she enjoys, and treat Rahul normally. **Not** spreading rumours, stalking his social media or posting sad messages about him.

steps.title: Older people and crushes
steps.body: If an adult or much older teen tells you they ‘like you’ romantically, asks you to keep it secret, or wants to meet alone — that is **not okay**, even if you like the attention. Tell a trusted adult or call **1098**.

a.text: Your friends dare you to message your crush something embarrassing from a fake account.

choices.label: Say ‘No, that’s not cool,’ and change the subject
choices.feedback: Clear and confident.

choices.label: Do it to avoid being teased
choices.feedback: Fake accounts and teasing can hurt others — and you.

choices.label: Shrug, laugh it off, and hang out with friends who respect you
choices.feedback: Strong friendships survive a ‘no’.

choices.label: Give in after all
choices.feedback: It’s hard, but giving in once often leads to more pressure.

c.text: Your crush gets upset and the message is forwarded around.

choices.label: Apologise honestly and ask an adult to help fix it
choices.feedback: Owning a mistake takes courage.

end1.text: You kept your values and found out who your real friends are.

end2.text: Mistakes happen. Next time, trust your gut earlier.

quiz.q: A crush on someone of the same gender is…
options: One of the normal ways attraction happens
quiz.why: A crush on someone of the same gender is one of the normal ways attraction happens. It isn't wrong, an illness or always a phase.

quiz.q: Which is a sign of an unhealthy friendship?
quiz.why: Controlling who you talk to is a sign of an unhealthy friendship. Respecting your no, helping with homework and laughing together are healthy.

quiz.q: A good way to say no to a dare?
quiz.why: 'No thanks, let's do something else.' is a clear no with a new plan. Giving in, crying or hitting doesn't help.

quiz.q: An adult says he ‘likes you’ and wants to meet secretly. You should…
options: Tell a trusted adult or call 1098
quiz.why: An adult wanting to meet a child secretly is a grooming red flag, so tell a trusted adult or call 1098. Don't keep it secret or feel flattered and go.

quiz.q: Your crush says no. Healthy response?
options: Respect it and lean on friends
quiz.why: Respect the no and lean on friends. Spreading rumours, repeated messages or sad posts about them isn't respectful.

lessons.title: Online safety: images, grooming and sextortion

scenes.text: Aditya, 13, from Ranchi gets a message from a ‘girl his age’ on social media. They chat for days.
She sends a photo and asks for one of him without a shirt. He sends it.
Immediately ‘she’ demands ₹5,000 or the photo goes to his whole school. It’s a scammer.
Terrified, he tells his father. They don’t pay; they screenshot everything, block, report on cybercrime.gov.in, and use the ‘Take It Down’ tool.
The threat fades. Aditya learns: telling was the strongest thing he did.

steps.title: How grooming and sextortion work
steps.body:
**Grooming:** someone builds trust (flattery, gifts, ‘you’re mature’, ‘nobody understands you like me’), then isolates (‘our secret’), then asks for images or meetings.

**Sextortion:** someone gets an intimate image — sometimes by sending a fake one first — then **threatens to share it** unless you pay or send more. Scammers often target boys 13–17 with fake ‘girl’ profiles.

steps.title: The law on images of under-18s
steps.body: In India, any sexual or nude image of a person **under 18** is treated as **child sexual abuse material** under the **POCSO Act** and the **IT Act**. Creating, asking for, keeping or forwarding it is a serious crime. A child who is **tricked or threatened is a victim**, not a criminal — tell and get help.

steps.title: If it happens: the 6 steps
steps.body:
1. **Don’t pay and don’t send more** — paying usually leads to more demands.
2. **Stop replying.** Don’t delete the chat yet.
3. **Screenshot** profile name, messages, payment requests.
4. **Tell a trusted adult** right away.
5. **Report**: on the app; at **cybercrime.gov.in** or **1930**; **1098** Childline.
6. **Take It Down** (by NCMEC) helps remove nude images of under-18s from many platforms without sharing the image itself.

steps.title: Prevention settings
steps.body:
- Private account; approve followers you know
- Turn off location sharing in photos and apps
- Don’t accept DMs from strangers
- Remember: anything sent can be **screenshotted, saved and shared forever**, even on ‘disappearing’ apps

steps.title: Worked example: spot the fake
steps.body: A new profile: 3 photos, all professional-looking; 2 days old; few friends; immediately flirty; asks you to move to another app; asks for a photo. **Five red flags.** Block and report.

activity.prompt: Put the sextortion response steps in the right order:
items: Stop replying and do not pay
Screenshot the profile and messages
Tell a trusted adult immediately
Report on the app and at cybercrime.gov.in / 1930
Use ‘Take It Down’ to help remove the image
Get emotional support — talk to someone or call 14416

quiz.q: What is sextortion?
options: Threatening to share an intimate image unless the victim pays or sends more
quiz.why: Sextortion means threatening to share an intimate image unless the victim pays or sends more. It is blackmail using images.

quiz.q: Should you pay a sextortion scammer?
options: No — paying usually brings more demands
quiz.why: No, don't pay a sextortion scammer, as paying usually brings more demands. Report it instead.

quiz.q: A 13-year-old is tricked into sending an image. In the eyes of the law they are…
options: A victim who should get help
Fine only if they delete it
quiz.why: A child who is tricked or extorted is a victim who should get help. They are not a criminal or to blame.

quiz.q: Which number is India’s cybercrime helpline?
quiz.why: 1930 is India's cybercrime helpline, and you can also report at cybercrime.gov.in. 112 is for emergencies and 1098 is Childline.

quiz.q: ‘Disappearing’ messages are completely safe because…
options: They aren’t — screenshots and recording are possible
quiz.why: 'Disappearing' messages aren't completely safe, because screenshots and recordings are possible. Anything sent can be captured.

lessons.title: Recognising abuse and getting help

scenes.text: Simran, 12, goes to home tuition in Ludhiana. Her tutor starts sitting too close, touching her knee and saying ‘You’re my favourite. Don’t tell anyone.’
She feels confused — he’s respected and her parents like him.
She remembers her school workshop and tells the school counsellor.
The counsellor believes her, informs her parents, and helps report it under POCSO. Simran is told again and again: ‘This is not your fault.’

steps.title: Types of abuse
steps.body:
- **Physical:** hitting, burning, hurting the body
- **Emotional:** constant insults, threats, humiliation
- **Neglect:** not given food, care, safety or schooling
- **Sexual:** any sexual touching, showing sexual images, asking for photos, sexual talk, or making a child watch or do sexual things

Most sexual abuse of children is by **someone the child knows** — a relative, neighbour, tutor, coach, or older child.

steps.title: POCSO in brief
steps.body:
The **Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012** protects **every child under 18**, any gender.
- Children can report to police, Childline **1098**, or a trusted adult
- Police statements should be recorded in a child-friendly way, and the child’s identity must be kept **confidential**
- Adults who know about abuse are required by law to report it

This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Warning signs of grooming by someone you know
steps.body:
- Treating one child as ‘special’ with gifts or attention
- Finding ways to be alone with a child
- Testing boundaries with ‘accidental’ touches
- Asking for secrecy
- Sexual jokes or showing pictures
- Saying ‘nobody will believe you’

steps.title: How to tell
steps.body: Choose an adult you trust. Say: ‘Something happened that made me uncomfortable. Can I tell you?’ If they don’t help, **tell someone else**. You can call **1098** any time, free. If a friend tells **you**, believe them, don’t promise to keep it secret, and help them tell an adult.

steps.title: After telling
steps.body: Feelings like fear, guilt, anger or numbness are normal. Counselling helps — ask the school counsellor, or call **Tele-MANAS 14416**. Healing is possible, and nothing that happened was your fault.

a.text: Your friend tells you a cousin has been touching her in ways that scare her. She says ‘Promise you won’t tell.’

choices.label: Say ‘I believe you. This isn’t your fault. Let’s tell a trusted adult together.’
choices.feedback: Believing and helping is exactly right.

choices.label: Promise to keep the secret
choices.feedback: Keeping it secret can leave her unsafe.

choices.label: Say ‘Are you sure? He seems nice.’
choices.feedback: Doubting can make her stop talking. Abusers often seem nice.

b.text: She agrees to talk to the school counsellor with you.

choices.label: Go together and let the counsellor take it from there
choices.feedback: You’ve helped her get protection.

c.text: Your friend goes quiet and seems more scared.

choices.label: Go back and say ‘I believe you. I want you to be safe — can we tell someone together?’
choices.feedback: It’s never too late.

choices.label: Call 1098 for advice
choices.feedback: Childline can guide you both.

end1.text: Your friend is supported and safer. You were a true friend.

quiz.q: Most child sexual abuse is by…
quiz.why: Most child sexual abuse is by someone the child knows. That is why 'stranger danger' alone isn't enough.

quiz.q: POCSO protects…
quiz.why: POCSO protects every child under 18 of any gender. It isn't limited to girls, under-12s or cities.

quiz.q: A friend says ‘promise you won’t tell’ about abuse. You should…
options: Believe them and help them tell a trusted adult
quiz.why: Believe your friend and help them tell a trusted adult, because safety comes before keeping a promise. Telling everyone or ignoring it is wrong.

quiz.q: Which is a grooming sign?
options: An adult giving one child secret gifts and wanting time alone
A doctor’s check-up with a parent present
A teacher giving the same homework to all
quiz.why: An adult giving one child secret gifts and wanting time alone is a grooming sign. Secrecy and isolation are warning signs.

quiz.q: Whose fault is abuse?
quiz.why: Abuse is the abuser's fault. It is never the child's fault.

questions.q: What does the R in FRIES stand for?
questions.why: In FRIES, R stands for Reversible, meaning consent can be withdrawn at any time.
Childline's number is 1098. 1930 is cybercrime and 100 is police.
Crushes are normal and part of growing up. They aren't dangerous or illegal.

questions.q: Which is a healthy friendship sign?
questions.why: Respecting your no is a sign of healthy friendship. Jealous control is unhealthy.

questions.q: A good way to resist peer pressure?
options: Clear no plus suggesting something else
questions.why: A clear no plus suggesting something else is a good way to resist peer pressure. Fighting or always giving in doesn't work.

questions.q: Should you pay a sextortion threat?
questions.why: No, don't pay a sextortion threat, because paying brings more demands. Report and get help.

questions.q: Consent to photos means consent to posting?
questions.why: No, consent to photos does not mean consent to posting. Consent is specific.

questions.q: Nude images of under-18s in India are treated as…
options: Child sexual abuse material under POCSO/IT Act
questions.why: Nude images of under-18s are child sexual abuse material under POCSO and the IT Act. It is a serious crime to make, ask for, keep or share them.
Most abusers of children are people the child knows, not strangers or other children only.

questions.q: Which is a fake profile red flag?
options: Account days old, flirty fast, asks to move apps and for photos
questions.why: A fake profile is often days old, gets flirty fast, and asks to move to another app and for photos. A school page or a classmate you know is not a red flag.

options: Remove nude images of under-18s from many platforms
questions.why: Take It Down is a free tool, run by NCMEC, that helps remove nude images of under-18s from many platforms. It is not for finding phones or blocking ads.

questions.q: A friend discloses abuse. Best first words?
options: ‘I believe you. It’s not your fault. Let’s get help.’
questions.why: 'I believe you. It's not your fault. Let's get help.' gives calm belief and support. 'Why didn't you stop it?' or 'Are you sure?' blames or doubts the child.

questions.q: Under POCSO, adults who know a child is being abused…
questions.why: Under POCSO, adults who know a child is being abused must report it. They can't ignore it or ask the abuser first.

questions.q: Which best describes the grooming sequence?
options: Trust → isolation and secrecy → boundary testing and requests
questions.why: Grooming often follows a pattern: build trust, then isolate and demand secrecy, then test boundaries and make requests. Knowing the pattern helps stop it.

courses.title: Relationships, consent and the law
courses.summary: For Class 9–12: healthy vs controlling relationships, consent and India’s age of consent (18, POCSO), sexting law and risks, and how pornography distorts — calm, factual and non-explicit.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish healthy relationships from controlling or abusive ones
Learners can explain consent and why the age of consent in India is 18 under POCSO
Learners can explain the legal and personal risks of sexting and respond to pressure or image abuse
Learners can critically explain how pornography distorts bodies, consent and relationships
Learners can name helplines: 112, 1098, 181, 1930, 14416
courses.guardianNote: For ages 14–17. Covers healthy and unhealthy relationships, consent and the law (age of consent in India is 18 under POCSO), sexting law and risks, and how pornography distorts ideas about bodies, consent and relationships — explained factually and non-explicitly. Follows UNESCO ITGSE 2018 objectives for ages 12–15 and 15–18.

lessons.title: Healthy and unhealthy relationships

scenes.text: Aisha, 16, from Mumbai starts dating Sahil. At first he’s sweet and attentive.
Soon he checks her phone, gets angry when she talks to male classmates, and texts 40 times if she doesn’t reply.
Her friend Lin says ‘That sounds controlling, not caring.’ Aisha isn’t sure — he says it’s because he loves her.
The school counsellor explains the signs of controlling relationships. Aisha decides to end it, with support from her parents.
Months later, she says: ‘I didn’t realise how small I’d become.’

steps.title: What healthy looks like
steps.body:
Healthy relationships (friendships or romantic) have:
- **Respect** for each other’s opinions, friends, time and bodies
- **Trust** — no need to spy
- **Honesty** and open communication
- **Equality** — decisions made together
- **Freedom** to have other friends, hobbies and goals
- **Safety** — you never feel afraid of the other person
- Disagreements solved **without** insults, threats or violence

steps.title: Red flags of control and abuse
steps.body:
- Checking your phone, demanding passwords or location
- Extreme jealousy, accusing you of cheating
- Isolating you from friends or family
- Insults, humiliation, ‘joking’ put-downs
- Threats (‘I’ll hurt myself if you leave’ or ‘I’ll share your photos’)
- Pressure for physical intimacy or photos
- Any hitting, pushing, grabbing

Control often starts small and grows. Love does not mean control.

steps.title: Worked example: caring vs controlling
steps.body:
- ‘Text me when you get home so I know you’re safe.’ → **Caring** (once, mutual)
- ‘Send me a photo of who you’re with right now.’ → **Controlling**
- ‘I miss you, can we hang out this weekend?’ → **Caring**
- ‘If you go to that party, we’re over.’ → **Controlling (ultimatum)**

steps.title: Ending a relationship safely
steps.body:
- Be clear and brief: ‘I don’t want to be in this relationship any more.’
- Tell a trusted adult or friend first
- If you feel unsafe, end it by message or in a public place, and keep evidence of threats
- Change passwords; review shared photos/accounts
- Help: **112** if in danger, **1098** (under 18), **181** Women Helpline

steps.title: Communication skills
steps.body: Use ‘I’ statements: ‘I feel hurt when you check my phone. I need trust.’ Listen without interrupting. Take time out if angry. Both people saying ‘sorry’ and changing behaviour is a sign of health.

activity.prompt: Healthy, or a red flag?

items.text: Supporting your partner’s exam goals
Demanding your passwords
Disagreeing calmly and finding a compromise
‘If you leave me, I’ll hurt myself’
Encouraging time with your friends
Getting angry when you talk to classmates
Pressuring you to send photos
Saying sorry and changing behaviour after a mistake

quiz.q: Which is a sign of a healthy relationship?
options: Mutual respect and freedom to have friends
quiz.why: A healthy relationship has mutual respect and freedom to have friends. Extreme jealousy, phone checking and ultimatums are control.

quiz.q: ‘I’ll share your photos if you leave’ is…
options: A threat and a form of abuse
quiz.why: 'I'll share your photos if you leave' is a threat and a form of abuse, since it uses fear to control. It isn't a joke or romantic; get help from a trusted adult or helpline.

quiz.q: Controlling behaviour usually…
quiz.why: Controlling behaviour usually starts small and grows over time, so early signs matter. It isn't proof of true love.

quiz.q: Women Helpline number in India?
quiz.why: The Women Helpline number is 181. 108 is the ambulance, 1098 is Childline and 1930 is cybercrime.

quiz.q: A good ‘I’ statement is…
options: ‘I feel hurt when you check my phone; I need trust’
quiz.why: A good 'I' statement describes your feeling and need, like 'I feel hurt when you check my phone; I need trust.' 'You're crazy' or 'You always ruin everything' blames.

lessons.title: Consent and the law: why 18 matters

scenes.text: In a Class 11 law-awareness session in Chennai, Karthik, 16, asks: ‘If two 16-year-olds agree, is it still illegal?’
The visiting lawyer explains the POCSO Act and why the age of consent is 18.
Students are surprised. Several had believed ‘if both agree it’s fine’.
The class writes the key points in their notebooks and discusses how consent works in real life.

steps.title: Consent in relationships
steps.body: For any physical intimacy — even holding hands or kissing — **consent** must be **freely given, reversible, informed, enthusiastic and specific** (FRIES). Consent **cannot** be given if someone is asleep, drunk, high, scared, threatened, or pressured. Being in a relationship does **not** mean automatic consent. Checking in (‘Is this okay?’) is normal and respectful.

steps.title: Age of consent in India: 18
steps.body:
Under the **POCSO Act, 2012**, anyone **under 18** is a child, and **any sexual activity with a child is an offence — even if the child says yes**. The law does not have a ‘close-in-age’ exception. This is meant to protect children from exploitation.

The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), in force since 1 July 2024**, also treats sexual acts with a girl under 18 as an offence regardless of her consent.

This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Why the law sets 18
steps.body:
Lawmakers chose 18 because younger teens can be more easily pressured, manipulated or exploited, especially by older people, and because consequences — pregnancy, STIs, emotional harm, images being shared — are serious. Many young people also say they later wish they had waited.

There is ongoing public debate in India about how the law should treat consensual relationships between teenagers close in age; courts have sometimes shown leniency. But **the law as written is clear**, and police and courts do act on it.

steps.title: Mandatory reporting
steps.body: Under POCSO, adults — including doctors, teachers and school staff — who know of sexual activity involving a child are **required to report** it. This can make teens afraid to seek medical help. **Still seek help**: your health matters, and doctors and counsellors aim to protect you.

steps.title: Worked example: is there consent?
steps.body:
1. A person is drunk at a party and can’t stand properly. → **No consent possible.**
2. ‘If you loved me, you would.’ → **Pressure; not freely given.**
3. Both say yes, then one says ‘Actually, stop.’ → **Must stop immediately.**
4. Two 16-year-olds both agree. → **Still an offence under POCSO.**

steps.title: Saying no and hearing no
steps.body:
Saying no: ‘I’m not ready.’ ‘No, and please don’t ask again.’
Hearing no: ‘Okay, thanks for telling me.’ Respecting a no is a sign of maturity, not weakness. If someone ignores your no, it’s not your fault — tell a trusted adult or call **1098** / **112**.

statements.s: In India, the age of consent is 18.
statements.why: POCSO defines a child as under 18.

statements.s: If two 16-year-olds both agree, it’s legal.
Someone who is drunk can give valid consent.
statements.why: Intoxication removes the ability to consent.

statements.s: Being in a relationship means consent is automatic.
Doctors and teachers must report known sexual offences involving children under POCSO.
You can withdraw consent at any moment.

quiz.q: Under POCSO, a ‘child’ is anyone under…
quiz.why: Under POCSO, a 'child' is anyone under 18. Below 18, a person cannot legally consent to sexual activity.

quiz.q: Which situation shows valid consent?
options: A clear, enthusiastic yes from someone who can change their mind
quiz.why: Valid consent is a clear, enthusiastic yes from someone who can change their mind. Silence, a sleeping person or 'If you loved me you would' is not consent.

quiz.q: Which current Indian criminal code replaced the IPC?
quiz.why: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) replaced the Indian Penal Code, in force since 1 July 2024. The other options are not criminal codes.

quiz.q: Someone says ‘stop’ midway. You should…
quiz.why: If someone says 'stop' midway, stop immediately. Consent can be withdrawn at any time, with no need to explain.

quiz.q: Why should a teen still see a doctor even though doctors must report?
options: Their health matters; doctors and counsellors aim to protect them
quiz.why: A teen should still see a doctor, because their health matters and doctors and counsellors aim to protect them. Mandatory reporting is meant to keep children safe.

lessons.title: Sexting: the law and the risks

scenes.text: Meghna, 15, from Kolkata sends a private photo to her boyfriend, trusting him.
After a breakup, the photo appears in a group chat. Dozens of students see it.
She stops eating and won’t go to school. Her mother notices and Meghna finally tells her.
They report to the school and cybercrime police, use ‘Take It Down’, and Meghna gets counselling. The students who shared it face serious consequences.

steps.title: What sexting is
steps.body: **Sexting** means sending sexual messages, photos or videos by phone or online. Many teens feel pressure to do it — ‘everyone does it’, ‘prove you trust me’. Surveys show most teens do **not** sext.

steps.title: The law for under-18s
steps.body:
Any sexual or nude image of a person under 18 counts as **child sexual abuse material** under **POCSO** and the **IT Act** (section 67B). **Making, asking for, possessing, forwarding or uploading** it is a serious crime — even if the person in the photo is yourself or agreed to send it. Forwarding someone else’s image adds to their harm and your legal risk.

For adults, sharing someone’s intimate image without consent is also an offence (IT Act and BNS). This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Why images escape
steps.body:
- Screenshots and screen recordings
- Breakups and revenge
- Hacked accounts and cloud backups
- Lost or repaired phones
- Friends showing friends

Once sent, you **lose control** of an image forever.

steps.title: Handling pressure
steps.body:
Replies that work:
- ‘No. If you respect me, you won’t ask again.’
- ‘That’s illegal for us — not happening.’
- Send a funny meme or a photo of your pet instead.

If someone keeps pushing, that’s a red flag. Block, and tell a trusted adult.

steps.title: If your image has been shared
steps.body:
1. It’s **not your fault** — the person who shared it broke the trust and the law.
2. Don’t delete the evidence: screenshot where it was posted and by whom.
3. Tell a trusted adult; report to the app and at **cybercrime.gov.in / 1930**.
4. Use **Take It Down** (under 18) or **StopNCII.org** (adults) to help stop it spreading.
5. Get support: school counsellor, **1098**, **Tele-MANAS 14416**.

If you **receive** someone’s image: don’t forward it, tell an adult, delete it after reporting.

a.text: Your partner says: ‘Send me a pic. If you trust me, you will. Everyone does it.’

choices.label: ‘No — I’m not comfortable, and it’s illegal for us.’
choices.feedback: Clear and confident.

choices.label: Send one to keep them happy
choices.feedback: You lose control of it forever, and it’s a crime involving under-18s.

b.text: They reply: ‘Wow, you don’t love me then.’

choices.label: ‘Love doesn’t mean pressure. Please don’t ask again.’
choices.feedback: Pressure isn’t love. If it continues, that’s a red flag.

choices.label: Give in to stop the argument
choices.feedback: Giving in to pressure often leads to more demands.

c.text: A week later, after an argument, they threaten to share it.

choices.label: Tell a trusted adult, screenshot the threat, report at 1930/cybercrime.gov.in, use Take It Down
choices.feedback: You are the victim here. Reporting protects you.

choices.label: Send more pictures so they won’t share
choices.feedback: Giving more usually increases the threat.

d.text: They now demand more and money.

choices.label: Stop replying and tell an adult now
choices.feedback: It’s never too late. Help works.

end1.text: You held your boundary. Healthy partners respect a no.

end2.text: With adult help and official reporting, the threat is contained. You get counselling and support.

quiz.q: Is sending a nude selfie legal for a 16-year-old in India?
options: No — it is treated as child sexual abuse material
quiz.why: No, sending a nude selfie at 16 is not legal in India, because it is treated as child sexual abuse material under POCSO and the IT Act, even if self-made.

quiz.q: You receive a classmate’s nude image. Best action?
options: Don’t forward; tell an adult; report; then delete
quiz.why: Don't forward it. Tell an adult, report it and then delete. Forwarding causes harm and is a crime.

quiz.q: Which tool helps adults stop intimate images spreading?
quiz.why: StopNCII.org helps adults stop intimate images spreading by using image hashes to block re-uploads. Calculators, maps and music apps don't.

quiz.q: ‘If you trust me, you’ll send it’ is…
quiz.why: 'If you trust me, you'll send it' is pressure and a red flag. Real trust doesn't require sending images.

quiz.q: Most teens…
quiz.why: Most teens do not sext, according to surveys. So the idea that everyone does is a myth.

lessons.title: Pornography: what it gets wrong

scenes.text: Farhan, 15, first saw pornography at 12 when a friend shared a link. Now he watches often and feels confused and guilty.
He’s started to believe real relationships should look like what he’s seen, and he worries his body is ‘wrong’.
A school health educator explains what pornography is and how it misleads.
Farhan sets limits on his phone, talks to a counsellor, and feels relief at learning the truth.

steps.title: What pornography is
steps.body: Pornography is sexually explicit material made to arouse, usually as a commercial product. **It is not sex education.** It is scripted and edited, often with performers chosen for unusual bodies, using camera tricks, and sometimes made without proper consent. Many teens see it by accident or through friends before they ever choose to. If you’ve seen it, you’re not ‘bad’ — but it helps to understand what it gets wrong.

steps.title: Five distortions
steps.body:
1. **Bodies:** performers’ bodies and genitals are often atypical or surgically altered; it can make normal bodies feel inadequate.
2. **Consent:** much content skips asking, shows people ignoring ‘no’, or presents aggression as normal. **Real intimacy needs clear consent every time.**
3. **Feelings:** it rarely shows talking, care, nervousness, affection or respect — central parts of real relationships.
4. **Safety:** it usually leaves out contraception and protection from STIs.
5. **Performance and stamina:** it uses edits, breaks and sometimes drugs; it sets unrealistic expectations.

steps.title: Legal points (India)
steps.body:
- Material showing anyone under 18 is **child sexual abuse material** — viewing, downloading, storing or sharing it is a serious crime (POCSO, IT Act section 67B).
- Sending explicit material to someone who didn’t ask for it, or showing it to a child, is an offence.
- Many porn sites are blocked in India and are common sources of malware and scams.

This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: When use becomes a problem
steps.body:
Signs that it’s becoming unhelpful: watching more than you want to, feeling unable to stop, it affecting sleep, studies or friendships, needing more extreme content, or feeling ashamed and anxious afterwards.

What helps: content filters and screen-time limits, keeping devices out of the bedroom at night, replacing the habit with exercise or hobbies, and talking to a counsellor (Tele-MANAS **14416**). Shame doesn’t help change; understanding and support do.

steps.title: Better sources
steps.body: For accurate information about bodies, relationships and consent: this course, WHO and UNESCO resources, trained school counsellors and doctors. Ask questions — no question is too embarrassing for a professional.

statements.s: Pornography is a reliable way to learn about sex and relationships.
statements.why: It is entertainment, scripted and edited — not education.

statements.s: It often leaves out consent, contraception and emotions.
statements.why: These are central to real relationships and health.

statements.s: Viewing or sharing material involving under-18s is a serious crime in India.
Performers’ bodies are typical of most people.
statements.why: They are often chosen for atypical features and may be altered.

statements.s: Feeling unable to stop watching is a sign to get support.
statements.why: Counsellors and Tele-MANAS 14416 can help without judgement.

quiz.q: What is pornography designed for?
quiz.why: Pornography is designed for commercial arousal and entertainment. It is not made for education, medical training or consent lessons.

quiz.q: Which is a common distortion in porn?
options: Ignoring consent and showing unrealistic bodies
quiz.why: A common distortion in porn is ignoring consent and showing unrealistic bodies. It doesn't explain contraception or show realistic emotions.

quiz.q: Which sign suggests problematic use?
options: Feeling unable to stop and it affecting sleep and study
quiz.why: Feeling unable to stop, and it affecting sleep and study, suggests problematic use, since loss of control is a key sign. Watching less over time isn't a problem.

quiz.q: Someone sends you explicit images without asking. This is…
options: Can be an offence; block and report
quiz.why: Unsolicited explicit images can be an offence and are harmful, so block and report. They are not a compliment or harmless.

quiz.q: Best source for accurate sexual-health information?
options: WHO/UNESCO resources, doctors and trained counsellors
quiz.why: WHO/UNESCO resources, doctors and trained counsellors give accurate sexual-health information. Porn, rumours and ads don't.

questions.why: The age of consent in India is 18, because POCSO defines a child as anyone under 18.

questions.q: Checking a partner’s phone constantly is…
questions.why: Checking a partner's phone constantly is controlling, because it shows distrust and invades privacy. It is a red flag, not care.

options: Can be saved and shared forever
questions.why: Once sent, a photo can be saved and shared forever, because you lose control of it. 'Disappearing' images can be captured too.

questions.q: Is porn a good teacher of consent?
questions.why: No, porn is not a good teacher of consent, because it often ignores consent and shows unrealistic behaviour.

questions.q: Which is a healthy relationship sign?
questions.why: Respect and freedom is a sign of a healthy relationship. Isolation and ultimatums are control.
No, a drunk person can't consent, because intoxication removes the capacity to make a free, informed choice.

questions.q: Two 16-year-olds agree to sexual activity. Under POCSO this is…
questions.why: Under POCSO it is still an offence, because anyone under 18 cannot legally consent and there is no close-in-age exception. Parental agreement doesn't change this.

questions.q: Your image is shared without consent. First steps?
options: Screenshot evidence, tell an adult, report at 1930/cybercrime.gov.in, use Take It Down
questions.why: Screenshot the evidence, tell an adult, report at 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in, and use Take It Down. Retaliating or deleting evidence hurts your case.

questions.q: Which law section specifically covers sexual material involving children online?
questions.why: Section 67B of the IT Act covers publishing or sharing sexual material involving children online. The RTI Act and Motor Vehicles Act are unrelated.

questions.q: ‘I’ll hurt myself if you leave’ is an example of…
questions.why: Get help; you are not responsible for their choices — tell an adult; they can call 14416.

questions.q: Which current law replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024?
questions.why: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024. POSH is a workplace law and 'IPC 2.0' doesn't exist.

questions.q: Which is a sign of problematic porn use?
options: Loss of control and impact on daily life
questions.why: Loss of control and impact on daily life are signs of problematic porn use, so seek support. Curiosity once or asking a doctor is not a problem.

questions.q: Under POCSO, who must report known sexual offences against a child?
options: Any adult who knows, including doctors and teachers
questions.why: Under POCSO, any adult who knows of a sexual offence against a child must report it, including doctors and teachers. It isn't only parents' duty.

questions.q: Which response to pressure for a photo is strongest?
options: ‘No — please don’t ask again,’ and block/tell if it continues
questions.why: Say a clear 'No — please don't ask again,' and block or tell someone if it continues. 'Maybe later' or a blurred photo leaves the pressure going.

courses.title: Sexual and reproductive health: the facts
courses.summary: Medically accurate, non-explicit facts on how pregnancy happens, contraception and effectiveness, STIs and HIV, and where to get confidential help in India.
outcomes: Learners can explain fertilisation, the fertile window and signs of pregnancy, and correct myths
Learners can compare contraceptive methods using typical-use effectiveness and explain emergency contraception
Learners can describe common STIs and HIV, prevention, testing and treatment
Learners can find confidential services (AFHC/RKSK, ICTC, helplines) and make informed decisions
courses.guardianNote: For ages 16–17 (and young adults). Factual sexual and reproductive health information as recommended by UNESCO ITGSE 2018 and WHO: how pregnancy happens, contraception methods and effectiveness, STIs and HIV including prevention, testing and treatment, and where to get confidential help. It does not encourage sexual activity, restates that the legal age of consent in India is 18, and is non-explicit. Research summarised by UNESCO shows accurate education helps young people delay sex and act more safely when they do become sexually active.

lessons.title: How pregnancy happens — facts and myths

scenes.text: Sneha, 17, from Pune hears a list of ‘facts’ from friends: ‘You can’t get pregnant the first time’, ‘not during periods’, ‘if you jump afterwards’.
She asks her biology teacher, who goes through each one.
Most turn out to be myths. Sneha shares the truth with her friends.

steps.title: The basic biology
steps.body:
Pregnancy begins when a **sperm** from a male fertilises an **egg** from a female, usually in the fallopian tube. The fertilised egg travels to the uterus and **implants** in its lining, where it can grow into an embryo and then a foetus. A pregnancy usually lasts about **40 weeks** counted from the first day of the last period.

Sperm can survive in the female body for **up to about 5 days**; an egg lives about **12–24 hours** after ovulation. So the ‘fertile window’ is roughly the 5 days before ovulation plus ovulation day.

steps.title: Myths vs facts
steps.body:
- ‘Not the first time’ → **False.** Pregnancy can happen the very first time.
- ‘Not during a period’ → **Less likely but possible**, especially with short cycles.
- ‘Withdrawal (pulling out) is safe’ → **Unreliable**; fluid released before ejaculation can contain sperm.
- ‘Washing, urinating or jumping afterwards prevents pregnancy’ → **False.**
- ‘Only if you’ve started periods’ → A girl can ovulate before her first period, so it’s possible.

steps.title: Signs of pregnancy
steps.body:
- A **missed period** (most common first sign)
- Nausea, sometimes vomiting
- Tender, swollen breasts
- Tiredness, needing to urinate more often

A **home pregnancy test** (from pharmacies) detects the hormone hCG in urine; most are accurate from the first day of a missed period. A doctor can confirm with a blood test or ultrasound.

steps.title: Options and help
steps.body:
Anyone worried about pregnancy should talk to a trusted adult and a doctor quickly — time affects options.
- **Government health centres** and **gynaecologists** provide confidential care.
- In India, abortion is legal under the **Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act**, amended in 2021: up to 20 weeks on one doctor’s opinion and up to 24 weeks for certain categories (including minors and survivors of rape) on two doctors’ opinion. For under-18s, a guardian’s written consent is required.
- Unsafe abortion (by untrained people or unverified pills) is dangerous.

This is general education, not medical or legal advice.

steps.title: Worked example: fertile window
steps.body: Riya’s cycle is regular at 28 days. Ovulation is typically about **14 days before** the next period → around day 14. Her fertile window is about days **9–14**. But cycles vary, especially in teens, so ‘calendar counting’ alone is an **unreliable** way to avoid pregnancy.

statements.s: Pregnancy can happen the first time someone has sex.
Jumping or washing after sex prevents pregnancy.
Sperm can survive inside the body for up to about 5 days.
statements.why: Which is why the fertile window spans several days.

statements.s: Withdrawal is a reliable method.
statements.why: It has a high failure rate.

statements.s: A home pregnancy test detects the hormone hCG.
statements.why: Most are accurate from the day of a missed period.

statements.s: In India, abortion is illegal in all cases.
statements.why: It is legal under the MTP Act within set conditions.

quiz.q: Where does fertilisation usually happen?
quiz.why: Fertilisation usually happens in the fallopian tube, where the sperm meets the egg. The embryo then moves to the uterus to implant.

quiz.q: Most common first sign of pregnancy?
quiz.why: The most common first sign of pregnancy is a missed period. Headache, rash and fever are not typical.

quiz.q: How long can sperm survive in the female body?
quiz.why: Sperm can survive in the female body for up to about 5 days. So pregnancy is possible even if sex occurs a few days before ovulation.

quiz.q: Is calendar counting alone reliable for teens?
quiz.why: Calendar counting alone is unreliable for teens because cycles vary. It can't safely predict fertile days.

quiz.q: Under the MTP Act (amended 2021), the general limit on one doctor’s opinion is…
quiz.why: Under the amended MTP Act, one doctor's opinion is enough up to 20 weeks. Special categories can go up to 24 weeks with two doctors.

lessons.title: Contraception: methods and effectiveness

scenes.text: Nurse Joseph runs a youth clinic in Thrissur. A poster asks: ‘Which method is best?’
Two 19-year-old students, Ritu and Sam, come in together with questions.
The nurse explains effectiveness, what protects against STIs, and emergency contraception.
They leave informed — and knowing they can come back any time.

steps.title: Why understand contraception
steps.body: Contraception prevents pregnancy. Knowing the facts — even if you are not sexually active, and the legal age of consent in India is 18 — helps you make safe choices later and correct friends’ myths. **Only condoms also protect against STIs.**

steps.title: Methods and how well they work
steps.body:
Effectiveness shown as approximate pregnancies per 100 people in a year with **typical use** (how people really use them):
- **Copper IUD (Copper-T)** — fewer than 1. Lasts 5–10 years.
- **Hormonal implant / hormonal IUD** — fewer than 1.
- **Injectable (every 3 months)** — about 4.
- **Combined oral pill** (daily) — about 7.
- **Male condom** — about 13 (about 2 with perfect use).
- **Withdrawal** — about 20.
- **Fertility-awareness (calendar)** — about 15–25, varies.
- **No method** — about 85.

In India, condoms, pills, injectables and Copper-T are available, many **free** at government health centres and through ASHA workers.

steps.title: Using a condom correctly (non-explicit)
steps.body:
- Check the expiry date and that the packet isn’t damaged
- Use a new one each time; never reuse or use two at once
- Store away from heat (not in a wallet for months)
- Use only water- or silicone-based lubricants with latex condoms (oil-based products can break latex)
- Put it on before any genital contact, and follow the packet instructions

steps.title: Emergency contraception
steps.body: If contraception failed or wasn’t used, **emergency contraceptive pills** can reduce the chance of pregnancy. The common levonorgestrel pill works best **as soon as possible** and should be taken within **72 hours**. It is available at pharmacies in India. It is **not** an abortion pill and **not** for regular use; it doesn’t protect against STIs. A doctor can advise on the copper IUD as emergency contraception (up to 5 days).

steps.title: Worked example: reading the numbers
steps.body: If 100 couples rely only on the pill for a year, with typical use about **7** may face a pregnancy. With implants, fewer than **1**. With nothing, about **85**. So long-acting methods are most reliable — but **condoms are still needed for STI protection**. Using a condom **plus** another method (‘dual protection’) gives the best protection against both.

activity.prompt: Which methods protect against STIs as well as pregnancy?

items.text: Male condom
Female condom
Combined pill
Copper IUD
Injectable
Withdrawal
Washing afterwards

quiz.q: Which is the only common method that also protects against STIs?
quiz.why: The condom is the only common method that also protects against STIs, because it is a barrier. IUDs, pills and injectables only prevent pregnancy.

quiz.q: Emergency contraception should be taken…
options: Within 72 hours, the sooner the better
quiz.why: Emergency contraception works best within 72 hours, and the sooner the better. Its effectiveness falls with time.

quiz.q: Which has the lowest typical failure rate?
quiz.why: The copper IUD has the lowest typical failure rate, being over 99% effective. Calendar, withdrawal and condoms depend on correct use each time.

quiz.q: Why not use oil-based lotions with latex condoms?
options: They can weaken latex and cause breakage
quiz.why: Oil-based lotions can weaken latex and cause condoms to break. Use water-based lubricant instead.

quiz.q: Dual protection means…
quiz.why: Dual protection means a condom plus another contraceptive method. Never use two condoms together, because friction can tear them.

lessons.title: STIs and HIV: facts, testing and treatment

scenes.text: Jai, 19, a college student in Delhi, notices burning while urinating after a new relationship.
He’s too embarrassed to see a doctor and searches online for days.
A friend convinces him to visit the government hospital’s STI clinic. It’s confidential and quick.
He has chlamydia, takes a short course of antibiotics, and his partner is treated too. ‘I wish I’d gone on day one,’ he says.

steps.title: What STIs are
steps.body:
**Sexually transmitted infections (STIs)** pass from one person to another through sexual contact — vaginal, anal or oral. Some also spread through blood or from mother to baby. WHO estimates **more than 1 million STIs are acquired every day** worldwide.

Common ones: **chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, trichomoniasis** (curable with medicines), and **HPV, herpes, hepatitis B, HIV** (viral — treatable or preventable, some not curable).

steps.title: Many have no symptoms
steps.body: Most STIs often cause **no symptoms**, so people pass them on without knowing. When symptoms do appear they can include: unusual discharge, burning when urinating, sores or blisters, itching, lower belly pain, or pain during sex. Untreated STIs can cause **infertility**, long-term pain and (for HPV) **cervical cancer**.

steps.title: Prevention
steps.body:
- **Condoms** used correctly every time greatly reduce risk
- **HPV vaccine** — WHO recommends it for girls aged 9–14 (ideally before any sexual activity); it prevents most cervical cancers. Available in India
- **Hepatitis B vaccine** — part of India’s routine immunisation
- Fewer partners and mutual testing
- Never sharing needles, razors or tattoo equipment
- **PEP** (post-exposure prophylaxis) for HIV: medicines started **within 72 hours** of a possible exposure, available at government ART centres

steps.title: HIV: what to know
steps.body:
HIV spreads through **blood, semen, vaginal fluids and breast milk** — mainly unprotected sex, shared needles, and mother to child. It does **not** spread by hugging, kissing on the cheek, sharing food, toilets, swimming pools or mosquito bites.

With **antiretroviral therapy (ART)** — **free at government ART centres in India** — people with HIV can live long, healthy lives. Someone with an **undetectable viral load** on treatment does not transmit HIV sexually (‘Undetectable = Untransmittable’). India’s **HIV/AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act 2017** protects people with HIV from discrimination. National AIDS helpline: **1097**.

steps.title: Testing is normal and confidential
steps.body:
- Government hospitals have **STI/RTI clinics** and **ICTCs** (Integrated Counselling and Testing Centres) offering free, confidential tests
- Test if you’ve had unprotected sex, have symptoms, have a new partner, or a partner has an STI
- **Tell partners** so they can be tested and treated too
- Finish all prescribed medicine, and avoid sex until treatment is complete

This is general health education, not medical advice. If something worries you, see a doctor, nurse or counsellor.

cards.back: Bacterial, often no symptoms, curable with antibiotics; untreated can cause infertility
Bacterial; painless sore early; curable with antibiotics; dangerous if untreated
Very common virus; vaccine prevents most cervical cancers; WHO recommends vaccinating girls 9–14
Virus causing sores; not curable but treatable to reduce outbreaks
Spreads via blood, sexual fluids, breast milk; free ART in India; undetectable = untransmittable
HIV-prevention medicines started within 72 hours of possible exposure
National AIDS helpline in India

quiz.q: Most STIs…
options: Can be seen in a mirror
quiz.why: Most STIs often have no symptoms, so testing is the only way to know. That is why infected people may not realise.

quiz.q: Which does NOT spread HIV?
quiz.why: Hugging and sharing food do not spread HIV. It spreads through unprotected sex, shared needles and from mother to baby without treatment.

quiz.q: PEP must be started within…
quiz.why: PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis) must start within 72 hours of exposure, as soon as possible. Later it is less likely to work.

quiz.q: Which vaccine prevents most cervical cancers?
quiz.why: The HPV vaccine prevents infection with the types of HPV that cause most cervical cancers. Polio, measles and BCG protect against other diseases.

quiz.q: Jai is diagnosed with chlamydia. What else should happen?
options: His partner should be tested and treated too
quiz.why: Jai's partner should be tested and treated too, so they don't pass the infection back. He should also finish the medicine and not keep it secret.

lessons.title: Getting confidential help and making decisions

scenes.text: Lakshmi, 18, a first-year student in Visakhapatnam, has questions about contraception and her irregular periods.
She finds the Adolescent Friendly Health Clinic (AFHC) at the district hospital, part of the RKSK programme.
A counsellor answers everything without judgement and keeps it private.
Lakshmi leaves with clear answers and a plan.

steps.title: Where young people can go in India
steps.body:
- **Adolescent Friendly Health Clinics (AFHCs)** under the national adolescent health programme **Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK)** offer counselling on puberty, nutrition, mental health and sexual and reproductive health
- Government **gynaecology** and **STI/RTI** clinics, **ICTCs** for HIV testing
- **ASHA** workers and ANMs in villages
- Qualified private doctors
- Helplines: **1097** (AIDS), **14416** (Tele-MANAS), **1098** (Childline), **181** (Women)

steps.title: Decision-making: delay is a valid choice
steps.body:
Many young people choose to wait. Good reasons: not feeling ready, values, wanting to focus on goals, wanting a deeper relationship, or the law (18). When thinking about any relationship decision, ask:
- Do I really want this, or am I feeling pressure?
- Do we both clearly consent? Are we both of legal age?
- Have we talked about protection from pregnancy and STIs?
- Do I trust this person to respect a ‘no’ at any moment?
- How would I feel tomorrow?

steps.title: Worked example: asking a doctor
steps.body: ‘Doctor, I’d like to understand my options for contraception and get an STI test. Can this stay confidential?’ Doctors hear this daily. You can ask for a doctor of your preferred gender.

steps.title: Avoid
steps.body:
- Quacks, ‘sex clinics’ advertised on walls and trains
- Unverified online pills
- Self-medicating with antibiotics
- Relying on friends’ advice for medical decisions

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Find the nearest government hospital or AFHC to you and save the helpline numbers in your phone today.

activity.prompt: Your sexual-health safety kit (knowledge, not supplies):
items: I know the age of consent in India is 18
I know condoms are the only common method that also protect against STIs
I know emergency contraception works best as soon as possible, within 72 hours
I know PEP for HIV must start within 72 hours
I’ve found my nearest government hospital / AFHC
I know how to say no and to respect a no

quiz.q: What is RKSK?
quiz.why: RKSK (Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram) is India's national adolescent health programme. It isn't a bank, sports scheme or school board.

quiz.q: Which is a healthy decision question?
options: ‘Do we both clearly consent and have we discussed protection?’
quiz.why: A healthy decision question is 'Do we both clearly consent and have we discussed protection?' Asking whether friends think you're cool or if it's on TV isn't a good basis.

quiz.q: Where should you NOT go for sexual-health care?
quiz.why: Don't go to wall-advertised 'sex clinic' quacks, who are unqualified. Gynaecologists, government hospitals and adolescent-friendly clinics are reliable.

quiz.q: Is choosing to delay sexual activity valid?
quiz.why: Yes, choosing to delay sexual activity is absolutely valid for anyone. Everyone sets their own pace.

quiz.q: Self-medicating with antibiotics is…
options: Risky — can fail and cause resistance
quiz.why: Self-medicating with antibiotics is risky, because it can fail and cause antibiotic resistance. See a doctor for proper treatment.

questions.q: Can pregnancy happen the first time?
questions.why: Yes, pregnancy can happen the first time, because ovulation can occur at any time. Condoms and contraception still matter.

questions.q: Only common method that also protects against STIs?
questions.why: Condoms are the only common method that also protects against STIs, as a barrier. IUDs and pills prevent pregnancy only.
No, HIV doesn't spread by sharing food. It spreads through blood, sexual fluids and from mother to baby.

options: As soon as possible, within 72 hours
questions.why: Emergency contraception works best as soon as possible, within 72 hours. Waiting a week reduces its effect, and it is not used only before sex.

questions.q: Most common first sign of pregnancy?
questions.why: The most common first sign of pregnancy is a missed period. Cough and fever are not signs.

questions.q: Many STIs have no symptoms. So…
questions.why: Many STIs have no symptoms, so testing matters. Ignoring them can let them cause harm or spread.
Typical-use pill failure is about 7 per 100 per year. It is not zero, because missed pills happen.

options: Pre-ejaculate can contain sperm and timing fails
questions.why: Withdrawal is unreliable because pre-ejaculate can contain sperm and timing often fails. It has a high failure rate.

questions.q: HPV vaccine is recommended by WHO mainly for…
questions.why: WHO recommends the HPV vaccine mainly for girls aged 9–14, before exposure to the virus. It works best given early.

options: People with HIV on effective treatment with undetectable viral load don’t transmit HIV sexually
questions.why: Undetectable = Untransmittable means a person with HIV on effective treatment and an undetectable viral load does not pass HIV on sexually. It doesn't mean HIV is cured.

questions.q: Under the MTP Act amended in 2021, certain categories (e.g. minors, rape survivors) may terminate up to…
questions.why: Under the 2021 amendment, special categories such as minors and rape survivors may terminate up to 24 weeks, with two doctors' opinion. The general limit is 20 weeks.

options: It protects against both pregnancy and STIs
questions.why: Dual protection is recommended because it protects against both pregnancy and STIs. Two condoms together aren't stronger and may tear.

questions.q: PEP for HIV must start within…
questions.why: PEP for HIV must start within 72 hours of exposure, and the sooner the better.

questions.q: A copper IUD can be used as emergency contraception up to…
questions.why: A copper IUD can be used as emergency contraception up to 5 days after unprotected sex. Discuss it with a doctor.

courses.title: Adult sexual and reproductive health and relationships
courses.summary: For adults: healthy relationships and communication, consent in every relationship, check-ups and screening, contraception and planning, POSH basics, and sexual wellbeing across the lifespan.
outcomes: Learners can apply research-based communication skills and spot the ‘four horsemen’
Learners can plan age-appropriate sexual and reproductive health check-ups
Learners can explain POSH Act rights and processes and act as bystanders
Learners can recognise common, treatable sexual concerns and find qualified help

lessons.title: Healthy adult relationships and communication

scenes.text: Rahul (31) and Priyanka (29) married two years ago in Bengaluru. Long work hours and money stress mean they barely talk.
Small arguments become cold silences. Intimacy fades. Each thinks the other no longer cares.
They try a weekly 30-minute ‘check-in’ with phones away, and later see a couples counsellor.
Six months on, they say: ‘We didn’t stop loving each other. We stopped talking.’

steps.title: What research says keeps relationships strong
steps.body:
Relationship research (for example, by psychologist John Gottman) highlights:
- **Turning towards** small bids for attention (‘Look at this!’ — responding instead of ignoring)
- **Fondness and appreciation** — regularly saying thanks and noticing good things
- **Gentle start-ups** — raising problems without blame
- **Repair attempts** — humour, apology, a touch, ‘Can we start again?’
- Managing, not ‘winning’, conflicts — many disagreements are about lasting differences

steps.title: The ‘four horsemen’ to watch
steps.body:
Gottman identified four patterns that predict trouble:
1. **Criticism** (attacking character: ‘You’re so selfish’)
2. **Contempt** (eye-rolling, mockery — the most damaging)
3. **Defensiveness** (‘It’s not my fault’)
4. **Stonewalling** (shutting down, silent treatment)

Antidotes: describe the issue + feeling + need; build appreciation; take responsibility for your part; take a 20-minute break and come back.

steps.title: Consent in adult and married relationships
steps.body: Consent remains essential in every relationship, including marriage: freely given, ongoing, and withdrawable. Pressure, guilt, threats or force are never acceptable. Partners also have the right to make their own decisions about contraception and their bodies. **Domestic violence** (physical, emotional, sexual, economic) is addressed in India by the **Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005**; help: **181**, **112**.

steps.title: Worked example: a gentle start-up
steps.body:
Harsh: ‘You never help at home! You’re useless.’

Gentle: ‘I’m feeling exhausted with the housework this week. Could we make a plan to split it?’

Same issue, very different result.

steps.title: When to get help
steps.body: Consider couples counselling if conflicts repeat with no resolution, contempt has set in, intimacy has stopped and it bothers either partner, or after a breach of trust. If there is **violence or fear**, safety comes first — contact **181/112** or a counsellor individually. Tele-MANAS **14416** offers free mental-health support.

a.text: Your partner says: ‘You’re always on your phone. You don’t care about us.’

choices.label: ‘You’re right that I’ve been distracted. I do care. Can we have phone-free dinners?’
choices.feedback: Taking responsibility and offering a fix is a strong repair.

choices.label: ‘Well you’re always nagging me.’
choices.feedback: Counter-attack (defensiveness) escalates conflict.

choices.label: Say nothing and walk away
choices.feedback: Stonewalling leaves your partner feeling alone.

b.text: Phone-free dinners help, but a bigger issue about money surfaces.

choices.label: Agree on a calm time to discuss finances with numbers and both views
choices.feedback: Scheduling hard talks reduces heat.

choices.label: Take a 20-minute break, calm down, then come back and apologise for your part
choices.feedback: Breaks and repair attempts work.

choices.label: Keep arguing until someone wins
choices.feedback: Nobody wins a fight with their partner.

end1.text: You built a habit of repair. Over time, trust grows.

end2.text: Try again with a break and a gentle start-up.

quiz.q: According to Gottman, which is the most damaging pattern?
quiz.why: According to Gottman, contempt, such as mockery and eye-rolling, is the most damaging pattern and the strongest predictor of relationship breakdown. Humour is not damaging.

quiz.q: A ‘gentle start-up’ is…
options: Raising an issue without blame: feeling + need
quiz.why: A gentle start-up raises an issue without blame by stating a feeling and a need. Blaming, shouting or avoiding does not.

quiz.q: Consent within marriage is…
options: Still essential and can be withdrawn
quiz.why: Consent within marriage is still essential and can be withdrawn. It is ongoing in every relationship, not automatic.

quiz.q: Which Indian law addresses domestic violence?
options: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005
quiz.why: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 addresses domestic violence. POSH is for workplaces, and the others are unrelated.

quiz.q: When flooding during an argument, a good step is…
quiz.why: When 'flooding' (feeling overwhelmed) during an argument, take about a 20-minute break to calm down, then return. Insulting or continuing makes it worse.

lessons.title: Sexual and reproductive health check-ups for adults

scenes.text: Dr. Nair, a family physician in Thiruvananthapuram, sees three patients one morning.
Anjali, 34, hasn’t had cervical screening. Dr. Nair explains and books it.
Mohan, 45, has trouble with erections. Dr. Nair checks his blood sugar and blood pressure — he has undiagnosed diabetes.
Ravi and Neha, newly engaged, ask about contraception and pre-marriage health checks.
All leave with clear next steps.

steps.title: Cervical cancer screening
steps.body: Cervical cancer is one of the most common cancers in Indian women and is largely **preventable**. WHO recommends screening from **age 30** (from 25 for women with HIV), preferably by an **HPV test** every 5–10 years; India’s national programme uses **VIA** (visual inspection with acetic acid) at government centres for women 30–65. Pap smears are another option. The **HPV vaccine** prevents most cases.

steps.title: Breast and testicular awareness
steps.body:
- **Breast:** know how your breasts normally look and feel; report a new lump, skin dimpling, nipple changes or discharge. India’s programme includes clinical breast examination for women 30–65.
- **Testicles:** monthly self-check for lumps or swelling, especially ages 15–45.

steps.title: STI testing and sexual health
steps.body: Adults with new or multiple partners benefit from regular STI/HIV testing; government ICTCs and STI clinics are free and confidential. Sexual problems — such as pain, erection difficulties, low desire or early ejaculation — are **common, treatable and worth discussing**. Erection difficulties can be an early sign of **diabetes, high blood pressure or heart disease**, so they deserve a check-up, not a quick fix from an advert.

steps.title: Contraception and planning for adults
steps.body: Adults can choose short-acting (condoms, pills), long-acting (Copper-T, implants, hormonal IUD, injectables) or permanent methods (**vasectomy** for men — a quick, safe procedure; **tubectomy** for women). Vasectomy does **not** affect masculinity or performance. Planning a pregnancy: start **folic acid** before conception (reduces risk of neural tube defects), check rubella immunity, blood sugar, thyroid, and anaemia.

steps.title: Pre-marriage / pre-conception checks
steps.body: Couples can consider: blood group, haemoglobin and **thalassaemia carrier** screening (especially important in India), HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis, diabetes and thyroid tests, and a frank talk about expectations and family planning. This is general health education, not medical advice. If something worries you, see a doctor, nurse or counsellor.

activity.prompt: Match each check with its purpose:
pairs: Checks risk of passing on a serious blood disorder
Lowers risk of neural tube defects in babies
Blood sugar test for erection problems
Detects diabetes, a common underlying cause
Free confidential HIV testing and counselling

quiz.q: From what age does WHO recommend cervical screening for most women?
quiz.why: WHO recommends cervical screening from age 30 for most women (25 for women with HIV). It is not needed at 15.

quiz.q: Erection difficulties can be an early sign of…
quiz.why: Erection difficulties can be an early sign of diabetes or heart disease, because blood vessel health matters. So see a doctor.

quiz.q: Does vasectomy reduce masculinity or performance?
quiz.why: No, vasectomy does not reduce masculinity or performance. It only blocks sperm transport.

quiz.q: Why take folic acid before conception?
quiz.why: Folic acid before conception reduces the risk of neural tube defects in the baby, which is proven. It isn't for hair or weight loss.

quiz.q: Which pre-marriage test is particularly important in India?
quiz.why: Thalassaemia carrier screening is important in India, since carrier rates are significant. Two carriers can have an affected child.

lessons.title: Consent and harassment at work: POSH basics

scenes.text: Nandini, 26, a software engineer in Gurugram, gets repeated ‘jokes’ with sexual comments from a senior colleague, and messages late at night.
She feels anxious and wonders whether to ‘just ignore it’.
She reads her company’s POSH policy and files a written complaint with the Internal Committee.
The committee inquires, keeps it confidential, and the colleague faces action. Nandini’s manager is trained not to retaliate.

steps.title: The POSH Act, 2013
steps.body:
India’s **Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013** (POSH) requires every employer with **10 or more employees** to set up an **Internal Committee (IC)**, have a policy and train staff. For smaller workplaces and informal workers, a **Local Committee** at district level handles complaints. The Act protects women; many companies extend their policies to all genders.

This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: What counts as sexual harassment
steps.body:
Unwelcome acts or behaviour such as:
- physical contact and advances
- a demand or request for sexual favours
- sexually coloured remarks or ‘jokes’
- showing pornography
- any other unwelcome physical, verbal or non-verbal conduct of a sexual nature

It also includes implied promises of preferential treatment or threats about one’s job, and creating a hostile work environment. **Impact matters, not intent.**

steps.title: How a complaint works
steps.body:
- Complaint in writing to the IC, usually **within 3 months** of the incident (extendable by 3 months for valid reasons)
- The IC may try conciliation **only if the complainant asks**
- Inquiry to be completed within **90 days**
- Confidentiality is required by law; **retaliation is prohibited**
- Interim relief (e.g. transfer, leave) can be requested

steps.title: Worked example: bystander at work
steps.body: In a team chat, a colleague posts a sexual meme about a teammate. Bystander actions: don’t react with emojis; message ‘Not okay — please delete’; check in privately with the teammate; support them if they want to report; report to HR/IC if needed.

steps.title: Look after yourself
steps.body: Keep a dated record of incidents, save messages, tell someone you trust, and use the company’s employee assistance programme or Tele-MANAS **14416**. You are not overreacting — workplaces must be safe.

statements.s: Employers with 10 or more employees must have an Internal Committee under POSH.
If the harasser ‘didn’t mean it’, it isn’t harassment.
statements.why: Impact on the person matters, not intent.

statements.s: The IC must complete its inquiry within 90 days.
Sexual ‘jokes’ at work can count as harassment.
Retaliating against a complainant is allowed.

quiz.q: What does POSH stand for in India?
options: Prevention of Sexual Harassment (of Women at Workplace) Act 2013
quiz.why: POSH stands for the Prevention of Sexual Harassment (of Women at Workplace) Act 2013.

quiz.q: Who handles complaints in workplaces with fewer than 10 employees?
options: The Local Committee at district level
quiz.why: In workplaces with fewer than 10 employees, complaints go to the Local Committee at district level. The CEO or neighbours don't handle them.

quiz.q: Within what period should a complaint usually be filed?
quiz.why: A complaint should usually be filed within 3 months, which can be extended by up to 3 more months.

quiz.q: A colleague posts a sexual meme about a teammate. Good bystander step?
options: Message ‘Not okay — delete’, and support the teammate
quiz.why: Message 'Not okay — delete' and support the teammate. Laughing, forwarding or ignoring helps the harassment continue.

quiz.q: Which is NOT required under POSH?
options: Mandatory conciliation even if complainant refuses
quiz.why: Conciliation under POSH happens only at the complainant's request, so mandatory conciliation if she refuses is not required. The 90-day inquiry, confidentiality and protection from retaliation are required.

lessons.title: Sexual wellbeing across adulthood

scenes.text: Dr. Sen, a sexual-health physician in Kolkata, gives a public talk for adults titled ‘What nobody told us’.
Anonymous questions come in: ‘Is it normal to have different desire levels?’ ‘Does intimacy end after 50?’ ‘Is pain normal?’
She answers each calmly and factually.
Many in the audience say it’s the first time anyone has spoken about this openly.

steps.title: Desire differs — and changes
steps.body: It is common for partners to have **different levels of desire**, and for desire to change with stress, sleep, illness, medicines (some antidepressants and BP medicines), childbirth, hormones and relationship quality. Desire is not a fixed measure of love. Talking openly, reducing stress and seeing a doctor if a change is sudden or distressing all help.

steps.title: Pain is not normal
steps.body: Pain during intimacy (dyspareunia) is **common but not something to endure**. Causes include infections, dryness (e.g. after childbirth or at menopause), skin conditions, endometriosis or anxiety-related muscle tightening (vaginismus). All have treatments — see a gynaecologist.

steps.title: Intimacy at every age
steps.body: Many people remain sexually active and value intimacy into their 60s, 70s and beyond. Changes like slower arousal, dryness or erection difficulties are common and treatable. Health conditions (diabetes, heart disease) and medicines matter more than age itself. Closeness, touch and affection matter at every stage.

steps.title: Common worries that are treatable
steps.body:
- **Erectile difficulties** — often linked to stress, diabetes, BP, smoking, alcohol; effective treatments exist from doctors
- **Early ejaculation** — very common; behavioural techniques and medical treatments help
- **Low desire** — multifactorial; check hormones, mood, relationship, medicines
- **Anxiety about performance** — counselling and sex therapy are effective

Avoid ‘sex tonics’ and unregulated online pills, which can contain hidden drugs.

steps.title: Who to see
