steps.body: A family doctor first; then gynaecologist, urologist, endocrinologist, psychiatrist or a qualified sex therapist depending on the issue. Ask for qualifications. This is general health education, not medical advice. If something worries you, see a doctor, nurse or counsellor.

activity.prompt: Questions adults ask about sexual wellbeing

items.q: We have very different levels of desire. Is our relationship failing?
items.a: Not necessarily — desire discrepancy is one of the most common issues couples face. Talking openly, scheduling time for closeness and seeking counselling help many couples.

items.q: Is it normal for desire to drop after having a baby?
items.a: Yes. Sleep loss, hormonal changes, healing and new responsibilities all affect desire. It usually returns gradually. Talk to your doctor if there is pain or low mood.

items.q: Are online ‘performance’ pills safe?
items.a: Many unregulated products contain hidden prescription drugs that can be dangerous, especially with heart medicines. See a doctor.

items.q: I’m 60. Is it strange to still want intimacy?
items.a: Not at all. Intimacy is a healthy part of life at any age.

items.q: Who do I see for sexual problems?
items.a: Start with a family doctor, who can refer you to a gynaecologist, urologist or qualified sex therapist.

quiz.q: Desire differences between partners are…
quiz.why: Differences in desire between partners are common and workable, through communication and sometimes help. They don't automatically mean cheating.

quiz.q: Pain during intimacy should be…
options: Checked by a gynaecologist — it’s treatable
quiz.why: Pain during intimacy should be checked by a gynaecologist, since many causes are treatable. Enduring it or hiding it isn't necessary.

quiz.q: Which factor affects sexual function more than age itself?
quiz.why: Health conditions and medicines, like diabetes, heart disease and some drugs, affect sexual function more than age itself. Hair colour and shoe size don't.

quiz.q: Why avoid unregulated ‘sex tonics’?
options: They may contain hidden drugs and be unsafe
quiz.why: Unregulated 'sex tonics' may contain hidden drugs and be unsafe. They are not proven to work.

quiz.q: First professional to consult for most sexual-health concerns?
quiz.why: The family doctor is the first professional to consult for most sexual-health concerns, and can refer further if needed. Friends, social media and wall adverts are not reliable.

questions.why: Contempt is the most damaging of Gottman's four horsemen. Appreciation and humour are positive.

questions.q: POSH applies to employers with how many employees for an Internal Committee?
questions.why: An Internal Committee is required for employers with 10 or more employees under POSH.

questions.q: Is pain during intimacy normal to endure?
questions.why: No, pain during intimacy is not something to endure, because it is treatable. See a gynaecologist.
A gentle start-up states a feeling and a need without blame. Silence and insults don't open a conversation.

questions.q: WHO recommends cervical screening from age…
questions.why: WHO recommends cervical screening from age 30, or 25 for women with HIV.

options: Sperm in semen, not masculinity or performance
questions.why: Vasectomy affects sperm in semen, but not masculinity or performance. It doesn't change voice or muscle.
Consent in marriage is still required and ongoing. It isn't automatic or irrelevant.

questions.q: Thalassaemia carrier screening is useful because…
options: Two carriers can have a child with thalassaemia major
questions.why: Thalassaemia carrier screening is useful because two carriers can have a child with thalassaemia major. It doesn't improve eyesight or prevent STIs.
Under POSH, conciliation happens only at the complainant's request. It isn't mandatory or banned.
Erectile difficulty may signal cardiovascular disease or diabetes, so get checked. It isn't caused by too much exercise.
Folic acid before pregnancy reduces neural tube defects. It doesn't affect twins or labour pain.

questions.q: A POSH inquiry must be completed within…
questions.why: A POSH inquiry must be completed within 90 days.

questions.q: Which law covers domestic violence including economic abuse?
questions.why: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act (PWDVA) 2005 covers domestic violence, including economic abuse. POCSO is for child abuse and POSH for workplaces.

questions.q: Desire changes after starting a new antidepressant. Best step?
options: Discuss with the prescribing doctor — alternatives exist
questions.why: If desire changes after starting an antidepressant, discuss it with the prescribing doctor, since alternatives exist. Don't stop suddenly or use online tonics.

courses.title: How to talk to your children about bodies, sex and safety
courses.summary: For parents, grandparents and teachers: what to say at each age, model answers to tricky questions, puberty talks with daughters and sons, abuse prevention, online safety and what to do if a child tells you.
outcomes: Parents can plan age-appropriate conversations from toddlerhood to the late teens
Parents can answer tricky questions calmly using the 3-step method
Parents can prepare daughters and sons for puberty without shame
Parents can prevent, recognise and respond to abuse and online harms, including POCSO duties

lessons.title: Why talk — and the big picture by age

scenes.text: Seema and Vinod in Jaipur grew up never hearing a word about bodies or sex. They plan to do the same with their children, Aarav (9) and Mira (12).
Then Seema finds Aarav watching a confusing video a classmate shared.
She reads that children who get accurate information from parents are safer and tend to delay sex.
That night she starts the first small conversation. It’s awkward — and it works.

steps.title: What the evidence says
steps.body: UNESCO’s review of research (ITGSE 2018) found that good-quality sexuality education **does not increase sexual activity**; it helps young people **delay** first sex, reduce risk-taking and increase use of protection. Children with correct body-part names and safety rules are better able to report abuse.

steps.title: What to cover at each age
steps.body:
- **0–5:** correct names for body parts, ‘my body belongs to me’, safe/unsafe touch, secrets vs surprises
- **6–9:** privacy, consent in daily life, families, simple answer to ‘where do babies come from’, online safety basics
- **9–12:** puberty for both sexes **before it starts**, periods and nightfall, emotions, grooming and image requests
- **13–15:** consent, relationships, pressure, sexting law, pornography’s distortions
- **16–18:** contraception, STIs, pregnancy, the law (18), where to get confidential help
- **Adult children:** respect their autonomy; stay a source of support

steps.title: Many small talks, not one ‘big talk’
steps.body: Use everyday moments — a TV scene, a news story, a pregnant relative, buying pads. Short, frequent, calm conversations build trust. If you don’t know, say ‘Good question — let’s find out together.’

steps.title: Common parental mistakes
steps.body:
- Waiting until puberty has already begun
- Using shame or fear (‘good girls don’t…’)
- Overreacting to questions — children learn not to ask
- Leaving it to school or the internet
- Only talking to daughters about periods and not to sons

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Pick one age-appropriate topic from the list and one everyday moment this week to bring it up for two minutes.

activity.prompt: Match the age group with a key topic:
pairs: Correct body-part names and safe/unsafe touch
Privacy, consent and a simple ‘where babies come from’
Puberty for both sexes before it starts
Consent, sexting law and pornography’s distortions

quiz.q: Does sexuality education increase sexual activity, according to UNESCO’s review?
options: No — it tends to delay sex and increase safety
quiz.why: UNESCO's review found sexuality education tends to delay sex and increase safe behaviour, not increase activity. Evidence shows protective effects.

quiz.q: When should you talk to a child about puberty?
quiz.why: Talk about puberty before it starts, around age 8–10, so children are prepared. Waiting until after is too late.

quiz.q: Best approach?
options: Many small, calm conversations from early childhood
quiz.why: Many small, calm conversations from early childhood work best. One big talk or avoiding the topic leaves gaps.

quiz.q: Your child asks something you can’t answer. Say…
quiz.why: Say 'Good question — let's find out together.' Honesty builds trust, while making something up or shutting the question down does not.

quiz.q: Who should learn about periods?
quiz.why: All children should learn about periods, since boys benefit too. It builds respect and reduces stigma.

lessons.title: Answering tricky questions calmly

scenes.text: Aarav, 7, from Nagpur asks from the back seat: ‘Mumma, how did the baby get into Chachi’s tummy?’
His mother Kavita’s first instinct is to say ‘God put it there’.
Instead she uses a simple, true answer she practised.
Aarav says ‘Oh, okay!’ and asks for a snack. It’s that easy.

steps.title: The 3-step method
steps.body:
1. **Stay calm and thank them:** ‘That’s a great question.’
2. **Find out what they’re really asking:** ‘What do you think?’ or ‘Where did you hear that?’
3. **Answer simply and truthfully** at their level — then stop and see if they want more.

Children usually want much less detail than adults fear.

steps.title: Worked examples by age
steps.body:
**4–6, ‘Where do babies come from?’** ‘Babies grow in a special place inside the mother called the uterus.’

**7–9, ‘How does the baby get there?’** ‘A tiny egg from the mother and a tiny sperm from the father join together. That’s how a baby starts. Some families also get help from doctors, or adopt.’

**10–12, ‘What is sex?’** ‘It’s a private, grown-up kind of closeness between adults that can make a baby. It needs both people to agree and is for when you’re much older. You can always ask me about it.’

steps.title: When they hear a rude or sexual word
steps.body:
Child: ‘What does ____ mean?’ (a word from school)

Parent: ‘Thanks for asking me. That’s a rude word some people use to hurt or shock others. It’s about private parts / a sexual act. We don’t use it, but you can always ask me about words you hear.’

You don’t need to give graphic detail — just enough to remove the mystery.

steps.title: Questions that need a closer look
steps.body: If a young child shows sexual knowledge or behaviour far beyond their age, or mentions a ‘secret game’, stay calm, ask open questions (‘Tell me more’), and consider that they may have seen something or been harmed. Seek advice from a paediatrician or counsellor; call **1098** if you suspect abuse.

steps.title: Phrases to keep handy
steps.body:
- ‘I’m so glad you asked me.’
- ‘That’s private — let’s talk about it at home.’
- ‘You can always come to me, and you won’t be in trouble.’

activity.prompt: Children’s questions — model answers for parents

items.q: ‘Why does Didi bleed every month?’ (age 6–8)
items.a: ‘That’s called a period. When girls grow up, their body gets ready to maybe have a baby one day. Each month a little blood comes out. It’s healthy and normal.’

items.q: ‘Why do you and Papa kiss?’
items.a: ‘Grown-ups who love each other sometimes show it by kissing or hugging. It’s one way people show love — and everyone gets to choose who they kiss.’

items.q: ‘Why does my penis get hard sometimes?’ (age 5–8)
items.a: ‘That happens to boys’ bodies sometimes. It’s normal and it goes away by itself.’

items.q: ‘Can two boys get married?’
items.a: Give a factual, respectful answer matching your local law and your values, and emphasise that every family deserves kindness.

items.q: ‘What is rape?’ (heard on news, age 10+)
items.a: ‘It’s when someone forces another person into sexual contact without their consent. It is a serious crime, it is never the victim’s fault, and if anything like that ever happens to you or a friend, tell me.’

quiz.q: First step when a child asks a tricky question?
quiz.why: Stay calm and thank them for asking. Your reaction shapes whether they ask you again.

quiz.q: How much detail do young children usually want?
quiz.why: Young children usually want much less detail than adults fear. Answer simply and stop.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old shows sexual knowledge far beyond their age. You should…
options: Stay calm, ask open questions, seek professional advice; 1098 if abuse is suspected
quiz.why: Sexual knowledge far beyond a 5-year-old's age may indicate exposure or harm, so stay calm, ask open questions and seek professional advice (1098 if abuse is suspected). Ignoring or punishing is wrong.

quiz.q: Responding to a rude word, a good approach is…
options: Explain it’s rude/hurtful and roughly what it refers to, without graphic detail
quiz.why: Explain that it's a rude or hurtful word and roughly what it refers to, without graphic detail. This removes the mystery calmly.

quiz.q: Why say ‘You won’t be in trouble for asking’?
options: It keeps communication open so children come to you
quiz.why: Saying 'You won't be in trouble for asking' keeps communication open, so children come to you. Open lines protect them.

lessons.title: Puberty talks with daughters and sons

scenes.text: Imran, a single father in Hyderabad, worries about how to prepare his daughter Zara (10) for her first period.
He reads up, buys a ‘first period kit’ with her, and asks his sister to be available too.
When Zara’s period starts at 11, she calls her dad first. He’s ready.
Meanwhile his son Ayaan (12) learns about periods and nightfall too — Imran wants him to be respectful and unafraid.

steps.title: Preparing a daughter
steps.body:
- Talk **before age 10** about breast changes, discharge and periods
- Make a **period kit** together (pads, underwear, wipes, bag)
- Show how to use and dispose of a pad; discuss cups/tampons when she’s interested
- Teach cycle tracking and when to see a doctor (very heavy bleeding, severe pain, no period by 15)
- Challenge myths (no restrictions are needed for health)
- Celebrate quietly — no shame, no announcing

steps.title: Preparing a son
steps.body:
- Talk **before age 11** about voice, hair, growth, erections and **nightfall**
- Say clearly: ‘Wet dreams are normal and **don’t make you weak**.’
- Teach hygiene, shaving and testicle self-checks
- Warn about quack ‘sex clinics’ and supplements
- Teach about girls’ puberty and periods too — it builds respect

steps.title: Any parent can do this
steps.body: Fathers can talk about periods; mothers can talk about nightfall. What children need is a **calm, informed adult**. Single parents can bring in a trusted relative, doctor or nurse as a second voice.

steps.title: Conversation starters
steps.body:
- ‘Some kids in your class might start periods soon. Want to know what happens?’
- ‘I noticed your voice is changing. When I was your age I had lots of questions — do you?’
- Leave a good book or this course on the shelf and say ‘Ask me anything.’

steps.title: Avoid
steps.body:
- ‘You’re a woman now, so be careful around boys’ (adds fear)
- Mocking a son’s voice or body hair
- Restricting a girl’s movement during periods for ‘health’
- Saying ‘We don’t talk about that’

activity.prompt: Parent puberty-prep checklist:
items: Talk about puberty before it starts (girls ~8–10, boys ~9–11)
Make a period kit with my daughter (or for the school bag)
Explain nightfall calmly to my son and bust the ‘weakness’ myth
Teach hygiene, shaving and self-checks
Teach each child about the other sex’s puberty too
Name a second trusted adult each child can ask
Know when to take them to a doctor

quiz.q: When should you talk to daughters about periods?
quiz.why: Talk to daughters about periods before age 10, so they are prepared. After the first period is too late.

quiz.q: Key message about nightfall for sons?
options: It’s normal and doesn’t cause weakness
quiz.why: The key message about nightfall is that it is normal and doesn't cause weakness. It isn't dangerous or shameful.

quiz.q: Can a father talk to his daughter about periods?
options: Yes — what matters is calm, accurate support
quiz.why: Yes, a father can talk to his daughter about periods. Calm, accurate support is what matters, not who gives it.

quiz.q: Which statement adds fear?
options: ‘You’re a woman now, so be careful around boys’
quiz.why: 'You're a woman now, so be careful around boys' adds fear. 'Periods are normal' and 'Ask me anything' are supportive.

quiz.q: Why teach sons about periods?
quiz.why: Teaching sons about periods builds respect and reduces stigma. Knowledge builds empathy.

lessons.title: Keeping children safe: abuse prevention, online life and disclosure

scenes.text: The Mehtas in Ahmedabad give their 11-year-old, Yash, his first phone.
Instead of just installing apps, they write a family tech agreement together.
Months later, Yash tells them a gamer asked for photos. Because of the agreement, he wasn’t afraid to tell.
They report it at cybercrime.gov.in and praise Yash for telling.

steps.title: Prevention basics
steps.body:
- Teach correct body names, the swimsuit rule and No-Go-Tell
- Know the adults in your child’s life; be cautious of anyone seeking **unsupervised one-to-one time**, giving special gifts, or asking for secrecy
- Choose schools, coaching centres and clubs with **child-protection policies**
- Prefer open-door, group settings for tutoring and coaching

steps.title: Online life
steps.body:
- Delay smartphones and social media where possible; check platform age limits (often 13)
- **Family tech agreement**: devices out of bedrooms at night, shared spaces, which apps, what to do if something feels wrong
- Use parental controls and privacy settings — but **conversation beats surveillance**
- Talk about grooming, image requests and sextortion **before** it happens
- Promise: ‘If something goes wrong online, you won’t lose your phone for telling me.’ (Fear of losing devices is a top reason children don’t tell.)

steps.title: Signs a child may be being harmed
steps.body: Sudden changes in behaviour, fear of a particular person or place, nightmares, bed-wetting after being dry, sexual knowledge or behaviour beyond their age, unexplained gifts or money, secrecy about devices, withdrawal or self-harm. Signs are not proof — but they deserve attention.

steps.title: If your child tells you
steps.body:
1. **Stay calm**; your reaction matters most
2. **Believe** them: ‘Thank you for telling me. I believe you.’
3. **Reassure**: ‘It’s not your fault.’
4. **Don’t interrogate** or ask leading questions; let them speak; note what they said
5. **Protect**: keep them away from the person
6. **Report**: police, **1098** or **112**; POCSO requires reporting; online: **cybercrime.gov.in / 1930**
7. **Get support**: counselling for the child and for you (Tele-MANAS **14416**)

steps.title: Your legal duty
steps.body: Under the **POCSO Act**, anyone who knows a child has been sexually abused must report it to the police or Special Juvenile Police Unit; failing to report is itself an offence. The child’s identity must be kept confidential. This is general education, not legal advice.

a.text: Your 9-year-old says quietly: ‘Uncle does a tickle game that I don’t like. He says it’s our secret.’

choices.label: Stay calm: ‘Thank you for telling me. I believe you. It’s not your fault.’
choices.feedback: Calm belief is the most protective first response.

choices.label: ‘What?! Are you sure? He would never do that!’
choices.feedback: Disbelief or panic can make a child stop talking.

b.text: Your child relaxes a little and says a bit more.

choices.label: Listen without leading questions; note what they said; keep them away from the uncle
choices.feedback: Protect and preserve their own words.

choices.label: Ask many detailed questions to ‘get the full story’
choices.feedback: Interrogating can distress children and affect investigations; leave detailed interviews to trained professionals.

c.text: Your child goes silent and says ‘Never mind’.

choices.label: Repair: ‘I’m sorry I reacted like that. I want to hear you. You’re not in trouble.’
choices.feedback: Repair is possible and important.

choices.label: Report to police / call 1098 or 112, and arrange counselling
choices.feedback: Reporting protects your child and others, and is required under POCSO.

choices.label: Handle it within the family quietly
choices.feedback: Keeping abuse ‘in the family’ often leaves children unsafe and is not allowed under POCSO.

end1.text: Your child is protected, supported and knows telling was right.

end2.text: Go back: children need protection and professional support, and the law requires reporting.

quiz.q: Which is the best first response to a disclosure?
options: ‘Thank you for telling me. I believe you. It’s not your fault.’
quiz.why: The best first response to a disclosure is calm belief: 'Thank you for telling me. I believe you. It's not your fault.' Shouting or doubting shuts the child down.

quiz.q: Why promise not to take away devices for telling?
options: Fear of losing devices is a major reason children don’t report problems
quiz.why: Promising not to take devices away matters because fear of losing devices is a major reason children don't report problems. It removes a barrier to telling.

quiz.q: Under POCSO, failing to report known abuse is…
quiz.why: Under POCSO, failing to report known abuse is an offence. Reporting is mandatory, not optional.

quiz.q: Which is a grooming warning sign in an adult?
options: Seeking one-to-one time and secrecy with a child
quiz.why: Seeking one-to-one time and secrecy with a child is a grooming warning sign. Open-door tutoring, group coaching and talking to parents are safe.

quiz.q: Who should do detailed interviews of a child?
quiz.why: Trained professionals should do detailed interviews of a child, to avoid leading questions. Relatives, neighbours or the suspected person shouldn't.

questions.q: Does good sexuality education increase sexual activity?
options: No — it tends to delay it and increase safety
questions.why: No, good sexuality education tends to delay sex and increase safety, as the UNESCO review found.
Talk about puberty before it starts, so children are prepared rather than surprised.
'I believe you' is the best first reaction after a disclosure. Doubting with 'Are you lying?' can silence the child.
Many small talks work best, because frequent, calm conversations keep communication open. One big lecture is less effective.

questions.q: A simple answer for a 5-year-old about babies?
options: ‘Babies grow in a special place inside the mother called the uterus’
questions.why: 'Babies grow in a special place inside the mother called the uterus' is true and simple. A stork story is untrue, and graphic detail is too much for a 5-year-old.
Childline's number is 1098. 1930 is cybercrime and 181 is the Women's Helpline.

options: Helps children report abuse clearly and reduces shame
questions.why: Correct body-part names help children report abuse clearly and reduce shame. They are not rude.

questions.q: A child hears a rude sexual word. Good response?
options: Calmly explain it’s rude/hurtful and roughly what it refers to
questions.why: Calmly explain that it's rude or hurtful and roughly what it refers to. Punishing or giving a graphic explanation isn't helpful.

questions.q: Online safety rule that most increases telling?
options: ‘You won’t lose your phone for telling me’
questions.why: Saying 'You won't lose your phone for telling me' removes the fear that stops children from reporting. Total surveillance or no rules doesn't build trust.

questions.q: Which is a possible sign of abuse?
options: Fear of a particular person, sexual knowledge beyond age
questions.why: Fear of a particular person and sexual knowledge beyond age can be signs of abuse that deserve attention. Asking for snacks or liking football doesn't.

questions.q: Under POCSO, a parent who learns of abuse should…
questions.why: Under POCSO, a parent who learns of abuse should report to the police or SJPU, or call 1098 or 112. Keeping it in the family is not allowed.

questions.q: Why avoid leading questions after disclosure?
options: They can distress the child and affect the child’s account and the investigation
questions.why: Avoid leading questions because they can distress the child and affect the child's account and the investigation. Leave detailed interviews to professionals.

questions.q: Which message to a teen daughter is best?
options: ‘Periods are normal; here’s how to manage them; ask me anything’
‘You’re a woman now, stay away from boys’
questions.why: 'Periods are normal; here's how to manage them; ask me anything' is calm, informed and open. 'Stay away from boys' adds fear.

wellbeing-unaskable.title: Ask the unaskable
wellbeing-unaskable.description: The questions people never ask aloud — for kids, teens and adults — answered calmly, factually and without judgement, with ‘see a doctor when…’ guidance.

courses.title: Questions kids wonder about but don't ask
courses.summary: Calm, true, child-level answers: where babies come from, why grown-ups kiss, what to do about rude or hurtful words, and why bodies are different.
outcomes: Learners can explain simply how a baby starts and grows
Learners know they choose whether to hug or kiss, and when to tell
Learners know what to do when they hear rude or hurtful words
Learners can name body differences and puberty without shame
courses.guardianNote: For ages 5–10, ideally read with a parent. Calm, child-level answers to questions children wonder about but rarely ask: where babies come from (sperm and egg join, baby grows in the uterus — no description of sex), why grown-ups kiss, why bodies differ, and what to do about rude or hurtful words heard at school (no slurs or swear words are printed). Follows UNESCO ITGSE 2018 for ages 5–8 and 9–12.

lessons.title: Where do babies come from?

scenes.text: Anya, 6, from Pune sees her Masi’s round tummy. ‘Is there really a baby in there? How did it get in?’
Her mother smiles. ‘That’s a great question. Let me tell you the true answer.’
She explains about a tiny egg and a tiny sperm, and the uterus.
Anya says ‘Cool!’ and goes back to her colouring. Later she asks one more question — and gets another calm answer.

steps.title: The true, simple answer
steps.body:
A baby starts when a tiny **egg** from a woman’s body joins with a tiny **sperm** from a man’s body. The egg and sperm are so small you can’t see them without a microscope!

The joined egg grows into a baby inside a special stretchy place in the mother’s tummy called the **uterus** (or womb). It takes about **nine months** for a baby to grow.

steps.title: How the baby comes out
steps.body: When the baby is ready, the mother’s body pushes it out through a stretchy opening between her legs called the **vagina**, or doctors help the baby come out through a cut in the tummy called a **caesarean** (or C-section). Doctors and nurses help keep mother and baby safe.

steps.title: Every family is different
steps.body: Some families get help from doctors to make a baby. Some adopt a child who needs a family. Some families have one child, some many, some none. All are real families.

steps.title: For grown-ups
steps.body: Answer simply and truthfully, then pause — children ask for more when they’re ready. Avoid stork or ‘found in a hospital’ stories; children later feel misled. If they ask how the sperm gets to the egg, a simple answer for this age is: ‘When grown-ups decide to make a baby, a sperm from the man’s body can reach the egg in the woman’s body. It’s something private for grown-ups.’

activity.prompt: Questions little ones ask about babies

items.q: How big is a baby when it starts?
items.a: Smaller than a dot made by a pencil! It grows bigger and bigger over nine months.

items.q: What does the baby eat inside?
items.a: The baby gets food and air from the mother’s body through a tube called the umbilical cord. Your belly button is where your cord was!

items.q: Can boys have babies?
items.a: Babies grow in a uterus, which girls’ and women’s bodies usually have. Men help make a baby with their sperm, and dads, uncles and grandpas can help look after babies.

items.q: Did I grow in Mummy’s tummy?
items.a: If your mum gave birth to you, yes! If you were adopted, you grew in another woman’s uterus and then joined your family — and your family chose you with love.

items.q: Why can’t I see the baby?
items.a: It’s safe and cosy inside the uterus. Doctors can take a special picture called an ultrasound to see the baby.

quiz.q: Where does a baby grow?
quiz.why: A baby grows in the uterus, also called the womb, inside the mother. It doesn't grow in the stomach or heart.

quiz.q: A baby starts when…
options: An egg and a sperm join
quiz.why: A baby starts when an egg and a sperm join. A stork doesn't bring it, and it isn't wished into being.

quiz.q: How long does a baby take to grow?
quiz.why: A baby takes about nine months to grow inside the mother before it is born.

quiz.q: What is your belly button?
quiz.why: Your belly button is where your umbilical cord was. The cord brought food to you before you were born.

lessons.title: Why do grown-ups kiss and hug?

scenes.text: Kabir, 7, from Delhi sees two people kissing in a film. He covers his eyes and giggles: ‘Eww! Why do they do that?’
His Papa laughs too. ‘It does look funny when you’re seven! Grown-ups who love each other sometimes kiss.’
‘Do I have to kiss people?’ asks Kabir. ‘Never if you don’t want to,’ says Papa.
Kabir feels better knowing he gets to choose.

steps.title: Kisses and hugs show love
steps.body: People show love and care in many ways — hugs, holding hands, kind words, cooking for someone, and sometimes kisses. Grown-ups who are in love may kiss each other on the lips. Families might kiss cheeks or foreheads. Some families and cultures show love more with words or namaste.

steps.title: Everyone chooses
steps.body: **Nobody has to kiss or hug anyone if they don’t want to** — not even relatives. You can wave, high-five or say namaste instead. And we always ask before hugging others.

steps.title: When it’s not okay
steps.body: It’s **not okay** for a grown-up or older child to kiss you on the lips, ask you to keep kisses a secret, or touch your private parts. If that happens, say **No**, **Go** away and **Tell** a trusted grown-up. Childline: **1098**.

steps.title: For grown-ups
steps.body: Normalise affection while teaching choice: ‘Would you like to hug Nani or wave?’ Respect a child’s ‘no’, even if relatives feel hurt.

activity.prompt: Okay or not okay?

items.text: Mummy kisses your forehead at bedtime and you like it
You wave instead of hugging an uncle
A big kid says ‘kiss me and don’t tell anyone’
Saying ‘no thanks’ to a hug
A grown-up asks you to keep a kissing game secret

quiz.q: Why do grown-ups in love sometimes kiss?
quiz.why: Grown-ups in love sometimes kiss to show love. It is a way of showing they care.

quiz.q: Do you have to kiss relatives?
options: No, you can wave or say namaste
quiz.why: No, you don't have to kiss relatives. You can wave or say namaste instead, because it's your choice.

quiz.q: Someone says ‘kiss me and keep it secret’. You…
quiz.why: Say No, Go, Tell. A request to 'kiss me and keep it secret' is an unsafe secret, so tell a trusted grown-up.

quiz.q: Before hugging someone, we…
quiz.why: Before hugging someone, we ask. That is how we show respect for their choice.

lessons.title: I heard a word at school that sounded bad

scenes.text: Rohan, 8, from Kolkata hears older boys shout a word and laugh. A teacher frowns. Rohan doesn’t know what it means.
At home he wonders whether to ask — maybe he’ll get into trouble.
He whispers it to his mother. She stays calm: ‘Thank you for asking me instead of using it.’
She explains why some words are rude or hurtful, without making a big drama.
Rohan feels relieved — and decides not to use it.

steps.title: Words have power
steps.body:
Words can make people feel happy — or hurt them. Some words are:
- **Rude words (swear words):** words people use when angry or to shock; many are about private parts, the bathroom, or grown-up private things
- **Hurtful words (insults or slurs):** words used to put people down because of their caste, religion, skin colour, body, disability, or whether they are a boy or a girl
- **Grown-up words** that you might hear but not understand yet

You don’t need to know every word. What matters is knowing **they can hurt, and we don’t use them to hurt others**.

steps.title: What to do when you hear one
steps.body:
1. **Don’t repeat it** to test it out — it might hurt someone or get you in trouble.
2. **Ask a trusted grown-up** quietly: ‘I heard a word, what does it mean?’ You won’t be in trouble for asking.
3. If someone uses a word **to hurt you or someone else**, tell a teacher.

steps.title: Why some words are about private parts
steps.body: Some rude words are just impolite names for private parts or for sex (a private grown-up thing). Using them in public is rude. The real words — like penis, vagina, bottom — are fine for talking to parents and doctors.

steps.title: Worked example: a grown-up’s answer
steps.body:
Child: ‘What does [word] mean?’
Parent: ‘That’s a rude word. Some people use it when they’re angry, and it’s about private parts. It can upset people, so we don’t say it. I’m glad you asked me.’

For a slur: ‘That’s a very hurtful word people use to insult a group of people. Using it is unkind and can be against school rules — and some insults based on caste or religion are even against the law.’

steps.title: For grown-ups
steps.body: Stay calm, thank the child, give a short factual explanation at their level, and explain the values. Overreacting makes words more exciting and teaches children not to ask you.

a.text: You hear a word at school that made everyone laugh and a teacher look angry. You don’t know what it means.

choices.label: Ask a trusted grown-up at home what it means
choices.feedback: Asking is the smart, safe choice.

choices.label: Say it loudly in class to see what happens
choices.feedback: It might hurt someone and get you into trouble.

choices.label: Search it on the internet alone
choices.feedback: The internet can show grown-up things that might confuse or upset you. Ask a grown-up instead.

b.text: Your grown-up explains it’s a rude word that can upset people.

choices.label: Decide not to use it, and say thanks
choices.feedback: Great choice — kind words make school better.

c.text: A classmate looks upset and the teacher asks you to stay back.

choices.label: Say sorry and tell the teacher you didn’t know what it meant
choices.feedback: Honesty helps — next time, ask first.

d.text: You see confusing pictures and feel weird.

choices.label: Close it and tell a trusted grown-up
choices.feedback: You’re not in trouble — telling is the right thing.

end1.text: You learned something and chose kindness. You can always ask about words you hear.

quiz.q: You hear a word you don’t understand. Best idea?
quiz.why: If you hear a word you don't understand, ask a trusted grown-up. That is a safe way to learn.

quiz.q: Slurs are words used to…
options: Hurt or insult people because of who they are
quiz.why: Slurs are words used to hurt or insult people because of who they are. They are unkind and never okay to use.

quiz.q: Will you be in trouble for asking a grown-up?
options: No — asking is the right thing
quiz.why: No, you won't be in trouble for asking a grown-up. Asking is the right thing to do.

quiz.q: Why not search unknown rude words alone online?
options: It could show grown-up things that upset you
quiz.why: Don't search unknown rude words alone online, because it could show grown-up things that upset you. Ask a grown-up instead.

quiz.q: Real body-part words like ‘penis’ or ‘vagina’ are…
options: Correct words, fine to use with parents and doctors
quiz.why: Real body-part words like 'penis' and 'vagina' are correct words, fine to use with parents and doctors. They aren't swear words.

lessons.title: Why are bodies different? Body questions

story.title: Pari and Ishaan at bath time

scenes.text: Twins Pari and Ishaan, 5, from Chennai notice their bodies look different in the bath.
‘Why don’t I have a penis?’ asks Pari. ‘Why don’t I have a vulva?’ asks Ishaan.
Their dad answers simply and calmly.
Then they ask why Papa has hair on his face. ‘That’s what happens when you grow up!’

steps.title: Boys’ and girls’ bodies
steps.body: Most boys have a **penis** and **testicles**. Most girls have a **vulva**, and inside, a **vagina** and **uterus**. These differences let grown-ups make babies one day. Some people have bodies that are a bit different from both — that’s natural too. Everyone’s body is special and private.

steps.title: Grown-up bodies change
steps.body: When children grow up (from about age 8–14), their bodies change — this is called **puberty**. Hair grows under arms and on private parts, girls grow breasts and get periods, boys’ voices get deeper and many grow beards. It’s normal and happens to everyone.

steps.title: Fun body facts
steps.body:
- Your **belly button** is where your umbilical cord was
- **Nipples:** everyone has them, boys and girls
- **Pee and poo** come out of different openings

steps.title: For grown-ups
steps.body: Calm, matter-of-fact answers with correct names teach children their bodies are nothing to be ashamed of — and help them speak up if anything unsafe happens.

activity.prompt: Match the question to a simple answer:
pairs: Why does Papa have a beard?
Grown-up bodies grow more hair in puberty
Why do I have a belly button?
It’s where your umbilical cord was
Why do girls and boys look different?
Most have different private parts, which can help make babies one day
It belongs to you — private parts are kept covered and safe

quiz.q: What is puberty?
options: When children’s bodies change into grown-up bodies
quiz.why: Puberty is when children's bodies change into grown-up bodies. It is normal, not an illness or a game.

quiz.q: Do boys have nipples?
quiz.why: Yes, boys have nipples. Everyone does.

quiz.q: Your belly button is…
quiz.why: Your belly button is where your cord was, which fed you before birth. It is not a sticker, mistake or switch.

quiz.q: Are private parts something to be ashamed of?
quiz.why: No, private parts are normal and private, nothing to be ashamed of. We keep them private but there is no shame.

questions.why: A baby grows in the uterus, not the stomach.

questions.q: Do you have to kiss relatives?
questions.why: No, you don't have to kiss relatives. It's your choice.
If you hear a rude word, ask a trusted grown-up. They can explain it safely.
A baby starts when an egg and a sperm join. A stork doesn't bring it.

options: Hurtful words about who people are
questions.why: Slurs are hurtful words about who people are. They are not kind.
Your belly button is where the cord was. It is not a button.

questions.q: How long does a baby grow?
questions.why: A baby grows for about nine months, not one week.

questions.q: ‘Kiss me and keep it secret’ — you…
questions.why: Say No, Go, Tell. 'Kiss me and keep it secret' is an unsafe secret.
Searching rude words alone online can show upsetting grown-up things. Ask a grown-up instead.
Puberty is when bodies grow into grown-up bodies. It is normal, not a disease.

options: When doctors help the baby out through the tummy
questions.why: A caesarean is when doctors help the baby out through the mother's tummy. It is a type of birth, not a name.

courses.title: Questions teens never ask
courses.summary: Calm, factual, non-explicit answers to what teens wonder but rarely ask: am I normal, masturbation, size worries, first crushes, being gay/bi/trans or questioning, and period myths.
outcomes: Learners can recognise the wide range of normal in puberty and when to see a doctor
Learners can reject masturbation myths and recognise compulsive use
Learners can counter size anxieties with facts and avoid scams
Learners can describe healthy first relationships and red flags
Learners can explain orientation and gender identity respectfully with Indian law
Learners can bust period myths
courses.guardianNote: For ages 13–17. Calm, factual, non-explicit answers to questions teens rarely ask aloud: am I normal, masturbation (common and harmless), size worries, first crushes and relationships, sexual orientation and gender identity explained respectfully with Indian law, and period myths. Restates the age of consent (18) and includes when to see a doctor and helplines. Follows UNESCO ITGSE 2018 and WHO.

lessons.title: Am I normal? Bodies, timing and comparison

scenes.text: In a Bengaluru school, a counsellor runs an anonymous question box for Class 9.
‘Am I normal if I haven’t got a moustache yet?’ ‘Why is one of my breasts bigger?’ ‘I sweat so much — is something wrong?’ ‘My friend got her period at 10 and I’m 14.’
She answers one theme: almost everyone wonders if they’re normal.
Students leave relieved — and realise how much they had in common.

steps.title: ‘Normal’ is a wide range
steps.body: In puberty, **when** and **how fast** changes happen varies by years between healthy people. Body hair, breast size, height, voice, skin, sweat and shape all differ. Your genes, nutrition and ethnicity play a big part. Comparing with friends or with edited images online gives a false picture.

steps.title: Typical ranges
steps.body:
- Puberty starts: girls ~8–13, boys ~9–14
- First period: ~10–15
- Voice breaking: commonly ~12–15
- Facial hair: may start in mid-teens and keep developing into the 20s
- Uneven breasts or testicles: very common
- Stretch marks during growth spurts: common
- Acne: affects most teens to some degree

steps.title: See a doctor when…
steps.body:
- No puberty signs by 13 (girls) or 14 (boys); no period by 15
- Very heavy or painful periods; periods stop for 3+ months
- Sudden testicle pain (emergency) or a lump
- Severe acne, or something that worries you and won’t go away

This is general health education, not medical advice. If something worries you, see a doctor, nurse or counsellor.

steps.title: Online ‘normal’ is not normal
steps.body: Filters, angles, editing, and in some content, surgery, make bodies online look very different from typical bodies. Many teens feel worse after comparing. Unfollow accounts that make you feel bad.

activity.prompt: ‘Am I normal?’ questions teens ask

items.q: I’m 14 and haven’t started puberty — am I behind?
items.a: Boys commonly start anywhere from 9 to 14. If there are no signs by 14 (boys) or 13 (girls), a doctor check is sensible — usually it’s just later timing, which often runs in families.

items.q: One breast/testicle is bigger. Is that okay?
items.a: Yes. Slight asymmetry is very common and normal. See a doctor only for a new lump, pain or swelling.

items.q: I sweat a lot and smell. Is something wrong?
items.a: Sweat glands become active in puberty. Daily washing, clean clothes and deodorant help. If sweating is extreme and soaks clothes even when cool, a doctor can help (it’s called hyperhidrosis).

items.q: I have stretch marks on my thighs/back. Why?
items.a: Rapid growth stretches the skin. Stretch marks are very common in teens of all genders and usually fade over time.

items.q: My friends look older than me. Will I catch up?
items.a: Most late developers catch up. Adult height and looks aren’t decided by when you start.

items.q: I have hair around my nipples / on my face (girl). Is that normal?
items.a: A few hairs are common. Lots of new dark hair, with irregular periods and acne, can be a sign of PCOS — worth a doctor visit.

quiz.q: Puberty timing between healthy teens can vary by…
quiz.why: Puberty timing between healthy teens can differ by several years. So being earlier or later than friends is usually normal.

quiz.q: Slightly uneven breasts or testicles are…
quiz.why: Slightly uneven breasts or testicles are very common and normal. They aren't dangerous or a disease.

quiz.q: Sudden testicle pain means…
options: Emergency — see a doctor the same day
quiz.why: Sudden testicle pain is an emergency, possibly torsion, so see a doctor the same day. Waiting can cost the testicle.

quiz.q: Stretch marks in teens are…
quiz.why: Stretch marks are common during growth spurts, because skin stretches quickly. They aren't always a disease or only in girls.

quiz.q: Comparing yourself to online images…
quiz.why: Comparing yourself to online images gives a false picture, because they are often edited. They don't show real bodies.

lessons.title: Masturbation: common, private and harmless

scenes.text: Dev, 15, from Lucknow has been touching his private parts for pleasure and feels terribly guilty. An older cousin said it causes weakness and blindness.
Similar worries come from Ritu, 16, who thought ‘only boys do it’ and felt ashamed.
At a school health session, a doctor answers anonymous questions calmly.
Both feel relief: it’s common, private and doesn’t harm the body.

steps.title: What doctors say
steps.body: **Masturbation** means touching one’s own genitals for pleasure. It is **common** among teens and adults of all genders, and doctors and WHO-aligned sexuality education describe it as a **normal, harmless** part of sexuality. Some people do it often, some rarely, some never — all are normal.

steps.title: Myths — all false
steps.body:
Masturbation does **not** cause:
- weakness, thinness or loss of ‘vital fluid’
- blindness, hair on palms, acne or hair loss
- infertility or damage to the penis or vagina
- harm to future relationships
- loss of virginity

The body continuously makes new sperm; releasing semen doesn’t drain health.

steps.title: Privacy and values
steps.body: It is a **private** activity — done alone, in a private place. Families and religions have different views, and those values are personal. Feeling guilty is common because of myths and silence, but guilt doesn’t mean you are harming your body.

steps.title: When to get support
steps.body: Talk to a doctor or counsellor if it feels **compulsive** — you can’t stop when you want, it interferes with sleep, study or friendships, it’s linked with heavy porn use you want to cut down, or it causes injury or pain. Also seek help if guilt or anxiety is overwhelming: **Tele-MANAS 14416**.

statements.s: Masturbation is common among people of all genders.
Masturbation causes weakness or blindness.
It can cause infertility.
It should be private.
statements.why: A private activity in a private place.

statements.s: If it feels compulsive and interferes with life, talking to a counsellor can help.

quiz.q: Doctors describe masturbation as…
options: A normal, harmless part of sexuality for many people
quiz.why: Doctors describe masturbation as a normal, harmless part of sexuality for many people. It is not harmful or illegal.

quiz.q: Which is a myth?
quiz.why: The belief that it causes weakness is a myth. It is common, private, and some people never do it.

quiz.q: When might it be worth talking to a counsellor?
options: If it’s compulsive and interfering with life
quiz.why: It may be worth talking to a counsellor if it is compulsive and interfering with life. Doing it once or not at all is not a concern.

quiz.q: Does releasing semen drain health?
options: No — the body keeps making sperm
quiz.why: No, releasing semen does not drain health, because the body keeps making sperm. It isn't harmful.

quiz.q: Feeling guilty means…
options: Often comes from myths and silence — not from harm
quiz.why: Guilt often comes from myths and silence, not from any actual harm. It doesn't mean you are ill or harming your body.

lessons.title: Size and shape worries

scenes.text: Aman, 16, from Delhi worries his penis is ‘too small’ after seeing porn. He searches ‘enlargement pills’.
Simran, 15, from Mumbai worries her breasts are ‘too small’ and searches ‘breast growth cream’.
Both bring their worries to the school nurse, anonymously.
The nurse explains facts, ranges and why the products are scams. Both feel far better.

steps.title: Penis size facts
steps.body: A large review of measurements from over 15,000 men (BJU International, 2015) found an average erect length of about **13 cm**, with most men close to that range. Size when soft varies a lot and changes with temperature. Size is **not** linked to manliness, fertility or the ability to have satisfying relationships. Most men who worry are in the normal range. Penises keep growing through puberty, often until the late teens.

steps.title: Breast facts
steps.body: Breast size and shape depend mainly on **genes and body fat**, and breasts may keep developing until the late teens or early 20s. Uneven size is common. Size has no link to health or the ability to breastfeed.

steps.title: Scams to avoid
steps.body: Pills, pumps, creams, oils, ‘exercises’ or ‘sex power’ products promising bigger penises or breasts **do not work** and some are harmful or contain hidden drugs. Wall-advertised ‘sex clinics’ exploit these fears. Pornography uses selected performers and camera tricks — it is not a guide to normal bodies.

steps.title: Height and muscles
steps.body: Height is mostly genetic; growth plates usually close in the late teens (often earlier in girls than boys). No pill or stretching adds height after that. Muscle builds with food, sleep and training — not with steroids, which are dangerous for teens.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: If there’s pain, a lump, a very real medical concern (such as a testicle not in the scrotum), or if worry about your body is taking over your thoughts — talk to a doctor or counsellor. Worry that’s out of proportion can be a sign of body dysmorphic disorder, which is treatable.

statements.s: Most men who worry about penis size are in the normal range.
Enlargement pills and creams work.
statements.why: They don’t, and some are harmful.

statements.s: Breast size is mainly decided by genes and body fat.
Porn shows typical bodies.
statements.why: Performers are selected and filmed to exaggerate.

statements.s: Height can be increased with pills after growth plates close.

quiz.q: Average erect penis length in a large review was about…
quiz.why: A large review found the average erect penis length is about 13 cm. 5 cm or 25–30 cm are not typical.

quiz.q: Is penis size linked to fertility?
quiz.why: No, penis size is not linked to fertility. Fertility depends on sperm and hormones.

quiz.q: Breast creams…
options: Don’t work and may be harmful
quiz.why: Breast creams don't work and may be harmful, so they are scams. Breast size is decided by genes and hormones.

quiz.q: Worry about appearance that takes over your thoughts may be…
quiz.why: Worry about appearance that takes over your thoughts may be body dysmorphic disorder, which is treatable. See a doctor or counsellor.

quiz.q: Steroids for teen muscle growth are…
quiz.why: Steroids for teen muscle growth are dangerous, since they disrupt hormones and can harm the heart and liver. They aren't vitamins.

lessons.title: First crush, first relationship

scenes.text: Zainab, 15, from Hyderabad has her first crush on Kabir from her tuition class. She can’t eat, keeps checking his online status, and feels silly.
She has questions she can’t ask anyone: ‘Is this love? What if he doesn’t like me? What’s okay in a relationship?’
Her older cousin Sana answers honestly over ice cream.
Zainab decides to enjoy the feeling, take it slow, and keep her studies and friends first.

steps.title: Crushes are normal
steps.body: A crush can feel huge — butterflies, daydreaming, checking someone’s status. It is a normal part of growing up. It may fade in weeks or grow into friendship or a relationship. Crushes can be on people of any gender.

steps.title: What a healthy first relationship looks like
steps.body:
- You feel **respected**, safe and free to be yourself
- You both keep friends, family time and goals
- Communication is honest; no pressure
- **No** checking phones, controlling clothes, or demanding photos
- Physical closeness only with **clear consent**, at a pace you both choose — and remember, in India the **age of consent is 18** (POCSO)

steps.title: Rejection and breakups
steps.body: If your crush says no or a relationship ends, it can really hurt. Cry, talk to a friend, move your body, and limit checking their social media. It gets easier with time. Respect their decision; don’t pressure, post about or follow them.

steps.title: Red flags
steps.body: Someone much older showing romantic interest, asking for secrecy, pushing for photos or meetings alone — this is **not** a normal relationship. Tell a trusted adult or call **1098**.

steps.title: Talking with parents
steps.body: Many Indian families find dating difficult to discuss. Even if you can’t talk about everything, having one trusted adult to ask helps you stay safe.

activity.prompt: Crush and relationship questions teens ask

items.q: Is it love or a crush?
items.a: Crushes are often intense attraction to the idea of someone. Love usually grows over time from knowing someone well, including their flaws. Both feelings are real.

items.q: Should I tell my crush?
items.a: That’s your choice. If you do, keep it simple and be ready for any answer. If it’s a no, respect it.

items.q: My crush is on someone of the same gender. Is that okay?
items.a: Yes. Attraction to the same gender is a normal variation. You don’t have to label it now.

items.q: Is it normal to never have had a crush?
items.a: Yes. Some people develop crushes later, and some people experience little or no romantic or sexual attraction (asexual or aromantic) — also normal.

items.q: My partner wants photos. What do I do?
items.a: Say no. Sending sexual images under 18 is illegal under POCSO/IT Act, and you lose control of them forever. Pressure is a red flag.

items.q: How do I get over a breakup?
items.a: Feel it, lean on friends, keep routines, limit stalking their social media, and give it time. If sadness lasts weeks or you feel hopeless, talk to someone — Tele-MANAS 14416.

quiz.q: Crushes are…
quiz.why: Crushes are normal and happen to people of all genders. They are not a disease or illegal.

quiz.q: A healthy relationship includes…
options: Respect and freedom to keep friends
quiz.why: A healthy relationship includes respect and freedom to keep friends. Phone checking, isolation and pressure for photos are control.

quiz.q: Age of consent in India?
quiz.why: The age of consent in India is 18, under POCSO.

quiz.q: An adult shows romantic interest and wants secrecy. You…
options: Tell a trusted adult or call 1098
quiz.why: An adult showing romantic interest and wanting secrecy is a grooming red flag. Tell a trusted adult or call 1098.

quiz.q: After a breakup, helpful?
options: Talking to friends and keeping routines
quiz.why: After a breakup, talking to friends and keeping routines is healthy coping. Not eating, posting about them or stalking their social media makes it worse.

lessons.title: Questions about being gay, bi, trans or questioning

scenes.text: Arjun, 16, from Chandigarh realises he has feelings for boys, not girls. He searches at night: ‘Is being gay a disease?’
He finds frightening websites selling ‘cures’.
He gathers courage to call Tele-MANAS. The counsellor tells him calmly what science and Indian law say.
Arjun doesn’t tell everyone — but he no longer believes something is wrong with him.

steps.title: Key words, explained respectfully
steps.body:
- **Sexual orientation:** who you’re attracted to — e.g. **heterosexual (straight)**, **gay** or **lesbian** (same gender), **bisexual** (more than one gender), **asexual** (little or no sexual attraction)
- **Gender identity:** your inner sense of being a man, a woman, both, neither, or something else
- **Transgender:** a person whose gender identity differs from the sex they were assigned at birth
- **Intersex:** born with natural variations in sex characteristics
- **Questioning:** still working it out — completely okay

steps.title: What science says
steps.body: Being gay, lesbian, bisexual or transgender is **not an illness**. WHO removed homosexuality from its list of diseases in 1990, and its ICD-11 no longer classifies being transgender as a mental disorder. Orientation is **not a choice** and not caused by parenting, films or friends. **‘Conversion therapy’** — attempts to change orientation or identity — doesn’t work and causes harm; India’s **National Medical Commission** declared it professional misconduct in 2022.

steps.title: Indian law
steps.body:
- **2014, NALSA judgment:** the Supreme Court recognised transgender people’s right to self-identify their gender
- **2018, Navtej Singh Johar judgment:** the Supreme Court decriminalised consensual same-sex relations between adults
- **Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019:** prohibits discrimination against transgender persons

Same-sex marriage is not currently legally recognised in India. This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Coming out — only if and when you’re ready
steps.body: You don’t have to label yourself or tell anyone. If you choose to, start with someone you trust and feel safe with. Have a support plan. Your safety comes first — if home isn’t safe, talk to a counsellor first.

steps.title: Being a good friend
steps.body: If a friend comes out: say ‘Thank you for trusting me,’ keep it private, use the name and pronouns they ask for, and stand up against teasing. Bullying for orientation or gender identity is still bullying — report it.

steps.title: Support
steps.body: LGBTQ+ young people face higher rates of bullying and distress because of stigma, not because of who they are. If you feel hopeless, talk to someone today: **Tele-MANAS 14416**, **112** in emergency.

activity.prompt: Questions teens ask about orientation and gender

items.q: Is being gay a phase?
items.a: For some people feelings change over time; for many they don’t. Either way, your feelings now are real and valid.

items.q: Can I be ‘turned’ gay by a friend or films?
items.a: No. Orientation isn’t caused by friends, films or parenting.

items.q: I’m attracted to more than one gender. Am I confused?
items.a: Not necessarily — bisexuality is a real orientation. You can take your time.

items.q: I don’t feel like the gender I was assigned. What can I do?
items.a: Talk to a counsellor or doctor experienced in gender health. Exploring feelings is safe; medical decisions are made carefully, step by step, with professionals.

items.q: Is it legal to be gay in India?
items.a: Since 2018, consensual same-sex relations between adults are not a crime in India.

items.q: Will ‘conversion therapy’ help?
items.a: No. It doesn’t work and causes harm; India’s NMC treats it as professional misconduct.

quiz.q: Sexual orientation is about…
quiz.why: Sexual orientation is about who you are attracted to. It isn't about marks, hobbies or clothes.

quiz.q: Is being gay an illness?
options: No — WHO removed it from its disease list in 1990
quiz.why: No, being gay is not an illness. WHO removed homosexuality from its list of diseases in 1990.

quiz.q: Which judgment decriminalised consensual same-sex relations in India?
quiz.why: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) decriminalised consensual same-sex relations between adults. NALSA (2014) was about transgender rights.

quiz.q: Conversion therapy…
options: Doesn’t work, causes harm, and is professional misconduct per NMC
quiz.why: Conversion therapy doesn't work and causes harm, and the NMC has called it professional misconduct. It is not medicine.

quiz.q: A friend comes out to you. Best response?
options: ‘Thank you for trusting me’ and keep it private
quiz.why: Say 'Thank you for trusting me' and keep it private. Telling others, laughing or telling their parents breaks their trust.

sources: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India 2018

lessons.title: Period myths — busted (for everyone)

scenes.text: In a Jaipur school, Class 10 starts a ‘period myth-buster’ club — boys and girls together.
They collect myths from home and school, then check each one against health sources.
Rahul is shocked to learn many things he believed weren’t true.
They present a poster at assembly. Several mothers ask for copies.

steps.title: Myths vs facts
steps.body:
- **‘Period blood is dirty/impure.’** — It’s normal blood and tissue from the uterus lining.
- **‘Don’t bathe or wash hair.’** — Bathing is hygienic and soothing.
- **‘Don’t exercise.’** — Exercise is fine and can ease cramps.
- **‘Don’t touch pickles / they’ll spoil.’** — No scientific basis.
- **‘Tampons/cups break virginity.’** — Virginity isn’t a medical state; using them doesn’t change it.
- **‘You can’t get pregnant during your period.’** — Less likely, but possible.
- **‘PMS is all in your head.’** — It’s linked to real hormone changes.
- **‘Irregular periods in teens mean infertility.’** — Irregular cycles are common in the first years.

steps.title: Quick facts
steps.body: Periods last 2–7 days; cycles of 21–45 days are common in teens; pads every 4–6 hours, tampons never over 8 hours, cups up to about 12 hours.

steps.title: How boys can help
steps.body: Don’t joke about periods. Keep a pad in a class kit; if a classmate leaks, tell her quietly. Help fight stigma at home.

steps.title: See a doctor when…
steps.body: Very heavy bleeding (changing every 1–2 hours), periods longer than 7 days, severe pain, no period by 15, or periods stop for 3+ months.

statements.s: Period blood is impure.
Exercise during periods is fine.
You can never get pregnant during a period.
Tampons should never be left in more than 8 hours.
Irregular cycles are common in the first years after menarche.
Boys can help reduce period stigma.

quiz.q: Is bathing during periods safe?
quiz.why: Yes, bathing is safe and hygienic during periods. Water temperature and the day of the period don't matter.

quiz.q: Pregnancy during a period is…
quiz.why: Pregnancy during a period is less likely but possible, because cycles vary and sperm can survive for days. It is not impossible.

quiz.q: Using a tampon affects virginity?
quiz.why: Using a tampon doesn't affect virginity. That belief is a myth, since virginity is a social idea, not a medical state.

quiz.q: How can boys help?
quiz.why: Boys can help by quietly helping and not teasing. Jokes or posting hurts.

quiz.q: See a doctor if…
options: Changing protection every 1–2 hours for hours
quiz.why: See a doctor if you need to change protection every 1–2 hours for several hours, which is very heavy bleeding. Brown blood at the end, mild cramps and a 4-day period are normal.

questions.why: Masturbation does not cause weakness. That is a myth.
No, being gay is not an illness. It is a natural variation of sexual orientation.
Crushes are normal, and many people have them as they grow up.
The age of consent in India is 18, under POCSO.
Enlargement pills don't work, so they are scams. Body size isn't changed by pills.
Bathing during periods is fine and keeps you clean.
Uneven breasts or testicles are common and normal. They aren't dangerous.
The 2018 judgment decriminalising consensual same-sex relations was Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India. NALSA (2014) was about transgender persons.

options: Transgender people’s right to self-identify gender
questions.why: NALSA (2014) recognised transgender people's right to self-identify their gender. It was not about marriage equality.

questions.q: Average erect length in a large review?
questions.why: A large review (Veale et al., 2015) found the average erect length is about 13 cm. 25 cm is far above average.

questions.q: When is masturbation worth discussing with a counsellor?
options: When compulsive or interfering with life
questions.why: Masturbation is worth discussing with a counsellor when it is compulsive or interferes with life. Otherwise it is a normal, private matter.

questions.q: Conversion therapy in India per NMC 2022?
questions.why: The NMC in 2022 treated conversion therapy as professional misconduct. It is harmful and not recommended.

questions.q: Worry about appearance taking over life may be…
questions.why: Worry about appearance that takes over life may be body dysmorphic disorder, which is treatable. It is more than normal vanity.
Sending sexual images of under-18s is illegal under POCSO and the IT Act, even if consensual. It is treated as child sexual abuse material.

courses.title: Questions adults never ask
courses.summary: Calm, factual answers for grown-ups: sexual-health worries and performance anxiety, low desire and loneliness in marriage, fertility, menopause and ‘andropause’, the ageing body, and money shame — with clear ‘see a doctor when…’ guidance.
outcomes: Learners can understand performance anxiety and common sexual-health worries and find qualified help
Learners can address low desire and loneliness in a relationship
Learners can explain fertility facts and when to seek assessment
Learners can recognise menopause and male hormone changes and their treatments
Learners can tell normal ageing from treatable problems
Learners can face money shame with a practical debt plan

lessons.title: Sexual health worries and performance anxiety

scenes.text: Suresh, 32, from Nagpur, newly married, has trouble keeping an erection when anxious. He hasn’t told his wife or anyone.
He considers buying ‘sex power’ capsules advertised on TV.
Instead he sees a urologist, who checks blood sugar and blood pressure and talks about anxiety.
With reassurance, couples communication and short-term treatment, things improve. ‘I wish I hadn’t suffered in silence,’ he says.

steps.title: Performance anxiety
steps.body: Worry about ‘performing’ triggers the stress response, which **works against arousal**. A single difficult night can start a cycle: worry → difficulty → more worry. It is extremely common, especially early in a relationship or during stress.

steps.title: Erectile difficulties
steps.body: Occasional difficulty is common. Frequent difficulty (**erectile dysfunction**) becomes more common with age and is linked to **diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, smoking, alcohol, obesity, some medicines and depression**. It can be an **early warning sign of heart disease** — so a check-up matters. Effective treatments exist and should be prescribed by a doctor, not bought from unregulated sources.

steps.title: Early (premature) ejaculation
steps.body: Very common at all ages. Behavioural techniques, counselling and medical treatments help. Anxiety often makes it worse.

steps.title: STI worries
steps.body: If you’re worried about an STI, **get tested** — government ICTCs and STI clinics are free and confidential. Many STIs have no symptoms; most are curable or manageable. Don’t self-medicate. HIV PEP must start within **72 hours** of an exposure.

steps.title: What helps
steps.body:
- Talk to your partner: ‘I’ve been anxious, and it’s affecting things. Can we take the pressure off?’
- Focus on closeness rather than ‘performance’ (sex therapists use ‘sensate focus’ exercises)
- Reduce alcohol and smoking; exercise; sleep
- See a family doctor, urologist, gynaecologist or qualified sex therapist

This is general health education, not medical advice. If something worries you, see a doctor, nurse or counsellor.

activity.prompt: Questions adults rarely ask about sexual health

items.q: I lost my erection once. Is something wrong?
items.a: Almost everyone has this sometimes, usually due to tiredness, alcohol or anxiety. If it happens often for weeks, see a doctor.

items.q: Are TV ‘sex power’ capsules safe?
items.a: Many are unregulated and some contain hidden prescription drugs that can be dangerous with heart medicines. Get a proper prescription from a doctor.

items.q: Can stress really cause these problems?
items.a: Yes. Stress and anxiety are among the most common causes, especially in younger adults.

items.q: I’m embarrassed to see a doctor.
items.a: Doctors discuss this every day. You can see a urologist, gynaecologist or sexual-medicine specialist confidentially.

items.q: I had unprotected sex and I’m worried about HIV.
items.a: Go to a government hospital or ICTC as soon as possible — PEP within 72 hours can prevent infection — and get tested at the right intervals.

items.q: Pain during intimacy (women) — is it normal?
items.a: Common but not normal to endure. Causes include dryness, infections, vaginismus or endometriosis — all treatable. See a gynaecologist.

quiz.q: Performance anxiety works against arousal because…
quiz.why: Performance anxiety works against arousal because the stress response opposes it, shifting the body away from the relaxed state arousal needs. It is physiological, not random.

quiz.q: Erectile dysfunction can be an early sign of…
quiz.why: Erectile dysfunction can be an early sign of heart disease, because blood vessel health affects both. So get checked.

quiz.q: HIV PEP must start within…
quiz.why: HIV PEP must start within 72 hours of exposure. The sooner the better.

quiz.q: Unregulated ‘sex power’ capsules may…
quiz.why: Unregulated 'sex power' capsules may contain hidden drugs, which can be dangerous. They aren't just vitamins.

quiz.q: A helpful first conversation with a partner?
options: ‘I’ve been anxious; can we take the pressure off?’
quiz.why: 'I've been anxious; can we take the pressure off?' is honest and open. Blaming, buying capsules or silently avoiding intimacy worsens things.

lessons.title: Low desire and loneliness in marriage

scenes.text: Meena (41) and Prakash (44) in Lucknow have two teenage children, demanding jobs and elderly parents to care for.
They rarely talk beyond logistics. Intimacy has faded. Meena feels lonely lying next to her husband.
One night she says, ‘I miss us.’ Prakash admits he feels the same.
They start weekly walks, see a couples counsellor, and Meena sees her doctor about tiredness — her thyroid is low. Slowly closeness returns.

steps.title: Low desire is common and complex
steps.body: Low sexual desire affects many adults at some point. Causes include stress, tiredness, caring duties, relationship conflict, depression or anxiety, hormonal changes (after childbirth, perimenopause, low testosterone), thyroid problems, some medicines, pain during sex, and body-image worries. It is **not** a failure of love.

steps.title: Loneliness inside a marriage
steps.body: You can feel lonely while living with someone. Common reasons: busy routines, unresolved resentments, no time alone together, poor communication, or growing apart. It is one of the most common reasons couples seek counselling — and very workable.

steps.title: Steps couples use
steps.body:
- Weekly **check-in** with phones away: ‘How are we doing?’
- Small daily **bids** for connection and responding to them
- Shared fun: walks, a hobby, a trip
- Talk about desire without blame: ‘I’d like more closeness. What would help you?’
- Medical check-up for tiredness, mood or pain
- Couples or sex therapy

steps.title: When it’s more than distance
steps.body: If there is control, threats, violence or forced sex, that is abuse, not loneliness. Consent is needed in every relationship. Help: **181**, **112**, **Tele-MANAS 14416**.

steps.title: Worked example: a gentle opening
steps.body: ‘I miss feeling close to you. I know we’re both exhausted. Could we take a walk on Sunday mornings, just us?’ — specific, warm, no blame.

activity.prompt: What’s one small thing you could do this week to feel closer to someone you love — partner, friend or family?
activity.hint: Think of a 10-minute action: a walk, a message, a question you’ve never asked them.

quiz.q: Low desire is…
options: Common and has many possible causes
quiz.why: Low desire is common and has many possible causes. It is not always a failure of love, and it can often be helped.

quiz.q: Which may cause low desire?
quiz.why: Thyroid problems or some medicines can cause low desire. Reading, eating fruit or wearing blue doesn't.

quiz.q: Loneliness in marriage is…
quiz.why: Loneliness in marriage is common and workable, through communication and support. It doesn't always mean divorce.

quiz.q: A gentle opening is…
options: ‘I miss feeling close; could we walk on Sundays?’
quiz.why: 'I miss feeling close; could we walk on Sundays?' is warm and specific. Sarcasm, 'You never touch me' or silence leads to defensiveness.

quiz.q: Forced sex within marriage is…
quiz.why: Forced sex within marriage is abuse, so get help. Consent always matters, in every relationship.

lessons.title: Fertility: facts nobody tells you

story.title: Riya and Aakash try for a baby

scenes.text: Riya (34) and Aakash (36) in Gurugram have been trying for a baby for 14 months. Relatives keep asking ‘good news?’
Riya blames herself. Aakash assumes it’s ‘a woman’s issue’.
A fertility specialist tests both. Aakash has low sperm count; Riya has slightly reduced ovarian reserve.
With treatment and lifestyle changes, they have options. ‘Testing both of us changed everything,’ says Aakash.

steps.title: What infertility means
steps.body: WHO defines infertility as **not achieving pregnancy after 12 months or more of regular unprotected sex**. WHO estimates that around **1 in 6 people** worldwide experience infertility in their lifetime. **Male factors are involved in roughly half of cases** — so both partners should be assessed.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body:
- After **12 months** of trying if the woman is under 35
- After **6 months** if she is 35 or older
- Sooner if periods are very irregular or absent, there’s known endometriosis or PCOS, previous pelvic infection, or known male problems (e.g. past surgery, mumps affecting testes)

steps.title: Basics of the tests
steps.body:
- **Men:** semen analysis — simple and non-invasive
- **Women:** checking ovulation, hormone tests (including ovarian reserve), ultrasound, and tests that the fallopian tubes are open

Treatments range from timing and lifestyle changes to medicines, IUI and IVF. In India, fertility clinics are regulated under the **Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Act, 2021** — choose registered clinics.

steps.title: What affects fertility
steps.body:
- **Age:** female fertility declines gradually from the early 30s and more steeply after about 35; male fertility also declines with age, more slowly
- **Smoking, heavy alcohol, being very underweight or overweight**
- **STIs** like chlamydia (can damage tubes)
- Some medicines, steroids and testosterone supplements (can lower sperm production)
- Timing: the fertile window is the ~5 days before ovulation and ovulation day

steps.title: Emotional side
steps.body: Infertility can bring grief, guilt, strain and social pressure. It is **no one’s fault**. Support groups, counselling and setting boundaries with relatives (‘We’ll share news when we have any’) help.

statements.s: Infertility is defined by WHO as no pregnancy after 12 months of regular unprotected sex.
Infertility is almost always a woman’s issue.
statements.why: Male factors are involved in roughly half of cases.

statements.s: Women 35+ should see a doctor after 6 months of trying.
Testosterone supplements can lower sperm production.
statements.why: They suppress the body’s own signals.

statements.s: Chlamydia can affect fertility.

quiz.q: About how many people experience infertility in their lifetime (WHO)?
quiz.why: WHO estimates about 1 in 6 people experience infertility in their lifetime. It is common.

quiz.q: Simple first test for men?
quiz.why: A semen analysis is the simple first test for men when investigating infertility. A brain scan or eye test isn't relevant.

quiz.q: Which law regulates fertility clinics in India?
quiz.why: Fertility clinics in India are regulated by the ART (Regulation) Act 2021. POSH, RTI and COTPA cover other matters.

quiz.q: Fertile window is roughly…
options: 5 days before ovulation plus ovulation day
quiz.why: The fertile window is about 5 days before ovulation plus ovulation day, because sperm survive up to about 5 days. Not every day is equally fertile.

quiz.q: A boundary with relatives could be…
options: ‘We’ll share news when we have any’
quiz.why: 'We'll share news when we have any' sets a polite boundary that protects privacy. Lying, avoiding family or blaming publicly harms relationships.

lessons.title: Menopause and 'andropause'

scenes.text: Sunita, 48, a teacher in Bhopal, wakes drenched in sweat, feels irritable, forgets words in class and her periods are erratic.
She thinks she’s ‘going mad’ and doesn’t mention it to anyone.
Her gynaecologist explains perimenopause and options, from lifestyle to hormone therapy.
Her husband Rakesh, 52, asks about his low energy — his doctor checks his weight, sleep, mood and blood tests before considering testosterone.
Both feel relieved to finally understand.

steps.title: Menopause basics
steps.body: **Menopause** is when periods stop permanently — confirmed after **12 months without a period**. It usually happens between **45 and 55**; studies in India suggest an average a little earlier than the global average of about 51. **Perimenopause** — the transition — can start years before, with irregular periods and symptoms. Menopause before 40 (premature ovarian insufficiency) should be assessed by a doctor.

steps.title: Common symptoms
steps.body: Hot flushes and night sweats, sleep problems, mood changes, anxiety, brain fog, joint aches, vaginal dryness and discomfort, urinary changes, lower desire. Over the long term, falling oestrogen raises the risk of **osteoporosis** and heart disease.

steps.title: What helps
steps.body:
- Regular exercise, including weight-bearing and strength training (bones)
- Calcium and vitamin D (diet first; supplements if advised)
- Limit alcohol and caffeine; stop smoking
- Cool bedroom, layers
- Vaginal moisturisers and lubricants; low-dose vaginal oestrogen if prescribed
- **Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT/HRT):** for many healthy women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause, guidelines say benefits for symptoms often outweigh risks — a personal decision with a doctor
- CBT helps hot flushes and sleep for some women

steps.title: See a doctor promptly if…
steps.body: **Any bleeding after menopause** (12 months without periods) — this must always be checked. Also very heavy bleeding in perimenopause, severe mood changes, or symptoms affecting daily life.

steps.title: ‘Andropause’ — what’s real
steps.body: Men don’t have a sudden equivalent of menopause. Testosterone tends to **decline gradually** with age (roughly 1% a year from middle age), and obesity, diabetes, poor sleep, alcohol and some medicines lower it further. A minority develop **symptomatic low testosterone** (low desire, erectile problems, fatigue, low mood, loss of muscle). Diagnosis needs symptoms **plus** repeated morning blood tests. Testosterone should be prescribed and monitored by a doctor — never self-medicate; it can cause infertility and other risks.

activity.prompt: Questions about menopause and midlife

items.q: Am I too young for perimenopause at 43?
items.a: No — symptoms often start in the 40s. A doctor can confirm and discuss options.

items.q: Is HRT dangerous?
items.a: For many healthy women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause, benefits often outweigh risks. Risks depend on age, health and type of therapy — decide with your doctor.

items.q: Can I still get pregnant in perimenopause?
items.a: Yes, it’s possible until 12 months without a period (over 50) or 2 years (under 50) — use contraception if you don’t want pregnancy.
